So...1984 by George Orwell, another book that everyone has read and everyone pretends to like likes. Personally, I adored it. Everything from the way it explores a very dark and cynical side of life, ruled by fear and oppression. Let's go a few years in the future (or the future-past? That's how I'd call it...). We're in 1984 (probably), and the world is split into three; each part is ruled by totalitarian parties. In Oceania, that party is Ingsoc, in Eurasia- Neo-Bolshevism, and in Eastasia- the Death Worship. The main character is Winston Smith. His job is something like replacing documents about the past with fake documents (doctrine, to be more exact). He hates the party and he keeps a journal about this. I have no idea how I really feel about Winston. On the one hand, he was rebellious and independent and super brave, but on the other hand, I failed to connect with him, which is not a tragedy, considering that I, unlike Winston, have never experienced the trauma of a totalitarian regime. One of the most important elements of the book is the affair shared by Winston and Julia. I thought it was amazingly written, showing how politics can influence even the purest people, morphing them and making sure they're as corrupt as everyone else. I was shocked by the fact that Winston and Julia betray each other. Only now I understand that their betrayals were proving a truly depressing idea: love can't save anyone. Ever. The people you trust can and will leave you anytime. The ending was bittersweet, yet perfect for this book. They don't overthrow the government. Instead, Winston feels a sickening admiration towards the Big Brother, welcoming his death, finally finding an escape from the horrendous world he lived in. Pessimistic and sad, but damn perfect The atmosphere of the book is impressively created: gloomy, insecure, frightening. 1984 is the kind of novel that stays with you, not in a nice, cozy way, but in a terrifying "overthinking-at-night" way. It never leaves your mind, it's haunting, and it's amazing.

ARC REVIEW: I've always been a fan of mermaid legends, they are such beautiful creatures! Monstrous Beauty is not just a typical mermaid story. It is a captivating yet haunting story of love, curses, family history, ghosts, and murder. Fama already grips you in the first few pages of the book with the introduction of Syrenka who has lived for hundreds of years. She has longed to experience what it's like to be human physically and has a strong yearning to love. However, to love is only but a misfortune for her as well as others. And in just the prologue, Fama has already successfully set the tone of the book that will keep you from putting the book down. Generations later, Hesther Goodwin is trying to piece together her own history and genealogy. She wants to find the answer as to why the women in her family die moments after giving birth. The consistency of those occurrences have kept her from being involved in any relationship, wanting to stay single from the thought of death. I have been able to piece together pieces while reading, looking back at previous chapters trying to make sense of certain details. It was refreshing and I felt engaged. This book is written in an amazing prose most young adult novels have yet to contest. The plots are intricate, strong character development and her eloquency is fantastic. The transition between periods may take time for some to get used to however for me it was easily understandable. Thoroughly executed from beginning to end, Fama is definitely one of the better writers I have come across in years!

4,5 stars I never intended to read a book like this. I've had enough of this kind of drama in real life to last a lifeline. More or less I've been forced to read this book and in the end I'm glad I did it. John Green has a gift of playing with words. His writing intellectually sarcastic and makes you laugh at the most inappropriate times. I was sucked into Hazel's world and didn't want to surface. I loved the way she views her surroundings, the sarcastic way she deals with the crap all around her, and together with her I fell in love with Gus. Though this book is about a bunch of kids who have cancer, it's not a throughout sad book. It is funny, witty and really sweet at times. Those kids try to as normal teenagers as they can be. They argue with their parents, do some very stupid things, and try to live a normal life. Obviously, because they aren't like other teenagers, they are not able to do so. But John Green manages to make his readers forget on many occasions the life threatening course, Hazel and Gus are dealing with. Sadly this all turns to dust when Gus is detected with new tumors and dies. This is really my only critique point. This book is a work of fiction and while John Green may have researched a great deal, for someone who watched a close friend die from cancer it is obvious that this story is not a real one. That is no problem at all but it would have suited the book much better if Gus had not died. After all this is fiction ;-)

A friend gave me this book years and years ago--I think it's a first edition. On Anne Osterlund's recco, I took it down to look at it. I can see why many love it still--the true star of the book is the scenery, rather than the characters. The way that Montgomery writes about nature shifts you to liminal space, within a heartbeat of the numinous. The reason, though, that I hadn't reread it in all these years was because the basic plot feels like a short story stretched out into a novel. That, and the two central characters are. problematical. I am not fond of the Wounded Animal hero or heroine, and Kilmeny is the apotheosis of the Wounded Animal--blind, beautiful, and utterly perfect, right down to her amazing violin talent. The schoolteacher who comes to town and falls in love with her at first sight just wants to look at her, because she's so perfect--and all the town immediately falls in love with him because of his heroic good looks. It's a comfort book--perfect for that dreamy thirteen year old in your life--and perfect for you if you really need a quiet novel at sustained pace set in the glories of nature.

It's very possibly my own fault for picking up a book called Twenty Boy Summer. But man, did I ever hate this book. The premise caught my attention: Anna has been best friends with Frankie and her brother Matt for years. She and Matt start liking each other but keep it a secret from Frankie. Then Matt dies tragically. Now Frankie wants Anna to go on vacation with her and meet some boys. Should Anna tell Frankie about her feelings for Matt? Is she ready to move on? OK, so there's potential for a lot of sappiness here. What I didn't expect was the level of bad behavior in the book. Frankie (who really annoyed me, especially in the way she always said the wrong word for whatever she was thinking) has been acting out since her brother's death. And apparently she wants Anna to act as bad as she does. What follows is a lot of sneaking out, lying to parents, and Frankie pressuring Anna to have sex with basically any random boy she can get to like her. Meanwhile Anna's conflicting feelings about Matt and his death pop up from time to time. Whatever. While I can accept that Frankie would have a bad reaction to her brother's death, there was just no real healing happening here. I got to a point where I just started skimming, and it seems there are no consequences to the girls' actions, either. What could have been a sweet look at friendship and secrets and loss and first love turned into a really bad teenage romp. AVOID IT! And try not to tell anyone I picked it up in the first place. Thanks.

Everything seems rushed and not explained. I didn't even get why they were in love. Was it because he brought her fairy tales to read when she was little? Through the whole book Esmerine wants to go and see her sister whom she was so close with (we are assuming because that is what Esmerine keeps saying....but we never got to see that relationship). When she finally reunites with the sister, the sister (was it Docia?) doesn't seem to care that Esmerine is there at all. Esmerine pretty much has to guilt trip her into talking privately at all. It was a disappointing read. The short blurb that Goodreads posts makes it sound interesting, but it's not. I just felt as if the whole book was kind of flat.

"BUCKETS OF BLOOD, WHEN DO I GET TO FINISH MY GREAT DISSERTATION OF TREASON?" Oh. My. Goodness. This book. Oh, my heart... I've made up my mind. I really enjoy reading WWII fiction and nonfiction. It's just so close to home, so real, so heartbreaking. Some of my favorite stories of this genre include Corrie Ten Boom's The Hiding Place and the popular film Life is Beautiful Now I can add Code Name Verity to that list. First of all, the writing style is masterful, but not traditional. Readers first get a glimpse at the story as the protagonist explains why she's a coward. Opening line: "I AM A COWARD". Immediately, I wondered why, and within a couple of pages, I'd come to like the narrator in all her traitorous, yet defiant narration as a prisoner of war. In many recent stories, especially YA, I've grown tired of reading stories where the narrator is almost completely without personality. Sometimes the story will go fifty pages, and I still hardly know anything about the character, but not so with the Wein's narrator. She's proudly Scottish, sassy, and truthful. Or is she? For the longest time, I couldn't really tell how much of the story I could actually believe. Perhaps one of the most heartbreaking parts of this book (and there were several, let me tell you) was the narrator's love for the German language despite her loyalty to her people: "You know, I speak German because I love German. What good was a degree in German literature going to do me? I was reading it because I loved it. Deutschland, das Land der Dichter und Denker, land of poets and thinkings. And now I will never even see Germany, unless they sent me to Ravensbruck" What breaks my heart about this part of the book is that I understand in some sense. I've actually lived in Germany, experienced the culture and heard the language. I love Germany. But even decades later, the scars from the war are still there. What would it be like to live in a time to have a heart for a place only to have it be ridden with bombs or people out to KILL you? Another thing I enjoyed about this book was the extent of the research. While Wein acknowledges that many of the places and even her characters are fictional, she gave me a very real sense of place and history and airplanes. Aside from all the commercial flights I've been on (which don't count really), I know next to nothing about planes. But Code Name Verity is full of planes and told in a manner that isn't overly technical. Did I mention how much I liked the writing style? And the ending... Enough! No spoilers. Saying it was well-written feels like an understatement. This book received 5/5 stars for masterful voice, storytelling, and research. I even had a similar story idea once, but there's no way I could have told the story better. I'd recommend this to anybody who enjoys WWII fiction; unusual narrators; and strong, independent--yet human--women. Who doesn't like reading about a woman pilot?

Sigh. So happy with this one. One of the best KA reads in a long time. I think I've learned how to enjoy a KA book. I'm not a very patient reader and I do not like long descriptions of rooms, outfit, makeup or mundane activities like grocery shopping. These parts I skipped. I seem to becoming an expert in picking parts with pertinent information. Cher came across rough to me at first, but as the book progressed, she grew on me ... or maybe her speech pattern softened. I don't know. What I do know is I liked the evolution of her relationship with Merry. First as friends ... and then as a couple. The shift in their relationship from friends to lovers was a bumpy one because both of them had their own baggage. What I liked in this book, we get a lot of Merry's POV so we knew exactly where his head was, otherwise a lot of things he did would have been considered a dick move. I think Cher's son Ethan was a little too perfect, but I did enjoy mother and son's relationship. I really liked that Cher was different--she was a straight talker, a fighter, she can definitely talk shit with the guys, and I enjoyed her funny quips with Merry, making her man laugh. The theme really was about "Holding on." Merry was a bit different from other KA heroes. He was alpha and badass, but he definitely had a vulnerable side. Besides loving Cher and Merry together, what really made this book click for me was we get lots of scenes with our past heroes of the Burg --Mike, Colt, Tanner, Cal and especially Ryker. God, I loved Ryker ... he's one crazy mofo. For me, I like guys talking business and shit with each other more than the female posse gatherings talking about outfits and makeup which can get old. There were several good conflicts interwoven into the storyline although there were a few spots that dragged, but not enough for me get impatient ... (remember I skipped long descriptions). Best of all, KA gave us what us fans have been clamoring for a time. A kidnapping! The title "Hold On" came full circle and I felt those words at that climactic moment. It was also emotional when something happened to a certain character. Ryker And the epilogue? Classic KA and a fantastic end to the series. Well done.

We're the middle children of the history Well that was depressing, but I finished it. Look I totally, 100% get it, I feel this crumbling existence and it feels like you're wading through death every day, and you just don't see how anything is going to last another century, and we've made all the wrong choices. You miss the cultish mysticism and freedom of old pagan religions, the organic quality of spirituality that is fake and forced or non-existent in the modern world by corporations masquerading as churches. You miss the feel of cold grass beneath your feet, and exertion of running after game, and cold dirt ripping at your skin as your dig by hand for food- even though you've never actually felt these things and it's just some sort of genetic memory. You want to look at a thunderstorm rolling in or the dark cloud billowing from a rumbling, quaking, shaking volcano and think this is god. God is angry, how do we appease it? and you want to not understand isobars and tectonic plates, and you want to forget all the science and all the facts and grasp at something primitive and mighty. This world is empty. You can trade a priest for an executive for a pastor for a celebrity, and one god for the next god, and a new hero and role model and father figure instantaneously, but we cannot seem to shift the leading role of our lives into our own hands. Most of all you miss the chance to prove yourself to you by simply surviving. I get it. But Fight Club largely revolves around domestic terrorism, and in a post 9-11 world I just couldn't connect to the disenfranchised message as I might have been able to if I'd been nearing thirty and read this in the nineties. Threatening to walk into your office with an automatic rifle and gun down all the corporate offices doesn't seem as revolutionary now. It almost doesn't even scary. It just seems like something that happens. and for fuck's sake, THAT'S whats scary. So here we are. I won't die without scars, I won't die without callouses, and I won't die without a fight. If you can honestly look around this world and not see something worth fighting for, then you are a lazy piece of shit. That's what Tyler Durden SHOULD have told you. We have no Great War, no Great Depression, bull shit. And fuck you. Life is shit, it always has been, you are not a unique snowflake, your pain, you wallowing pity, it's not unique either. Tyler Durden was a lazy ass, and his followers were lazy self-absorbed assholes. Don't wait for life and an opportunity to fight to come to you. Don't be Tyler Durden. We are the middle children of history, and we need to realize that there is a vast and terrible world beyond city limits and go fight for something that is worth it. As for the book itself- the writing style was gritty and educated middle class. It fit the plot and characters perfectly. Its entirely believable, and I think Chuck grasps exactly how people feel, and as this was satirical look on modern society, I don't think Chuck is endorsing Tyler Durden either, other than his message that we need to change society, and we have a large group in a particular age that is still grasping at what direction we should go from here. Honestly though, I thought the movie was better. I was bored by the overly cultish feel of Project Mayhem and I even rolled my eyes once or twice at the repetitive rhetoric. Three stars because it was good, great for a freshman go, but doesn't live up to the hype or age gracefully.

I've enjoyed the Soul Screamers series up to this point. But I have to say I was sorely disappointed with If I Die. I know that it was a crowd pleaser because of the ending, but the whole set up was sort of ridiculous. Kaylee is scheduled to die pretty soon and Tod and her dad think it's a good idea to tell her? Who does that? Her dad could try to find a way to change her appointment with death without telling her the truth. But this is the first point from a very long list of things that went wrong with this book in my opinion. There wasn't any character development on Kaylee's part. Even in the face of death, the girl could not enjoy her last few days with her boyfriend. She had to try to save someone. She is a martyr, I get it, but I think that her need to be the world's savior just went a bit too far this time. Yes, she traded Nash for Tod, which it was her act of entitled recklessness. But really? A love triangle between brothers? Could the book get more predictable? And the way it was done wasn't romantic, it was just sad and made me lose faith in RV as an author. It seemed to me that Kaylee dumped Nash because he didn't play the hero part well enough for her. Because he wasn't perfect, he had problems. I'm not saying that you should stick with a person just because he or she needs you. Is Nash a weak character? Absolutely. Did he deserve what happened to him. Hell no. That was my other beef against the book, why did Nash have to fall in disgrace in order to make the transition from him to Tod easier? I thought he was a pretty decent boyfriend in the beginning of the series and if there was any relationship problems it was also due to Kaylee's insecurities. Finally, I didn't like how Kaylee ended up looking like the victim when she was the one who got Nash exposed to Frost in the first place and abandoned him when he was fighting the addiction and needed her the most. She subsequently went on to string him along even though she couldn't trust him anymore so that Sabine couldn't have him, but the moment a better candidate appeared (Tod), she didn't have any qualms about trading poor Nash. I thought that Nash reactions to her at the end of I I Die where justified and the things he told her while under the effect of Frost were absolutely true. She was a frigid bitch with him. It is really a sad affair when you dislike a book so much that you have to abandon a series all together. But my time is too precious to dwell on something I don't enjoy anymore.

The premise is interesting---a story unfolding over the course of a dinner---but I'm not sure it worked well in practice. The narrator established himself as a liar fairly early on, and once I stopped believing him, I found I couldn't believe anything he said and was no longer invested in the story. I couldn't tell which were the narrator's lies and which were mistakes on the author's part. Even if the Dutch criminal justice system is ridiculously lenient, I can't imagine some of the things the narrator claims to have done just being brushed under the rug with no consequences. And what the heck kind of mental illness can be detected by amniocentesis? It reminded me a little of Donna Tartt's The Goldfinch; the reader couldn't trust anything that narrator was saying either. I liked Tartt's novel more than I did this one. It felt more like a puzzle, and I enjoyed trying to spot the lies, but both novels leave me wondering what the point was. I think that means that the novels are postmodern. I don't think I like postmodernism. At least The Dinner wasn't as long as The Goldfinch.
Now I just wonder, who ended up having to get what tattoos?

At BEA, I waited in line for about an hour to get an ARC Prodigy, which I also got signed by Marie Lu. Though I was excited for her series, mostly I just wanted an excuse to sit down for an hour so I wouldn't have to be a pack mule for tote bags full of books for a while. At that point, I hadn't yet read Legend so there really was only a certain amount of excitement that can be mustered, even with all the good reports. Well, finally having read the ARC, shortly after publication because I fail, I can report that, with Prodigy Marie Lu solidifies her good start in Legend. Her plotting and characterization both improve, and the action and dystopian elements are just as strong as in the debut. The plotting of Legend follows a pretty standard dystopian outline, but, in Prodigy, Marie Lu really does something different. The first book set the pieces perfectly for her to branch out. Without spoilers, I really cannot tell you much specifically about what is awesome, but just believe me that it is. The ending leaves the plot poised to be completely epic in the next book, but I hope Lu is cutthroat enough to do what she needs to do, because that's where a lot of young adult authors miss the mark in dystopian novels. Where June spent most of Legend being an annoyingly perfect, almost robotic, girl, completely devoted to her role in the Republic, she really develops in Prodigy. Torn between her childhood leanings and her new alliances, June has to learn how to evaluate the world on her own, no longer accepting what other people tell her to be true. Smart as she is, she has to learn about independent thinking. Readers will find June much more sympathetic and likable in Prodigy. Day, of course, we all loved from the beginning. In some ways, I don't think I like him as much now, but in others he's even better. Where Day is practically perfect in Legend, the reader now gets to see more of his flaws, giving him depth and perhaps ultimately making him more admirable. The budding relationship between June and Day, thankfully, does not become a huge focus of the plot. Lu does capture both their strong feelings for one another (or how strong they think they are) and the insecurity of their relationship. She stresses how little they've known each other, and how their mutual trust suffers as a result. Lu does introduce a love triangle or two (love square? ), and I hope she uses this wisely. For those who like their dystopian novels full of explosions, I have good news for you. There are fist fights, chase scenes, bombings, jumps off of high objects, and even aerial battles. Lu does a really nice job with her action scenes, keeping them tense and exciting. Also, I never felt confused about what she was describing, which can be tricky to accomplish. And was that a reference to Joss Whedon there towards the end? I hope so. The only real detractor for the Legend series remains the youth of the protagonists. I know I complained about this in my review for Legend, but it really does bear reiterating. Both Day and June are 15, but they are brilliant, gorgeous, strong, and respected by all. Now, a prodigy can certainly be clever than adults, but I really question both of them being incredibly gorgeous on top of that. Seriously, just take a moment and think back to your yearbook from freshman year of high school, or, even better, go look at it. Do any of those teens look model perfect at all times and anywhere near capable of taking on the Republic? Shouldn't at least one of them suffer from acne? I also question their incredible physical abilities. At 15, odds are, they wouldn't even be done growing yet, and they're not at their physical peak. I mean, at one point, June jumps onto a door knob and from their onto the top of a door as it opens without anyone noticing. Unless she's secretly a member of the X-Men with cat powers, I just cannot buy that. As for the respect, well, even as a prodigy, I really do not see everyone in a country rallying behind 15 year old rebels. At most, they would be cute figureheads, not viewed as actual leaders. Katniss, for example, powerful though she is at 16, she doesn't lead the revolution; she just serves as a symbol of it. The story would make so much more sense with main characters in the range of 18 to 20, and every person I talked to said that they also kept forgetting that Day and June were so young. Obviously, that can't be changed now, but how about we make it more realistic by giving them some pimples or something? Marie Lu's Legend series is an excellent choice for readers looking for an action-packed dystopian novel. After that ending, I am pretty much desperate to read the next book, which is poised to be even better!

Pushing the Limits was what I would term a 'breath of fresh air' it was a YA Contemporary with a bit of edge, however I wasn't a MASSIVE fan, I enjoyed it but felt there was more it could do. I was hoping that Dare You To would prove to be an improvement. Firstly - you do not need to have read Pushing the Limits (PTL) to read Dare You To (DYT) they are linked in a way, DYT is written from the POV of PTL secondary character Beth and a new face, Ryan. Isaiah, Noah and Echo all make appearances, but you don't need to know their background when reading this, any link is explained for the new readers. DYT follows Beth as she tries to save her drunk mother from her boyfriend Trent, and she ends up in jail because of it, she's bailed out by her Uncle Scott, who is a big time pro-ball player (or was), and their relationships strained to say the least. Scott takes Beth into his home, and forces her to cut all ties with Isaiah and Noah, and starts her off at a new school. Ryan is a baseball jock, who cannot turn down a dare, and when he is dared to get a snarky girl's number at taco bell, he tries and fails. When she (of course its Beth) shows up at his school, the dare is back on. Ryan is determined to get that date with her, he NEVER loses a dare. Throw in a number of revelations about Beth's past and her inability to let go of her mother and you've got 500+ pages of a story. The whole plot for me felt a little 90s teen movie (with added bad language and drugs), she's all that, 10 things I hate about you, etc etc. The guy is dared to get the longer/strange/odd girl at school to date him, to believe he likes her, and of course he then falls for her. Thats the first half of the book, the second half is him convincing her that he's no longer in it for the dare, he's reformed and that she likes him too. Like I said. 90s Movie. I loved 90s movies, so its not necessarily a bad thing, just a little predictable. I know a lot of fans will panic when they realize that Isaiah and Beth are not going where we though they would in PTL, but believe me when I say that is a good thing, McGarry has been really brave in separating two characters that in the first book you think will end up together.But don't worry - it doesn't go the way you think it will either, McGarry handles their complex relationship with respect, and because of that the results are believable. Where McGarry excels is bringing the hard hitting reality that is the underclass youth into the real world. She doesn't hide the fact that there are many struggling teens out there, and these are issues they deal with every day. He character building is again, excellent, the reader sees the characters grow, Beth in particular, and you care what happens to them. The major moans I have (and its the same in PTL) is the possessive language used over the girls. The guys talk to each other about girls being 'mine' and 'my girl' as if they are objects, not people. I struggle to believe a character like Beth would be owned in such a way, I certainly wouldn't. The other issue is the whole 'forever' and intense level of the relationships portrayed in both books. These characters are teens, yet they are getting involved in relationships most adults would struggle to cope in, lets face it teen romances are usually short lived, yet the stories are written as if this is their only chance. I don't think it sets a particularly good example for the Ya reader, authors should be telling the reader that teen relationships can be fun, light and if they end, thats OK. Not putting pressure on teens to find their soul mates by age 16. This is not an issue that is solely related to McGarry, many teen authors do it, the pair meet, a week later they are in love and then its forever (or in the case of many paranormals, destiny). Over all a good read, I was flicking between 3 and 3.5 stars, so went for the higher in the end. I read it quickly, it was entertaining, and the character building was great. There was however very little in it to add to PTL, the story doesn't go above and beyond the first book, its more of an extension of the story. Ally Carter writes the some of the cutest literature. Don't take that the wrong way, it's a compliment. If you need something light-hearted and simple to read curled up somewhere on a rainy day, Ally Carter is your way to go. I'm going to say her Gallagher Girls series didn't start of that well, but it's definitely much better in the later books. However, Heist Society is good throughout the series. The plots are very simple; there's a bad guy, then Kat's adorable family gets involved. They pull the biggest con ever attempted, and they win YAY. It's very suitable for younger kids, (except for when Hale gets drunk). But even then, it's written for a more juvenile audience. If you're looking for a complex. emotional plot, with twists and turns this is not it. BUT, it's still so, so enjoyable. It's fun and adventurous. The names of some of the Heist capers are ridiculous (ex. Three Blind Mice, the Anastasia, Cat in the Cradle, Count of Monte Cristo). It's so much fun imagining all the different cons those could possible refer to! The characters are definitely one of the best aspects of this book. Kat, Hale, Uncle Eddie, Bobby, Gabrielle (who I really love), Angus, Hamish, Simon, Silas Foster, Marcus, Marianne. They're all fantastic and whimsical and hilarious and very, very lovable. And the bad guys are fun to hate too! Hale's entire family is horrible, Garrett was despicable. But it was all so lighthearted. Although, there was a scare towards the end, there is nothing awful that happens in these books. They'll just make you plain old laugh in amusement. The relationships are beautiful. Kat and Hale go through some bumps, but they still love each other. Kat and her Uncle Eddie are always there for each other. Kat and Gabrielle...I adore them and their little cousin bickering. The characters never let each other down though, they are loyal to the end. In these books, family is everything, and it just adds a bright spot to your day. Overall, these books are simple, delightful, and heartwarming. It's just a pleasure to read, and will take your mind off your problems.

Jessica Park, you are an amazing author. I loved "Flat-Out Love" and "Relatively Famous". Your writing is so easy to read and your story is so well paced. No a boring moment in my opinion. I thought I could predict what's really going on but I didn't and that's what made this book so good. LOVE it! Kudos! My Review: Flat-Out Love, what a weird name right? This is the second book I've read from Jessica Park. From what I've seen in her books, they were both easy to read and you can easily relate to her characters in some way. This story was so well paced and well put together. I was never bored once even when nothing big was happening, I still was flipping through the pages. Julie finds herself stranded after trusting a Craigslist ad for an apartment. Right away my heart went out to her. How scary that would be to get stranded in a new city. But no worries her mom's college friend comes to the rescue. This is where the story gets interesting. Julie is now living with a family who has more secrets than a mystery thriller. As she adapts to this new family, her heart has found a new love. And while she's going through these emotions, she wants to help the youngest family member. Like Julie, I'm a fix it girl. So I quickly understood her when she wanted to help Celeste become a bit more independent. My favorite parts of this book is the Facebook statuses and emails back and forth. I really enjoyed reading their statuses. They were really funny. I loved to read the interaction she has with Finn. The sexy older brother who is off exploring the world. Then you have Matt, a nerd, (luckily, not a font nerd...gotta read the book to understand this joke) who is just the most responsible young adult I have ever met in any YA book. Matt is my favorite character in this book, because I wanted to love him and hug him the minute he came on the page. I absolutely LOVED Flat-Out Love. Ms. Park invested well into her characters. Each character was written perfectly. The characters grew and the story was a little richer because of that. The story line was unique. Flat-Out Love is a 5 stars read and a definite Good Choice for Reading! http://www.goodchoicereading.com/2012...

"You think some rabble with kitchen knives makes you a queen?" Caspida glances back at the people, fighting tooth and nail against the better-equipped soldiers. "They're exactly what makes me a queen." Well, that was a bit of a surprise. The Forbidden Wish is a romantic Aladdin retelling with added romance, yes, but it's also a story about women and their power in the world. Talk about passing the Bechdel test - this absolutely killed it with badass girl leads. I'm tired of living for the dead. I want to live for you. There is a major romance here, but it's one I enjoyed far more than usual. I really loved the developing romance between Zhara and Aladdin. Not only is their relationship building slow and high-quality; they're also just very good for each other. I felt invested in their relationship just by the virtue of how sweet they are. I could spend the rest of my life discovering you. I also really loved Zhara's character arc. She's a girl who believes she's a monster and hates herself for it. I know this kind of character is bit of a archetype, but it's an archetype I personally love when done well. This book definitely did the archetype well. I really loved the way Zhara was written and developed. You can't choose what happens to you but you can choose who you come because of it. I have to admit, though, this whole thing felt a little insubstantial. But I can't even really complain about this, because that was the intention!! It's a romantic fantasy. This book was so clearly not for me to analyze!! It's not necessarily meant to be serious. It's a romantic fantasy, and it's a good one at that. I rushed through this and absolutely enjoyed it. That should be enough for me. Hopeless romantics will enjoy it maybe more than me, but this is was certainly very high quality as these books go and I can't recommend it enough to anyone who feels interested. How to best enjoy this book: 1) Forget it was written by the same author who wrote "The Thirteenth Tale" and 2) disregard the words "A Ghost Story" in the title. It was engaging and I wanted to love it, but I just didn't. There were times when I felt sympathetic towards the main character, William Bellman, and there were times when I disliked him passionately, which is either a great compliment to the author for painting a rich character or a horrible criticism for creating a character so confused. It was not a BAD book. The intro was amazing and foretold of dark things to come. I enjoyed the look back in time to Victorian London. I enjoyed the glimpse of mill life. While it wasn't a ghost story, William's life was certainly haunted and it was fascinating to see how it drove him forward (or backward) at times. There were bits that I expected to turn up later or perhaps become a larger plot point that didn't really develop as expected. Again, is that kudos to the author or the opposite? As for the author, I do feel badly for her. Setterfield's first book, The Thirteenth Tale, was so well-received that fans couldn't wait for her next novel. I think that would be a lot of pressure and there was really no way to succeed. People were going to be disappointed because expectations were set so high. Hopefully with her second book out of the way, book #3 will be written with less pressure. I look forward to it very much. It's not that this book was bad - it just wasn't The Thirteenth Tale. And for that it's going to be ripped to shreds.

This is not the worst thing I've read, but one star was close. The book has some good qualities, and I got to the end, so that's why it got 2 stars.

I devoured this. I read it, then I read it again, and now I want to read it for a third time. I've really got to move on, but this was just so Good with a capital G. This book takes such an interesting perspective on what is, in my opinion, an overly written about period of history. Having Death as the narrator for parts of the story really took it to the next level; it made it utterly unique. It also created a sense of detachment from the events, and evoked the message that death is unavoidable and will eventually come for all. I loved it, and I think the heroine is just superb. A book thieving heroine? Say no more! For me, one of the most important aspects of a well written character is someone I can sympathise with and feel vast quantities of empathy for. So, when the protagonist is in love with reading and appreciates the freedom it can grant, I find myself somewhat immediately won over to her cause. Liesel's story is woe begotten and tragic yet she always seems to carry on; she always seems to realise that there are good things in this world. And they're not just books; they're people too. She doesn't give up and fall into a pit of self-pity. You've got to hand it to her for that. For a young girl she is incredibly strong. She's written so well; it's so easy to invest in her story and wish for her to have an ending she deserves. But, death, by its very nature, doesn't work that way. "A small fact: You are going to die....does this worry you?" Indeed, Death is cold and undiscriminating; he can come at any time and take anyone. I should have known this was going to be a sad one. Death pretty much said so from the start. But one can hope: one can hope that someone who has gone through so much will get a happy ending, though that's not the point of this book. I'm saddened by the ending, but it was necessary. This book's impact would have been marginally lessened if the deaths didn't happen at the end. At least Liesel found some degree of comfort, which lifted the veil of misery somewhat. The ending of this book is precisely what made it so powerful. I wouldn't want it's sadness any other way. A fantastic story Liesel is an orphan, and when she was adopted I expected her to have an absolutely terrible time. I expected her adopted parents to be awful. This just seemed like the predictable route this story would take, and I'm glad it didn't go that way because Liesel learnt the value of human kindness. In the Hubermann household she received warmth and comfort. Hans Hubermann is an excellent man; he is open-hearted and genuine in his affection. He is everything the young orphan needed in a parent, and he is everything that was needed to balance the darkness in the book. He is a true figure of strength and someone who represents the underappreciated resistance to Nazism within Germany during WW2. He refuses to become a member of the political party and even hides a Jew in his basement. He's a good man, a great man. He is Liesel's rock and figure of morale guidance. He's a great character. I know I keep saying that but it is so true. Everything about this book is just brilliant. I think this is such an accomplished story. It takes a lot to write a book like this, and to end it like this. The temptation to end it differently must have been humongous. It's refreshing to see a modern story actually end how it should rather than the easier route of a happy ending. This certainly won't be the last book I'll be reading by Marcus Zusak. An outstanding five stars

2.5 stars This was a not-at-all-subtle modern take on Pride & Prejudice. Unfortunately, it did not work for me. The characters are just awful. Julia is one of the most annoying, uptight, pretentious female protagonists I've ever read, especially in a contemporary YA. She is so OCD and know-it-all that she makes Hermione Granger look like a lazy simpleton. It's beyond obnoxious. And her character has absolutely no growth throughout the story. Her opinions regarding certain characters change when she learns their true character, but she is just as insufferable at the end as she was in the beginning. Jason was terrible too. He acted like an 11-year old kid rather than a 17-year old. He continually acts out and makes Julia feel awful. I hate that he calls her Book Licker. What the heck is that? Am I supposed to think that's cute? Cuz...no. Just no. The plot was silly, the ending was rushed, and the 'love story' felt rushed and inauthentic. This is the author's first story. I could possibly see myself giving her another chance in the future, but this story just did not work for me. I would say that it was a fast read, but I don't know how much of it was a 'fast read' and how much was that I couldn't stand being in Julia's head and found myself skimming a lot of her inner dialogue.
Well..it was good enough to read through the end, but not appealing enough, as much as it should be, to inspire me to continue reading the other sequels.

"The Shadow of the Wind" is everything you would want from a book set in Spain about the sense of mystery and wonder that books give us. This is the story about Daniel who wants to know the story of Julian Carax, the author of a book that he discovers in a place where books go to "die." Really, I suppose they come back to life again in the hands of someone who really cares about them. Anyway, because he has never heard of Carax he wants to know what happened to him. In many ways, Daniel and Carax's lives reflect each other. It is really exciting how Carlos Ruiz Zafon weaves the different pieces of information, misinformation and action together. The only reason I rated it four stars was because there were times when something didn't quite fit the way I thought it could (always very slight and nothing anyone but nitpicky old me would notice)- and I predicted who the man with no face was from the introduction of him. Otherwise, this book was stellar, A-level material. What are you waiting for? Go read it!

If this book were more creative and intriguing, this is exactly what I would wish I could expect from all fantasy books. Although Eldest generally receives harsh criticisms, I applaud Paolini for his brilliance in the Inheritance series. Originality may be something he is lacking in, but what author doesn't take certain concepts from past literature and transform it to create his own? If there's one thing that I've learned from language arts classes, it's that no written work is ever truly authentic. What matters is that the author molds each theme or idea to match his own interpretation. In my humble opinion, Paolini does just that. I'm certainly no expert when it comes to reviewing novels, but I enjoyed reading Eldest in the simplest regard. It was well-written, interesting (for the most part), and artful. I felt a deep emotional attachment to the main characters, and the plot was exciting enough to arrest my attention. After all this, I still don't quite understand the hype around these books; however, I wouldn't say that I would ever dissuade anyone from reading them. I liked it, but it's definitely not something I would place among my favorites.

Once again, I dislike the book everyone else obviously loves. First of all (and I NEVER thought I'd say this about a book) - it is too long. It would be fine if it had action-driven plot, but for a story like this I think that reducing the number of pages would be a significant improvement. This way, I had a feeling that I was reading the same thing over and over again - every encounter between Gabriel and Julia looked almost exactly the same like the previous one. It just dragged on and on and I was seriously worried that I will have to break my own rule of finnishing every book I start and put this one aside. I didn't, but even if I did, it wouldn't make any difference because the second half was even worse than first. Second, it was waaay too predictable. I usually don't mind that, but this was just too much. There wasn't a single moment of surprise and at some point it just came down to waiting to happen something that I already knew is going to happen. It became boring. Third - I hated Julia. She's just too ''perfect''. That amount of perfection just doesn't work for me, it made her dull and annoying and I was irritated by her from the beginning . There are two different personalities in her and for a while I hoped that she was just acting in some situations. Unfortunately, she wasn't. So, one side of her is a (virgin) pocket Venus, too sexy and beautiful for her own good. Even the way she eats is so sensual that noone - men, women, boys, professors, students - you name it - is able to resist that amount of beauty and sexiness. On the other hand, she is pure, naive, caring, nice, shy and innocent (this one was repeated so many times it made me nausious). So, we have a pure, innocent virgin who is sensual and sexy beyond reason. I'm not saying it isn't possible, I'm saying that in this story it wasn't presented in a way that would make her interesting (or credible). And she is just too damn sensitive and fragile for my taste. Instead of unique, interesting and exciting girl, she just seemed boring, at least to me. I didn't care for her one bit. Fourth - I had a hard time liking Gabriel. I tried, I really have, but still failed. I am a big fan of bad, disturbed and dark characters and I expected to fall for Gabriel at instant, but it didn't happen. Instead of being dark, all he did was talk about how he's dark. Some parts of his past fit in that description, because what happened to him and what he did to others made him edgy and dark, BUT... With Julia he was just too corny. He was too gentle, too sweet, too careful to say and do the right thing at every moment. He didn't want to hurt her so much that he was afraid to tell her the truth about his past, and he just dragged on and on with it. He praised her beauty and innocence and appologised for him being... well, him, so much I wanted to vomit every time. And he gave her too much presents. Again, I'm not saying that there's anything wrong with all that, but it just doesn't fit in a damaged guy he is supposed to be. Bad boys just aren't like that. Yes, they do want to change when they feel there is something worth the effort. Yes, they can be ridiculously romantic and sweet. Yes, they can be overprotective. I know all that from experience. But they don't talk like Gabriel talks. They don't compare people to roses, they don't repeat how someone is innocent and sweet in every single sentence and they don't apologize for who they are all the time. Gabriel did that all the time, he was like ''I am dark, and not good enough for you. Sorry for who I am. Oh, you are so pure and innocent and sexy at the same time. I'm sorry I'm not worthy of you. You are a beautiful, INNOCENT rose and I need to keep my hands off of you. But I am bad, so I won't do that. Sorry.'' He just didn't seem real. The emails and messages they sent to each other were... Well, I had a few (actually more than a few) ''kill me now'' moments. And the sex thing - oh they planned their first time for weeks, talked about it through pages and pages, and finally, it lasted forever while they were doing it. And of course, it was PERFECT. It wasn't exciting. It was boring. They made sex so... not sexy. Fifth - changing the POV so much made my head spin. It wasn't that difficult to follow, but all that jumping from one POV to another... I don't know, I just didn't like it. I could go on and on about what I didn't like, but I'll stop being negative and say what I did like. So here we go. I liked the title, as soon as I saw it I couldn't resist reading this book. I liked the writing style, it was clever, detailed and funny AT TIMES and I can see a great potential here. If the writer didn't repeat himself so many times, I would like it even more. Anyway, there are some good sentences in this book and they are not to be ignored. The author's knowledge of Dante and Italian art is really impressive. Actually, I would like to read a book about that and ONLY about that, becouse while describing some pieces of art he managed to show his talent somewhere in between all that crap with Gabriel and Julia. 1 star from me, because I was annoyed by Julia and Gabriel and their boring relationship.

I wanted to like this book. I really did. But the plain truth is that I didn't. My book-dud rule is if the plot is still unclear by page 50, you are allowed to abandon. But I really wanted to like this book, so I pushed the rule aside and read up to page 150, waiting for some substance. But I finally gave up and closed it. To be fair, there was a plot - a political seat needed to be filled because of a counsillor's death - but waiting for that dull concept to become riveting simply didn't happen. To begin with, there were a lot of characters - so many that I had to write a cheat sheet and refer to it often. Each character seemed to have a complex history with the dead guy and each character had some reason to be angry, jaded or mean-spirited. All of this 'character development' slowed the plot down to a crawl. I mean who really cares about a bunch of whiney townsfolk who have nothing to do but scheme and complain? Aren't there any good running trails nearby? So after Miles or Howard or whoever shreded someone else's election application form for no good reason, I decided that I would close this book for good and go out for a run on my town's fabuous running trails. As for the famous J.K. Rowling, I think I am done with her. I know that I am one of the very, very few people who did not enjoy the first two Harry Potter books and didn't bother completeing the series. I really do not enjoy reading children's lit (for pleasure) and I felt like I was reading it because of peer pressure. But I really thought that her adult book would allow me to enjoy her obvious talent as a storyteller. Sadly, this is not the case.

I have to say that this book wasn't what I was expecting. I knew the general premise of killer plants but I didn't expect it to be over such a long drawn out period of time. In my head I thought it was like war of the worlds in as much as a quick invasion and a battle that was the deciding end. Instead the book is written over years which the plants having a much more sneaky and gradual arrival. The book starts in a very horror provoking way. The main character is in hospital awaiting to have his eye patches removed to see if his vision is intact after an incident with one of the plants. No one comes, he cannot hear traffic or the normal bustling noises that London has. He cannot see what has happened. Does he take the patches off and risk his sight? Does he stay in the dark and image all kinds of horrors creeping round his vulnerable self? To me this is the worst part of the book for the horror of the unknown. The book goes on to document his struggles with a very different world to the one of yesterday. The entire order has changed and humans are having to adapt all over the world. This book shows whether as a species, we sink or swim. It brings out all the good and bad characteristics in people and the interactions between characters are a fascinating study of the physcology of coping. I liked this book but wouldn't say that it reached one of my favourites.

A disappointing book written by a usually reliable author, Afterworlds is actually two full-length novels inter-cut with each other. The first is a tiresome wish-fulfillment fantasy for wannabe writers, depicting an 18 year-old author, Darcy Patel, who moves to New York City after selling her first manuscript. The second is the novel Darcy has written - a bland supernatural romance about a girl who discovers the ability to see ghosts. Let's start with Darcy. Darcy's story is totally devoid of conflict and therefore the most boring story I have ever read. She gets everything she wants without any effort whatsoever. She gets $300,000 dollars for a crappy first draft she wrote in a month, she moves to NYC and finds the perfect apartment, everyone loves her books - from her instant girlfriend to distinguished authors she barely knows, she goes on an amazingly successfully pre-publicity tour, blah, blah, blah, blah. Honestly, the only obstacle that Darcy ever faces is the occasional slight insecurity which she quickly overcomes. She's the most boring character of all time! She never faces any hurdles; she never has to try particularly hard. This fact is made ever more deeply ironic because at one point in the story Darcy tries to convince a crowd that conflict is the most important element in any story! Maybe the author should have listened to his own advice and actually included some conflict in Darcy's story. I appreciate that Westerfeld has tried to show what "real" YA writing is like - the pressure from editors to make books marketable, the long delay before publication, the pressure to write sequels, the total necessity of publicity and networking. All that is great. But without any conflict, Darcy's story is just a series of unengaging events. By the end, I was actively irritated by her for getting everything she ever dreamed of without any cost or consequence. In addition, while I appreciate the gesture of a 50 year-old straight white man deciding to write a teen lesbian romance about a woman of colour, I was utterly underwhelmed by Darcy and Imogen's romance. Most everything about their relationship was unconvincing, inauthentic and unmoving. I don't want to criticise Westerfeld for attempting to write a YA lesbian romance - the world most definitely needs more of them - but I honestly wished he cared enough to make the romance real, not some ridiculously diluted-down version of lesbian romance written by a straight man for a presumably straight audience. And as for the story Darcy writes... Well, that's a whole different level of atrocious. Darcy's novel about Lizzie Scofield, a teenage girl who survives a terrorist attack and acquires the ability to see ghosts, has got to be the most horrendously generic supernatural romance I have ever read in my entire life. Lizzie's love interest has no personality whatsoever - he's a hot guy who shows up and Lizzie falls instantly in love with him. There's no substance whatsoever to their relationship, just PG-rated kisses. Lizzie's relationship with him isn't even that relevant to the plot and plays such a minor role it could easily be dropped entirely. Lizzie's friendship with the ghost of a murdered girl takes up much more time and it's also more emotionally engaging and actually drives events. Except that Lizzie's story is so shapeless! She gains the ability to see ghosts and then hangs out in her house for a while. Every time she gets into a problematic situation she just summons her hot boyfriend to save her instead of solving things herself. Lizzie appears to have a few plot goals involving a serial killer and a ghost collector, but even those plot lines turn out to be too brief and insubstantial to amount to much. And THIS is the story that all the characters in Darcy's story are crazy about!? It's absurd! The worst part is that Westerfeld is very obviously aware of the shortcomings of his book, but he just doesn't care. The book features a lot of meta-commentary about YA writing in general and, in particular, about cultural appropriation. Darcy wonders if it's okay to include a Hindu god in her story "for the purposes of YA hotness." But the book never properly resolves this issue, nor acknowledges that it's actually Scott Westerfeld who has appropriated a Hindu god into his story for the purposes of YA hotness. Lampshading a trope doesn't suddenly make it okay. Lampshading is not a get-out-of-jail-free card. And what's more, there's very little point to inter-cutting the two stories. They never really influence each other; they never intertwine; they are always merely the sum of their substandard parts. I was longing for the moment that the two stories would mesh together and become some mind-bendingly post-modern self-parody of YA literature. That was honestly the only thing that could have saved this book. Alas, Scott Westerfeld is not so self-aware. This book has totally changed my opinion on Scott Westerfeld. Previously I saw him as a solid, varied writer who occasionally misses the mark. Now I see him as a mediocre, generic writer who occasionally finds a decent idea. This is definitely one of Westerfeld's worst.

** spoiler alert ** It's always an excitement to read anything that has to do with J.K. Rowling and the magical universe she's created, she never runs out of ideas. The story of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is no exception. I loved the plot, but the writing itself lacks emotion and creativity. I know, J.K. didn't write the actual book, but I can't help being angry at all this. This is not the 8th Harry Potter book! There is no such thing as 8th Harry Potter book! Since it's a theatre play, I had to focus a little bit extra on the characters, and I was kind of disappointed to realise that they're not exactly themselves. Ron, whom I loved in the HP series, doesn't look like Ron at all. He's barely there, actually, and he seems so bland and so not himself. Don't blab that he's a grown-up now and he got mature, I know Ron, and this certainly isn't him. Also, the most important question I have, WHERE IS GEORGE? I mean, he was supposed to run Weasley's Wizard Whizzes, not Ron. I so wanted to read about George again, to see how he's doing after losing his other half, but he wasn't there! He's not even mentioned. I was expecting so much more from Albus's friendship with Scorpius! I wanted to see some development, some chemistry, some intrigue, and I got none of that! I believe there's so much more to a friendship between two persons whose fathers used to be arch enemies! Since Scorpius is Draco's son, I wanted some angst (how can you speak of Draco Malfoy without mentioning how angsty he is? Speaking of Draco, who's a beloved character of mine, I was actually happy with him in this novel. He got the redemption he deserved, but he kept his old habits of teasing The Golden Trio. I missed this, and, fortunately, I got some of it. I have believed in Draco all this time... Delphi was not very predictable, but she's definitely not worthy of being a Harry Potter villain. Once again I found a plot hole and ruined everything: if Voldemort is not capable of love, then how on earth did he leave Bellatrix pregnant? Voldemort was hungry for power, he'd never wanted a heir, he wanted to live forever and rule the world. Then how was this Delphi actually born? Hmm... But I can't end this review without mentioning the biggest and most obvious mistake in the book: how did Albus and Scorpius manage to prepare Polyjuice Potion is a few minutes, when preparing it takes at least one month. You can't fool me, muggles, I've read Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets...

GOLDEN is everything I want in a contemporary: heartfelt, thought-provoking, charming, and real. Curiosity getting the best of her, Parker reads the journal. I related with Parker more than I have with any YA heroine in a long, long time. Perhaps because I was a lot like her in HS-graduating near the top of my class, taking only carefully calculated risks. My parents were not nearly as overbearing as Parker's mother, but I understood Parker's desire to never disappoint. I won't say much about the journal because the mystery surrounding it is one I don't want to spoil. This is a novel about how small moments can lead to big ones, how chances can be seized as easily as missed. It also features a wonderful friendship-Parker and Kat felt like real girls, real friends, real teens. I adored this story. Originally posted here.

The basic premise of this story is that there are two types of people - Reds and Silvers. Reds have red blood, no special abilities, and are slaves to the silvers. Silvers have (you guessed it) silver blood, all sorts of special abilities - like super strength, water powers, fire powers, basically whatever you can think of someone has it - which give them all the power in this society. Also, there's a big war that's been going on for a hundred years with a neighbouring country, and thousands of Red lives have been sacrificed over the years due to the conscription of every Red who turns 18 and doesn't have a job. Enter our hero, Mareena Barrow! A seventeen-year-old girl who doesn't have a job, and so she steals from all the people in her neighbourhood (who are just as poor as she is) and helps to support her family - which, if you think about it, means she's actually a really horrible person. But it's ok! She's our hero! We forgive her everything! She has three older brothers who have all been conscripted, and she has resigned herself to her fate until her best friend loses his job and is conscripted. To stop this, she comes up with a plan to escape with her best friend, which involves having to steal a lot of money from Silvers. Obviously, this is very dangerous, and a terrorist attack by Reds thwarts her plan and ends up ruining her sister's sewing hand (she has a younger sister who is a very good seamstress, and is about to make a lot of money from it, but alas, it is not to be). Then, she goes on a stealing spree in her local pub, until she steals from the wrong man and is caught, she tells him all her sorrows, he gives her a bit of money, walks her home, and that's that. Again we forgive her. The next day palace guards appear, and she finds out she's been given a job as a servant there, and then she finds that the guy who helped her out the night before is Prince Cal! Yay, she didn't have to change her ways at all, a man saved her! And in the process of choosing his wife, she falls on a big electric shield and discovers she has powers over electricity - which is quite fortunate or she would have died. This earns her the apparently terrible nickname little lightning girl...hmmm... Anyway, the Queen makes her become engaged to the second prince, Prince Maven. Who is called the shadow to the flame in comparison to his older brother. Deep-seated resentment on Prince Maven's side to his older brother, poor little princeling. To cut a long story short, Maven and Mareena join the rebels, Mareena and Cal like each other, hate each other, kiss each other, hate each other, etc, Maven and Mareena then fall in love, they start kissing too (at the same time she's still kissing Cal), lots of people are killed. All of this is interspersed with lots of martial training, because even though the nobles don't join the army, they all spend hours training to become amazing killing machines (I know, this doesn't make sense. You would think the less noble Silvers would do all the training and fighting and the nobles would be involved with other things, as they aren't going to war. I think it's to make it more along the lines of Mockingjay and Divergent that these scenes are brought in). By the way, I am SO over strong female characters being incredibly weak and unable to do anything without the love of their life. Of manipulating the people around them by pretending they're in love with them. Of being massive users and actually really selfish and horrible, but being portrayed in a way where that is their only available choice! Actually, you know what, it's not. Rely on yourself! Stop being so dependent on a man! Grow up! Ugh. Anyway, eventually the big twist is that Maven - shock horror! - is not actually on the side of the rebels but wants to be king, so he and his mother get rid of the king and Cal and Mareena go on trial. The only surprise is how long it takes for the book to get to this stage. Cal and Mareena feel very betrayed and Mareena decides that she doesn't want to be with either Cal or Maven, even though you can tell she still likes Cal. At this stage was one of my favourite ridiculous lines about Maven "Murder helps him sleep". Ooookaaaayyy Anyway, they go on trial, end up killing their opponents, and then escape with the resistance where I'm sure they will live to fight in another book. So basically, it's a rip-off of Mockinjay and Divergent with a little fantasy thrown in.

I originally rated this book a 3 out of 5 stars. With Only An Abundance of Katherines left to read, Paper Towns is my least favorite so far. I didn't think that the story was that great. I read through the entire book in one sitting. I thought I liked Quentin and his friends and I thought I liked this story, but the more I worked on this review, the more I realized that this just isn't the case. First off, John Green has pretty much recycled the characters from his first book Looking for Alaska and inserted them in a new story. Alaska for Margo and Miles for Quentin. It was very hard to read about Margo dramatically leaving vague clues when she decided to run away and not think, "Yup, that is what Alaska would do." We are introduced to younger versions of our main character at the beginning. Still in grade school, young Quentin and Margo are walking to the park together when they accidentally stumble upon the body of a man who had committed suicide. When I first read this my mind went "oooo!! This is cool!" But this scene contributed nothing to the story line. It was some weird prologue that meant nothing. We fast forward to Quentin and Margo's senior year of high school. Although the two characters grew up next door to each other, at some point after the discovered suicide in the park, they drifted apart. I'm not sure if it's the idea of the girl next door, but Quentin has this fixation on Margo. For some reason, he fancies himself head over heels for this girl that he doesn't talk to. I feel like Quentin doesn't even try to approach Margo or get to know her, not because she has a boyfriend (although that seems to be the excuse he uses), but because if he were to express his feelings for her she would shoot him down. So he's content to worship her from a distance. The only part of the book that I found 100% believable was the night of shenanigans. I completely accepted that a young man, whose life long crush crawls through his window after dark and asks him to help her with a project, would totally agree. I especially liked how Margo presented her case. Eleven tasks, no laws will be broken (serious ones, at least), live a little! However, as the tasks were being checked off, it became clear that Margo was nothing more than a manipulative mean girl. I get wanting revenge because find out your boyfriend is cheating on you with your friend. But the third fish, the one that was smashed in Lacey's car; that was just malicious. Margo assumed that Lacey knew about her cheating boyfriend, but she never actually asked her. We find out later that Lacey didn't know a thing about it. The worst part is Lacey just forgives Margo! When Margo runs away, Quentin is determined to find her, which is admirable, but lost its charm quickly. Quentin becomes obsessed with finding her, with reading as far into these supposed clues that Margo scattered before she left. It wasn't the first time she's done this either. Shortly after she goes missing, a case worker shows up at Quentin's house and tells him that the last time she ran away she left the letters M, I, S, S in her empty bowl of alphabet soup. She had run off to a town in Mississippi. Her parents didn't get the message; they just cleaned the bowl and reported her missing. If that's not narcissistic, I don't know what is. Then there was the flop of an ending. I enjoyed the build-up, these friends skipping their high school graduation to go find Margo. But, of the four people who are traveling to a paper town in New York (from Florida, mind you), Lacey is the only one can truly claim to be Margo's friend (and I've already stated my opinion on that definition of 'friend'). Upon being discovered, Margo admits that she didn't want to be found, that she didn't think anyone would know where to find her. Although impressed by Quentin's detective work, Margo just brushes them off; like I said, manipulative mean girl. That's it. That is the end of the book. I thought the buildup was great and then was so anticlimactic that it hurt. I love YA books. I don't always like what is popular, but I love what these books are doing. With all the technology in the world today and other fun distractions, the target audience these books aim for can sometimes be hard to encourage picking up a book. I love author who can get a young person's attention and I respect an author who can influence that same young person to pick up another. I first accepted this book because it was YA. But now, after really sitting down and thinking about it, I'm going to have to say that I didn't care for this book. It romanticizes abusive relationships and glorifies the abuser. Margo may not have hit or verbally assaulted anyone, but she sure did send them into a frenzy. That is just not something that I can, with a good conscience, recommend.

Teased was actually a very good read, but it could have been an excellent one... The story was complex and full of mystery, suspense, intrigue and drama. Plus, it felt so very real that you could have been watching the story's movie instead of reading its book...The characters were shaped beautifully and had a very interesting journey throughout the book..So, I loved the story in general... However, I didn't like the gaps in the timeline and I even noticed a couple of emotional gaps. For instance, we read how attracted to Vida Colton was, even when he were acting indifferent towards her. But suddenly he stopped hesitating and questioning his feelings and simply started to pursue her incessantly. That moment, when a character changes course of action when he realizes his true feelings is such an important moment in the book and it really saddened me not to have it. Up until that moment, I really loved the book. However, the lack of processing Colton's feelings and decisions really let me down, because for me that is a huge moment in the story. Indeed, there were a few gaps in the timeline that took me a while to adjust. They were mainly focused on Sawyer and her story, but they bugged me a bit. Especially in the ending right before the epilogue...Perhaps that gap is in the next book of the series..But the movement towards the epilogue was not smooth and I felt very startled by it and annoyed that I didn't really get any significant answers. Again, all of this may be in the next book, but I merely state my breaking points... But those remarks do not change the fact that the story and our characters are pretty amazing!! Let's Go Meet Them! >>Vida is such a strong, loyal, stubborn, decent and sweet person..You cannot not love her! She has fierce determination and so many dreams for her life that make her awe-inspiring..Because she wasn't dealt with a good childhood..She didn't have many resources and she certainly did not have the best environment every child deserves to have when growing up..She is an admirable young woman who will also keep you very entertained... >>Colton is such a strong, confident and devoted man...He also didn't have the best environment to grow up in and he certainly was not the best judge of character..Tessa was the worst decision he ever made and he paid it dearly..But we can't stop wondering that his awful decision did land him with Vida, so yeah I will leave it to that.. I will give you a fair warning that he might make you want to slap him..A lot...In the first half of the book, anyway..So you could enjoy a glass of wine, while reading that first half... In conclusion, Teased is a really great story..It has some negative points ( in my opinion, at least)...But the story and the characters more than make up for them!

Most of all I loved some of the quality character development seen in this issue. Especially Rick, Carl and Michonne. Rick and Michonne have definitely gone through more than their fair share of suffering and we've watched how this has affected them. Watched how they've become more numb to the world, more cut off from who they once were. In Here We Remain, we get to see a much more psychological change taking place - something more than just numbness and I really appreciated this development. Last but not least, Carl. Carl has been an important and central character throughout the entire series. He's survived when so many others haven't and yet we haven't got to know him very much at all - UNTIL NOW!! It makes me wonder what time period is occurring in the waking world... but once Villett gets there, even though it is made clear that time moves differently in the waking world and dream world, it is clearly present day, like 2016, which just blows my mind if you remember these comments about women not dreaming earlier on in the book. Just... WHAT?! The whole premise of the dream world and the waking world, and that the dream world is a physical place, and that some people live only exclusively there was really interesting, but the overall plot was kind of boring, and it took me quite a while to get into the story even though it was only 166 pages.

Actual Rating: 2 I put off reading this for so long. I had LOVED An Ember in the Ashes and I just wanted the story to pause there for a little while longer. After reading this book, I haven't changed my mind. In my opinion, book two suffered - terribly - from second book syndrome. After the events in An Ember in the Ashes, Laia and Elias are on the run and heading towards Kauf to save Laia's brother, Darin. But an infinite amount of obstacles stand in their way, ranging from otherworldly spirits to Elias' childhood friend, Helene. The book also contains chapters from Helene's perspective this time - and it follows her emotional struggle between herself, her family, Elias, and the Empire. I've read several reviews and they all seem to agree that Helene's part in this book was powerful. I have to agree; there was a lot of character development for her especially, and I loved seeing how she tried to fight back even when the entire world was against her. Other than that, I'm afraid I liked book two a LOT less than its prequel. The pacing was a lot slower, firstly; while the first one was full of action and I felt like the story was going somewhere, the first half of A Torch Against the Night just felt like Laia and Elias were running away over and over again, never really getting anywhere. It's true that the book did start to pick up a little later, but it still just didn't have the same spark for me that book one did. Many of the twists were predictable, and when the book ended, it just felt like a bit of progress slowly drawn out over 500 pages. Due to the slower plot, I felt like Tahir's writing style was also less engaging. There were definitely several beautiful quotes, but in the long run, I just wasn't as captivated. Another thing that really bothered me was the romance. In book one, I felt it. I felt every emotion between Elias and Laia, and I just LOVED them together. Their relationship felt a lot weaker in this book, and while I understand the circumstances, it made me feel as though all the emotion I had invested into their relationship was being put on hold, or even slowly erased.
