This review originally posted at Improbable Chuck: Canucks on Comics I've been hearing more and more about East of West as the months go on so when the first trade paperback was available I figured it was about time for me to check it out. East of West in a nutshell is the story of the four horseman of the apocalypse. Well actually it's about three of the Horsemen (War, Famine and Conquest) trying to track down the fourth (Death). But it's also about this group called "the Chosen." The world leaders of the future, who are purposely working together to bring about the end of the world. And it's about Death's missions to retrieve what was taken from him and be reunited with his wife. Ok so there's no "in a nutshell" for this series. As you've probably determined, there's a lot going on. But the action is very slow going, there's a lot of set up, a lot of characters to be introduced and a lot of relationships and back handed deals to be explored. At first I wished it would just tell me what everyone was after but as I kept reading I began to appreciate the deliberate style, as it meant there was a surprise around every corner. Death is the character that most of this book centres around. He takes the form of a wild west cowboy in a futuristic world and he is pissed! There is a lot of violence committed because of him or at his hands. I guess this shouldn't be surprising -he is death after all. (But seriously - violence!!) He's also a very real and interesting character - which was a nice surprise. He has very clear goals and motivations and the love he feels for his wife is downright moving. I appreciated that Hickman didn't make this character cliched or boring. You can tell from these first five issues, he not going to be what you expected. There is some really fascinating world building in this book - a futuristic world blended with the Wild wild west. And it's complexities are communicated through some very crisp, very detailed artwork. Dragotta is very talented and though I loved all his work throughout this book, I was particularly a sucker for the full page spreads that would appear throughout. Such as this one: It is both complex and straight forward all at the same time. These first four issues are excellent set up and they have me curious about what's to come. This is a dark and gritty book and if that's your style you're going to love it. However the slow pacing makes me feel like buying the monthly issues could get tedious and frustrating while you wait for something big to happen. This one might be better in trade paperback form.

One summer night the stars abruptly blink out. Three young people are lying on the grass behind the splendid house belonging to the parents of the twins, Jason and Diane Lawton. With them is Tyler Dupree, a year younger, son of the housekeeper to the Lawtons. They react, like the rest of the country, with a variety of emotions, and everyone wonders if the sun will come up. Jason is excited about the scientific questions; Tyler and Diane are on the phone when there is indeed a dawn--but the sun they see is not the real sun. Tyler is the first person narrator, which gives the necessary infodumps a human voice. Tyler has a crush on Diane that never quite abates, and Jason is their tycoon father's heir apparent, raised with the burden of expectation. Thus the Lawtons get drawn into the political and scientific side of the mysterious 'Spin'--probing the membrane that suddenly shrouded the Earth--and so Tyler, Jason's best friend, gets the inside track on the unfolding discoveries and secrets ahead of the rest of the world. Interspersed with Tyler's life story are snips of present-day action, when he is quite a bit older. We get hints of breakthroughs to come, in a book chock-full of sfnal ideas and explanatory passages. Meanwhile Diane goes off and joins a religious cult, Jason is buried in scientific work, and Tyler pursues a medical degree. The only discovery I'll mention here (it's revealed on the book jacket) is that only a few years pass on Earth while millions of years pass outside the Spin barrier, making it possible to do really long-duration experiments once they figure out how to penetrate the membrane. Wilson keeps his focus tightly on his three protagonists, which avoids the cast-of-thousands cliche snapshots of most endtimes novels. Who set up the Spin? The scientists call the unknown perps the Hypotheticals--and the novel does eventually provide answers to all the questions. The narrative voice comes down with all the subtlety of a hammer in making its point that a male-gaze secular humanist POV is the only way to think. I found the questions raised in this book more interesting than the answers--and I did feel zaps of impatience when it seemed to me that females were rewarded with the accolade of being smart and worthy of success only after they agreed with the 'right-thinking' males. (The one major wrong-thinking male being Diane's Simon, who shares her faith--a one-dimensional character who seemed to be there only to lose encounters with Tyler.) My own feeling of sense of wonder was evoked in the first chapter; the rest of the book never quite matched.

So clearly, Margaret Atwood can write a sentence. She can write a paragraph. And she can write a damn good story. I'm just not sure this is one of them. I've been an Atwood fan since I picked up The Edible Woman for a quarter at a yard sale when I was 18, and I've loved how Atwood can take on such a wide variety of stories and characters and personas. It can't be boring to live in her head, not for a second. The problem with The Blind Assassin for me was that it just dragged. I "listened to" this book rather than read it, although I have a copy on my bookshelf. If I remember correctly, I've picked up and abandoned this book at least several times during the years, and I almost abandoned the audio version as well. Which would have been a shame, because the book is quite good -- at the beginning and at the end, and here and there, in the middle. It's actually a story within a story within a story, and at least two of those stories are quite compelling. But for way, way too long, an elderly woman wanders the streets of Port Ticonderoga and Toronto, ducking into coffee shops and squabbling with the sweet woman who looks in on her. During these long segments, I found myself drifting off to ponder such things as the national debt and what I might put on my Christmas list, if I end up making a Christmas list this year after all. But the payoff is there, and ultimately worth the time it takes to arrive.

Add me to the list of girls who love Sinclair Vinemont. ARC provided via Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. For more of my reviews visit Carlene Corrupted. Stella Rousseau would do anything for her father, anything to keep him from prison for crimes he didn't commit. Sinclair Vinemont is up for the Acquisition, a tournament held every 10 years by the wealthy and elite of Louisiana. Vinemont will do anything to become the next Sovereign to rule them all, even enslave Stella. One thing is clear, the Acquisition always ends in bloodshed and Stella refuses to be dragged down easily. I read Counsellor in one sitting and by the next day I had already purchased book two in the Acquisition series by Celia Aaron. With incredible writing and graphic detail Aaron brings to life a powerful and dark tradition in the beautiful scenery of Louisiana. My favorite thing about Counsellor wasn't the characters, though they were fantastic, it was the detail into how the Acquisition trials worked and how the character thought processes worked through it all. The scenery was beautiful, easy to imagine, even during the horrific times when hundreds came together in a game of blood and kink. I felt the heavy stares of outsiders and the terrifying horror as the main characters watch the ball turn into a whipping ground. My emotions sat heavy on my chest through out the entire book, with twists and turns heightening my fear for Stella and pulling me between hatred and lust for Vinemont. Aaron makes the reader feel the anticipation Stella is going through as she wonders what is to become of her and what the Acquisition really is. On top of that, the ever shifting mood of Sinclair Vinemont left me wondering what was true and what wasn't and how evil he truly could be. I definitely found myself rooting for Stella, for her to keep herself out of the darkness and see it through the end, even when the hits kept coming. While Vinemont should own the asshole alpha title, I found myself liking him as glimpses of his hidden self came out. The two characters, and even the secondary, make this fictional novel feel so realistic and shows that even in horrors a romance can blossom. Counsellor is a very dark and erotic fiction, it contains slavery, BDSM, and violence, however it is a stellar novel. Though it is a work of fiction, Celia Aaron makes the traditional Louisiana wealth and Acquisition come to life, pulling you into a realistic story that you won't want to put down. Counsellor is book one in the Acquisition series and does end in a cliffhanger. Book two, Magnate, available for purchase now and both novels are highly recommended.

"Lizzie Borden took an axe..." On the 4th August 1892 inFall River, Massachusetts Lizzie Borden calls out to the maid, 'Someone's killed father.' This new fictionalised retelling of the story of Lizzie Borden makes for compelling reading. Told from the first person viewpoint of several of the characters (suspects??) whom the author so cleverly brings to life you really get a real feel for this dysfunctional family. The house is peopled by adults who are angry, sad and resentful in some way but can see no way of escaping their miserable, interlocked lives. Mirroring this atmosphere the oppressive, claustrophobic heat of an malodorous, overblown summer makes people sweat, food goes rancid, fruit rots and blood congeals as the household go about their daily business. The writing creates a noxious atmosphere that literally rises off the page into the reader's mind creating a feeling of dread and unease. Undeniably compelling - I highly recommend this book to any reader whether they have an interest in the Lizzie Borden case or not just for the quality of the writing - superb . Short Review In many ways a step down from the first book Storm Front. Convoluted, but strangely dull at times more from an overabundance of action than a dearth of it. Still a bit of a fun read despite its faults and the fact that I've been told by several fans of the series this is one of the, if not the, worst books in the series. Long Review It wouldn't be a Dresden Files review if I didn't remind everyone that everyone tells me these books don't get really good until book four. Now that that's out of the way, we can talk about this particular book. I'm not sure where to start here. The book, admittedly, was hard to put down. That in and of itself is a bit confusing to me, because simultaneously I often felt... well, bored with it. The premise is basically a copy of the first book, spooky murders mean Murphy is calling Dresden for help, it puts him in severe mortal peril, turns out the bad guy isn't who you thought it was the author wanted you to think it was, Dresden saves the day, etc. Shortly after the book starts, Checkov shows up at your house and smacks you across the face with that gun of his before he puts it over the fireplace. You're introduced via Bob to like five or six types of werewolf and then subsequently every single one of them has to show up and be involved in the story, including an additional type that isn't mentioned. I could practically hear Oprah yelling, "You get a werewolf! And you get a werewolf! And you get a werewolf!" Like the first book there's some general misogyny. Murphy gets so close to being a strong character, but I felt like her mistrust of Harry and Harry's self-righteous over-protectiveness of her was blown way out proportion to infuse some quick and easy drama there. The other thing that got to me a bit was that Harry spends so much time where he's one gentle push away from death, that it starts to lose a lot of its tension. It's a similar problem to heroes who are so perfect (think Superman) that it's hard to make them seem like they're ever in real danger. Harry is the opposite end of the spectrum in that him being almost dead becomes the norm, and I got to feeling like there weren't any real stakes there. That made a lot of the book feel a little dull, even though there's all sorts of action. People say this is the worst in the series, so I'm hoping that bears out. I'll stick with it through all fifteen or so books though still.

THAT COVER. *wants it now* I was drawn to Sybella in GRAVE MERCY and her story sounds every bit as amazing as I expected! I cannot WAIT to read it! Sybella was a fabulous, flawed heroine who I loved, and the romance was genuine, if a little fast. Full review coming soon. Final Review (also appears at Once Upon a Prologue) Grave Mercy was one of the books I fangirled over the most in 2012; it was just beautiful, macabre, and unlike anything I'd ever read. I don't read much YA historical fiction but when I do, I tend to fall in love with whatever book I choose in that genre. I loved Ismae and Duval in Grave Mercy, and waited forever, and EVER for Dark Triumph. The publisher was generous enough to allow me to read an e-galley but as much as it pains me to say, I wasn't quite as enamored with Dark Triumph as I was with Grave Mercy. Dark Triumph picks up hot on the heels of Grave Mercy, and we see so many characters - good AND bad - and familiar events from the first book through Sybella's eyes. I think part of my problem is, although I loved Sybella, and wanted to hug her and protect her, because we only saw her from Ismae's point of view in Grave Mercy, I think I expected something MORE from her. She's a very sympathetic character, but she was built up so much in Grave Mercy, so for me she fell a little short of the mark in Dark Triumph. Maybe I was expecting her to still be "half mad from grief," as the synopsis alluded, but whatever was missing, I wrestled with my conflicting emotions about Sybella throughout Dark Triumph. That said, I DID like her - she's very fierce, and very loyal to those she cares about, which earned her lots of points with me. Dark Triumph was one of those books that I read slowly, because despite not clicking with Sybella as much as I wished, I was once again drawn right into Robin LaFever's gorgeous, heady writing, and brilliantly alive descriptions of Brittany, and various historical figures. My heart went out to so many characters - Beast, Duchess Anne, Sybella, Julian, and more. Dark Triumph hit me hard, and kept beating up my heart-strings. Plot-wise, Dark Triumph is a stellar read. The pacing is spot-on as in Grave Mercy, and never feels hurried; at the same time, I was never bored while reading Dark Triumph. Anne's perilous hold on her power has never been in more danger, and although a large portion of Ms Lafever's novel focuses on Sybella trying to survive in her father's household, there was still the over-reaching plot of Duchess Anne's struggles, which tied everyone together. We also learn more about Mortain, and the old religions, and what the convent's true purpose is. *cue sinister music* My heart went out to Sybella, seeing how she lived. A cossetted noblewoman on the surface, this facade hides Sybella's tortured childhood, her escape to the convent of Saint Mortain, and her return as an implant for the convent in her father's house. D'Albret is a monster, and I despaired, as did Sybella, if Mortain would ever marque him for the death he deserved. Robin LaFevers knows how to write her villains, her heroes, and her flawed characters. Amidst everything else going on, including Sybella questioning Mortain's purpose for her, there's a beautiful undercurrent of self-acceptance and romance in Dark Triumph. We're reunited with one of my favorite characters, Beast of Waroch. Beast is just unfettered, and wild, and I adored him. It was very lovely, seeing him come to care for Sybella, although I preferred the slow-burning affection between Ismae and Gabriel in Grave Mercy. Best and Sybella developed feelings for one another so quickly I could *almost* call it insta-love, which frankly, irritated me. But at the heart, what's between them was genuine, so I did like the romance. I have to mention Julian. Oh Julian. Right away I knew I was either going to love him or hate him, but I ended up getting so invested in him. He did terrible things, but dammit all to hell if I didn't end up tearing up a few times over him. Maybe it's because I read several books as a teen that showed character under intense duress where incest happened in a way I could support *only in the book, never in real life* or maybe it was just how tormented Julian was, but I couldn't help but believe he DID love Sybella. Oh, my heart though. It BROKE for Julian, especially as he finally started to see things from Sybella's point of view. Her memories of him as her protector throughout childhood contrasted with his love for her just killed me. They were so tragically beautiful. Dark Triumph wasn't quite the sequel the Grave Mercy I hoped it would be, but it was still a lovely read that I really did enjoy. And I have no doubts that I'll be adding a physical copy to my collection soon, while I wait - impatiently - for the third and final book!

A Hollows series short-Kim Harrison. This short story is an breakfast outing between Kisten and Rachel that becomes a run. Kisten's sister Chrissy crashes the breakfast date with her son Audric. Audric's father is trying to take permanent custody of the 6 year old as a gift to his Master. *sorry about the spoilers* This story was not about the plot at all for me. I miss Kisten so very much. Reading this brought forth so many emotions. I wish I had a time machine and I could go back into time and beg Harrison not to take him away from us. I will hold out hope since the series has not completed yet, that somehow Harrison brings Kisten back from the true death. The dialogue between Kisten and Rachel is heart wrenching. It would have been difficult to read even before Kisten's death, now it is pure torture. The discussion runs the gamete, from marriage to children. Kisten's nephew, Audric, looks exactly like his uncle. That is a picture I can not remove from my mind. It is amazing as I read book that I find such a strong connection with characters and not so much with others. It is all about the journey. Here are a few of the quotes that almost had me bawling like an idiot! "I told you, Rachel." he said in my ear to start a warm spot in me. "I've got your back. Nothing alive will ever hurt you if I have breath in me. And nothing dead will hurt you if I don't." He leaned in to give me a kiss, and this time, I let him, my lips moving against his to turn it into a spine-tingling, stomach quivering kiss that delved deep and set my pulse racing. "Are you and Ms. Rachel going to get married?" he asked from nowhere. My mouth dropped open, and Kisten started. "Ah, not today. Sport. Maybe someday." Oh God, I'd forgotten kids were like that, and I warmed. "Do you kiss her?" the boy asked. Kisten grinned as his hand fell from Audric's shoulder. "Every chance I get." Audric thought about that for a moment as he picked at a bit of mortar and dropped it into the water for the bridge troll to eat, "Mommy says if you love someone, and you like kissing them, and they don't ever, ever hurt you, you should marry them" If only it was that simple. Audric squinted up at me, and I panicked, not knowing what had come into that little brain and was now going to come out his mouth. "Do you hurt Uncle Kisten?" he asked. I opened my mouth to answer--it was a disturbing question for anyone but a vampire child--but Kisten beat me to it. "Only my heart, Audric," he said. "Ms. Rachel is like the sun. See her sparkling there with the wind in her hair and fire in her eyes? You can't catch the sun. You can only feel its touch on your face. And if you get too much of it, it burns you." Scrolling through the reviews of this book, I couldn't find a single negative one--Yet I was completely underwhelmed by this book. I would have put it down after the first chapter, if it wasn't for my weakness for post-apocalyptic fiction. Mullin didn't seem to get the memo that there is more to writing young adult fiction than just writing dumbed-down adult fiction. The main character's voice was inconsistent and completely unbelievable--I was constantly distracted by out-of-place thoughts and actions, and some phrases and word choices made me want to groan out loud. The writing itself was plain, blunt and expository in a way that felt unfinished, not clean or effective. The book oscillates between long bouts of trudging and sudden bouts of abrupt action--and the ending highlights this inability to explain meaningful portions without rushing through them. I was left dangling off the end of a book I hadn't really wanted to keep reading anyway.

Oops. I totally didn't mean to read this all tonight but here we are anyway. Listen. Have you ever read Pride & Prejudice and thought, "There should be more magic." The thing about this was it was so readable. Like, I flew through the first 150+ pages without hardly taking a break to eat dinner. (Okay, so I definitely took a break to eat dinner, but let me tell you, I went straight back to this when I was done.) But whatever, this book is forgiven because it was ridiculously adorable and super fun to read.

** spoiler alert ** So in the beginning it was, well what is that, what are these words, how am I suppose to know what's happening with this many made-up words!? Then I couldn't figure out who was really the main character and what was happening. Then Chronicler came in & it started to make sense. I love Rothfuss's writing, it was sometimes very much fantasy/celtic & often very modern with superb barbs, 'I hear you three times' & 'You lack the requisite spine & testicular fortitude to study under me'. & 'To deem us simply enemies is to lose the true flavor of our relationship. It was more like the two of us entered into a business partnership in order to more efficiently pursue our mutual interest of hating each other.' & 'Music is a proud, temperamental mistress. Give her the time and attention she deserves, and she is yours. Slight her and there will come a day when you call and she will not answer.' Once I started getting a feel for the mythology of the world with everything having a 'name' and Kvothe and his antics and learning at the University, I kept thinking, this is a lot like Earthsea. But I was really glad that Kvothe's twists/turns were very different from Sparrowhawks, though still a familiar tale. 'So Taborlin fell, but he did not despair. For he knew the name of the wind, and so the wind obeyed him.' [Ok, literally I started counting the number of times 'name of the wind' was mentioned in the book then had to stop because it was really racking up] Elodin & Kvothe and the 'will he teach him won't he part' was insanity. Obviously, It made sense Kvothe was going to need to study Naming under Elodin because he wanted to know the name of the wind [coming back to the title, always, in this one] but then this happened instead: 'As I lay there, counting my blessings & broken ribs, Elodin stepped into my field of vision. 'Congratulations, that was the stupidest thing I've ever seen. Ever'. And that is when I decided to pursue the noble art of artificing.' Loved it. I have no idea how I read this book in 6 days, but Rothfuss/Kvothe kept ending certain chapters with cryptic thoughts about how much he underestimated Ambrose, when Ambrose decided to kill him, and then that bombshell, Ambrose did get him kicked out, oh no he just did, no wait he didn't, but he later? Driving me insane, so I couldn't really stop reading. H-O-O-K-E-D. Like the best books really get us. There were times that I started to drift when reading about Kvothe's poverty, his cleverness, Ambrose, Denna & the Chandrian but each subject would get a respite from/for another that I think that made it all work. I'm very intrigued by the over all plot of three books, three days (Ye, Gods a lot happened on that first day, didn't it?) hopefully finding out something concrete about the Chandrian & this king killing business in the end.

Those of you who have been friends with me for awhile know that I love to dissect books about mental illness, especially when the author has done a terrible job at the research involved in the book (for examples, see this review of The Asylum Prophecies or this review of Switching Time). There was none of that nonsense in A Cure for Madness. (Can I tell you how much I adore authors who present a realistic picture of mental illness??) Anyway. I think what really caught me up in A Cure for Madness was not so much the fact that there was a pathogen that created an extremely contagious and incurable disease that was very similar to schizophrenia... but was more the relationships. I loved seeing how Clare slowly realized that her brother, Wes, was right in a lot of what he said, regarding her running away from Clarkeston. I loved seeing her character growth throughout the novel. And I loved Wes' brotherly jabs at her ("my friends aren't dickheads... unlike yours"). I would've liked to see more romance between her and Kenneth, but given the hectic and tense situations that they continuously faced, it makes sense why there wasn't (and honestly, given the setting of this book, it would've been more of a distraction had there been more of a spark between them). That being said, the book ended on such an amazing cliffhanger-but-not-quite-cliffhanger so if there is a follow-up/sequel to A Cure for Madness, I definitely want to see more Clare-and-Kenneth interaction in there (even if it's not super romantic). My honest opinion - Jodi McIsaac has a lot of talent. And I'm very interested to see where she will go from here. I'm definitely going to be putting some of her others books on my TBR pile (which is about the size of Mt. Everest now... and growing!

Read this and other reviews Ampersand Read The Sculptor is delightful. You can definitely see that McCloud knows his stuff. The artistic style is really on point. The character's expressions, and the inventive way McCloud utilizes speech bubbles (so skillfully that you forget it's a comic, that it's a speech bubble spouting from someone's head), are impressive, to say the least. And the way plot twists are laid out really gets you turning pages. You really start to feel for the characters, and you ache a little when the story ends. The premise alone sets you up for some heartbreak: this guy is going to die in 200 days, and partway through that, he meets and falls in love with someone (who just happens to be a little damaged too - character flaws are well-rendered here too). But the journey to this deal's end is a long and tangled one. David's success doesn't come as easy as he would hope. In fact, his first exhibition kind of flops. He's crazy awkward around women, he makes misstep after misstep when it comes to his lady love, and he's moody and depressing and somehow, still brilliant. The book had a lot to say about art and commercialism and living in the big NYC. I liked that it was a gritty graphic novel. It dealt with real, complex issues in a way that was visually beautiful. The ending felt a tad clumsy...without spoiling the whole thing, you have to pause at the end to suss out what's real, and how the book really...ended. For such a solid book, it was an ambiguous ending, and I felt the story deserved more (and the sunshine and rainbows half of me wanted it of course to end happily for everyone!) Great art, that has a lot to say about art itself. The ending brought the work down a little, but it's a story that makes you think about it long after you've turned the last page.

Cat is on the run, trying desperately to hide her sought-after magical powers. But a hunky warrior named Griffin discovers one of her powers, kidnaps her, and tries to force her to work for his queen. They have a tempestuous relationship that inevitably ends with them in love. The plot is fast-paced. The world building and magic system aren't stale; they're actually my favorite part of this. And I could totally understand why Cat and Griffin are attracted to each other. This is certainly a 4+. I wish Goodreads would let us use fractions. For me at least there is a broad divide between 4 and 5. 2s are novels I struggled to complete. 3s usually are technically sound but lack some key ingredient to make them great. 4s are great but lack that special something that makes them masterful. If I'd had to rate this thirty pages in, I'd have given it a 2. God, I hated the protagonist and the present tense narration (with flashbacks no less, also in present tense!). I loathed the strawman that was her "relationship" with some bland boy who's every mention just made me scratch my head and ask: "Why are they together?" And her perky friend, who my mind immediately cast as Amanda Seyfried (more on that towards the end)...Ug. There is an almost lack of realism to the story in that, with the one notable exception of the aforementioned "boyfriend", everyone quickly rallies around Hermione. This made for a niggling, uncomfortable reminder that the secondary characters lacked much depth. Not because depth would necessitate a lack of empathy or support for the main character, but because the ready-made, indelible support never seemed to extract any expense. It was literally what they were made for. And then it all worked. I can't quite put my finger on the author's voodoo, but she drew me in and I cared deeply about everything that happened. I liked Hermione (the narrator), I felt for her and her parents; I liked her friends--even Lilly! (OOPS!) --and most of all I wanted her to get her life back on track after the truly terrifying thing that was done to her. Just a final word about the Veronica Mars/Amanda S connection: As I said I immediately cast A.S. as the best friend, and it didn't occur to me until the author's note at the end, when she mentioned Veronica Mars, that I realized what an inspiration for this story one of that show's greater arcs had been. (That's vague because Spoilers. Tho VM fans who read the book will certainly see it. And, if you haven't watched Veronica Mars, what are you waiting for? Also, read this book. Well worth it.)

Then I frantically searched for a note somewhere in the book saying that there would be another one-thankfully, it's the first of a quartet. I'll agree with some of the other reviews that some of the background world building was lacking slightly. However, I didn't feel that the lack of background info really detracted from my appreciation of the story at all (which was mostly plot and character driven, my favorites!). And I bet that we'll learn a little bit more about the world in the next books. I did wonder a little bit about how no one could tell that she wasn't really from New Beijing, since she wouldn't really look Chinese, but I just assumed that this happens so far into the future that the predicted melting pot phenomenon had occurred so that there are no longer distinct races of people (well, other than Lunar and Earthen). As to the distinction between Lunars and Earthens, I thought it was described fairly well. No, the reasons why Lunars moved to the moon were only mentioned once in passing, but I'm not reading an alt history textbook here, I'm reading a re-telling of a fairy tale. And it's a re-telling with a kickass female character who would rather save millions of lives than pursue her own crush--and her crush is willing to do the same thing! It's a rare book with such strong, consciously-motivated characters with so much depth. And what a cool idea to have a cyborg mechanic Cinderella!

King can say he wanted it out of print because of all the school shootings in the last couple decades but I have to wonder if quality wasn't also a contributing factor. Charlie Decker is a bit of a outcast and has a whole dresser drawer full of issues. His classmates, seemingly normal, aren't without problems themselves. John Hughes at gunpoint is a good way to describe most of what goes on in the book. If snipers were watching the windows of the library in the Breakfast Club, Rage is probably what the result would be like. I don't have a lot to say about this one. The ending was unexpected. I'll give Bachman/King that. Other than that, I'm glad it was short. 2 stars. I hope this doesn't lead to Stephen King rejecting my friend request.

Someone has stolen the Darwin Centre's Architeuthis dux, the giant squid or kraken, and now an apocalypse is imminent. Only no one knows who stole the squid or which apocalypse it might be, though the Londonmancers have divined it involves fire. And with that China Mieville takes us on a roller-coaster ride through London as we follow various characters and their attempts to figure out what's going on. I had fun reading this book. Mieville has fun with the language and with conspiracy theories, and you have to pay attention or you'll become hopelessly lost. And even if you do pay attention, you might have to come up for air occasionally and take your bearings. The style and climax of the book are reminiscent of Umberto Eco's Foucault's Pendulum - self-engendering conspiracies and self-fulfilling prophecies - with a Cthulhu-like twist. And as a bonus there's a Trek-obsessed teleporter and a working phaser. The final observation I'll make is that Mieville has also created one of the most disturbing psychotic killer in the character of Goss and Subby (and you'll understand why I use the singular if you read the book). Very highly recommended to Mieville fans and those urban fantasists.

Actual rating 2.9. A very average collection of very average love stories. Then again, if you're reading a book of summer-themed love stories, it's exactly what you'd expect. There are the bittersweet tales of heartbreak and separation contrasting with hopeful tales of reunion, characters of all sexualities and colours making it a fully representative anthology. I gave a few of the stories 5 stars ('The End of Love' by Nina LaCour, Stephanie Perkins sequel to her short story in 'My True Love Gave To Me', and - surprisingly - 'Inertia', the short story by Veronica Roth) but the rest of them only merited 2/3 stars at best. My least favourite stories (and the two stories that I only awarded 1 star) were 'Love is the Last Resort' by Jon Skovron (which features extremely stilted language that makes the characters the least authentic teenagers I've ever experienced) and 'Sick Pleasure' by Francesca Lia Block (whose characters are only given initials instead of names, making it one of the most unemotional and disconnected short stories I've ever had the displeasure to read). If you enjoyed 'My True Love Gave To Me', you'll probably like this collection, but I kind of wish Stephanie Perkins had left her foray into anthology editing as a one hit wonder.

This is the second book in a row that I've read that I've been someone torn on. You see, like What Happens Next, the good elements of this book were phenomenal. I'll go into more details later, but Sloane's mental state and the raw character interactions were some of the best I've ever read. This almost made it to my list of all-time favorites. But there were also elements that bothered me, enough that I couldn't put it on the list. Granted, the bad elements here were fewer and further between than the ones in What Happens Next. But they were still present, and the book would've been better without them. But right off the bat, the book is excellent. The book is told from Sloane's point of view, and ever since her sister ran away and left her with her abusive father, she's been suicidal. Summers's portrayal of Sloane's mental state is very accurate and poignant. In everything Sloane does, everything she thinks about, Lily and her father and her suicide are in the back of her mind. Her attitudes to it are appropriately bitter, but unlike some books about suicide I could name, Sloane is still very sympathetic. All of this comes through most noticeably in the prose. It's written in present tense, giving us the impression that we're seeing Sloane's thoughts and actions as she has them. On a very consistent basis, her thoughts are completely believable and interesting. It helps that the prose goes into stream-of-consciousness in some of the more emotional moments. It was here that I was most strongly affected, most constantly aware of how well-rendered Sloane is, where I was the most moved. Because of all this, reading This is Not a Test is a truly unique and immersive experience. Nowhere else have I ever seen anything like this, but I'd love to. Which is why I'm going to be reading another Summers book at some point. Another thing the prose did that I loved so much, that made the reading experience so unique, is that it purposely kept little things from us, so that we were constantly surprised. This rarely kept me at an arm's length from the story, because the things that Summers kept from us were never necessary to the story, and we were given enough information to enjoy the individual scenes. Instead, this technique left me guessing, and enjoying the book further. I suspect that this technique won't appeal to everyone, but it certainly did to me. There were a few prose problems - Summers occasionally used sentence fragments or run-ons, making the prose choppy at some points and runny in others - but the other prose elements far more than made up for it. Most of the other characters were as well-rendered and interesting as Sloane. The one exception was Harrison; I kept waiting for Summers to add more depth to his character, to develop him beyond a crybaby stereotype, and it just never happened. But everyone else is great. In particular, I really loved Trace's character arc; his parents were killed on the journey he and the others took to the school, and he blames Cary for their loss. Trace isn't always entirely sympathetic, but his mental state is always fascinating. Likewise, Cary, Rhys, and Grace are also interesting in their reactions to the apocalypse and their desire for, above all else, survival. It reminded me of The Way We Fall, only more intense; Crewe redeemed her characters and their mental states, but Summers is merciless to them. (Not that this makes The Way We Fall any less effective - the books are both honest portrayals of two completely different situations.) Summers's eye for characters and their psychology is almost flawless. Because of all this, the plot isn't very action packed, and it doesn't have a traditional dramatic structure. The dramatic structure is built entirely around the characters' emotions. I'm sure some readers who are less interested in psychology and emotions will find the plot boring; after all, they don't have to work too hard to survive, and the events that happen often occur simply to give the characters an interesting situation. It's most notable in the enemy - this is technically a zombie novel, but we don't actually see that many zombies, until the very end. Yet there's still an overarching sense of tension. The characters are still aware of the constant threat around them; after all, that's what they're reacting to. Summers created a tense situation and characters to respond to it; I need nothing more from my books. But remember when I said that there were a few problems that prevented me from considering this one of my favorites? Because there were a couple, even apart from the minor ones that I mentioned above. I said before that the story rarely kept me at an arm's length, but occasionally it did. The biggest way was probably in the worldbuilding; we never get a clear picture of the exact effects the virus that created the zombies, and I never quite understood their exact capabilities. We see so little of the world around Sloane and her friends, it's hard to say whether it made sense or not. However, that problem is insignificant compared to the biggest problem: there's no theme. There's lots of potential for a theme (the heroine is suicidal, for the love of god), but Summers never really says anything about her situation, other than "This is what it's like to be suicidal." The same goes for the rest of the character interactions: Cary's sex with Lily and involvement with drugs, Tracy's slow decline... all of it should lead up to some grand message, but it never does. I wouldn't want the message to be anvilicious, John Green style, but I want something, and I never got it. That causes a lack of focus in the character interactions; without something for Summers to say, there's nothing her to focus on. And if that's the case, what's the point? Why read about characters in such a depressing situation if it's not going to teach me something about life? Still, that doesn't change the fact that the book is beautifully written, with wonderful character interactions. Reviewers more familiar with the zombie-apocalypse genre than I have said that this book didn't add much new to the genre for them, and that they'd recommend it for people who aren't familiar with the genre. Well, this is my first zombie book, and I loved it. So if you're like me in that regard, this is definitely the book for you. You'll love it, I promise.

I waited two months to get my hands on this book. Constantly when I tried to check it out from the library, someone else had already checked it out before me. It just built up my expectations for this book, and the hope that it was going to be something spectacular and awesome. I hoped that the characters would be phenomenal and well-developed, the plot surprising and creative, the writing interesting and fresh. Turns out that the only thing that this book had familiar with any of these words, was a creative plot. But then again, the 39 Clues series follows a similar pattern. Perhaps this is where my great sadness and semi-hate for this book originates. 39 Clues. Last year, a bunch of my classmates in school were freaking out about the 39 Clues series. It was like a phenomenon that spread from one student to the next, all of them checking out all of the 39 Clues books just to try and read them. It was pretty hard to check out those books from the library at that time, let me tell you. Even then, I read three of the books, and didn't have the eagerness to finish. I'll be trying again sometime, though. When that is...well, you can see how low The Maze of Bones is on my to-read list right now. But they were enjoyable. The 39 Clues series was different, creative, and I enjoyed the global aspect of it. It was good to know the rivals, and although they were portrayed a lot like villains, I saw that there were different sides to them. The main characters were developed well. There was humor! The humor succeeded in making me laugh! The characters' pasts were intriguing! And this is all stemming from a series whose books are only a hundred-ish pages long. None of this, unfortunately, holds true in The Forbidden Stone. Perhaps I shouldn't have waited two months and just dumped it, had I known what a boring journey it would be. This took me an ENTIRE WEEK to read. Granted, that's because I had so few opportunities to actually, you know, read it, but that's mostly because it annoyed me so much. Tony Abbott tried to make the story center on four main characters--five if you count Wade's dad. Unfortunately, this fails, because NONE of the characters get ANY character development WHATSOEVER. Except for the villain, Galina Krause. And even she got, like, a smidget? There's something that's going to happen to her in six months. Do we know what? No, of course not. All we know is her past, and that she...well, she's a standard world domination villain. And she could have been two-dimensional! The main characters, Wade, Darrell, Lily, and Becca, are infuriating. We hardly know much about them at all. Abbott never reveals to us the past of these characters, and if he does, it's not much. He's hiding something, clearly. But he should have given it away by now! After all, the first book in a series is always meant to develop characters and build the world, right? It does build the world. But I found a whole 2% of character development in this book. And you know what 1.5% of that character development comes from? Krause. The other 0.5%? Becca, at the very end. That's IT. The four main characters, along with Wade's dad Roald, are very bland. Wade is...well, he's Wade. I would call him a __-year-old boy who's fascinated with stars here, but we don't even know his AGE! That's when you know it's bad. And we can't tell what his age is, either. As far as we know, he's eighteen and hasn't gone to college yet, or is seven, and has skipped a few grades. Has the answer been hinted at all in the story? No. Because screw those tiny details that MAKE UP A CHARACTER'S ENTIRE BACKGROUND! We don't need that. All we need is CHARACTERS! Perhaps we should look at this tad bit of advice: Strong characters can carry a weak plot, but weak characters can't carry a strong plot. --Anonymous Abbott, apparently, overlooked this very important advice when writing The Forbidden Stone. Or, you know, he twisted it the other way around. Darrell is completely comic relief, and no matter how much Abbott tries to conceal it, it's obvious. Which brings up another issue of this book I'll get to in a moment. But back to Darrell. He freaks out about spies. And spouts "jokes". And he's Wade's cousin! Yeah, that's all there is to poor Darrell here. And Lily is just frankly annoying, both as a character and as what she does. Let's look at her computer and her tablet for a moment, shall we? Unless this takes place in the distant future--which it probably doesn't, given from the technology we've seen, but heck, does it tell us? No!--Lily SHOULD NOT be able to use internet or anything to do with internet in foreign countries without Wifi. And her phone wouldn't be able to do this, either! Because guess what? Your phone ain't got no data in foreign countries. Don't believe me? Drive to Canada with your iPhone 6 and see for yourself. Because you can't even CALL in foreign countries without Wi-Fi! But she does. She uses Google Maps. In Germany. And we can PRETEND that's on her phone. But we can't PRETEND that she is Googling stuff up in a taxi/bus/train/whatever! ON HER COMPUTER, it blatantly states! And, as I'm pretty sure is common knowledge, computers don't got no wireless. Who knows? She might have hacked a wifi network in Germany or something. Possibly the only character of the bunch that I found tolerable was Becca. She's a reader! You've got to love her! But she's, what, twelve, and has learned...five foreign languages? Is that right? I know people who are younger learn languages better, but my father came from China to America. He spoke Chinese first. He has been in America for nearly 30 years now. And his English STILL isn't perfect! 30 years later! If Becca can learn five foreign languages in twelve or so years, that's just plain unrealistic. Unless she's Einstein. Which she isn't, clearly. That's just the characters. But Abbott tries so hard to be humorous, it's actually kind of laughable. The humor is so stupid and dumb in this book. It doesn't make you laugh. It makes you groan! And that is NOT a reaction you want when you're trying to make a joke. I also found zero plot twists in this entire thing. Zero. That's right, zero. Perhaps there would have been a plot twist if it had been revealed what would be happening to Galina in six months? Maybe we could actually USE a double agent? No? Okay... But let's be real here. We NEED a part where we are actually surprised. Is there such a part in this book? No. Never. I think Abbott just tries to mimic Riordan and other author legends of middle grade adventure so much that he starts to forget about other things. All that is important in this book is the chase and relics, I guess. And perhaps that's all we need in the end. Adventure, chases, and relics. ...I will credit this book for having a slightly creative plot. But the 39 Clues has such a similar plot and surpasses this book in all ways possible that you should really take that over this any day. Other than that, I give up. This is possibly my longest review to date. Sorry for all the words and characters you had to read. I just had to vent about this thing, and I couldn't hold it in. And there are STILL things I want to say about this 400-page long disappointment!

Book two in Julie Ann Walker's Black Knights Inc series and I'm enjoying. This is a black ops suspense type series, but it is on the lighter side with lots of humor and over the top situations. This is Frank and Becky's story, who we meet in book one. Frank is the top dog at Black Knight Inc, a group of ex-military men who go on super secret assignments. Years ago, Becky's brother suggested to Frank they use Becky's custom motorcycle shop as a front for this secret op group. While Becky obviously knows these men are involved in secret government affairs, she has never been asked to be an operator for the group, nor is she allowed to sit in on their meetings. This frustrates Becky to no end, as she thinks she is just as tough as everyone else involved in this operation. Frank is 12 or 13 years older than Becky and has had a crush on her since the first day he saw her. But being that much older than her and kind of being her boss of sorts, he has stayed away from her. But the sexual tension between them is off the charts. Becky feels the same way about him, and yet his huge, serious demeanor and presence has scared her enough to keep her distance over the years. When this book starts, Becky is on vacation with her friend Eve in the Indian Ocean when their fancy boat is over take by Somalian pirates. Kidnapped and held for ransom, all they can do it wait and hope the Black Knight inc boys can find them and rescue them (which they do of course!). Frank and Becky's brother Billy along with the hottie Angel, come to their rescue. During this event, Frank becomes badly injured, and everyone arrives back in Chicago, all more beat up then when they started. From here, it is just a story of the two of them dancing around each other until one of them finally makes a move. I liked this one a little more than book one. I think the sexual tension is better and the suspense part is more fun to read about. All the characters are very likable and the author does a nice job with bringing in supporting characters to make the world feel very full. They joke around a lot, and I like that all the men are so intense and bad ass. What can I say? I'm a black ops ho. I did have a few disappointments. First, while there is great sexual tension, there is not a great pay off with the sex. There is really only one scene. Fail. I needed more. And I needed the sex to be a little intense and dirtier. I guess you can say the sex scene fit the tone of the book, a little silly. But I don't want that kind of sex. I want hard core sex that only super secret black op military men know how to have damn it! So I really hope books in the future bring that part out more. Second, and I mentioned this is the review of the first book - there is a lot of over the top, slang words used, and in particular slang words for curse words in this book. Frank says 'Keerist' instead of Christ. Becky says 'dill-hole,' and Eve. Oh god Eve. On multiple occasion she says 'cheese and rice' instead of Jesus Christ. Just fucking curse people!! (see what I did there?). Seriously, y'all are bad asses, cuss like one. Please. Otherwise this is a fun book, and I very much look forward to book three. Rating: B

I don't know how to feel about that I guess shit always has to go down on that day haha (even if it's like 5 centuries later) This only took me a year and a half to read it completely but totally loved it. I LOVED Illuminae, so I was weary to judge this because I didn't want to hate it, you know? Nik definitely grew on me (but if it wasn't for Ella, I wouldn't have). I took to Ezra and Kady wayyy faster than Hanna and Nik. But the plot twists and side plots BLEW my mind. Seriously. I felt, like, shocked and betrayed. God damn you, character I cannot name. Also. So many of the main characters did the "died then is revealed to be alive" that it's kinda funny at this point. "I'm not typing another word until I change my name back." "Oh no. That is terrible." "Sounds like a plan with no flaws to me." I really, really loved Marie Lu's drawings. I think they added a sense of personality and the character's thoughts that were absent in Illuminae. You would feel kind of disconnected to the characters sometimes, and this finds a way around that. It's bloody brilliant. The only solid thing left in all her worlds. I don't know if the authors understand that people could, like, not be sarcastic people. I mean. I love sarcastic characters but if their voices sound the same, there's no point in having separate characters you know? It's like when you read a book with multiple point of views and they all sound the same. But still. And she's not breathing a word of it. Not complaining, not crying herself to fucking sleep. She's fighting. Kicking and screaming. You got her picked for the spoiled little rich girl, I get that. But in case you haven't noticed, she's lost just as much as you. And she's punching back just as hard." Did I mention that I freaking love Hanna? What an iconic princess. Also, I loooove the Illuminae Group. Loved the diversity on the ship, even with the BeiTech group and everything, but wish we got some like non-binary or at least one LGBT character? I mean...it's been FIVE centuries...surely there's at least one that we come across on these hundreds of people in space. Right? P.S. YAY EZRA AND KADY ARE BACK THATS MY BABIES P.S.S. Ella deserves that one star. This was so a 4 star. But Ella. My god. What a girl.

It's been more than twenty years since I read this book the first time in my late teens. I remember loving it, thinking it was so edgy. I was in a Dostoevsky phase then and maybe I just liked grappling with heavy lit. I was probably insufferable. Reading it again as a 40-year-old, I find it much harder to relate to and enjoy. Part of me wants to give The Trial five stars for being such an important piece of literature, but did I enjoy it? Did I really love reading this? Or am I giving stars because it's Kafka and intellectual and canon? After much soul-searching, I think the truth is I want to award stars because it's Kafka, not because of my own personal experience of the book. It was hard to follow, the dialogue is stilted, most of the story is in heavy allegory and makes no sense unless you're willing to invest a huge amount of time placing it in context and picking it apart. If I picked up this text today thinking it was written by an unknown contemporary author, I doubt I would even finish it and it would get two stars at most. This doesn't mean I don't think it deserves its place in the literature world - there's a definite genius to Kafka. I think it's become so famous that everyone should read it once. I would recommend it to anyone. But I did not find my re-reading to be enjoyable.

Glad this book picked up a bit more. Cinder suffers from a MAJOR, MAJOR case of a great premise, but poor writing. ("She eyed her with a critical eye." EYED her with an EYE, you say! My heavens! How does one manage such a thing?) There are more plot holes and logic problems than you can shake a stick at. (Doop dee doop! I am a great mechanic! Now watch as I fix a car and neglect to fix the headlights!) Cinder has the most inconsistent skill and ability set I have seen in a long time. (Why go on about how her brain can connect to access all of this information so quickly and search it so well if she literally can't take five minutes to educate herself more on Lunar customs before running headlong into a plan heavily involving them? Why just take the doctor's word at face-value and do almost nothing to form a solid plan?) The relationship is...irritatingly written in such a manner as to tell us it is complex when there is not a lot there to support it and frustrating to read. (Telling, not showing.) The book itself is agonizingly predictable, flashing neon signs in place of good foreshadowing. Alllll of this being said...it was a pretty cool take on Cinderella, and I was thrilled to see that she had larger concerns in her life than just a cute boy. Cinder was pretty good about sticking to her own guns and her own needs first before dropping her slipper-- er...foot-- for the first boy who called her pretty. Good on you for having priorities, kiddo! It is really kind of a shame that the book was not in more skilled hands. I absolutely will try the next, though, as this one gets good points for creativity and I would like to see more world-building before I write off the others.

3 Very Generous Stars for story. 2 Stars for narration. Ugh. This is gonna be hard to review. Let's make a list. Things I liked: The trailer. It's why I love the houses in Harry Potter and the factions of Divergent, etc. As a self-declared narcissist, I like the conflict of the realms Firstlife presents. The male narrator Zachary Webber. This character was written FLAWLESSLY for me. I agreed with all of his choices. I think as a character, he's different from most guys in YA. There's a reason for this. He's not a love interest. He's a friend. A GREAT friend. I love him. The last hour or so of the story. The major conflict comes to a head and I really like how it played out. It made me want to read the next book when at least 70% of it made me go, DEAR LORD MAKE IT END. So now I'm torn. Ugh. The use of prophecy. I'm writing a story with a prophetic element, and I learned a lot from how she wove in very in-your-face foreshadowing that still surprised me and had me going oooooooh, that's what that meant. What I didn't like: Emma Freaking Galvin. She on my list of terrible narrators. When I listened to her voice the Divergent series, I had thankfully already read the books, so I knew the story and tolerated her butchering of it. This time, she may have actually RUINED this book for me. Her inflection is terrible. She reads every line at the same over-eager pitch and cadence and ends every sentence like she's surprised. It's awful. And I hate to tell people DO NOT LISTEN TO THIS BOOK because Zachary Webber was so freaking perfect. But I have to. Really, if you want to read this book, do it with your eyes. Killian. This might be kind of spoilery. So I'm hiding it. But ultimately, I didn't think this character was fleshed out effectively. Also Killian and Ten. Also Killian's perfect perfect perfect sexy bad boy with a angsty sad past and heart of gold or what-freaking-ever. I HATE this character. This isn't even about teams. This is about this bro being a douche bag and me not buying anything the author tried to make me believe about him. There wasn't enough SHOWING of this good guy he's supposed to be. Just a lot of Ten TELLING me how she felt about him and I guess I was just supposed to swallow that. But I didn't think they had any chemistry AT ALL. I hated their romance; it seemed entirely without substance or authenticity. I hate him, okay. I did appreciate that this wasn't really an instalove story. At the end when the 3 MCs go through the final battle together at the end, I liked how that played out. But I just don't think he's a lovable character. If he'd died, not a single crap would be given by me... The "my parents are evil and torture me" thing is getting old for me. Parents play a role in YA fiction by NOT BEING THERE. This is necessary. But I'm a mother now. And it's just a lot to buy into every time someone's parents are so evil they'd sell/hurt/kill their kid for stupid reasons like fortune and fame... The world building...Sigh. I just didn't get the world. there's a lot of questions--the main one being why Ten is a Supah Speshal Speshal Gurl. I may have missed exactly what that was about. Something about light and darkness. But it was not described and expressed in a way that I as a reader understood and cared about. The writing. I take a lot of issues with the writing. This is my second Gena Showalter book, and I felt this way about it too. I like her ideas. I can even see the overall plot structure and how it's working. But the writing just doesn't do it for me. Maybe it's the first person. Maybe it's just stylistically not for me. Not one or the other: --I'm curious about the metaphor/spiritual undertones here. A lot of the language is stuff I know from the Bible. As a Christian, it's an interesting treatment of evangelism and how your eternal destiny shapes your current life and the concept of spiritual warfare. I expected an anti-biblical message. But it really wasn't. More of a "what if" exercise. All in all, this book broke my streak of epically awesome books!

4.5 Stars (LOL Asshole Jake knocked off half a star) Ah yes, Jake, the love interest/ex. A character you love to hate, but can't get enough of. You want Jake on every single F**** page, but that's not possible. Jake, who you want to reach through the pages to strangle. I'm floored. A tidal wave. A roller coaster as relationships struggled for meaning through a murder mystery. It was a nice balance. Another reason I think this series drew me in was it actually was a mystery novel with romantic (detailed) interludes peppered through the story instead of highlighting a sexfest that most of the male/male novels I've read so far are. I've been trying to find books like Lanyon's for a long time now. While books 1-3 also really toyed with the reader's emotions, this one really felt like the finale of a fireworks show. To me, at least. The ending of this was just... wow.. wow..., and I will say I was fooled until the last! Parts of this book were slow and dry, but the main character Adrien kept the reader engaged and interested. (So did his interactions and struggles with keeping his ex-Jake at a distance.) As an extremely picky fantasy reader, the only other series I can recall ever burning through was Paksenarrion and October Daye. This is my first journey into the mystery genre, and I'm pretty certain Lanyon has me ensnared as a permanent reader. The chemistry between all the characters is vivid and believable. Adrien's new (step)family is just so adorable! And with the very minor character Angus hopefully coming back, I am hoping there might be sparks with Natalie. I will be diving into book 5 tonight, the last book in this series, then it's probably onto Lanyon's Sherlock and Holmes ones... I'm really sorry to see the Adrien English series end. Oh, wouldn't it be grand to see a book or two from Jake's POV?

Ilsa J. Bick is one of the authors that is so raved about that I knew that I am going to have to begin reading a book of hers sooner or later. When I spotted this in the bookstore a few weeks after it was released, I knew that I had to read it. Sadly, I DNFed it at 107 pages and I don't regret it at all. "Something has bled into this world, all right. Something is storming after them. Something is running them down. Not an aurora. Not clouds. What is coming for them is the fog." So for once, I'm not the black sheep in this situation. Most of the times, I actually am and it frustrates me because I can basically agree with my own opinion and that's about it. For this book, I've read so many negative and DNF reviews before reading, and I kind of expected it even though I still wanted to give it a try. So I did--and it was okay for like two chapters, and then I just let go of happiness. You see, the thing is I feel confused and mentally abused. I didn't even really understand the plot and the formation of POVs or anything of that sort. All I did catch to understand was that there's a Mirror and something happened that got Lizzie and Emma's dad nuts and no one believes him so the family moves to a remote place far away from London. That's just about it. When the author introduced a new character, the event was never memorable and I didn't seem to even know who was who or who was telling the story at the time since it was confusing. And whenever I'm reading a POV in a book, I always feel like I need a sense of direction of who's reading. This was a total The 5th Wave situation again. Why waste my time being confused by reading an almost 600-paged book? That's horror of readers. Lately I've been finding that I've been DNF-ing a lot of books, and that kind of frightens me for the future of YA. "People are always dying for him to hurry up and write the next book already. They love that feeling of being lost somewhere and somewhen else. Sometimes Lizzie doesn't want to pull herself out of a book-world at all, just like kids who pretend to be superheroes and run around in costumes." Probably the only thing that was positive in this book was the actual writing. No, I don't mean the plot or characters, but the actual words. We can all tell that Bick is very talented at it, but doesn't do a really good job at actually capturing the reader's attention greatly. You see, if the book wasn't as confusing or improbable, then maybe I would've enjoyed the plot and actual story. But since that was out of the story, why just keep on going to read some random mumbo-jumbo that doesn't mean anything to you? Aren't words supposed to mean something and possibly inspire you? So, the plot was out of the question. Don't even ask about my experience, because I'm as frustrated as a scared cat. I probably had to like Lizzie better than Emma, but I think Emma was telling the story more often? I'm actually not even sure of what was happening more than half of the time, haha. If you're like me and get easily confused with POVs then I'd suggest to run away as fast as you can. This book wasn't even worth a dollar. I wouldn't even take it if someone gave it to me for free, honestly. As most books that I DNF, this had a total potential to become something great. In ways, this definitely reminded me of Afterworlds, by Scott Westerfield with the whole book aspect. Don't you just love it when authors write about characters who actually write books themselves? Of course I do, but this was a blur. I can't seem to barely get anything out of it. Not recommended--stay away and trust the reviews. I have to admit, adult historical fiction genre is one I rarely read. I think I'm afraid that it'll involve melodrama, inaccuracy too flamingly bold to ignore and far more sex than is appropriate to the story (really, where do I get these ideas?). Lily of the Nile proved to be absolutely none of these things and left me craving the sequel. This was definitely a book that I didn't want to set down--the one upside of the 2 feet of snow in 12 hours blizzard was that I had every excuse to stay on the couch all day and immerse myself in Dray's world. With that being said, I confess that I set the novel down once, about 50 pages in, just to look in my old Roman history textbook and see what I could find about Cleopatra and her daughter, Cleopatra Selene, who the novel focuses on. Turns out I could hardly find a thing about Cleopatra Selene, so I think it's safe to say that Dray writes about a period that isn't often touched on. Dray's novel is fantastically paced. Some might wish that she was more descriptive, but I think she did a nice job of briefly touching on events that are best summarized as opposed to described play by play. The descriptions of the Roman feasts definitely made me hungry. To top it off, Dray creates complex characters that were interesting to read about and kept me guessing. My only real complaint about this book is that I questioned how realistic a couple of plot points were, but after turning the final page I still really wanted to get my hands on a copy of the sequel. Lily of the Nile surprised me in the best way possible. It may not be the most thought-provoking book I've read, but it approaches history from a new angle and kept me turning the pages.

This was an interesting book. It's hard to describe how I feel about it, which is one reason why this book floats between 3-4 stars for me (marked as 4/5 on Goodreads because I rounded up :p). I like big tomes I can really dig into, and this story did it for me. The story flowed pretty well throughout, and I think that's what really kept me going. King's Folly was super long; over 500 pages in about a 6x9 format, and the font size is probably 10 pt. at least. Just think Wheel of Time: the Great Hunt long, and you'll get an idea of how long this is. I think this is supposed to be a YA novel, as I think Bethany House Publishers intends to publish YA (correct me if I'm wrong), but due to the length and more mature themes, this definitely came off as adult level to me. For some background, this is a story about a land that's falling apart due to the greediness and general immorality of its people. The story focuses on royal families, most of which are involved in sleeping around with concubines and mistresses. Normally a book with this sort of content, even though it's not explicit, would have made me set it down pretty early on. However, I have a habit of looking at the end of the story/book soon after I start reading it, where I found the Author's Note. Basically, she explains this is a story about a people slowly turning to the true God of this fantasy world, so that helped me see all the immorality and corruption, and the eventual turning to truth and godliness, in the right light. There were a lot of characters, at least named characters, and I lost track of some at times when they reappeared after hundreds of pages of first meeting them. I'm glad the author took pains to list the major characters before the beginning of the story; I referenced it quite a bit, along with the map. I liked the character development in this book. The main protagonist, Wilek, strains against living the way his father, a morally corrupt king, wants him to. Instead of having many concubines and such, he has one, and boy is she more questionable than she first sounds. In the beginning, Wilek considers her a friend, but she is very manipulative, so I never really saw her the way Wilek did, but that may have been intentional on the author's part; she didn't present any of the immorality as acceptable, and other characters blatantly condemned immoral behavior. After his concubine Lebetta dies , Wilek really starts to develop positively as a man and slowly starts to turn to one of the gods, who is the only real god in the pantheon while the rest are evil spirits whose name is Arman. He is captured by a magic user, or mantic, named Charlon, who is supposed to be impregnated by him to fulfill some prophecy for her tribe and the spirit she serves; however, she's terrified of men from past traumas, and has a hard time persuading Wilek, or herself, to sleep with her. She was my least favorite POV, as she was so focused on doing this one thing that it disgusted me; good thing she's not one of the good guys, so it's okay to dislike her. My favorite character was Trevn. He's also one of the princes, and Wilek's half-brother, as the king has several wives. Right from the beginning he sees through the corruption and immorality in his father's court, and is highly reluctant to practice having concubines and a harem and whatever. He's taught by a goodly priest who has just barely preserved the true teachings of Arman, and though Trevn didn't realize that at first, comes to look to Arman and risks his life to preserve what's called the Book of Arman. I also liked his interactions with this love interest and one of the main characters, Mielle, who I also enjoyed reading about and had good development. There were several other characters, some of which didn't seem to be important, at least not to this story. I'm assuming they'll play a larger part in the second collection of the Kinsman Chronicles, King's Blood. The story itself flowed pretty smooth, but I thought the last several chapters were pretty rushed. The action and plot were pushed really fast and condensed, so much so that some of the descriptions confused me and I had to reread them. A lot of the story focused on the sexualization of characters, and while I feel the author portrayed it in the right light, it got pretty repetitive after awhile, and I became eager for more plot points and devices. It wasn't until probably the last half to the last fourth of the book that we got some really interesting action and a better look at the spirits of the world and their relation to their magic users. I liked how much the setting played into the story. The whole land is riddled with tunnels from a huge plant called evenroot, which, when ingested, helps the mantics interact with the spirits and use "magic," which is really the spirits interacting with things invisibly. Because of the excessive mining of this plant, among other things, the land is literally falling apart. It presents a desperate background for the characters to develop in, and really shows a hopelessness from greed and power struggles. There's a lot more going on in this story, including a prophecy, but I won't go into all of that here. Once you understand the moral of this book, and why the author wrote what she did, it's an interesting read. I look forward to seeing where this series goes next year. I'm not comfortable giving this book a rating, so I won't. I haven't read a YA book since I was of its target demographic, mumble years ago. I have to take it at face value, without any context to let me know if it's a decent thing of its kind or not. I was first drawn to it because of this guest post on Malinda Lo's blog, written by Rose Yndigoyen, that talks about Emily, one of the main characters, who is LGBT. And the series looked like trashy fun during a time where that's been the only type of entertainment I can muddle through. Reading this was almost like reading fantasy or SF, giving me a peep into an alien world. Never a fashionable person, and certainly not up on the latest trends, all the details of designer clothes and bags etc. flew right over my head. "Remember when Juicy sweats were popular?" Um, no... Maybe it's a good thing, since this story didn't feel dated to me. Its being from 2006, I'm sure there are plenty of references that would make a teen today look nostalgically back on the old days. As an adult reading a YA novel, there are things that come across as peculiar. Teens smoke cigarettes and weed, throw f-bombs, drink and drive, get naked with men. But the author goes out of her way to not have them actually have sex. They'll use their decision-making power to do utterly stupid things, but won't cross that line. The four main girls aren't characters per se, more like collections of tricky situations and hair colors. Once or twice, I was picturing the wrong girl in a scene and had to backtrack to remember which one was the shoplifter , for example. The boys (and man, in one case) fare even worse: an indistinguishable mass of lanky bodies, abs, butts and names ending with "n" (Sean, Ben, Wren). The writing style is simple, very suitable for popcorn reading. But just like popcorn, too much of it and you realize you're choking down something that has no flavor and wonder why you're bothering. There's an awful lot of squeaking in the latter chapters of the novel (the only stylistic bobble that really stuck out to me.) The suspense plot is interesting, though. Who is "A," now that we know Alison is dead?

Vlad and Leila meet under difficult circumstances and there is an instant draw to each other. Some things made me chuckle and some made me gasp but the connection between the two of them was the best part of the story. The two of them work well together...most of the time, and I can't wait to read more of their adventures.

The fourth book continues in very much the same vein, and is consistent with the rest of the series, although the lumbermill setting was just... less enjoyable to me. Also, I know that the series is surreal at times, but I like to imagine that that is mostly just Lemony Snicket's hyperbolic narration. But a man whose entire head is covered by smoke at all times and nobody ever saw his real face, was slightly more surreal. There was also less Olaf this time around, which in some ways lost a little edge, but then at the same time it meant there was more intrigue and mystery to be unravelled. {Read 28/09/2015}
