The difficult thing about Empress of the Seven Hills is that I can't decide whether or not I like it more than Mistress of Rome. I definitely like it just as much; I may like it more, which I can't say about the prequel to Mistress, the immensely enjoyable but slightly frustrating Daughters of Rome. Empress is exactly the kind of book that I've always wanted. It has everything I like: flawed main characters; Women Who Do Not Please; multi-dimensional villains; and long, drawn-out drama. Long live the love/hate relationship of Vix and Sabina. (I can't say the same of his marriage, which while realistic and appealing, made me grind my teeth. And that has nothing to do with my preference of the former pairing.) Much of our story takes place from the perspective of Vix, son of Arius and Thea from Mistress. He is our hero, moreso even than his love interest and counterpart Sabina. Of course Vix is likable. We as readers are already sentimental about him due to his many adventures as a child in the previous book. But Vix is also deeply, deeply flawed. And I've got to say that I feel that a lot of reviewers seem to miss that when critiquing Sabina's every move and decision? Sabina's lack of effort and sacrifice in their relationship is constantly criticized; in fact, the pair are two of a kind. Just as Sabina chooses duty to Rome over Vix, so Vix consistently chooses duty to Rome over his lovers and loved ones and later his wife and children. No matter how happy Vix becomes with Mirah (and really, they aren't that happy because she deserves better treatment and he's too practical for someone so tied to her Jewish heritage and the symbolism in Masada) he will ultimately leave her for orders from Rome--and the sickly loving arms of Sabina, who is Rome. Vix constantly made decisions that kind of disgusted me. He's really quite the asshole, which sort of surprises me considering the kind of mother he has. But at the same time, he made decisions that I admired and I loved him for being him. He loves blindly and is distracted by the next shiny sparkly thing that catches his eye. His only consistent loves are Trajan (and Trajan is Rome) and Sabina, who he also hates (and don't forget, Sabina, too, is Rome). Sabina is an even more complex character. And she's a complex female character! Who, thus far, hasn't been raped! She controls her sexuality and she weaponizes it and she does what she wants because she wants to! How much do I love that Sabina can be in love and still choose to do something other than follow that man wherever he goes? Sabina accepts that she loves Vix. She also accepts that she can't be with him the way he wants her to be, not just because it's not in her nature, but because she, like him, has other duties. (And how much do I love that Vix is incapable of seeing his own hypocrisy, just as a real person would be?) Their relationship is just captivating to read about because it is so obviously doomed and yet so obviously the most important relationship, platonic and romantic, in their lives. For all the action and plot that happen in this book (and do they happen) the key of it is character and that particular relationship. The novel would be nothing if it didn't work. And oh, does it work. The other characters are strong as well. Plotina is a sort of foil to Domitian's empress: a wannabe kingmaker who is as mad as "Domitia" was cool, as well-treated by her (admittedly sexually uninterested) husband as "Domitia" was abused. Hadrian, a man Vix hates as soon as he sees him (at first due to petty jealousy and then, slowly, because of much deeper and more founded reasons) is one of those lovely Quinn antagonists who is very. slowly. unveiled. He doesn't walk onto the stage cackling, though you know from the freaking summary of the book that he's the "bad guy". Hell, Hadrian is recorded as one of the Good Emperors, and the book certainly gives an explanation for that as well. The one thing I will say is that I didn't completely buy Vix and Sabina's devotion to Trajan. I understood it more from Sabina, who spent so much personal time with the man. I couldn't get why this very obviously flawed man so captured Vix's attention. Then again, perhaps that's a part of what makes Vix so wonderfully flawed. He clings to the flaws of people like Sabina, and is blind to many others (including his own). But hey, he grows up. We see a lot of returning favorites like Marcus and Calpurnia, and a few (nicer than the others I mentioned) new darlings like Titus and Faustina. I am biting my nails on that one. As for Mirah--as I said before, I'm not crazy about her relationship with Vix, though I think it is necessary and at times likable enough. (It seems a bit plot device-y, and sometimes it reminds me of the Michael/Apollonia marriage in The Godfather.) I also found Mirah herself incredibly frustrating in her lack of practicality. Her religious fervor is admirable, but made me want to shake her by the shoulders sometimes. And a lot of her traits made me imagine that she's meant to be the "good woman" next to Sabina's "bad woman". Not that Quinn views one or the other as either. But it's there, nonetheless. That aside, Empress is a really, really great book. I loved it to pieces and am biting my nails until the next installment. (I need some kind of resolution to my Vix/Sabina relationship, though I can't imagine that it'll be good.)

I read this during my second year of college. I knew not of Hubbard's schemes, but saw the movie coming out and knew that I enjoyed dystopias and aliens. My friend saw me reading it and became concerned. She had an intervention with me, to let me know there might be subliminal messages in the book and that I should be wary of reading Hubbard. The story was okay--I know there were better books in the wild world that I could have wasted my time on. This one was a tome. It kept me distracted during a flight. The movie was definitely awful.

I was bored. It really tried to keep the suspense on how May died but it actually annoyed me than made me anticipate about the story. Sometimes I feel that the person Lauren's writing to doesn't really have a connection to what she's about to say. Poor character development (Wow, am I really saying this?) AND, she (Lauren) talks to the dead person about their own lives. Why would the dead person want to hear his life from Lauren, eh?

Probably my least favorite book in the series. The entire time I thought that I was going to absolutely hate the ending, but then right as it was getting ready to end horribly it just wrapped up. And the worst part was that it didn't even explain HOW it wrapped up, just one minute things are going wrong and then oh we switched back and now things are fine. Yeah, not that great.

unlike John Green's other books, I didn't enjoy this one NEARLY as much. and that is so saddening. maybe it was the fact that it was the last one i read... or i don't know what. but it was just really hard to get into. and the characters were just inexplicably unlikable. all of them. I can't blame Alaska for pulling him out of his freakin shell. goodness knows he needed it. i've never met a character like that. and he was just infuriating. it pretty much got worse from there... I'm a huge freaking john green fan. like everyone needs to reads his books RIGHT NOW. but this was just disappointing compared to his other words =(

Definitely a middle book of a series. Way too much sitting around worrying about politics, not enough happening. There were definitely some good fight scenes, but overall, this book just dragged along while Eland tried to negotiate between several armies, political problems within his new government, and his own desires. Vin has some good fights, but she spends a lot of time being indecisive and, to be honest, mopey. I do want to know how the series ends, before the 4th book (set in the distant future) comes out, so I will be reading the Hero of Ages, but this one didn't really wow me.
Wilde's fiction is really just a delivery mechanism for bon mots, but what bon mots they are.

Meh. I thought this book was quite mediocre. The overall plot was fairly cheesy and didn't feel very original. I also found Sophia pretty annoying. She was so naive and unsuspecting I couldn't help but want to shake some sense into her. The whole "I've never even used a flyswatter" claim was super pathetic. I guess I'm just not too keen on wussy main characters lol. I feel a little guilty considering some of the rave reviews I've read, but sometimes I can be honest to a fault.

Library copy. Found it hard going, the narrator is a very peculiar girl and I struggled to connect when things started to get a bit incesty I ran screaming! Tempting to skim to end / read reviews to find out what happens as this central mystery was very interesting and I wondered if if it was going to follow a 'Babadook' style ending the 'Magical' elements are all a way of coping with her mother mental illness

Well, it's bittersweet; I've finished the series. It was absolutely fantastic. I loved it so very much. The characters were very well done, and their progression through the series was perfect. The artwork continued to be excellent, and as suspected, the story was phenomenal. Well done, Joe Hill & Gabriel Rodriguez, well done. You created a world that entranced me from page one, volume one until the very final page of the last volume. I'm very pleased with how the story wrapped up. The final volume was epic. I couldn't put it down. I was on the edge of my seat needing to know what happened next. I have no complaints. Don't be fooled into judging this by appearances - this isn't a kids story. This is a story that features adults, teenagers, & children. The subject matter is mature, and they also address some very serious real-life issues. The story had gearth to it, and I'm sad it's over. This is easily one of my favorite graphic novel series, and something I see myself reading again. I would recommend this for both graphic novel fans and newbies.

This is Volume One of the Malazan Book of the Fallen, and there are an awful lot of fallen by the time you're fifty pages into the book. There are maps that I did not find necessary, a list of Dramatis Personae which is quite necessary, and a glossary at the end which is not a frivolous addition. The Malazan Empire is either about to swallow the last holdouts against its power, or start breaking up due to imperial overreach and poor personnel management of military class necessary to its expansion. This is a complex fantasy world, with a multitude of different cultures, different species, gods taking an active role in the world, etc. What's more, the characters are reasonably complex, with a plausible mixture of good and bad tendencies in at least all the major ones, and the conflicting interests between cultures and between factions within cultures are reasonably plausible, too. If there are few too many major ones, well, that's a tendency shared by many fantasy series, and at least each of these major characters appears to be worth spending some time with. All of which makes it especially unfortunate that all these fairly interesting pieces didn't really come together, and left me not caring how many more volumes there are in the Malazan Book of the Fallen.

Love Me in the Dark by Mia Asher is a standalone romance that borders on a love-triangle trope without ever fully stepping into that darkness. It is beautifully written to showcase the depth of conflict between the lead married female, Valentina, her apathetic husband, William, and the successful Parisian artist, Sebastien. Valentina thought she had it all. The happy marriage, the doting husband, the comfortable life. When she catches her husband, on their anniversary, cheating on her, the next year is spent dissecting their years together and trying to move past this heartbreaking event. When he offers to get away with her and go to Paris for some much needed time together she finally thinks things are on the mend and is willing to open up and maybe let him back into her heart. When he gets held up by meetings and sends her on ahead then never shows she is left to discover her true self, alone, in Paris. Sebastien is a troubled man who has suffered much loss in his life. He is a successful, renowned and wealthy artist who hasn't opened himself up to love in years. When he meets Valentina, by coincidence, at a gallery party, the attraction and intrigue is instantaneous for him. He wants more but they go their separate ways only to have fate play it's hand and have Valentina staying in his same apartment building. They build a solid friendship through the months she stays there all the while knowing that a reckoning is coming in the way of William and none of them will like it. Magical. I loved every word. I have laid out the gist of the story above without letting any of the sordid details loose and it is the sordid details, Sebastien's past, William's own nasty secrets, and Valentina's true desires, that make this story so amazing. Enjoy!
Three words: NOT. FOR. ME I grew so frustrated with every page. I just couldn't continue on. 1.5 stars!
You can find my Italian review of this wonderful book here: http://www.leggereromanticamente.com/...

This had the potential to be a good book - the writing style was engaging and the story was going somewhere but it was just like ... Bam... one minute Ryan was straight and what felt like half a page later he was gay forever. It was instalove to the power of a thousand! It all just happened so quickly that I felt like I was cheated out of the middle half of the book. I prefer a bit more thought behind the scenes so it didn't hit my buttons, which is a shame because had there been more to it, it probably would have.

A much more intimate look into the brothers that previous books. The Beast delved deeper into each of these characters that us BDB fans love, more focused on personal growth and development. Most of it I liked, some of it I loved, and some I was indifferent to, but overall, it was a pleasure to visit my brothers. Full review to come...

Me after finishing this series: [Disclaimer: I'm angry. And I won't hold back.] I've never been the biggest fan ot the Queen of the Tearling series but I enjoyed the plot and mostly the whole world Erika Johansen build. But then, what happened? Did the story get to complicated for her to finish it properly. Was she exhausted and thought this cheap cop-out was necessary? This was not a "hipster" way to end a story, this was pure laziness. The author didn't want to answer the burning questions. Maybe she got lost in her story. I'm frustrated. I regret spending so much time reading book 1 and 2 and getting invested in the characters (and I can't believe I was invested in The Fetch! Thanks Erika.). For what? That Kelsea is the only one left and everyone doesn't remember her or the whole plot that happened in the books before. Ridiculous. ABSOLUTELY RIDICULOUS. No recommendation from my side. Stay clear from this series. It's way to unsatisfying and dissapointing.

Rosemary and Rue was a good debut UF. It was an intro into the world of October Daye. Much of it felt like just that, an introduction into her fae world where, in the midst of solving a murder, we learn about the many, many different types of fae and fae lines, including changelings (half breeds, like Toby). There were times where I was a bit lost. But, for your reference, there's a long list of types in the front of the book. (I sometimes cringe when I see those, wondering how easy it'll be to follow the story without first memorizing all the info thrown at us before the first "Hi, how are ya".) If you removed all of that {world-building} the book would've been short, but still interesting. That being said though, now that we have all been fully educated on Toby's world and the inhabitants in it, I'm hoping book #2 will be heavier on the character interaction and lighter on the world-building. October said, "I live in a city by the sea where the fog paints the early morning, parking is more precious than gold, and Kelpies wait for the unwary on street corners. Neither of the worlds I live in is quite mine, but no one can take them away from me. Stuck between two worlds ... her journey to find "home" continues in book #2, A Local Habitation.

This was a great book, one which builds a new world for Jim's Urban Fantasy series, with the fresh concept of Libriomancers drawing magic out of books, but it was great for another reason - I completed my Goodreads goal of 100 books in a calendar year for the first time with this one, and it makes me proud as hell! On to the book itself, it has good, solid writing, with good worldbuilding, memorable and fleshed out characters with unique motives and a concept which is unique. Plus the fact that the author has used some real world personas and characters along with favourite books to 'channel' magic makes it even better. As the first book in a series, this has all the markings of a fantastic saga, one which I can't wait to get on with the second book. 5/5 for you, Mr Jim C Hine! Verdict: Urban Fantasy readers, give this a read, you will surely love it.
I loved the characters and the writing was good but the story was slow for me. I might've enjoyed it better at a different period in my life.

It is Ilona Andrews, so you know the world building is going to be amazing. The action is also outstanding and is served up in a cast of quirky and interesting characters. The downside is that it pushes as close to PNR as you can get without tipping over the edge. In the Kate Daniels series, the romance is the blurry background to the action-oriented focal plot. I wish this series was more like it. In this book, Nevada is once again pulled into a deep and dangerous case. She knows things can get hairy when she accepts the job to look into the murder of her client's wife. In the process she stumbles upon a deep and deadly conspiracy, as well as Mad Rogan. It was a fun ride. I blew through it.

Fall 2018. The awaiting begins. Gods. Now I advise you not to read further unless you've finished ACOWAR -- seriously, what are you even doing on the internet if that's the case?? I think it's high time we started the game of who will be featured in the next book? I mean, obviously, it's a healthy and not-obsessive past time hobby. Right? *smiles innocently* Nesta & Cassian? Honestly, my money's on them. Maas loves them and there were so many things left unfinished regarding their status. Plus, tell us they're mates already! Or Lucien and Elain and possibly Azriel? I cannot be the only one sensing something iffy about these three, like a pseudo-love-triangle thingy morphed with the free-will issue regarding mates. Or, for goodness's sake, not so appealing but certainly plausible, Tamlin? The guy's a douche but even I have to admit his only fault was that his love was toxic. Maybe he changes his love. Maybe he finds his happiness. Or or or, one of my personal faves, Hellion????? I mean, just imagine! OR JURIAN AND DRAKON AND MYRIAM, GODS YES. That would be one hell of a prequel. Or just Amren and Varian, in one of their vacations. The firedrake needs to find her hidden talent. Or Kallias and Viviane. And how most likely Viviane will relentlessly ask to be made High Lady. Girl power FTW! Or Eris's story, the one with his regrets and all that bullshit -- the prick managed to intrigue me. OR MOR'S. This angel of Velaris that deserves so much love <3 Or Tarquuuuuin. He needs to find himself a chick ASAP. Perhaps Jurian and Vassa!! (Can Vassa's curser be Koschei, the last piece of the death-gods Triumvirate?) Or the Bone Carver's vision coming to life. That would be amazing. But I'm pretty sure SJM is saving that for last. Let's be honest here, though -- I'll devour the most basic of scenes with these characters. Them going shopping or getting drunk or training or bickering. I'll gobble it up in 2 seconds. So yeah -- HOLY SHIT THE POSSIBILITIES. What's your guess?

I'm not a Sparks fangirl. I don't have to read everything written by him. A few of his stories have caught my interest and The Choice is one of them. What is the choice? There are two of them in this story and the one I believe the title came from is not what you'd expect. I should also point out that this story actually defies regular Nicholas Sparks logic. I won't tell you how, though! Gabby moved in next door to a single man, Travis. Travis's closest friends are all married with children. He was very attractive, very adventerous, and very much the vet she goes to when her dog is in trouble. One can only guess what's going to happen next except Gabby has a boyfriend. There is a second part to the story, but I'm not going to tell it to you because it gives away too much of the first part of the story. All I will say is it has a lot do with the choice. I wasn't too thrilled with the second part of the book. Honestly, it felt like it came out of left field and didn't connect well with the first part. As its own story it's nice, I just don't feel it fits with the first part too much. I read this book for pure pleasure. All opinions are my own. I was not compensated for this review in any way.

SO MANY STARS YESSSSSSS This book gave me life and reminded me why I love reading so much and deserves every freakin' star possible. Visually, this thing is also a masterpiece. The cover? GORGEOUS! The pages and different styles of telling the story? AMAZING! This book is absolutely stunning in every way. I had tried to read this one as a hardback several times before because I saw all the hype and just couldn't do it for whatever reason. I think it was through BookBub that I found out that this one was $1.99 on Kindle and I figured I would give it a try on there. I think I also tried on Kindle before the last time and again, to no avail. But this last time, something changed. Once I got through some of the rougher parts, I was racing through the book and even finished it in record personal time. One thing that I did not enjoy about the Kindle version was that it hindered my enjoyment and visuals of the more visual things in this book. I didn't figure out how to zoom until the last 30% of the book and before them, had to squint and guess as to what they said or find a copy in a store and check them out. Anyways, back to my thoughts on the actual book. Like I previously said, the beginning to this one is a little rough. I wasn't too into the interviews and was unused to the style. But, I quickly eased into it and I think I most enjoyed the chats and pages that involved text woven within an image. The other styles I did not enjoy as much but they really do add the story and serve to give the reader multiple perspectives as to what is happening. And these perspectives really work and again, add to the story. I do like fantasy and science fiction YA but have found it hard to find ones not ruined by cheesy romance or in a style that I love (Some perspectives just bug me and I can't get into them.) but I've never read one like Illuminae before. Not just because of the style but also in terms of the content. I don't generally read into space books as it's hard to find them or to find good ones. This one was a step out of my reader comfort zone that I am so glad I took. I raced through it, devouring every cute romance bit of Kady & Ezra's story, every whacked AIDAN moment, and every twisty turn of the Beitech v. Alexander & Hypatia crew battle. The authors really excelled at writing all of those aspects and drawing me in using them. At first, I wasn't so into Kady+Ezra, but as the book went on, I really enjoyed it and found myself becoming a hardcore shipper in no time. As for AIDAN, it was kind of the same thing. In the beginning, I hated it and what it was doing to the people it was supposed to protect. But towards the end, especially in the scenes with Kady, I actually kind of liked it a bit and almost felt sorry for it. Although, I hated the fact that it impersonated Ezra and claimed he was dead (Holy shiz, I'm glad he wasn't. I was actually scared he wasn't. I found this one to not be predictable, except for a few minor things, but otherwise it was completely unpredictable and intriguing. I highly recommend this one and have added it to the high honor of being on my favorite shelf. All the stars in the universe for Illuminae, my friends.
fairly predictabe, but I don't regret having read it.

If you're already skeptical about a person someone being in deep, dark mourning lasting a year over someone they knew for only a few weeks then this is definitely not going to be a book for you. Although normally that would put me off I really, really wanted this book to work. Considering Wolitzer is well established in adult literary fiction, I suppose I figured she was likely to have a shot at creating a truly wrenching story of lost love even if that love was so brief. There were a couple of clear ways this scenario could work and I was curious to see if Wolitzer would pull it off. She didn't. Everything about this story is surface level only. There is no depth of emotion, no character development, limited growth, stunted pacing, and one hell of an obnoxious ending that had me going, "Seriously?!" Full review at The Midnight Garden.
It was pretty average...
UPDATE: Woah, that cover. This sounds freaking amazing.

This book was such a welcome break in this weird string of flop books I've been reading. Ahh, so good. The dialogue was great. The love/hate was adorable. And the mystery was intriguing. And the COVER. Overall, love.

~sigh~ It pains me to think the third book hasn't even been released yet. 4.5 for this one. I really, really liked it. We meet 3 new main characters all of which I liked for their variety of personality differences. We follow Scarlet and Wolf as they try and track down Scarlet's grand-mere. Lies, deceit and love all intertwined between the animalistic Wolf and independent Scarlet. I loved how tender and vulnerable Scarlet was when it came to her grandmother, it made for a nice and realistic balance. Meanwhile Cinder is escaping with the arrogant and very funny Thorne whose ship they take as they make their way around the globe in search of answers. I think I liked this book even better than the first.

I'm really loving this series and world. The third installment does not disappoint. If you have enjoyed the series to date, this is another excellent addition. We continue the journey with Ty, Kinsey, and Bode as they discover more mysteries of Lovecraft and their father. So far each volume has introduced new keys and new adventures. It's been enjoyable how the story unfolds. I don't feel bored or annoyed at the pace. Instead each volume feels like the next piece of the puzzle being explained strategically. The artwork continues to amaze me. I love the interplay between it and the story. They enhance each other. It's well done and on my list of favorite artwork. I can't wait to read the rest of the series!

A glance of a terrible place to live - 1933 in Russian - where people are so hungry they eat their pets. Skip to 1953 - and he horrors continue. I don't know much about Russian history and I'd like to think it wasn't as bad as Mr. Smith shows us but I suspect it was. Not so different from Nazi Germany where neighbour was encouraged to spy on neighbour and even Hilter Youth kids betrayed their parents. Child 44 was chilling view of Russian society - a bleak landscape in all respects. Leo was really well drawn, the relationship between him and his parents and his wife - all heart rending. I knew the opening had to link in somewhere and I'd sort of guessed partly but not completely. I think I felt the end a little rushed somehow but maybe we'd had enough of the horror by then. I was completely engrossed in this book from start to finish. If you like thrillers with meat - this is definitely one to read.

I so loved this book! Sure I generally liked Shelly Laurenston's books but this one is special for 3 reasons! 1) Zach Sheridan -Our hero. Well if you can call an arrogant jerk a hero exactly. He is the typical bad but not BAD boy! Sexy, sinister and more than a little wicked he has females swooning! 2) Sara Morrighan -Our bitc...heroine. Sara is in one word nuts! You don't really know if she will love you or stab you in the back! Not the typical romance heroine and all the more refreshing for it! 3) The girlfriends! I loved Sara's friends. We have the "Barbie" and the mental "geek"! Both interesting and more than a little out there...

Hero and heroine didn't do anything smart and had bad luck all the way through. Too much of a helpless victim feel. I want to root for my hero and heroine. I want to see them do at least some things competently. In this book it was disappointment after disappointment after disappointment. The good guys had bad luck or stupidity in every part of the investigation. When they had an information source they didn't get to it quickly enough which allowed the bad guy to kill, burn down, or obstruct it. Examples are in the Spoiler below (I don't give away the bad guy's name). They had the name of a suspect. They should have immediately gotten his picture from the license bureau, but they didn't. They would have recognized the bad guy. They had a deputy guarding a witness. But he stepped away to flirt with a girl for ten minutes which allowed the bad guy to get in and kill the witness. They had a lead on a suspect. Two good guys went there alone without any back up. It was a set-up/ambush. When they arrived the bad guy shot one of them. The other should have immediately taken cover and shot back, but he didn't. He went to tend to the wounded guy and got hit. The heroine was keeping a secret from her past. If she had opened up about it, it might have let someone else discover clues. You need to suspend disbelief about the bad guy's consistent good luck. As John Gibbs another reviewer said "the villain's almost supernatural omniscience, omnipresence, and invisibility were not adequately accounted for." This was not fun unless you're rooting for the bad guy. I'm reminded of a scene from a Harry Bosch book (author Michael Connelly). Harry's friend was confined to bed. The friend complained that his wife was mistreating him. So Harry bought a spy camera clock which he placed in the room. A rogue FBI agent showed up and made serious threats which were caught on camera. This led Harry to something new. It was unexpected, neat, and lucky. Deadly Fear was missing unexpected things like that. There were several sex scenes. Somehow I wasn't interested. I skimmed them. The author is a good writer. Her dialogue and action were well done. She just needs some good ideas to write about. DATA: Narrative mode: 3rd person. Story length: 385 pages. Swearing language: strong including religious swear words, but not often used. Sexual language: strong. Number of sex scenes: 6. Setting: current day Mississippi, with a little Washington D.C. and Louisiana. Copyright: 2010. Genre: romantic suspense.
One of the lamest flattest vampires I have ever read. Just horrible.

Holy moly this was dark. I'm not sure what to say. If this is intended for young adults I'm thinking it is the 18 to 23 range young adult. There were numerous graphic and disturbing scenes (the bed!). In fact, I went to go see Gone Girl and afterwards I told my sister-in-law that Scowler was darker and more horrific. Definitely not for the faint of heart. Two stars only because this was not my cup of tea.
Ugh. This one seemed EVEN MORE ridiculously sexist than the others, if that's possible.

Unfortunately, this second book was a read that I just couldn't seem to get into. One of the reasons was that there was so much time spent apart between Emma and Carter. The other reason was that I felt there was a lot of repetition with how characters were feeling about certain situations. I was very disappointed, especially because I had really enjoyed the first book.. I am going to leave this review short as I don't feel like bashing or anything.. I will leave this as I was very bored! Will I ever read another Tijan book again?? Absolutely! I have enjoyed a few of her books, and I have faith that there will be more that she writes that will be just as good as the ones that I fell in love with! Carter Reed #2 was a let down, but I look forward to see what is next for the talented Tijan..

After a terrible ending to a party Hayden decides to take his own life. His best friend Sam, ready to apologize, is the one to find Hayden lying dead in his bedroom the next morning from a drug overdose. The only clue he left behind was a playlist, specifically for Sam. Now Sam immerses himself in the playlist trying to figure out why his only friend was so desperate enough to kill himself. Soon Sam starts figuring out that Hayden had some secrets that he didn't even share with him. Full of bullies, amazing songs, revenge, and puzzles this book is sure to keep readers entertain. My only problem with this book is the revenge aspect, and who is dishing it out. Especially since things end so flatly and almost as if done quickly to run away from the story itself. 3 out of 5 stars. Thanks Edelweiss.
I am soooo excited to read this! Jennifer Donnelly is one of my favorite authors, and it has been WAY too long since I read one of her books! I may even throw in a SQUEEE for good measure... ;)

Despite growing up in a small PNW town not far from where this book takes place, I didn't really connect with this one. I did really love this bit towards the end: "Small-town life is loving the wide roads one day and wanting to leave and never look back the next. But you accept that's how it is, because you're a part of something. And because... it's home."

This book is overwhelmingly disturbing. I want to give Cynthia Bond positive stars for her writing. But the story is about really terrible things.. things we all are against. I believe there should be resources in the back of ways to get involved and help stop this type of violence. In a Goodreads video Author Cynthia Bond describes Ruby's life as very difficult. That is certainly an understatement!!!! Ruby now 30 has lost her mind as she is been physically and mentally abused. She is possessed by the devil Dybou.. Story deals with women violence, child abuse, and devil worship. . This is an Oprah recommendation so I knew the story would be emotional. Oprah states that she has never read anything like this book. THAT I agree ....100%. I finished the book as I wanted to know what happen to Ephram. I read and finished this book on March 18 while traveling by plane to DC. I had downloaded two light books on my Nook so was delighted I could pull up another book quickly..I knew if I had this book on my mind there is no way I was going to sleep that night. The light read was Angels Walking
Okay, I think my little romance novel run has come to an abrupt end. Wow, this was trashy & ridiculous! DNF & skimmed to the end. Pretty bad stuff.

Either the first two books really weren't as good as I thought, or this one just didn't compare, but either way I almost quit this book several times. Sara turned into that scary movie actress that runs up the stairs when she's being chased by the bad guy. Every time she did something incredibly stupid, I just wanted to shake her. I kept hanging on thinking we would find out what happened to Ella, who hasn't been seen since page 1 of the first book, but no. Jones does throw out a little tidbit at the end to get you to come back, but I just don't care that much.

This was such a fun, exciting book to read! It really had the feel of a summer blockbuster action romance movie to it! You've got con artists, political machinations, extremely handsome & sexy royal princes, and lots of hot, sexy, fun times! What more can you ask for? Well, I suppose you could ask for the next book in this series, but it is already out, so I'm buying it now! Can't wait to see how this turns out!

A fast-paced page turner full of mishaps and laughs,Becky Bloomwood style. [3.5 - 4 stars] You'll find no bigger Sophie Kinsella fan than this girl right here. I have loved every book I've read of hers, especially her Shopaholic series. So when I was able to early read this book, my excitement knew no bounds. I was ready to jump into this crazy, hilarious world of too much shopping and too much laughing. Because Becky Brandon (nee Bloomwood) is back in all her stylish glory and this time she's heading to Hollywood! Luke takes on a celebrity client, and moves the family to Los Angeles, temporarily. And while Luke's focus is on learning the ins and outs of managing a celebrity, Becky is seeing stars. She's ready to lunch with the who's who of Hollywood, ready to hit Rodeo Drive, ready to talk films, fashion and the latest must-have handbag. "Imagine having that job. Working on films; choosing outfits for actors; styling stars for appearances... Forget department stores, I should aim higher! That's the job I should have. I mean, it's perfect. I love clothes, I love films, I'm moving to LA... why on earth didn't I think of this before?" In a new city that thrives on yoga, working out, clean mind and body, movies, wheatgrass smoothies and fashion, Becky finds herself immersed in all things LA, especially when she runs into a shoplifting celebrity who happens to be the nemesis of Luke's client. And as fate would have it, an old enemy shows up to make things even more difficult. As her world begins to spiral out of control, Becky faces her challenges with irresistible wit, unfailing positivity and her infamous shopping cure-all attitude. Becky... being Becky, works hard to land a celebrity client... which of course means shopping, shopping and more shopping. And shopping undoubtedly leads to secrets, which she of course keeps from Luke as the complicated becomes more complicated. Soon, she finds herself making some bad choices and ostracizing the people who love her the most as she pursues her dream to be a stylist to the stars. "This is what it's like to be a celebrity. Your family don't understand. No one understands. No wonder they say it's lonely at the top." I so enjoyed the book. I laughed out loud so many times. But there were a couple things that kept this from being my usual 5-star shopaholic review. One, there were a number of different story lines in the book and not all of them were resolved. It felt as if too many issues detracted from the primary plot. And secondly, after six books in, I wanted to see Becky evolve a little more. Perhaps it's that I've read too many of these books and seeing Becky fall into the same old traps repeatedly bothered me. I expected to see more character evolution across the series even though I certainly don't expect Becky to lose the tendencies that we've grown to love. I just wanted to see more learning from her mistakes. I will continue to read more from Sophie Kinsella, whose keen mastery of romantic comedy enlivened by witty dialogue and enchanting characters, always leaves me feeling happy long after the flip of the final page. Perhaps one of the most jarring, exquisite, books I've read all year. I don't where to start but I can say this: The alternating povs of the past and present were amazing. Not only did it navigate the reason for the main plot; it navigated through all the characters. Every single one fleshed out completely. The phrase "morally grey" does not begin to explain the mold of these characters. Each one of them, terribly, terribly flawed- maybe to the exception of Sydney- but, nonetheless, no one in this book has that hero flare, the kind you really root for. And it's funny, considering it is a book about superheroes. But superheroes is the lightest term that could possibly be thought of. Especially when it's titled Vicious . The book follows the darkness, the gritty, raw parts of you that you don't want to touch. The type of parts that is concealed. The kind of aching that devoid you of emotion. No character is left untouched; the darkness is everyone and it's unleashed one way or another. I loved loved how Schwab captured that concept. The characters were written tragically, painfully. hollow and broken. There was no room for the lightness that superheroes (or the concept of) usually bring because this book wasn't about hope; it was about revenge and the satisfaction of a kill. It's scary reading this book, how empty and numb these characters can really get, but I think that's what made this book so good, Schwab never held back and I'm so glad for it.

Why was it, she asked herself, that 'animals can sometimes subdue their predatory ways in only a few months, while humans, despite centuries of refinement, can quickly grow more savage than any beast'? I was super excited when the book club I'm in decided upon this book as our last one of the year (& my last one in high school ever). I thought it would be super interesting to hear about WW2 from the POV of some Polish zookeepers, protecting Jews from the hands of Nazis. I was right. It was such a docile book in a way, with extended descriptions of animals and their behaviors. In other ways, it was raw and honest with the way it mentioned the amount of death and destruction brought about by Hitler. It took me awhile to get into this book. It wasn't even that it was bad, it just wasn't really capturing my interest. The first thirty or so pages is mainly talking about the zoo and the villa and the animals they have, in the actual zoo and the house. This by no means was a wrong move on Ackerman's part. It definitely set the scene and put me in the mindset for this book, but I didn't feel like picking it up every chance I got. Once I got around 1/3 of the way into the book, I was way more intrigued. I became fully engrossed when the Ghetto is put into place and Jan begins to smuggle them out and bring them to the zoo where they would hide in animals cages or the basement of the villa. The selflessness of both Jan and Antonia was mind blowing. They were both so brave and kind, and it really upset me that Jan would sometimes brush Antonia's fears and worries to the side, as if she was in the wrong to feel this way. I did like them both a lot, I just didn't understand why he always had to have superiority over her success. As a nonfiction book, many people will probably shy away from this one. Along with the density that it appears to possess, many won't even bother and just go see the movie. However, as you're reading, it feels almost like fiction for a majority of the book. There were definitely parts dominated by facts and statistics that bogged down the story and strayed from the plot. I understand that Ackerman was trying to establish her ethos and show how much research she had put into this novel, but I definitely think that some parts could have been cut out. There definitely are a lot of names. Although there is an index in the back and you can see the page they were first mentioned, I would definitely have started a character chart myself if I had known how overwhelming it was going to get. This is especially true because a lot of the names are similar in the starting letter or last name, which definitely got frustrating because I would have to flip to the index and find when they were first mentioned. Towards the end when there is a sort of recap of all the characters and where they ended up, I just gave up. Oops. Although I'm only giving this book three stars, it really , which is hard to do when there are already so many out there. It wasn't the most exciting thing to read, but I learned a lot about the way the Nazis not only wanted a superior Aryan race, but also wanted to have certain animals bred so that they would remain in the bloodlines of the world. Some of it definitely went over my head, but that also might have been because I ended up skimming a bit occasionally. Better than Code Name Verity, which was our first book club book.

Looking for a fun, new adventure loosely based on a classic fairy tale? FROGGED might be just the book for you. In an E.D.Baker/Disney-esque spin, kissing a frog has a way of rebounding and turning oneself into a frog. Unlike the former two, however, the frog turns back into a human, leaving his savior as a frog in his place. Harry is no prince, either, but a wainwright's son. He doesn't care that he's turned the royal princess into a frog, either. He's from a poor family overrun with kids. Why shouldn't he have a little luck, too? Our plucky princess, Imogene, refuses to curse another human into frog form in order to save herself. Instead, she sets off to find the witch who cursed Harry, only to find that it can't be undone. Imogene will remain a frog unless she can get someone else to kiss her and transfer the enchantment. As she tries to make her way home, she's captured by a couple of teenagers named Luella and Bertie, who are running away to be actors and want to add a talking frog to their act. Imogene has no way out, especially when the troupe's owner realizes that Imogene is who she says but doesn't care, so long as a talking frog brings in the money. Will Imogene ever find a way to return home and become a human frog again? FROGGED is great for middle-grade readers and will appeal to children as they follow Imogene on her journey. There are a couple of small adult elements slipped in, but they're done in a way that kids won't notice or wonder about, but adults will pick up on. They can relate to Imogene, who doesn't want to read about a stuff book about how to be a princess that her mother's making her study. They'll feel bad when, only trying to help, she's forced to give her first kiss away to a frog, who turns out to be a mean boy. They'll feel as mad as Imogene does when she's tricked, handfed lies, and held against her will. FROGGED is a fun, light read about a princess forced to masquerade as a frog after being caught up in an unfortunate curse.

I'm just not sure how to rate this book, having now finished it. I think some people will get a lot from it, mainly in the realm of insight into the Ohio/Kentucky region's culture and community. My mother is from this part of the country and much of her family still lives there today, so I didn't really benefit from an illustration of what life there is like. Though this is not a flaw in the writing, it made me a lot less able to excuse what I felt were weaknesses, and glaring ones at that. I thought the writing itself was sub par--a lot of cliches and clunky exposition. A lot of bland descriptions of what must have been formative events in the author's life, relying on the reader to fill in with their own emotional impressions rather than describing how he felt exactly. Saying something to the effect of "You can imagine how that made me feel," does not count. Many people and events are credited with "saving him," ostensibly from becoming a drunken, abusive patriarch of another dysfunctional hillbilly clan. Also most of the descriptions of his "beautiful, kind, and brilliant" wife rubbed me the wrong way, as she rarely appeared without the qualifier of beautiful. This would not be a problem at all if we actually got a sense of who she was... being a stable presence for Vance while he was at Yale, and being beautiful, do not make up a whole person. This is a pet peeve of mine so maybe others weren't as turned off by this but... yikes. I don't know, maybe this was a case of inflated expectations, but I was left utterly unimpressed by this book. For the record, I do agree with his assessment of the societal ills of hillbilly country, so it's not a matter of being offended by what he's saying. (A baffling number of low ratings on this book included something along the lines of "I am from this area and I work very hard, and so does my entire family! This book is WRONG!" These readers seem to be missing something vital, either about this book or their communities at large.) About 3/4 of the way through: Wow, this Obama section feels unbelievably tone-deaf. I mean. It's not Obama's skin color but the fact that he benefits from meritocracy that makes people in Middleton, OH feel that he's an alien? This segment of the population firmly believing that he's a Muslim despite all evidence to the contrary isn't necessarily due to skin tone either, but the fact that his accent is neutral and he went to an Ivy League school...? Even as an argument that it's not ONLY racism motivating the Obama mistrust/hatred in the white working class completely crumbles when you consider that he ran against ROMNEY in 2012, who received this population's outright support on top of avoiding its scorn. Romney absolutely ticks all of those "alienating" boxes that Obama does. This is just really rubbing me the wrong way. Oh, and they hate Michelle because she's starkly against feeding your children junk food, which is a hit below the belt... except that if she were moralizing as an older, well made up white lady I highly doubt it would be taken with the same kind of offense (see Mrs. Nancy Regan). The Obamas are "otherized" by the white working class for all the reasons Vance cites, sure, but any claim that skin color isn't the principle dividing line is demonstrably false.

Original review at Gabic Reads. Review copy received via Netgalley. Bryn is set up to be this bad-ass, snarky girl who doesn't take crap from anyone. But several times, she finds herself in tears. When Zavien tries to manipulate her, she gets mad and tells him to just talk to her plainly. But when he does that, she explodes at him and does the opposite of whatever he tells her. Also, who goes to boarding school and only contacts their parents and friends after the first day of school? I mean, you don't feel the need to talk to your parents after almost dying three times? I would really want to go home at that point... So many unanswered questions. I want to know if the Directorate forces Bryn into an arranged marriage. Or if the lighten up on their archaic rules. Nothing was resolved at the end except we know who tried to kill Bryn. Do Bryn's parents return to the dragon community? I really need a sequel to answer these questions, but I have seen no indication there's going to be one. If there turns out to be a sequel, I will reconsider my rating, because the main reason it's a two star is the unanswered questions and the underdevelopment. There were so many things about this book left unexplored. I wanted to know more about the knights. Chris had so much potential with that and it was only mentioned a few times. And Valmont, the knight who binds himself to Bryn, only shows up to protect her once. And that was after she almost died the first time and before the second time. He wasn't around for any of those times. I want to know more about the Orange dragons. Why are there so few of them? Is there really an underground community in hiding? Despite these things, Chris has created a world that has the potential to be magical and fantastical. I hope to see more from this world that answers the questions I've posed.

It will come as a shock to absolutely no one that Danny Torrance, the little boy whose alcoholic father was so unlucky as to become the caretaker at The Overlook hotel, grew up to be an alcoholic. King, himself a former denizen of the bottle, writes Danny a rock-bottom that serves as one of the few truly impactful moments in Doctor Sleep, the long-belated sequel to The Shining. Unlike his famously testy father, Torrance gets himself into AA and manages to crawl back to sobriety. He even lands a job and earns the title moniker at a small New England hospice that just happens to be up the road from the home of a little girl with a Shine of her own, one so bright it attracts the attention of a herd of psychic vampires known as the True Knot who travel the country in RV campers and polyester pants. The Shining tells the story of the destruction of a family. Thirty-six years later, in what might seem almost a gesture of amends to his protagonist, King builds a new family for poor Danny Torrance in his adopted community. Strangely for an author with such a generally Dickensian gift for character, none of these new additions ever truly come to life - perhaps because King devotes far more time to his anti-family, the True Knot, whose lovingly-detailed camaraderie undercuts their creepiness, and who pale in comparison to the shades of The Overlook. In fact, despite multiple heavy-handed references to the original, Doctor Sleep bears more resemblance to King's son Joe Hill's novel NOS4A2, released back in April. The two discussed their books with each other while writing them, and seeded cross references in each text, though whether they intended to produce such similar narratives (now-adult damaged gifted child confronts ancient vampiric threat via road trip in order to save the next generation) is debatable. Frankly, NOS4A2, while flawed, works better, perhaps because it's not chained to now-classic source material. King's The Shining stands as one of the great horror novels of all time, and perhaps the most terrifying parable for alcoholism ever written. To expect the sequel to live up to that kind of visceral impact is perhaps unfair, and if you can divorce yourself from the original I suppose Doctor Sleep isn't bad - it's just a bit of a snooze.

Those sentimental Hallmark greeting cards that bring a tear to your eye when you read them at Target? If whoever wrote those also wrote a novel about a crusty old curmudgeon, it might turn out something like this book. The characters are typically described by one word (pregnant, overweight, homosexual, etc) then spend the rest of the book behaving only in behavior that directly supports the initial description (ie eating a sandwich or asking about food in every scene). Character interaction is so slapstick that Ove might as well be a man called Elmer Fudd. There's at least one eye-rolling, exasperating moment in each chapter. And yet there are moments that transcend the morass, moments where we genuinely feel for these characters and their absurdly cartoon-like lives, moments where we reflect on how little we really know about the people around us and what they've been through in their lives that affects who they are and how they interact with others. And those are the moments that make this book worth reading in spite of its faults.

As Emma fights to be the "perfect" assistant she finds there are times when its best to take chances--no matter the consequences. I was looking for a book like this--it has a bit of everything--lots of tension, great dialogue, humor, and characterizations. I laughed out loud in places, gasped (yes, I did) in others and stayed up until the wee hours of the morning reading this book. It had a fabulous happy ending--and the best part--Alaric and Emma stayed who they were. The writing was exquisite--with emotion and description creating a vivid, visceral picture. Very well done!! I can't say enough about it. Ok, so you don't think I'm just waxing poetic--there were some moments of reading where I wasn't sure what the characters positions were: Standing or Sitting--because at times it was confused--(not enough to make me stop reading)---but the emotion was such I didn't care and the characters didn't either; because that was the point even they were caught up in the moment.--and that's all that mattered. Just a wonderful fabulous read. I am looking forward to more from this author.

I love every one of Olivia Cunning's Sinners Rock Star bad boys. She has their personalities down to a fine art. And although this story is primarily about Jace and Aggie, the entire band is all over this book. They are sexy, perverted, loveable, perverted, effed-up, perverted, hilarious, perverted, and just plain fun. Oh yeah, did I mention perverted? I chuckled throughout the whole book at their perversions. Not only is there plenty of fun,kinky erotica, but there is a good dose of drama and humor thrown in for your reading pleasure. If you ever need a pick-me-up after a sad book or a bad day, you can always count on the Sinners Rock Band.

The thing I took away from this book is the idea that teenagers are some twisted mofos. Nothing is about the meaning and meaninglessness that we feel as humans. That's pretty much the entire story. How the author gets there, however, is disturbing and--at times--straight-up sick. I felt really uncomfortable reading this book, but not in a 'wow, what an amazing message' kind of way. By the time I finished the book, I wanted to wrap myself in a blanket and sit in a corner, rocking back and forth and muttering to myself. The book is *that* troubling. I think I only finished it because it's pretty short (227 pages)--if it had been much longer, I might have left it unfinished. I think we all know that humans are capable of very depraved acts, but it's that much more troubling when those acts are committed by teens or children. I can't say that I recommend this book because I just found it really depressing and soul-sucking. The author's point hit home; I just didn't like the manner in which it was revealed to me.

I am a huge fan of Sarah Ockler's - Twenty Boy Summer is exceptional and so is Fixing Delilah. What I love about this novel is the multiple layers of the characters from the MC Delilah to her mom to Patrick, the boy who falls in love with Delilah. The story unfolds one page at a time, pulling the reader into their lives and at the same time allowing us to examine the relationships in our own lives. Ockler does such a fabulous job presenting the depth of each characters wounds, challenges, joys - their strengths and weaknesses - while giving way to a hope that things can work out despite the muck we trudge through in life. Every family has its secrets, and we all know that it's nearly impossible to keep them hidden. Once they're revealed one must decide if they're going to destroy or, after picking up the pieces, strengthen the core of your being. A beautiful, powerful, and hopeful novel. Way to go Sarah!

I have no idea how to rate this book. I thought TINY PRETTY THINGS was supposed to be a snarky competitive ballet novel and I was looking forward to something that would make me laugh and instead this story was awful and savage and terrible and cruel and stressful. Very few positive or happy moments exist in this tale. I had a lot of speculation about what was happening and by whom and after that ending I may or may not be right. I'll have to read the sequel to find out. But holy wow that won't be for a while. This book was murder on my ability to be calm. The authors give this life a sense of reality in a way, the harsh drive to be perfect and more talented than the rest, to come out on top, but it's also totally unreal, the intensity of the bullying and the lengths the girls (and boys) will go. Not for the faint of heart.

3.5 stars for "Swift and the Black Dog" by Ginn Hale 4 stars for "Everyone's Afraid of Clowns" by Jordan Castillo Price because it's a Psycop story and I miss Victor and his endearing quirks I don't know how to rate this anthology. How do people rate anthologies when they read only two stories all the way through and sample the rest? 3 stars? Seems kinda harsh since I did really like those two stories. Both are great, and I got this anthology just for them. Worth it even if the rest of the anthology falls into writing exercise territory. Prose-wise they fall short of GH and JCP, but story-wise, they don't seem that bad, with one exception--the one that reads like fanfic. That aside, a few have interesting settings and world building, or rather interesting enough that I might come back to finish them later on, but the rest needs a more thorough edit to smooth out awkward clunky prose. Another thing is it's not clear if these stories are stand-alones or part of a series. Since I wasn't that invested, I didn't bother looking them up. So for now this is a DNF, but I might return later. Maybe. I really hope the haunted theater will play a part in the next Psycop book. It would be awesome to see Vic and Jacob renovate another old building.

4.5 stars This is the second book the the Combative series and I loved it. I'm going to try and write a spoiler free review but it's going to be hard not to give anything away. This time the story focuses on Nate and we get more into his background with Bailey. I was hooked from the very beginning and I certainly couldn't tell where the story was going. It was great to get a background to Nate and seeing his relationship with Tiny his right hand man and then also his growing relationship with Bailey. The story didn't really answer any questions I had left over from book 1, if anything I have more. I can't wait for book 3 to see where the story goes and what happens to these characters. The story is told from duel POV which was great and really added to the story. I really liked Nat's characters after reading his POV's and now I really hope for a HEA out come for all the characters. I can't wait for the next book because I don't have a clue where Jay McLean will take the story. Overall another great installment in the series and hopefully the wait for book 3 won't be too long. * I received an ARC in exchange for an honest review

Page 44: The main character is being stalked by somebody after leaving a bar, and I just. don't. care. I could take the infodumping (I've seen worse). I don't mind werewolves and vampires, at least in theory (I've read some good books featuring them). I could live with the garden-variety urban-fantasy writing (I've seen much worse). Vigilante anti-vampire vampire with her very own techno-Igor? Okay, sure, let's see how it goes. It's the world-building. I'm kind of a world-building connoisseur, I guess. In these 40-odd pages, we are informed that not all that long ago, the vampires and werewolves rose up and took over the night (and in the werewolves' cases, part of the day). The "Pureblood" authorities don't even bother to try reining them in, so folks cower inside their houses every night, hoping their number doesn't come up. This, in the United States. (Somewhere. It could be anywhere in the U.S., as long as it's a city and basements are standard issue, because there is nothing in the text that identifies the location.) As I was saying, in the United States, the best-armed nation in the world outside of actual active war zones, we are asked to believe that supernatural creatures that are completely vulnerable during the day are able to run wild and uncontrolled. Ruling the night and all that. Nuh-uh. Sorry. Not buying it. The military, police, random citizens, and the CDC would all have a lot to say about it. Then there's the fact that we are also asked to believe that in this context, there is still gasoline for motorcycles, electricity, and all the accoutrements of modern life. I don't buy that either. The industrialized world has a 24-hour economy; take 8 hours or more out of it, add a terrorized populace, and things would totally fall apart. The fact that I don't care about the main character may be due partly to my trying to ignore these world-building flaws, but upon reflection I think it's also because the character comes across to me as flat, like a typical action-movie hero. The world-building, now that I think about it, is movie-level too - if everything moves fast enough, the viewer won't notice the flaws till it's over (and maybe not even then). It's not bad enough to deserve one star, but I'm not going to finish it or seek out the sequels. It's just not for me.

Eh, this is like Sarah Dessen lite. It had some good parts but the characters were really flat. The story wasn't compelling, even though the premise (in love with your best friends dead brother but can't tell her) was interesting. Also Frankie's word mistakes were annoying.

Ink and Bone is a fantastic page-turner that made me a new Lisa Unger fan. I can't believe that I haven't read her novels until now! This book keeps you reading from start to finish. It has those amazing ups and downs. It has those moments when you think the big resolution is about to happen, but then it's quickly taken away from you. I love those teasers! There is so much going on in this story that I'm not even sure where to begin. It's one of those novels that has multiple layers. It has the main storyline, a missing girl, Abbey, but it's also has multiple family dynamics that's going on under the surface that adds more depth. I love the storytelling and the characterization. When you're reading it, you feel that you're living the story instead of feeling as if an author is telling you a story. It takes a lot of talent for an author to write a novel, but remove herself from the story. The writing style makes all the difference. Sometimes an author will write something in the story that inadvertently tells the reader, hey, I'm still here. You never get that sense in this novel. Merri Gleason's daughter Abbey disappears while the family is staying in The Hollows, New York. The Hollows is almost a character, an evil one. On top of that, Merri's husband Wolf is a cheating bastard. She's desperate to find her daughter, but the police have searched extensively for her with no luck. She doesn't believe in psychics, but she's willing to try anything. Detective Jones Cooper has worked with psychics before, although he's a nonbeliever. He's worked with Eloise in the past, but Eloise recommends her granddaughter Finley for this particular assignment. Finley second-guesses her abilities constantly, but she feels like something is pulling her towards certain investigations. She accompanies Jones a few times, but she's not sure which vision belongs to which investigation. It's all a big jumbled mess in her head. She's covered in tattoos that represent her visions, all inked by Rainer, a man she loves, but also wants to avoid. Poppa is the creepiest and best-developed character in this novel. Calling him mentally disturbed is an understatement. He and Momma are so demented and unhinged that for a moment you think they can only be characters, but then you remember that there really are screwed up people in this world who are like them. Their daughter Penny died and Momma never recovered from the loss. I don't want to give too much away, but there's so much more I'd love to say about them. This novel has addictive qualities that keep you reading. I couldn't wait to find out what happened to Abbey. I love that moment when you find out how a novel got its title. It gave me goosebumps, especially since the title is mentioned in the last paragraph before the epilogue. If you love psychological thrillers, you'll want to read this one. Blog | Facebook | Twitter

Kitty Norville is a twenty-something girl with past guy issues, a distant relationship with her mother, and no female friends. In the course of living her everyday life, she somehow manages to threaten the bad guys and earn the attention/respect of the good guys. And, oh yeah ~ these guys are sexy, and Kitty likes to wear sweats & grungy jeans. Sound familiar? Of course it does. Kitty and the Midnight Hour is not that different from so many other UF novels on the shelves right now. Although I didn't despise this book, I doubt I'll continue with the series. First, we really don't get a feel for Kitty other than what I mentioned in the above paragraph. What does she look like? What does she do? All we know is that she hosts a radio show and helps the good guys while butting heads with the bad guys. Again, been there, done that. Well, except for the radio show. And that unique aspect of this story is what makes it most unbelievable for me. Kitty's radio show is, of course, called The Midnight Hour. It is a call in show to discuss all things paranormal (with a heavy preference for weres and vamps) and airs once a week from 12am-4am on public radio. As in NPR. I won't go in to a long rant here, other than to say I'm not buying it. NPR? Not likely. What, does that make Kitty smarter? More convincing? Apparently, because when she admitted on air that she is a werewolf, people believe her. Gee Paw, if the girl says she's a mythological beast, she must be telling the truth, right? It's never 100% clear whether weres & vamps are "out of the closet" in the beginning of the novel. You get the idea they aren't. But Kitty's radio show gets them all sorts of attention. Uh huh. Cause her show is so different from all of the other Art Bell's, George Noory's , and other people who believe in the paranormal. But I said I wouldn't go into a rant. Had this book been published when the market wasn't already saturated with so many other UF novels, I might have been more excited about it. But Kitty and the Midnight Hour has the misfortune of being so similar to other (and frankly better) series. The book isn't bad, but it's not great. And it's not unique enough, nor am I emotionally invested enough to want to continue right away. Yeah, I'll add the second book to my TBR, because sometimes I feel that a series needs at least two books to really get going. Just like the pilot episode of a tv show isn't fantastic, sometimes the "pilot" book isn't so great either. So I'll give this one a second chance. Eventually. Probably.

Orphan Train tries to put a face on the process. It's a good book well-researched and told. The connection between the modern teen and the aged survivor is crafted to connect that far away time to today. The development of the protagonists is good, if stereotypical. In fact, all the characters suffer from two-dimensional characters. The various men and people of faith especially suffer from formulaic characterization. Quibble: several anachronisms. I love Attack on Titan,but one scene that really irked me is Hannes' death. Eren already watched the smiling Titan kill his mom the first volume and now that Hannes decided to fight, he gets killed right off the bat while Eren sits and watches. I know a lot of people don't like Eren because of his indecisiveness and whining, but that never really bothered me until this volume. Eren knew Hannes didn't stand a chance, but he just sat there feeling sorry for himself. Other than that this was a pretty good volume that left me wanting more. I know the author is trying to draw out his story and keep us interested, but we still know nothing! Where's Eren's dad? How did the Titans get created? 4.5 Stars This regency romance is a lot of fun, and sweet at the same time. It's a really good mix of fluffy romance with a lot of heart and tender feeling as well. Will is really a different sort of hero, which a good thing. He's so ordered and punctual almost to a fault. I really liked this side of his personality, especially when we get to know why exactly he acts that way. At the same time, he can be very very cold, especially to Juliette, which isn't so good. However, there is one point where we really understand where he's coming from, when he admits his true feelings for himself as well as why he covers them so much, and it is just absolutely heartbreaking. He has to do a lot of apologizing to Juliette, but he does find a way to apologize, and he definitely redeems himself. Juliette is the perfect contrast to Will, she is such a free spirit. I love that this aspect of her character isn't watered down. She really is pretty reckless, it's not like she says she's reckless, but then in reality she's just a cultured 'miss' of the ton. The author does a really great job with both characters and makes them both interesting to read about and unique from the norm in historical romance. They butt heads quite a bit, and it is really fun to read about. Overall, a fun regency romance with a lot of heart and two unique and likable leads. ARC sent by publisher in exchange for honest review reviewed for http://inthehammockblog.blogspot.com

Yeah no. I tried, I really did. The love triangle has literally suffocated my interest in this series entirely. The constant "pick me, pick me" of the love triangle only reinforced my feelings about Evie's strong reliance in the attractive men around her. She identifies so strongly with how she loves Jack and Aric, and yet when it comes down to choosing, she automatically goes back to Jack because that's who she loved first. After she spends 90% of the book agonizing over the decision. In my opinion I find both of them to be kind of garbage characters that are constantly trying to rationalize their actions. It's the apocalypse and you're playing a game 'to the death' against 18 super powered people now (something like that, I lost count), how do you even find time to worry about your romantic life? Priorities. OKAY. Not a lot happened in this book. Stuff happened but we didn't experience any massive time jumps. I literally skimmed over half of this book because I was waiting for the plot to physically move along. That cliffhanger? Predictable and pretty easy to see through the deception. 1.5 stars, because I honestly couldn't contain the constant eye rolling and the awful love triangle.

Once again R.S. Grey proved to me that she is the queen of romantic comedies. The Foxe & the Hound is laugh out loud and delightful book. Must read for summer times and really all times! I don't exaggerate if I write that the dog stole the show. The heroine, Madeline adopted a small and furry puppy, and named him, Mouse. A puppy that was growing with rapid pace and became difficult to keep in check dog. But still a beloved friend. In fact, our heroine is also a mess. She is trying to make a good live for herself and raise her adorably dog. A dog who collided with a stranger on the street who turned out to be her new, handsome vet. Adam Foxe ended a longtime relationship and moved from the big city to a small town somewhere in Texas. He's starting a new job, and wants to be closer to his family, but he has trouble adjusting. And now he meets this crazy girl with a crazy dog, who intrigues him, but it is a totally wrong time for a new relationship. It is light, with only a hint of tension, and so funny story. They have their sweet and sexy moments. And despite the small perturbations that will take away your smile for a moment, it is just a delightful reading. ARC kindly provided for an honest review. The first in a new series by Katie Ashley shows a new side to her writing. This is a high octane, intense, gritty view into the heart of an MC set in a small town. The scenes where they play together and study together, amid all the danger, bring a peace to the story that makes it very well rounded. This review originally appeared on Heroes and Heartbreakers. After receiving a copy of The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight a few months ago for review, and really enjoying it, I was excited to try more work by this author so I was excited when I happened to come across it on NetGalley and even more excited when my request got accepted. However, no matter how much I wanted to like this book, I just couldn't and I did struggle to finish it. Right from the start I had problems. I just couldn't connect with the characters or their situation and I found the story was too jumpy. I never really felt the author developed scenes which in turn led to a lack of emotions, plot and relationships. There just wasn't enough detail for me and it led to me not caring either way about what happened to the characters--even the parts that could have been emotional were either ended abruptly to jump scenes or were just bland with hardly any depth. I hate saying this as I really like the author's style in the first book I read by her and I had none of these problems. However, by 15% I was already thinking about giving up on The Geography of You and Me. The only thing that kept me reading was the hope of it getting better because I've read the author's previous work. Sadly though, by the time it became obvious it wasn't going to pick up, I had to finish it out of necessity because I had spent so much time on it already--in fact I wish I had given up because the book became even more jumpy and disjointed towards the end. I just felt there was no consistent flow to follow and that the overall plot was lost on mini tangents that to me had no relevance. I'm not sure what else I can say about this book really as the only word that comes to mind is bland as it drew no emotions from me whatsoever--not even anger or frustration. I just found myself not caring for the characters or the story and I never got into the book; I'm not sure why, it just didn't happen. This won't stop me reading the author's other work, I just hope they are more like The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight.
