I don't normally write pre-reviews but I feel like this needs to be adressed. I am currently in the middle of reading this book, while I have pdf document of Twilight open on my laptop so technically I am reading two books at once (GAHHHH it's massive, my kindle version is 13000 locations long! That's longer than The Final Empire). Why I want to read this is because I want to see how much of the backlash is truly deserved. I'm not one for defending Twilight, I still think it is pretty shitty and it goes against feminist principles. HOWEVER! Being closed minded to a potential re-written version of Twilight that might actually make if not the story at least the readability of the book better is not the way to go about this. In my honest opinion, this idea of genderbending Twilight should not be discredited. If it is Meyer's way of redeeming herself from the God awful Twilight book, I dunno how it can be a bad thing. Yes it is basically fan fiction, and yes it's still Stephanie Meyer writing it, and yes, it's the same story all over again and YES it may not do well in dismantling every element Meyer created that went against feminist beliefs. But it can also be a step up from Twilight. And I can come with a few examples of the top of my head: - Beau is more of an opinions guy than Bella, who always complained about everything when we got into her mind - Beau is a handyman and may also show signs of having a potential job, which gives him more responsabilities than Bella ever had (though this might not rub well with feminists either, because by changing how well Bella fares, Meyer may be suggesting that boys are active and girls are reactive (thanks Misuki and Andre for the observations)) - I personally don't see it that way though, I see it as an improvement - Beau doesn't whine about everything around him, this makes him a tad more sympathetic than Bella - the purple prose is dumbed down in this book, instead of using over complicated words and unnecessary adjectives and adverbs the text is more often than not to the point. - we get some interesting sense of confusion with his name and an actual backstory to why he prefers Beau to Beauford (which made me chuckle btw) - he also displays some troubles with his being really tall. This was only in the first chapter. I will give my full thoughts on it when I do manage to finish it, I'm at the second chapter! (sheesh)

Mild spoilers ahead, I will warn you in each line before giving them. I'm going to ignore all the hub-bub the negative reviews give about this being a Twilight rip-off because A/ all YA paranormal fantasy I've heard about since Twilight's release is as well (note those I've heard about, not every single one) B/I don't beleive it intentional because to be honest you pick any two books in the same genre and you can come across similarities eg, 'The Wheel of Time' vs 'The Belgariad' both have farm boys forced to leave their farms by dark forces only to discover their own magical power, and also feature a woman from back home who has incredible magical power and a red-headed princess as a possible love interest. See what I did there? And that was with only five minutes thought on books I last read years ago. So to sum up, not paying attention to it because I DON'T CARE. Now onto the actual book review. I read this book based on a four star review from a book blog I like/respect. That and the cover art caught me. I became even more enamoured when I heard the writer was discovered online. The dreamer in me desires that so I felt obliged to get the book despite having already spent my book alowance on manga. I enjoyed the fact that the book was set in Ireland and really loved that there were Celtic myths woven in. However I would have liked some more mythos personally or to see the realtionship more closely bound to a myth, but that's personal taste. I loved the fact the school system in Ireland seems to be very similar to the Australian system and it made me nostalgic for those good old school days. I like that the author pointed out these differences to show Megan (the protagonist) was American in a foreign country. What makes it impossible for me to give this book anything more than three stars is the relationship between Megan and Adam. Yes you saw it coming, I had no problem with that, what I struggled with was the fact I couldn't connect with their romance. I thrive on romance in a book. A good couple in a book/tv show/ movie will keep me watching/reading even when other plot points are falling apart because as much as I may deny it I LIVE for romance. Megan and Adam were not that couple for me. I couldn't feel the love. At all. Normally I'll enjoy a giddy feeling at the moment of confession and anticipation for the first kiss and if it goes further well I'm not complaining ;p However very quickly I got bored with the PDA's all over the place and even the private expressions bored me. Yes, bored me. I skipped paragraphs wasted on what should have been passion. I skim read some pages to avoid getting bogged down in it. I gave a few pieces a try to see if I could catch the spark but the last page (literally) was the only page I liked the romance on. Perhaps it's because I'm nearly thirty and reading a book aimed at teens and maybe teen romance doesn't thrill me anymore and I'm happy if you think that and want to give the book a try. The end felt a bit rushed, like she realised she needed some action to end the book with and I hate that she leads us into the book with a snippet of said action but when you get to the action it only lasts a few pages. Then again I hate when books lead you in with a snippet of the action near the end of the book regardless of the book. Start your book in medias res a different way people! /rant, sorry. I will give Fallon props that Megan has appropriate injuries after the action with (mild spoilers) a puffy swollen face, stitches and burns on her hands. I hate it when characters come out of danger unscathed and she obliged me by wounding her heroine. Overall I feel the book lacked the romance needed to pull off a paranormal romance. Their love felt farcical to me. However I did like the writing itself and the ideas of (SPOILERS AGAIN) people being bred like animals to propagate a line of people able to carry the magic and linking genetics with magic. I think teens would better connect with the romance and thus this book in general.

** spoiler alert ** I liked this book enough to recommend it as a "good book", but it had some issues. The story idea was fabulous. The book was fun, engaging and entertaining... for the first 2/3 of the book. Then it climaxed a little early and sort of fizzled as there was nothing left to tell. Wacky story arc. In the end, the characters basically come to the realization that they were unhappy with their former lives, knew what they needed to do to make themselves happy but refused to do it, but after gaining lifetimes of experience they were able to finally make that leap of faith into a happier life. Gumdrops and rainbows all around. Despite the happy (and long-time-coming) ending, there was some genuine emotional torment for the characters, and it made them more interesting and likable. My biggest peeve with the book is the misplaced sex. It read like some of Heinlein's more jarring works, where the story is moving along and then all of a sudden there's a hot-and-heavy sex scene that seems totally out of place. It made sense in some places as the characters were discovering themselves and living lives fueled by drugs and sex, but the scene in the train? What was with that? It was so incredibly disorienting that it's the main thing I'm taking away from the book, and that's a shame. It could have been much better with a little bit of editing for story flow.

Argh this review got deleted ! Sorry to repost guys. "We die a little every day and by degrees we're reborn into different men, older men in the same clothes, with the same scars." Oopsy another unpopular opinion from me *evil cackle*. Firstly I must start this review by saying this book was extremely overhyped imo. Everyone raves on about how great this book is, but to be honest it was just okay for me. I once again went into this book with high expectations as I did with Prince of Thorns and once again I've been left wondering what all the hype was about. Hype is a very bad thing. Seriously like FUCK THE HYPE (it's misleading & terrible). I don't know if it's just me but everytime I read something by Mark Lawrence, I feel the book is missing something. Please don't get me wrong Mark Lawrence is a brilliant writer and very talented, I love his no bullshit style and I think Jorg is an extremely quotable character, however some things in his books just didn't add up or were left unexplained. I won't go into details because of spoilers but that ending was fucking shit. Sorry. Why wasn't anything explained? Why does Jorg always get out of ridiculous situations? Why is it so unrealistic? Honestly I have no answers to my own questions and it's bothering me. Yep I want to swallow glass and die after this book BECAUSE IT ANNOYED ME. Some random ass shit happened and everything is left unexplained so I'm really confused about everything, I also hate magic systems that don't have repercussions, it's just so unrealistic. For me this book has more cons then pros, but I did enjoy it. The story itself lacked a lot of gore and action which the first book possessed and I found the plot kinda boring, it's basically about Jorg trying to take over an empire and anyone who stands in his way will die. Sounds awesome ? Yeah I no. But it was very mellow basically this book was Jorg looking for artefacts. ZZzzzz. However I did enjoy some components of this story, Jorg is my demented hero that I love with every inch of my black heart, seriously I feel guilty for loving him so much. "A Dark time comes. My time. If it offends you. Stop Me." Back to the bad stuff, another major issue I had in this book, I feel this isn't a spoiler more a warning but this book did have an animal torture scene. Yep I got the beef about it... Hollywood say "don't shoot a puppy" for a reason. I felt offended by the torture scene it was so unnecessarily disgustingly descriptive and disturbing, I felt it went abit too far, but hey when reading grimdark you want to be shocked and disgusted I just didn't imagine that type of scene and kinda really wish I didn't read it, seriously where the fuck is the eye bleach at ? this book is very unique and definitely left a huge impression on me which wasn't very good. However it wasn't enough to stop me from reading this. I read grim dark for a reason and that's to be shocked and to be offended. So if you don't have a hardened heart this book is definitely not for you. The plot is so intriguing, I couldn't get enough. The story is very dark and when I say dark I honestly mean it, it has basically no relief definitely lacking humour and the romance is actually FUCKED UP. This book is actually kinda scary but in an awesome way. I love having goosebumps and feeling creeped out, I think Mark Lawrence does a wonderful job of weaving together interesting and compelling ideas that have you on the edge of your seat, it has the right amount of everything (except of course animal torture, I could do without). It is pretty much the bible of badassery if it was better explained but most importantly it's realistic with grey characters and Jorg defines the word 'anti-hero'. The plot is extremely complex, I must admit I was really confused at times due to the POV switching back and forth from four years earlier to present. I hate first person POV, it's a peeve. I want to secretly burn all first person POV books because i hate it. I don't know how to rate or review this book because I loved and hated it at the same time so I'm just gonna say it's average. I love Mark Lawrence's writing style, I love his beautiful sentences, I love his complex characters. I'm so taken by the interesting main character Jorg Ancarth. Seriously, I can't even cope with myself when I read about him. Some of the background characters especially Sir Makin stole my heart. He is definitely a genius when it comes to writing characters. Most of the plot was interesting, a lot of parts ending up being flat for me but it was intriguing and different. If you have read this book I recommend going to google and looking at the beautiful fan art, it is all so beautiful. The covers also give me heart eyes, I LOVE THEM. I recommend this book to lovers of grimdark and anti-heroes. All you vegetarians and animal activist should stay away. Definitely will continue with this series but I'm not in a rush. Ratings; Prince of Thorns - 3.5/5 King of Thorns - 3.5/5 Total rating for the series so far - 7/10

** spoiler alert ** I really enjoyed "One of Us is Lying"! It was very fast paced and I probably could've read it in one sitting if I really tried. Although the writing was meh--there were a few blips here and there that I would change--overall, I really enjoyed this one. I was taking notes throughout the entirety of this wild journey and figured the whole thing out less than one hundred pages in (spoilers btw): pg 88- BEFORE I THOUGHT IT WAS JAKE CAUSE I HATE THAT POSSESSIVE CONTROLLING ASSHOLE BUT NOW I'M THINKING ITS SIMON HE PLANNED THE WHOLE THING AND HE KEPT THE HOT GOSS SECRET FOR SO LONG AND DID THE PHONE PRANK CAUSE HE WAS SAD AND FOR THE D R A M A Very eloquent notes from Julia once again. Though I solved the mystery early on, I wouldn't call this a predictable read--when the big reveal came I felt satisfied, not let down, y'know? I also really enjoyed reading about all of the characters! At first the whole different POVs felt kind of weird, but it grew on me. I liked how we started and ended with Bronwyn, as it made the story come full-circle quite nicely. Moreover, the relationships the characters formed with each other were so lovely; watching all of these completely different personalities bond was the best. Addy was probably my favourite in terms of development--she really pissed me off at the beginning but once Jake was gone, she truly stepped up to the plate. Her character development was just A+. She turned into the ultimate badass and I couldn't be happier about it. I don't have much else to say about "One of Us is Lying", other than that all the little pieces Karen M. McManus put into place came together perfectly. This gets a thumbs-up from me.

To be honest: I was bored and I really had no interest in finishing this book. The only reason I continued, was the fact that I buddy read this book and I didn't want to do that to my buddy. The last 1/3 of the book got a lot better, the story came together and the characters became a little more interesting, but by that time I was already annoyed and just wanted to finish the book. The characters are underdeveloped for the most part of the book, the magic system is just weird and as a reader you're pretty much left to figure it out on your own, using your imagination. This book just barely scraped a 3 star rating from me. Sure, it had its moments. It was cute at times and admittedly I giggled aloud once or twice. Plus, it took place in London! I was more interested in reading about the Globe and the Tate than anything else. First of all, I absolutely despised the main character. Julia was the type of protagonist that never ceases to infuriate me. She thinks she's better than everybody else, constantly judges those who don't reach her ridiculously high standards, and lives inside her completely fabricated fantasy world! I'm sorry, but there is no such thing as a MTB. Nor is it realistic for a girl to have a crush on three guys at once. At least, not in my personal experience. And the way the story wrapped up made me so friggin irritated! Julia spends literally half of the novel looking her nose down at her classmates! Like the fact that she reads classic novels and likes the Beatles and doesn't doll herself up makes her superior! Pretentious people, I find, are the most superficial. And Julia just SCREAMED pretentious. The entire time I just wanted to grab her and shake her, yell: GET OFF YOUR HIGH HORSE! The only character I even SORT OF grew to like throughout this book was Jason, though he often got on my nerves as well. Out of the handful of characters that were given to me, though? He's definitely a shining star. It was a shame the author didn't incorporate the side characters more into the story, or at least show them in a better light than Julia's twisted mind made them out to be. And yet, I gave this story 3 stars! I do this because as much as it irritated me and ground on my nerves, I still found myself enjoying it at times. It has some cute elements on it and a few moments that made me laugh out loud. Some of the situations Julia finds herself in are so completely ridiculous it ends up being very entertaining to watch it all unfold. So, despite my lack of interest in the main character and my issues with the love story, I maintain the statement that I did like this book. Just not as much as I wanted to, I guess. Would I recommend it? I wouldn't go as far as to say that.

***MAJOR SPOILER ALERT!!! I was more than a little disappointed in this book. The other two were very good I thought and I really felt for Katniss and the love triangle, the Hunger Games, the people in the Capitol, everything. This book, not so much. First of all I hate war books. Books where there is some fighting sure, but when the whole country is at war and the story reads more like the evening news doing a play by play of whose winning, I tune out and lose interest. Then Katniss spends the majority of the book either in shock, crazy, medicated, or hiding from everyone. Gale has become a killing machine and Peeta has quite literally gone insane. Then the ending was awful. The final scene with the parachutes was incredibly disturbing, as was the knowledge of who gave that command. Then at the very end we're just supposed to be happy with her going back to 12 alone, eventually marrying Peeta (whom we hope is cured and doesn't relapse and kill her in her sleep), Gale gets a "fancy job in District 2" and there's a mass grave in her meadow. I honestly can't think of a single part of this book that I found enjoyable. Even the resolution of the love triangle was tragic and disturbing rather than romantic and fulfilling. I now regret making my book club read yet another futuristic dystopian society teen novel next month directly after this. So...sorry! Oh, one thing I did like was the quote about how the people in the capitol had given up their interest/voice in politics in exchange for food and entertainment. I think that was directed at our society.

I requested this because it seemed right up my alley - a thriller that features a character who a) has, in a strange turn of events, "reconnected" with a childhood friend of hers who was abducted as a young teen and, as a result of this abduction, has been lying in a hospital for decades with severe brain damage and b) is an alcoholic. Not sure if a) and b) are connected, because I didn't get far in the book. If you know me, you know how much I love thrillers and police procedurals. In books like this, the alcoholic investigator (official or amateur) is a huge trope (in Lawrence Block's Scudder books, The Girl on the Train, Jimmy McNulty in The Wire, Harry Hole in the Jo Nesbo books, Jane Tennyson in Prime Suspect, and the list goes on and on and on...) I see why main characters are given a flaw like this -- it humanizes them and puts their job at risk and typically works very well in this kind of story. But maybe too many of these books downplay (or even romanticize?) alcoholism, because when I got to the part where the main character in Try Not to Breathe has to put on some Depends* when she starts drinking because she knows she'll black out and wet her bed, I just couldn't read on. That may be accurate but ... I just can't. Life is depressing enough, thanks. I can see that others on Goodreads have enjoyed this, but not sure I can continue reading. Anyone out there who could get past the Depends? *It's a British book, so she uses something called DryNites which seems to be a British bed-wetting product. Can I read book this out of series order? No, you really can't. This story wraps up the story of Cat's heritage, answers questions I didn't even know I had and shows how far Cat and Bones relationship has progressed. Did the ending make you feel happy? Yes. The ending was not one I predicted, nor one I thought I would want, but I think it was perfect to what is the ending of their love story. Is Bones's still dreamy? I wanted to punch Bones at multiple points in this book. The one thing I respected in this series is Jeaniene Frost's consistency of character; there is no massive character change to either of them because they fell in love, they stayed the same, and it was who they were that got them through all the shit that love brought with it. Bones is a selfish bastard and what he wants, with no apologies and no excuses, is only to keep Cat safe. Is everyone in it? Yup, the whole gang. When I first heard about Slide, my thoughts went straight to Lisa McMann's WAKE. While I believe it would appeal to fans of this series, Slide is a very different creature. I've heard quite a few favourable comparisons to Veronica Mars, and it deserves them. I can see the similarities: we have a smart, snarky protagonist, sharp witty dialogue, murder, mystery, and some pretty dark issues for a YA audience. But Slide is not derivative and, rather than being predictable, kept me guessing to the end. Exciting and fresh, Slide is utterly gripping and a total page turner. I loved this book. Can I just say Slide has some of the best cover copy I've ever read. I'd normally try and give you a quick synopsis of a book from my POV. But this? It sums it up perfectly. Are you hooked yet? Excited? Guys. You should be. I liked Vee immediately. Her open and friendly voice and unique personality (and situation) make her fun to read. From her pink hair, to her atypical taste in music (read: awesome taste in music), she's different, she's not your typical teenager. Somehow, where Vee could easily have felt contrived, she didn't once come across this way. To me, Vee felt real, and I loved her for being herself. This is a girl who's suffered a lot in her life. She should be jaded, but she doesn't feel that way. She knows more than she'd like to about the nature of the people around her, and this, combined with the loss of her mother, and an absent father, have forced her to grow up. She cares deeply about her sister, Mattie, while not approving of the path she's been taking, and despite knowing what they are capable of, has a great deal of empathy for the people around her. It's the murder of Sophie, Mattie's best friend, that kickstarts the mystery driving the story of Slide. So many clues and threads, and pieces of information kept me guessing, and, like Vee, I truly didn't know who to trust. Jill Hathaway has nailed the pacing of this book, and knows when to move it along; speeding it up, or slowing it down for a quiet, tender, human interaction. It's enthralling. Riveting mystery and storyline aside, one of the things I loved most about Slide was the cast of characters, and the human interactions. Vee's love and concern for her sister shines through in their tender scenes together. The tension between Vee and her best friend, Rollins, is palpable. My heart broke a little when I discovered a secret Rollins has been keeping of his own. I kept wishing that each one would reach out, and take a gamble on trusting one another. You could feel Vee's ache for her father's presence and support, and the need their broken little family had for him to be there. As the book progresses, characters like mean-girl cheerleader, Amber, and jock, 'Scotch', develop personality (for good or bad). I came to care for characters I didn't even like, as Vee's caring pulled me in. Slide has a perfect balance of funny and sad, touching and terrifying, and truly tender and sweet moments. On top of this, Slide is beautifully written. Vee's left-of-field images and descriptions are gorgeously realised, her voice unique and refreshing. Hathaway shines a writer. Slide, again like Veronica Mars, deals with some pretty heavy issues: suicide, substance use, date rape, death, loss and grief. These issues are handled well, but I could see some concerns with Vee popping caffeine pills like they're candy, instead of her prescribed narcolepsy medication. I understand why, and none of these activities are glamorized. In fact, I thought these issues are all handled well, but, for these reasons, this book is clearly for older teens. Simply put, Slide is everything I want from a book. Gripping and thrilling, exciting and achingly beautiful. It dragged me in and made me feel. From page one, Hathaway had me in her thrall and still, with the last page turned, hasn't let me go. This book left me very split. My first reaction to it was hesitancy. I wasn't really sure I felt okay with a white woman portraying a black woman facing modern day racism. Which this feeling still holds true. I have only ever interacted with Jodi Picoult as an author that the white, Christian women that I was surrounded with growing up were obsessed with. I have never really experienced any person of color talking her praise. Now, I'm aware that this is unfair of me to hold her readers against her but this was what I was feeling to start. Then as I read, I felt a little less queasy about it as I saw that Ruth seemed like a real person that I actually know. BUT, I was still annoyed that the main interaction of racism was with a white supremacist. Obviously, these people still exist in our society but it is openly shunned and I feel like the systematic racism in America would have been the bigger story. Thankfully, Jodi eventually does address this even though I found it to be a little too on the nose. As the story progressed, I did find an easier time in reading it although I started to find Ruth to not be as real as I found her to be in the first 100 pages. I also felt like the outcome of the book was wholly unrealistic. I didn't think that the twist or the outcome of the trial or the epilogue were realistic AT ALL. Call me a pessimist but there's no way that the charges against Edison would have been dropped, that Turk would have changed completely and now does talks regarding hate and that Judge Thunder would have acquitted Ruth completely. I also thought it unlikely that Edison would have gotten into Yale considering how much he skipped school as well as the arrest (although I know he wasn't charged) wasn't erased from his permanent record. I found the ending to be so unrealistic that it actually brought my rating down from a 4 to a 3. Despite all my critiques, I did enjoy it enough to not just drop the book and I think that this is a great first start to a discussion on modern day racism to all those white women who are her readers. And to her credit, Jodi addresses her privilege and limited POV in the Author's note.

*Please note: The quotes used below are taken from an Advanced Review Copy of the book. The content may differ in the actual published version. When I began reading 'Shatter Me' I wasn't too sure what to expect. It helped that only two of my fellow Goodreaders had read the book, one who loved it and one who didn't love it, so I went into it feeling fairly neutral and open minded. I will say here and now that I was absolutely hooked from the very first line. This review will be a long one - there are so many passages that gripped me, and I want to share them with you. Tahereh Mafi has such a beautiful writing style - it was lyrical, so different and unique and utterly original. I loved the way she was able to convey Juliette's conflicting emotions, you know, head versus heart, or "this is what they tell you but this is how it is", with the way she struck out words or lines, for example; It's a home, a center for troubled youth, for neglected children from broken families, a safe house for the psychologically disturbed. It's a prison. The way she described emotions and feelings by comparing them to nature conjured up some gorgeous imagery, and she did it in such a great way, constantly leaving me entranced. A couple of examples; The sun drops into the ocean and splashes browns and reds and yellows and oranges into the world outside my window. A million leaves from a hundred different branches dip in the wind, fluttering with the false promise of flight. The gust catches their withered wings only to force them downward, forgotten, left to be trampled by the soldiers stationed just below. I step into the slight breeze and clutch a fistful of wind as it weaves its way through my fingers. Bliss unlike anything I've ever known. The air is crisp and cool. A refreshing bath of tangible nothing that stings my eyes and snaps at my skin. The sun is high today, blinding as it reflects the small patches of snow keeping the earth frozen. My eyes are pressed down by the weight of the bright light and I can't see through more than just two slits, but the warm rays wash over my body like a jacket fitted to my form, like the hug of something greater than a human. I could stand in this moment forever. For one infinite second I feel free. Sometimes sentences are long and without commas which I had initially thought was a grammatical oversight, however I was quick to realise it was just a tool to allow the reader to grasp Juliette's reactions and better understand her emotions. Words were repeated when she's nervous, excited, scared etc. His lips his lips his lips his lips his lips (go figure which of the three this is, ha!) I think this is something that readers are going to either love or hate. I personally am for the former, I just felt as though it made Juliette feel that much more real, it was clever. Everything flows, the transitions are easy, I just couldn't get enough of it. When we are first introduced to Juliette, she is broken. She has been kept locked away, in solitary confinement, for 264 days. She was trying to help an innocent person and despite her good intentions, they ended up dead. She feels so alone, her thoughts are filled with sorrow and fear - my heart broke for her. Despite everything she's been through, though, she's so good. She doesn't hate, yes, she's confused, but she is still so human. She doesn't wallow in self pity, she just wants change. She wants to love. She wants to feel wanted. I always wonder about raindrops. I wonder about how they're always falling down, tripping over their own feet, breaking their legs and forgetting their parachutes as they tumble right out of the sky toward an uncertain end. It's like someone is emptying their pockets over the earth and doesn't seem to care where the contents fall, doesn't seem to care that the raindrops burst when they hit the ground, that they shatter when they fall to the floor, that people curse the days the drops dare to tap on their doors. I am a raindrop. Sometimes I think the loneliness inside of me is going to explode through my skin and sometimes I'm not sure if crying or screaming or laughing through the hysteria will solve anything at all. Sometimes I'm so desperate to touch to be touched to feel that I am almost certain I'm going to fall off a cliff in an alternate universe where no one will ever be able to find me. It doesn't seem impossible. I've been screaming for years and no one has ever heard me. The world is flat. I know because I was tossed right off the edge and I've been trying to climb back up for seventeen years but it's nearly impossible to beat gravity when no one is willing to give you a hand. When no one wants to risk touching you. As you would expect, there is, of course, a bad guy here. His name is Warner. He's evil, he's manipulative, he's sleazy. His father is the leader of a group called The Reestablishment - the group who have taken control of the population, the food, resources and government. The Reestablishment had come in guns blazing, taking over in an effort to convince the masses that their way was the only way to survive. Without much else to do and having little way to fight back, society crumbled - what with diseases destroying the population, food being hard to find, the absence of birds that fly, and clouds that are the wrong color. Warner believes that by 'saving' Juliette from a life in a cell, by convincing her to help him torture trouble makers, he will gain better control over the people. He is cold and harsh and craves power. Everything a bad guy should be. The thing is, he's 19 and incredibly good looking. If you weren't so repulsed by him, you'd be attracted to him. I personally hated the guy. As the book progressed though, his layers (if you will) are peeled back and you begin to understand him and the reason for his actions better. I actually ended up feeling a little sorry for him. His glassy green eyes glint in my direction. "Are you not hungry?" Words dipped in sugar. His gloved hand touches my wrist and I nearly sprain it in my haste to distance myself from him. I could eat every person in this room. "No, thank you." He licks his bottom lip into a smile. "Don't confuse stupidity for bravery, love. I know you haven't eaten anything in days." Something in my patience snaps. "I'd really rather die than eat your food and listen to you call me love," I tell him. "I like my clothes," I tell him. I'd like to punch you in the eye, is what I don't tell him. Warner's smile slides back into place. "No one asked you what you like, love. Now eat. I need you to look your best when you stand beside me." I'm very interested to see where things go with him in book 2. Of course, what good is a young adult book these days without a swoon worthy male? Cue Adam Kent. Adam is a complex individual, with a past as emotional and upsetting as Juliette's. He's gorgeous, sensitive, toned and tough. He's compassionate and caring and has secrets of his own. He and Juliette have a past, not the kind you may think. I don't want to delve into it as it was such an emotional story, revealed in bits and pieces, something that I want everyone else to have the opportunity to learn themselves. Two tips of two fingers graze my cloth-covered shoulder for less than a second and every muscle every tendon in my body is fraught with tension and tied in knots that clench my spine. I stay very still. I don't move. I don't breathe. Maybe if I never move, this feeling will last forever. I open my eyes and he's standing right in front of me. My heart is a field of lilies blooming under a pane of glass, pitter-pattering to life like a rush of raindrops. His jaw is as tights as his eyes as tight as his fists as tight as the strain in his arms. "You've always known?" Three whispered words and he's broken my dam, unlocked my lips and stolen my heart all over again. I can hardly feel the tears streaming down my face. I stare at the strength in his jaw, in his eyes, in his body. I try to understand the confidence he has in who he thinks I am and realise his reassurance is the only thing stopping me from diving into a pool of my own insanity. He's always believed in me. Even soundlessly, silently, he fought for me. Always. I honestly loved this book. I cannot wait for more, I mean, the ending was great but wow! Hurry up book 2! Such a great debut for Tahereh Mafi, I can hardly believe that it is only her first published book. ARC issued by Allen & Unwin

This book was fantastic! It was intense and slow at some points, but overall, I can't say many negative things about it. The descriptions were beautiful without being boring and the magical system had a logic set of rules, while at the same time maintaining an aura of uncontrollableness... I guess it could be said that the whole book felt like a build up to something. Like nothing really impactful was actually happening. Though, that's not true, since every detail in it is important for the story, but it feels that way because of the way it's written, with Kvothe telling his story (and in my opinion, choosing deliberately to tell the much lighter parts that paint him in a good light). Not many really dark things happen in this book, especially not if you compare it to other fantasy tomes of the likes of Game of Thrones. Which is a good thing for me - in that sense, this book is kind of like a breath of fresh air. My (probably) only problem with this book was the lack of strong/interesting female characters. "The world does not deliver meaning to you. You have to make it meaningful...and decide what you want and need and must do. It's a tough, unimaginably lonely and complicated way to be in the world. But that's the deal: you have to live." On Beauty is a novel of keen observation that unfolds slowly, offers humor and tender insight along the way, and bonds firmly the reader to characters by its close. Told in three parts, the original source of central tension between Howard Belsey and his wife Kiki has already occurred when the story begins: an affair with a colleague puts Howard on trial for his devotion to a marriage of 30 years. Howard, an Englishman and professor at a small New England college, is in many ways the opposite to his bold, curvaceous, African-American wife Kiki ("He was bookish, she was not; he was theoretical, she political. She called a rose a rose. He called it an accumulation of cultural and biological constructions circulating around the mutually attracting binary poles of nature/artifice"). They have three children: Jerome; sensitive and spiritual; Zora, outspoken and zealous; and Levi, street-cool and big-hearted. The novel follows the Belseys over the course of a year, zooming in on each character's search for self-reckoning and a voice to claim. Zadie Smith's astute writing, splashed with clever humor, draws out the human narrative through connecting the individual to the universal, touching on identity, race, culture, academia, politics, relationship, and a motif of the beautiful and true vs. the ugly and inauthentic. A parallel glance is given to the Kipps family, with whom the Belseys seem to be inexorably connected through academic competition (Monty vs. Howard) and romantic pursuits (Jerome vs. Veronica vs. Howard). Interestingly, the matriarchs (Kiki and Carlene) break down this familial nemesis with genuine friendship. In other instances as well, Smith gives weight to the raw and real moments that emerge from places of surface or masked meaning. While parts of this novel felt slow to reveal, I found the third part to bring everything together in such a beautiful way that heightened my sense of appreciation for the way in which Smith introduces her characters and tells a story where not much and yet everything happens.

Samantha moved to a new school to work with a better swim coach. She's still the new girl and still getting to know everyone. Her teammate, Zee, on whom she has been crushing for some time, invites her to a party but ends up making out with another girl right in front of her. Samantha decides to make him jealous by making out with his best friend Alex, who seems more interested in her than Zee. Suddenly, he can't breathe and they're calling an ambulance. He dies on the way to the hospital and now Samantha is the girl who killed Alex. Samantha was an interesting character to get to know. She seemed strong and confident, but struck me as a bit immature. After Alex's death, she punished herself much more than anyone else could. She became introverted and lost all confidence and refused to be persuaded that his death wasn't her fault. That aspect seemed a little out of character for her, when compared to the beginning of the story. I liked Zee, Samantha's crush, until he started making out with another girl. That was an asshat thing for him to do, and she seemed to forget about that part of the night rather quickly. Casper, who became interested in Samantha after that night, was a bit of a mystery to me (for a while). He was nice to her even after almost everyone else stopped speaking to her, but he could also be distant for no apparent reason. I loved Taylor, the one friend who stood by Samantha. She was nice and kind and there for Samantha no matter what. Samantha's dad and aunt were wonderful parents for her. It was nice to have a dad who's not only in the picture, but actually a very good dad! Aunt Allie was just quirky enough. The plot was interesting, and I liked the direction Janet Gurtler took with it. It's hard to imagine something as simple as a kiss causing someone's death, but she made it believable. There were facts and statistics, and they help you see how often something like this may actually happen. One part I really liked was that Samantha started to see a psychologist, which was a smart thing for her to do. We see some of the things he did to help Samantha through her guilt. One thing that bugged me about the story was that nobody ever called out Alex. Since he had such a severe allergy, I would think he might mention that to a girl before he started swapping spit. Maybe they never thought that was a concern, but surely his mother would wrestle with some guilt over not thinking about it? There are scenes of underage drinking and drug use. There's also a v-card losing situation, which was not at all graphic. The sum up: A cautionary tale filled with sadness and hope.

"War. Such a little word, such a depth of agony." "Liberty is valued only when it is threatened; therefore, it is the threat that highlights the value." Ugh! I wanted to like this book so much more than I did. There were sentences, even paragraphs that I found brilliant, such as the ones I quoted above. But overall, I just didn't connect with any of the characters, and therefore I just didn't get into the book. It's your basic storyline: different people converging toward the same place and point in time. Each character has their own goals and reasons for going to said place, but overall I wasn't that caught up in any one story. I can't fault any one thing in this book. The pacing was nice, action scenes were good and frequent enough, the world was built nicely, and the characters were fleshed out. As I mentioned, there were a few sentences that I loved and the writing was solid and at times beautiful. The dialog was ... how should I put this? Epic, maybe? They seemed grand, like something you'd hear in some old movie; Gone with the Wind, or something. I don't know how else to put it. Especially when we're in Druss's PoV. Which brings me to another point ... Oh, the horror of PoV changes. I actually didn't mind it was much as I usually do in books. Gemmell stayed with a character a lot longer than some of the others I've read. Still, it's jarring when you're in one character's head and then in another's the next paragraph without warning. I always find it an unpleasant experience unless the author gives me a heads up. I must say, I'd love to read a Gemmell book done in first person. Now, one thing that really turned me off pretty early on was the romance. Don't get me wrong, I like romance in my books. I do. But when it happens overnight, literally, I just can't get into it. I've said it before: if the characters have sex the first night they meet each other, super. If they feel some sort of connection, I can get behind that as well. After all, when I meet someone I can tell pretty early on if they're going to drive me crazy or if I'll be laughing with them by the end of the night. But professing undying love after one night? I just can't. After that moment, I admit I checked out. Now, I do understand that this is fantasy and we must suspend belief sometimes, but for some reason fast romance has always bothered me, no matter the genre. About those characters ... What can I say? They were developed, each having their quirks and flaws. I liked Rek right off the bat and was excited to hear his story, but the tone that started out faded a bit. I was more interested in his PoV than any others, but it still didn't drive me to keep reading. Druss is a character I liked, though I wasn't obsessed. His over-the-top badass-ness was kinda fun, but it did wear a bit the farther I read. I guess my tastes are changing over time. Had I read this ten years ago, I might have liked it more. Now, I like something a bit darker, grittier, or with a lot more humor. I can't fault Gemmell at all. He's a legend (ha...see what I did there), and I have massive amounts of respect for his career achievements. His writing was solid, his pacing great, his storytelling pleasant. It's just not the type of story I want to read these days. So overall, if you're into a bit more high fantasy, you'll likely really enjoy this. What started out as getting revenge on Kai, slowly turned into a series of online interactions between the two. Kai makes his living live streaming his gaming online for his thousands of subscribers. What we soon find out is that Kai is a bit of a recluse, possibly undiagnosed agoraphobia, and hasn't left his apartment except for a handful of times over three years. I guess, for the most part, talk about video games and all that is just boring to me. I don't play video games and it's just...not interesting. I also find it unrealistic that Garrett could do half the stuff he's getting away with while talking to Kai and almost no one finding out when he's on Base? Even the "sexy" scenes in the book were a little too much somehow and I found myself skimming through most of it. At first, their interactions were cute with the emails and the GChat, but the secondhand embarrassment I got from reading the two interact once the web cam parts started up should have been enough for me to put the book down earlier. I don't know, the book makes me uncomfortable. I just couldn't finish it even after the Garrett and Kai meet up in real life because I just couldn't find it in myself to care about either of the two characters and their problems. I know I'm in the minority on this one, since there are so many people who love it. I've loved all of Santino's other books, but in the end, this just really wasn't my kind of book.

Have you also checked out my fab interview with Jodi Picoult and Samantha van Leer? I'm so excited to share an early review of BETWEEN THE LINES with you for FTF! I've been looking forward to this novel for so long and was ecstatic to receive a copy early. I wasn't disappointed, either. BETWEEN THE LINES is everything I could want and more. I love books that are about books, and this one really left me thinking. What if characters really did have their own lives and personalities outside of the story? What if they were trapped and bored? What if the characters I write and bring to life resent the shape of the story they're acting in? It gave me a lot of food for thought. BETWEEN THE LINES weaves together three intersecting sections: One that features pages from a book entitled BETWEEN THE LINES, about a heroic prince named Oliver, complete with beautifully illustrated photographs, a second section in blue from the "real" Oliver's POV, and a third section in green from reader Delilah's POV. Oliver is a unique book character because he knows he's inside a story...and he's not content to remain there. He harbors no love for his princess in reality, but has fallen for a beautiful reader despite the fact that their worlds can never cross. Delilah, on the other hand, is an ordinary girl in our world. I loved seeing her talk about her homework and mentioning THE HUNGER GAMES, which is very current. Delilah isn't like the other girls at school and obsesses over a children's picture book, wishing characters such as Oliver could be real. When Delilah and Oliver find themselves able to communicate with one another, they try to find a way to be together in reality despite the odds stacked against them. If you were following me on Goodreads, you saw me sharing a lot of quotes I liked as I was reading (And looking at it now, my spelling is atrocious. I apologize and blame my cell phone with its itty-bitty keys!). The story is absorbing, and I loved the creative ways used to show that Oliver was in the book from the way his world bent, to the way he could interact with letters (It brought Disney's WINNIE THE POOH to mind!) to the way he viewed Delilah as she read the pages of the book. The novel was also gorgeously illustrated by Yvonne Gilbert and Scott M. Fischer. My favorites are an image of Oliver at the very beginning (Which is Delilah's favorite as well) and an illustration of Oliver with three mermaids because, well, you know how much I love mermaids! I also like the way smaller illustrations adorn the page such as when a bug moves from one world to the other. I can't wait to see the final version of these images. If you like novels about book characters such as INKHEART and STORYBOUND, you'll enjoy BETWEEN THE LINES. Even though the novel doesn't feature a court room or the hard-hitting moral issues Picoult has become famous for, her debut YA is fun and refreshing and well worth the read. I can't wait to see what Picoult and van Leer dream up together next!

Review By : Sarah W (grade 10) Grade Range: 9th grade and up (mainly because of high vocabulary use) Genre: Fantasy / Science Fiction Literary Merit: Very Good Characterization: Very Good Nix is back on her journey through the water, but this time with a new mission: to change the past. With her father's fate looming ahead of her she must make the decision to lead the rest of her life weeping for her long lost love like her father, or to take her fate in her own hands. She makes her decision and sets out to make it a reality, while Kashmir fights to make her realize that she has made the wrong one. Her voice of reason is seen in him, though with all the fighting whether or not they make it through this journey is a mystery in itself. As all of the characters fight through individual battles, their fates are inevitably laid in the hands of one man. The Ship Beyond Time is a fast paced novel that keeps you on your toes throughout the entire read. The inclusion of Kashmir's point of view adds missing information from the first book. This makes it an easier read that also makes more sense than The Girl from Everywhere and is better paced. One specific thing I loved about this book was how it handled the theory of time-travel. Whenever I read a book that includes time travel I am left pondering all the "what if's" that time travel includes. What if something changes in your future because you went back to the past? What if someone from the future recognizes you from when you visited in the past? The Ship Beyond Time answers all those questions in a logical manner that helps the reader be able to let go of their "what if's" and enjoy the book for the story it brings. The problematic characters have just the right mixture of bad and good morals for readers to both connect with the characters and form their own opinions on them based on the reader's own morals. Heilig captures the essence of the young but brave girl who has never been on her own to the core and shows the inner turmoil that is realistic for the situation. Heidi Heilig's writing allows readers to experience the story in their own individual way, making it worth reading, and rereading, as you grow and the meaning of your life changes. Recommendation: This is a good book that could relate to many teens and is worth a read. If you love adventures that keep you guessing this is the book for you.

4.5 stars I was pleasantly surprised with how this Little Mermaid retelling went, like REALLY HAPPY that all the reviews I read of The Summer of Chasing Mermaids lived up to the book. This is truly a diverse novel, with a person of color who has a disability (in that she is mute). For me, seeing Elyse without her voice, with all her dreams and plans crushed because of it, literally crushed my heart. It constantly made me think of my own future, and what would happen if that was all taken away from me. However, I realized, like Elyse, that having a home and finding your family is what really matters. Which is why it is not only the love interest, Christian, that helps her recover what she's lost, but also her family and friends. Even though the plot revolved around Elyse helping Christian fix up his boat to win the Pirate Regatta, a race that the both need to win due to an idiotic bet his father made with the mayor, it mainly focused on Elyse's recovery. As she hung out with both Christian, his adorable little brother Sebastian, she learns to look forward to the future again and face her fears with the sea. Speaking of the adorable little child---I mean brother, I can't really put into words how much of an impact he had on Elyse. First off, CHILDREN. You don't normally see such well developed children in YA, especially in the form of a younger brother. And he definitely had a personality. He loves mermaids, and he always wants to go searching for them in the cove. My favorite part is that this is not gender stereotyped at all, especially his love for dressing up as a mermaid. And everyone's support for him (Except the father and the mayor because ugh). So here's a sum up so far of all the amazing things going on in this book. - Diversity - Feminism in Gender Equality/NO Gender Stereotypes - Awesome friendships and family - Romantic interest is not a jerk, and actually APPRECIATES Elyse for who she is, even though she can't talk. I felt like my reading comprehension for this novel was on par with where I stand trying to fight my way through a novel written in French. I know what all of those individual words mean, but when they go together, the results occasionally become baffling. This was partially true because of the thick use of Yiddish words and phrases, sprinkled liberally throughout with no explanation for the unfamiliar reader (would have been nice to realize there was a glossary in the back before finishing...) But also, Chabon's writing is hugely poetic. Not just lyrical, but dipping occasionally into phrasing so metaphoric and uncommon that I would have to reread a paragraph to see if I really understood what had happened. It was beautiful, but got a little exhausting, so that I stopped doing such rereads and just left off thinking "well, I probably have the main gist" and moved on. And THEN there's the alternate history. Five chapters in, I paused to do some reading on Sitka so I could at least understand how far the separation from reality goes. I didn't really come to grips with any of it (beyond "there isn't really a population of 2 million Jews living in Alaska") until I read the wikipedia article about the book after finishing. I feel like all these comments are terribly condemning of myself as a smart human and professed lover of history, but World War Two was never my era, and I'm frightfully out of touch with current events. I have no cultural connection to Judaism of any sort, and event my forays into hardboiled crime fiction are pretty sparse. All that being said, I liked the characters and the writing really was lovely. The resolution (as far as I understood all the problems that needed to be resolved) seemed satisfying, offering closure where it was absolutely necessary, but allowing for speculation on some of the wider world concerns.

5 amazing stars! KJ Charles has become an auto buy author for me. Her books always hit the right spot for me and A Fashionable Indulgence is no exception. There was a lot for me to adjust to with the 1800's historical settling and politics, but I soon found myself falling into the story and enjoying it more and more. I loved Harry. The lost soul who was so easy to love, for me at least. He'd been through a lot in his life and had done things he didn't really want to do, but had no choice. All he wanted to do is belong and when that chance comes in the form of a wealthy grandfather, he jumps at it. Julius is the man who has to teach Harry how to be a gentleman, something he's not exactly thrilled about at first. He was a bit more difficult for me to love in the beginning, but as I learned more about the closed off grieving man, the more I found myself liking--and eventually loving--him. The relationship between these two is beautiful. It starts out as student/mentor, develops into a reluctant friendship and finally evolves into lovers who so deeply need each other, it had me rooting for them through all the BS of the historical setting. Harry changes Julius in many ways. He helps him loosen up and see the world differently. He brings out the man behind the grief. "It's not that. I've made such a mess of matters and to embroil you any further--You know I love you. I don't want to entangle you." "The problem is, you already have." Julius's fingers twined with his hair, "You have entangled me so thoroughly that I doubt I shall ever be satisfied with solitude again. I am well aware that you are storm-tossed, my dear. I merely wish that you will permit me to give you a port when you need it." He kissed Harry, gently. "And I have rarely seen a more precious sight that you lying like a mountebank to save your friend." "What?" "Utterly shameless." Julius kissed him again. "Quite magnificent. I was proud to stand with you. And talking of stands..." He moved his mouth to Harry's ear. "Next time you wish to lie to agents of the Crown, I insist you let me watch." I enjoyed seeing all the secondary characters and how they shaped the story. Especially Verona, Harry's cousin, who was such an amazing, likable and strong character. She was a bit of a surprise to Harry, but not to me. I couldn't imagine the story without her and quite honestly, I would have been happy to have more of her. She especially endeared herself to me in the last chapter, where she did something I knew she would do. An ARC was provided by the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for a fair and honest review. There are all kinds of people in this world, and we can constantly divide them in groups of two. So here's my division: there are people who like the Twilight series and there are those who don't. I'm the latter. So, if you're a fan searching for a nice review, you might get disappointed. I first read the first part of the series, Twilight, during my first year in college. All the girls were hyped about it and, as a fan of books, I decided to give it a try. I began reading and I must say, at first I was interested. That is, until the sparkling thing came along. I have always been a Dracula fan (when I mean always, I mean since I first read the Stoker classic, roughly at about the same time), so my idea of a vampire is pretty much set to a cunning, treacherous monster who kills (so you could probably guess my reaction to the movies... but oh, well). So when presented a teenaged vampire who goes to high school time and time again, and a girl who barely even blinked when told she had been stalked for weeks at night... Well, you get my gist. I was about to stop reading during the second half of the book (something I seldom do) but then again, my friends kept telling me "Keep on reading! It gets better!" And then I finished the whole book, and it never did. Bunch of liars. Ha, ha. So, then you might be wondering why on Earth did I read the sequel? Funny story. I was in my third year of college and working part-time at a bookstore. A dream come true, right? Well, certainly not in my case. I was working "part-time" (36h. a week!) for some people who obviously didn't love books but thought of them as market value only. Those people had me on my feet for 6h. in the children's section (the most abandoned of them all) while behind me there was construction work going on. Drilling, drilling, drilling. Migraines, migraines, migraines. And what is a 21-year-old girl going to do for 6h. a day, Sat. included, in a room full of children's books and with sounds which might have completely damaged my hearing? Well, read. And what kind of book was I to read in that section of the store? Well, Twilight. Because, trust me, Twilight was the only book with more or less complex sentences and in which there were relative clauses and passives. So there you go, I read the second. That was five years ago, and I don't even remember the plot of the book. So yes, that is why I read the book and why I gave it 1/5 stars. I'm good at remembering things, plots, characters... but I've got zero memories connected to this book. Freud would have a field day. Oh, and for those who were wondering, I got caught several times reading and was sacked. Best thing that happened to me that year.

Reading the novella first, I was intrigued. There was a large amount of mystery around Sculpt/Logan which had me very curious to find out what his deal was. I enjoyed the build-up of the relationship between Emily and Logan. The fighting lessons were cute and enjoyable - and the chemistry was very obvious between the two. Of course, we couldn't go into too much details - as it was mostly saved for the main book - but I did question Emily's utter faith in a guy who doesn't really reveal much about himself. But, I left my faith in the story telling and would hope it would be brought to light when I read the following novel. And now I'm angry. BEWARE: Rant and spoilers ahead - read at your own risk. FIRST OF ALL... I went in expecting some really dark things to happen. I had mentally prepared myself for some content that would make me bleed on the inside. I didn't bleed at all. In fact, I barely got scratched...and here's why. Things actually started out fairly rough for Emily. She's been kidnapped, manhandled, hit (yaddi yaddi yadda) and then, she thinks her saviour has come when she hear Logan's sweet, sweet voice. Alas, he seems to be in on it. And then... well things get less...interesting... Yeah, yeah.. I'm screwed up, what else is new? Maybe I'm just used to books with darker content. Or maybe I have a sick and twisted mind (which I've never denied before). But everything that happens to Emily afterwards seems really fucking tame to what I was anticipating. Like what? Well, she gets released to Logan, who pretty much holes her up in their own room during the day and then parades her around at night. Oh yeah... and they have sex practically all the time. Seriously....all the time. You know, because her body still wants him, and she sometimes sees the Logan she 'use to know' when they're by themselves in their own private room. But when he's out in public he's cold and mean. Then there was that one time that they had no choice but to have sex in front of everyone else. For the record, in no way am I saying that she didn't get through some sort of hell. Because no one wants to be held against their will and get threatened to be sold. Especially when you're being held against your will by someone you used to love. What I AM saying is, if you're gonna try and sell me something that has 'dark content' well... I'm expecting dark. Not an overcast grey. Despite what I was told, I was expecting half of the book to be about Emily' kidnapping, and the other half about Logan trying to repair the relationship. No, only 37% of it is about her kidnapping. And I kid you not, about 15-20% of that is them having sex. I feel as though there could have been more brought to Emily's predicament, and what she had to go through. There were so many opportunities for Emily to have experienced something, while harsh - would also made her strong. To top it all off, there was a whole Novella on her becoming stronger by asking Logan how to fight and defend herself. WHY WAS THIS NOT INCORPORATED INTO IT SOMEHOW? She had some moves, but I didn't see her build herself up. I didn't see her do what she had to do to survive. I wanted more from her, but I felt as if she depended on seeing her 'old Logan' far too much to be able to do anything else. Which brings us to... After Emily's escape - Yes, with Logan's help...cause we did NOT see that coming It's two years later, and Logan decides that it's enough time for Emily to heal and for him to 'claim what's his'. Worst. Fucking. Apology. Ever. Let me make myself very clear. Just because you act like an asshole, does NOT make you an Alpha. Logan barely apologises to Emily. Keeps giving excuses on why he did what he had to do. Trying to make out that what he did was okay and how'd he'd do it again. There was no compassion, no wishing he didn't have to do it. Fair enough, the situation came up and you had to do what you had to do to protect her. That doesn't mean that you can't regret what you did. That doesn't mean that you can't sympathise with her pain and prove to her again that you are the person she first met, and not the person she began to hate. No, it was 'I had to do it, so just accept it.' I wasn't satisfied with how Logan came back into Emily's life. And the loop of him trying to convince her what he did was right was repetitive and frustrating. Oh, and the whole 'she's my trophy' thing, yeah - way to objectify her even more after she escapes a fucking sex slave ring douchebag.

Real rating: 3.5 stars I went into Turtles All the Way Down with much trepidation. I tend to feel that John Green bites off more than he can chew in his novels. In past novels, he would try to expound very "deep, philosophical" themes. Worse than this, he loves using the Manic Pixie Girl tropes. So I started this novel expecting to be hit by these two problems. Instead, I was pleasantly surprised. Aza/Writing Aza is probably the best John Green protagonist I've encountered. She grappled with so many internal demons. She also had her external battles that resulted because of those internal demons. Her mental illness was so written in such a realistic way that reading it caused me anxiety. It felt so real, in ways that John Green's books have never really made me feel. It was because of these issues that those deep, philosophical thoughts that are a staple of John Green novels felt substantial. Aza seems like a character that could actually have these thoughts. She had seen so much, been through so much, that when she had thoughts like, "Anybody can look at you. It's quite rare to find someone who sees the same world you see," I didn't scoff. Instead, I mulled it over. Davis/Romance I didn't consider Davis a main character. I say this because I feel like this was not a romance novel by any means. This is a book about Aza and Aza's war against her thoughts. Davis is merely a side character, pushed into the wings most of the time (and rightly so). Yet, I need to point out how cute he is. He is not perfect, he is sad, he is confused. But he is so eloquent. His love of astronomy and his thoughts on it was heart wrenching. My heart broke a bit when he said favorite star was his favorite solely because it was seeing 12 year old light, light in which his mom was still alive. Like, first of all, ouch. But let me just thank John Green for not making this a love story. He put the idea out there but he didn't push it. He let Aza take center stage. I loved how the story was all entwined. The way both conflicts merged into one at some points. Though it wasn't 4 star worthy, I will say this is the best John Green novel I've read so far.

this book is a perfectly good bit of entertainment, if you can disarm your logic and incredulity buttons. it's about phoebe hall; a newly single and disgraced celebrity biographer, who has fled the glamor of new york, world travel, and talk show appearances after a plagiarism scandal to teach writing at a private college in a tiny town in pennsylvania. glenda johns, one of her oldest friends from her own boarding school days, is the president of the college, and when a girl is found murrrrrderrrred, she asks phoebe to quietly investigate the rumors of a secret society of girls known only as "the sixes" to determine if there is a connection. phoebe is reluctant, because she herself had been victimized by a similar group of girls in her youth, but since researching celebrity dirt is pretty much the same thing as solving violent crimes, she agrees. here's the thing - just as celebrities don't like it when you spill the secrets from what little they have of private lives, post-adolescent girls do not like having light shed on their own less-than-ladylike behavior. as her investigation progresses, phoebe becomes the target of several invasive scare tactics - break-ins where increasingly-creepy things are left behind for her to find, harrowing adventures in the dark, and then - more murrrrrderrrrr. but phoebe is plucky, and she will not quit the hunt just because half-frozen rats spring out at her face from her freezer . oh, and is there a love interest? is he dreamy with a dark past, a psychology degree, and a habit of doing all sorts of suspicious things in her presence?? check and check. and why does the feminist studies teacher seem to dislike her so much? and why does the dean of students keep throwing wrenches into her investigation? and why is glenda's husband acting so shady? and what about all the other students who drowned or near-drowned or went missing in the past? and what's with the campus police? and what's up with the townie bar that seems to have been the "victim last seen at" point in so many cases? and why is that new york post reporter sniffing around? and why are all the boys at the school so dumb? and how have the sixes been able to operate in secrecy for so long when some of their rituals are kind of high-profile? i mean, really - if there were more than forty members this one year alone, wouldn't they have run out of "important" people to seduce and destroy? and if this had been going on for as long as it had, would none of it have come out before?? it's a small town, but in the cloistered world of academia, there would have been rumor mills a-chugging. red herrings abound. there are a lot of things that usually drive me mad, but they are pretty minor incidents. it's weird that a first fight, albeit one with serious accusations, translates into a breakup and communication blackout between two adults, especially when one ends up in the hospital right after that. it defies normal human behavior that duncan would call glenda and say "yeah, we're not together anymore, but how is she? tell her i asked about her but nooooo i can't contact her now or for a long time after this because - WEIRD!" that's just one of my personal bugbears, and it's one of those things so common in books and so completely removed from the way people actually behave. someone with whom you have been having the intercourse with a couple of days ago ends up in the hospital, you call. a case with which you have both been preoccupied comes to a close, you call. i don't care who accused whom of what. again - this is just something that bugs me, and it's not a huge part of the story, but it speaks to a certain kind of writerly laziness. tana french wouldn't go there. now, i have this on my "books claiming to be just like secret history" shelf, but this book doesn't actually make that claim. and it's not ultimately anything like secret history except that it involves a ritualistic secret society in an academic environment and there is a murder. which is enough for it to go on the shelf, but it is not at all a readalike. it's a diversion-read - it holds the interest and it only takes a couple of hours to read, so it's a good vacation, beach, airplane, or wine-bath book. they can't all be life-changers.

** spoiler alert ** WELL. I wanted to like this so badly, you guys. I went in with an open mind and read the book with "it's a play, don't forget it's a play, don't forget how much the actors will bring to this" going constantly through my head but it just wasn't enough. I love everything about the HP series and spent a huge amount of time reading fan fiction in high school. Honestly, even 16-year-old me wouldn't have wasted my time on fiction this bad. As soon as I saw that it was an alternate-universe-time-traveling story I had to close my eyes from preventing them from rolling right out of my head. It had me hoping that at the end it would be "all a dream" and not real canon. It's not only not interesting, but it's lazy. This is every cliche you could think of piled into one play without any of the magic and whimsy of JKR's writing. It's static, two-dimensional characterizations and reads like a Doctor Who Christmas episode -- corny and entirely reliant on reader nostalgia. Some set description might have helped, and I'm sure that seeing this live would've helped quite a bit, but it doesn't save that the plot is throwaway and has been done a million times before. How is this the story that needed to be told? I love JKR immensely, and the HP books are not ever entirely unique in plot but the writing and characters and world-building is what makes them so magical. This play has none of the good writing, none of the characterizations, none of the world-building (seriously, there are NO new magical details; all we learn are what characters do as their jobs!!) and all of the lazy tropes of a cheesy Christmas special. I'm getting repetitive now, but this was truly disappointing. I thought there would be a kernel of something wonderful, but to me, there wasn't even that. Just a lot of lazy writing that honestly ends up feeling like kind of a money-making scam. Also, Voldemort's daughter? Are you kidding me?? To end on a positive note, here are some things I did like: Harry being bad at being a dad; Ginny telling Draco that she doesn't use the kitchen and only Harry cooks; Harry's fear of pigeons? (which also somehow feels contrived? ); learning that drunk floo-powdering can get a bit messy.

Rachel is a hopeless alcoholic divorcee. Despite losing her job, she still takes the train into London every day, passing the house Tom, her ex, lives in with his new wife, Anna, and their kid - a child she couldn't give him herself. Then Rachel sees their married neighbour, Megan Hipwell, from the train window kissing a man who turns out to be her therapist. When Megan goes missing, the secrets of her life reveal a startling link to Rachel's own... I couldn't finish this so-called "thriller". It's not a long book either at just over 300 pages but, some two weeks of picking it up, reading a few miserable pages, and quickly putting it down again, I'm ready to admit defeat at the 180 page mark. Paula Hawkins' novel is full of seedy, unlikeable people in a "plot" that reads like an overlong episode of Eastenders. Rachel's ex Tom and his missus Anna argue with Rachel in the street while Megan's cheating on her husband Scott who argue at home and Cathy, Rachel's housemate, wants her to get help, and blah blah blaaaaah who finds this interesting! No real story appears until well over the halfway mark and even then it's really only the hint of one. Most of the time it's this soap-opera dogshit as the dimwits bicker like the dreary suburbanites like they are about dull nonsense. Paula Hawkins' writing is pedestrian at best, rendering it all in flat, un-evocative prose. Quite why The Girl on the Train is such a runaway hit, I have no idea. It's tedious claptrap of the lowest order. Then again Eastenders is incredibly popular too so there's probably a crossover between those audiences. Don't listen to anyone who compares this crap to Gone Girl, they are nothing alike and at least Gillian Flynn can write. Exhausting and boring, The Girl on the Train is a total waste of time.

To be honest, this is not what makes a book remarkable, yes it gets it off the shelves, but it will not remain as a memorable story in the heads of avid readers. She had a lot of world-building and new ideas, and I was interested in the whole society... but thats about it. The Negatives: (which seem to outweigh the positives) The plot. Which seems to be nonexistent. Sure, we get some information on the Vittra or whatever they're called, but they play a very small part in the entire story. Most of the time we're centered around a) Wendy's complaints about who she is or b) Wendy's obsession with Finn. Which leads me to my next issue. Wendy. What a frustrating, irritating, annoying character. From the beginning she came off as immature and vapid, and I had trouble connecting to her in any way. Finn this, Finn that, oh no! Don't leave me Finn!! Get a grip. If I were Finn, I'd be running away from such a train-wreck. And some of her choices are completely stupid. For example: if I were to stab someone in the back with a shard of glass, it would be smart to jump on his back and impale myself on the way. Obviously. The writing. The story has regular pacing and fluency, but there are frequent info-dumps throughout it. Try showing instead of telling, or at least have it more evenly spaced. In addition, some of the dialogue and narration is choppy and immature. Parts that were supposed to be touching or swoon-worthy had me choking and rolling my eyes. And although the author had some good ideas, they could have been much better executed. The ending. After the central conflict, all of a sudden Wendy makes (*another*) random, stupid decision. The book suddenly ends in 2 pages in a cliffhanger and I'm thinking, did that actually just happen? Out of all the random things... Whatever. Overall there were a lot of annoying parts of the story. While I admire any self-publishing author, this clearly could have used a lot more work. Props to her, though. The author had some very unique ideas, but this could have been a much better story. Overall: 2.5 stars. I'm being more generous.
