I kind of just sit at the edge of the fandom pool and dip my feet in. Although, I have been known to, on occasion, talk at great lengths about the latest Naruto chapter. That's only when I'm with the right person. Like Cath had her sister, Wren. So yeah. I can relate to Cath from the fandom side. Really, what got me was the writing and the characters, oh man the characters. There wasn't one I didn't like (except maybe Laura but fuck her). I loved that Cath grew up thinking she was the crazy one, like her dad, but really it was Wren who eventually had a meltdown. I love Reagan and how she pulls Cath out of her comfort zone. I love Art and his quirky little habits and how his girls have to bring him back to earth sometimes, but they always manage to do so. It's like he's getting lost, but he sees his girls and remembers where he is and where he needs to be. And I absolutely adore Levi. Pretty much as soon as he was introduced. He's such a sweetheart and it's great that his relationship with Cath builds naturally and it wasn't another "insta-love" romance. These characters were so wonderful and their relationships and lives seemed so real, it was such a relief from what I've been reading lately. This is actually the first time I'm having trouble with understanding why people don't like this book. I mean, if it's not for you it's not for you I get that. But people are saying it's such a slander to us fangirls and I really didn't see it that way. I can relate so much to Cath. Without my awesome roommate, I probably would have been holed up in my room, on my computer (doing who knows what because I made a point not to have a tumblr while in school), refusing to leave even to brave the dining hall. And I went to a small school. As in, there was about a 350 dorm capacity. And it was an all girls school. So there wasn't much to be afraid of. I had my small group of friends in high school and we'd all geek out together, so when we all went our separate ways in college, I felt lost. Those first few weeks were horrible. I think I did actually hole myslef up in my room the first week or so. I distinctly remember sitting in the dark room watching anime (Yakiyatee Japan!! thank you very much) while there was a big new semester celebration festival going on outside. There were moonbounces and everything. My roommate coaxed me out eventually, as Reagan did with Cath, so I mean when I say I can relate to this main character, I mean it. The one thing that kind of bugged me was when she had to walk back alone to her room from the library at midnight she dialed 9-1-1 on her phone but kept her finger on the send button in case anything happened. I honestly thought that was a little extreme, especially considering she had never gone through any experience where she might need that. But then we got more insight on Cath and her mannerisms. Especially the checking if the front door is locked at 3 am. We learned about her mother and what a bitch she is and how she left their manic father to care for these girls on his own. This left a lasting impact on Cath leaving her with anxiety and paranoia. So even though that little quirk of hers irritated me at first, and honestly it kind of still does, I understand it and accept it. It also explains why she would rather stock up on food and hide in her room than go in search of the dining hall and find "real" food (I use that term very loosely as I know from experience that college food is worse than high school food and probably has fewer regulations). Although there isn't that high school mentality of "oh my god where do i sit" in college, your first few weeks, it's tough to lose that mindset. So yeah, I get it. I really loved that Rowell made an alternate series to Harry Potter. I'd actually like to read it. I'd also love to read Cath's fanfiction. I loved the little snippets we got and how they tied into the main plot, although sometimes the way it tied in was lost or hard to find. I'm not a huge fan of her making this spin off of HP only to mention Harry later on, because then what's the point of the spin off? I'm kind of bummed we didn't get to hear the ending Cath wrote, but I understand why we didn't get that. Okay I'm going to take this paragraph to just talk about Levi for a bit. He is so damn respectful, okay. He has a key to Reagan and Cath's dorm room. But it was given to him for emergencies only, so when he gets there and no one's inside what does he do? He sits outside the door and waits to be invited in. If he's told he's not welcome in, he leaves or sits and waits for Reagan. He makes everyone happy. That's what he likes to do. He lives for it. There's a scene at a bowling alley where he just talks to everyone there. Not for any other reason than to see people smile. He's a genuinely good person and I just find it so adorable that Cath reads to him because he can't process words when he reads them. He is absolutely perfect and adorable and I want one. Okay, glad I got that off my chest. Honestly, I think it had a good representation of one side of fandoms. Did it focus on fandoms? No. It was more about Cath growing up and how her fandom life was affected by it than the fandom itself. So I'm really not sure why people are so upset about this being a poor representation of a fandom, because this is how I was (minus the fanfiction). I really did enjoy this book, and it easily earned a spot on my favorites list. Can't wait to read more of Rainbow Rowell's books!

Pale Fire is a deeply and profoundly strange novel. I enjoyed this much much more than Nabokov's earlier and more famous Lolita because it is equally (if not more) staggeringly impressive from a craft perspective, just as thought-provoking (at least for me, who studies literature at school for the same reason he reads--being head-over-heels in love with the English language), and infinitely less distressing. Where Lolita, for all of its beautiful prose and interesting ideas, made me feel physically ill, Pale Fire fascinated me and made me excited to discover what was going on in the lives--and heads--of the characters. About Pale Fire in isolation. This novel takes the form of a 1000-line autobiographical poem by the fictional John Shade and an associated Foreword and Commentary by Charles Kinbote. The plot of the novel proper really plays out in the comments, where Kinbote is unafraid to veer off into unrelated territory to express what he deems necessary to understand his perception of Shade's motives and inspiration, as well as reveal a story about the exiled king of his home country of Zembla. Kinbote is said exiled king, which becomes apparent about halfway through the novel or a little earlier and is actually revealed in the last third or so The plot is fairly straightforward: Shade's life in the poem, Kinbote's tale and a narrative of his brief friendship with Shade in the comments. Outside of the strict confines of the plot is where the novel really shines. Nabokov's formal device allows the two plots to be read absolutely contrapuntally, jumping back and forth between poem and comments. It also makes the whole work a statement on the act of commentary itself--Kinbote, while sympathetic and, when you get down to it, the protagonist of the novel, is somewhat fatuous and egocentric, indicating a careful disdain for the tendency of critics (of whom I would count myself) to overread and inset themselves into the author's words. While I do not necessarily agree with the full force of understated harshness that Pale Fire levels, it is an interesting line of thought to explore. The meta-fictional elements are somewhat difficult to engage with, but do make Pale Fire particularly intriguing in terms of what it says about fiction and engagement with it. The novel also brings up some interesting considerations about station and importance--through the tale of kingly exile and attempted regicide and the thread of Shade's popular and critical reputation, that play out through the story. I will admit to being occasionally confused by the treatment of sexuality in the novel--Kinbote's attitude is clear, but the tone regarding Kinbote is not, which makes for an odd, but not particularly discomfiting (for me) experience, and is actually a fairly minor element of the work, although I believe it is one that adds to the complexity of position regarding the meditations on personal role and social station within the novel. I was a bit hesitant to shelve this under "poetry", because the bulk of the text is actually a work of prose fiction, but I did so because the poem forms an integral part of the novel as a whole. Kinbote's commentary could have been structured as a narrative that told the same story without the eponymous poem or the conceit of being commentary, instead of a narrative. But Nabokov chose not to do that, and instead worked the fiction around this long and carefully crafted (if--I suspect deliberately--rather conventional) poem. This makes the poetic element of the work a central part of the story, even as the plot primarily occurs inside the prose comments. Pale Fire is a fascinating and complex novel, one that is as much a work about literature as it is a work of literature.

Pretty Girl-13 is a disturbing psychological mystery that is not for the faint of heart. At the age of 13, Angela 'Angie' Chapman is kidnapped. Three years later she returns home, with no memory of where she has been or what has happened to her, completely unaware that any time has passed and with a fractured blank space in her mind. In order to mend the missing pieces of herself she must journey into the dark and dangerous labyrinth of her mind, filled with horrifying secrets hidden in only the darkest of corners. I quite enjoyed this book, although it's definitely a mature read. It is reasonably well paced and filled with plenty of tension, although the beginning is a bit disorientating and tries too hard to confuse the reader before the narrative really finds its feet. I thought the overall premise of the story was interesting and very ambitious, although it perhaps missed the mark on being truly fantastic. At its core this is a story about dealing with trauma and it explores how the mind reacts to horrifying experiences (such as sexual abuse). I really enjoyed the psychological aspects of the story and the process Angie goes through to understand and accept what has happened to her as she tries to rebuild her life. However, while this is a story that tries to grapple with a lot of big concepts I don't think some of these ideas were handled with as much sensitivity or finesse as they could have been (for instance, 'slut' references in the context of rape - a pet peeve of mine - and an experimental procedure performed as part of Angie's therapy which completely opposes the idea of acceptance the book is trying to explore). I also think that this book fell down in places because the plot tried to be overly convoluted in an attempt to really dissect the psychological aspect of the story. If you're going to pin a novel on the psychological exploration of trauma then it needs to be extremely well refined. Similarly, if you have a story that explores rape and child abuse then you need to deal with those concepts carefully and thoughtfully, and that requires significant discussion, not avoidance or outright 'deletion'. There were also a few plot holes that stood out, for instance the lack of media attention after Angie returns home. I mean, really? It just didn't make any sense given that she was attending high school surrounded by hundreds of students who were aware of her situation. Overall I found it to be a compelling read but it could have more nuanced and deal with certain topics more effectively. I would recommend it to people with an interest in psychology or stories about dealing with traumatic experiences.

"Meanwhile John Cole says he loves me more than any man since the apes roamed. All the news in the Grand Rapids Courier is that a man was once an ape which John Cole says is no surprise to him considering." This book begs to be read out loud and in fact I did so many times. The rhythm of the narration is pretty genius. The story is told in first person conversational style by Thomas McNulty , who stowed away on a ship bound for Canada as a child in the mid 1800's when the Irish potato famine made him an orphan. When the book opens, he and his lover and best friend John Cole are still in their teens and are troopers in the U.S. Army, which then as now is sometimes a choice for those who have no other options. It is a beautifully written book, which amid the brutality and hardship of mid-18th century American life, begs the reader to consider tolerance and love where you can find it. The three main characters, Thomas, John Cole and their adopted daughter Winona are all orphans who were maybe lucky in the sense that they are free of familial and/or cultural values and so are able to make their own family without gender or racial restraints on who and how they are allowed to love. For such a short book, it took me a long time to finish it. And it only covers about a 10 year period (and a lot of ugly U.S. history) in real time. In that span, Thomas and John Cole crisscross the country from Missouri to California to Michigan to Virginia to Tennessee to Wyoming and fight in both the Indian Wars and the Civil War. I enjoyed reading it and I loved the language but the nuts and bolts of the plot were sometimes a little too tidy, ie unbelievable. Also, once or twice Barry had Thomas using some pretty highfalutin vocabulary which didn't mesh with his barely educated character.

So after a week spent reading Patrick Rothfuss, I felt a longing for the fantasy I choose for myself as a teenager. It wasn't this book, but Owlflight and Brightly Burning that drew me in and refused to let go, but like many series in outdated country libraries, they didn't have all the books. Maybe they did at some point, but over the years theft and use had dwindled the collection down to a few titles. It is with great shame that in my adulthood I haven't hunted more of these down, now I have the opportunity. I have a physical copy of this one, but had to download the other two on Kindle. Boo! I loved this as a first novel for Valdemar. All the links are there, even if they aren't as fleshed out as they are later on. I even had that heart stopping moment when Lavan Firestorm was mentioned (never forget ;_; ) I loved how even though this was in the 80's, Mercedes doesn't shy away from having gay/lesbian relationships. In fact, sex is always an underlying theme in Valdemar books, and not just as a way to show 'true love' like many books these days. The Heralds get up to hanky panky for many reasons; lust, comfort, physical relief, friendship. It's just never a squick factor. These books were never over the top battles and action, and always seemed to focus more on the characters and letting them grow into the heroes and legends they become. They remain human, with faults aplenty. Knowing what I know now of later books, it is with glee that I see where it all began for the first time. It is this love that drags me through what some readers may find boring; the development. As I mentioned, I did download the next two books on my Kindle. I read through the Last Herald Mage books a few years ago in order, so why not these? Keep an eye out for future reviews ;) Five stars, there is a reason Mercedes Lackey is my second favorite author (The first being Piers Anthony)

I read the Twilight series as a teenager and, admittedly, enjoyed it. As I got a little older and the movies began to came out I started to see all of its problems and slowly came to strongly dislike it. That said, when beginning The Chemist I made a conscious decision to leave my opinions for Twilight at the door, so to speak. I never read The Host so I don't know how that book is but it has been several years since Twilight came to a close (not considering all the stuff from Edward's POV and the genderswapping, none of which I have read). Surely after so many years of developing as a writer and diving into a new genre there is bound to be something good. That's what I told myself. And I was wrong. This book is a mess. From the line "hating what I do gave me the power to do it best" it is clear where this is going. For the record, she tortures people. Somehow hating torturing people makes her better at it? It begins in an alright place, with the main character running for her life. The only real problem with this section of the book is that it is a lot of info-dumping. Tons of telling rather than showing. But it was still early and there was still a chance that things could be turned around once the story got going. Yeah...no. The telling v. showing did improve but never really went away. The plot was basically a chunk of swiss cheese with all the holes that were in it. The book contains one of the most moronic love interests ever. Seriously, the only fictional character that comes to mind while reading about him is.....wait for it....Bella freakin' Swan. Both are in a relationship that they really shouldn't be in. In Daniel's case, he falls in love with the woman that literally freaking tortured him! He rationalizes it with "she did what she had to do" but other characters do things that upset him and the exact same argument could be used for what they did, but he gets stupid angry at them. He actually tells Alex at one point as she is trying to tell him that she is bad for him "I loved you before you were the only woman in my life." Okay, let's set this straight here. You knew her for a total of 5 minutes before she became the "only woman in your life." Also that magical before time was also the time before she had tortured you! But somehow this does not change his opinion of her. The plot was a little all over the place. There's a terrorist thing going on in the background that is the excuse used for all this stuff happening to Alex. You would think that the possibility of a biological weapon being used to murder a few million people would play a fairly major part in a book that is referred to as a spy thriller but no. Everything having to do with it is pretty much entirely off screen including the climax and conclusion of that plot line. The book instead focuses on Alex and her relationship drama with some action thrown in. A lot of the book is pretty much an action scene followed by a makeout scene which is followed by an action scene which is again followed by a makeout scene. Rinse and repeat ad nauseam. Finally, Stephenie Meyer's attempt at creating Alex's character completely failed. As mentioned, Alex is a trained torturer. She describes herself as being a bad person because of this. Yet it is obvious that she really wanted the reader to like Alex and be able to relate to how she feels. Creating a character that is both dark and likable is a fine line to walk and requires balance and hard decisions. Those hard decisions were not made here. Sure, Alex thought an awful lot about doing the heartless thing but she never really actually did it (well, she did one thing toward the end of the book that was a little messed up but by that point the reader knew it was all going to be fine anyway). Too much effort went into making Alex likable and into makeout and love confession scenes and not enough into actually developing a dynamic character. This sounds really harsh even to me but I actually doubt that this book would have been published had it not had the name Stephenie Meyer attached to it and so was guaranteed to sell.

See this review and more like it on my blog, Written Permission My first thought upon completing this book was that it belonged alongside the likes of 1984. I was actually quite stunned to find it had been published in my lifetime. The Giver is a really interesting book to me, because it sparks so much discussion among those who have read it. I read it over a month ago, so some of the finer details are already fuzzy, but I recall thinking it wasn't really a children's book. Then I encountered people who felt it was too simplified, which is well within their right to think of course, but hard to determine. Where do we draw the line? I don't dabble in politics much (or really, at all) so the claims of The Giver being simply a piece of anti-socialism propaganda are a little outside of my realm of comfort and knowledge. But I will say it is hardly the first time a book has shaken things up in the political sense, and I doubt it will be the last. For me, I enjoyed The Giver. The quick change from utopia to dystopia is not something I have seen very often, at least in contemporary works, and it was a really refreshing change. I find a lot of the dystopian novels I read are very cut and dried that they are dystopian. There is not something missing, there is not something more. Yet, here we have a distinct lack that is pointed out in a big way. I don't want to give away the whole book, so I won't go into any more detail, but I loved the way it was told. In some ways, The Giver is very much a children's novel. The characters are not really delved into very much, though I was very appreciative that Jonas was portrayed very much as a standard young man. He didn't read as older or younger than his years, which is something that can be hard to do when writing a younger character... especially in a situation where the world they are dealing with is so heavy. The writing was technically fine, and I enjoyed the narrative voice. It kept the story moving at a good pace. The story of The Giver is hard to define. I really wanted more details, and that is where I feel it very much fell flat. Given more details, more worldbuilding, this novel could have been truly magnificent. And the ending was the kind that drives readers insane, and not in a good way. Bottom Line: A children's utopian/dystopian novel surrounded in so many opinions that I hesitate to add my own voice. I feel like you will either really like it or really not, and I encourage you to pick it up and see which category you fall into.

Whenever a new Juliet Marillier book is released I pretty much drop everything else I am doing and devour it in a single sitting and this is more or less what I did with 'Flame of Sevenwaters'. This book is about Maeve, one of the daughters of Lord Sean of Sevenwaters, who was last seen in 'Child of the Prophecy'. I really loved Maeve's voice. She was prickly and definitely not afraid to speak her mind. The story begins with Maeve returning home to Sevenwaters after a long absence. After suffering grievous injuries in 'Child of the Prophecy', Maeve went to live with her aunt Liadan in Harrowfield. Ten years have passed and Maeve now finds herself, somewhat reluctantly, returning home to Sevenwaters. She returns home to find Sevenwaters in turmoil. Mac Dara, the leader of the Fair Folk, is causing all sorts of strife for her family. A visiting chieftain's two sons and travelling companions have been snatched out of thin air and war could be on the horizon. Maeve has many scars, both physical and emotional, but she must confront her demons if she is to survive this ordeal and put an end to Mac Dara's reign once and for all. I really enjoyed reading about Maeve's journey. I also liked spending more time with some of the familiar characters from previous books in the series, notably the young Finbar and also Ciaran, who has long been my favourite character. Romance takes a bit of a backseat in this novel, although it is certainly present (though the love interest may not exactly be who you would think! I get the impression this may be the last Sevenwaters book and although this would make me sad, I think 'Flame of Sevenwaters' would be a fitting conclusion to the series. Five stars *****

I was disappointed with this novel. When I read the description I thought it the idea seemed like a really good one. A coma patient with a previous head injury awakes and finds himself with physic like abilities. I think that sounds like a great story! There were several things that I didn't care for with this particular Stephen King novel. The first being I felt the entire story was being told one long ramble. There were so many extra tangents off the main plot line that I felt were unnecessary. One example of this being keeping Sarah, the love interest for Johnny, involved in the book. I understand the sense of lost love between these two characters, but I felt like after the "What If" moment they shared after Johnny was discharged from the hospital should have been the end of her character. She had the opportunity to be released from the rest of the book as she drove away that evening. But instead, she kept popping up randomly in the future. Another thing I had trouble with was the exponential character growth for Greg Stillson. I have a hard time seeing how he went from Bible Salesman to a foreseen presidential winner who is going to drive the world into nuclear war. It was like The Omen, except with a backwoods bumpkin at the helm. It just didn't seem plausible to me. Personally, I felt the best part of the book was when Johnny gets involved with the small town strangler. I thought that Frank Dodd was a successful version of the growth style that King used for Stillson. He was portrayed in the same glimpses into random points in the characters life, however, I felt that the development of Dodd was way more believable than Stillson (This fact alone maybe why I didn't care for Stillson in the first place.). It makes sense, to me, for a young boy to be so effected by his mothers abusive treatment of him that it shapes a murdering rapist. That is a psychological path that makes sense. I feel like this book would have been a lot better if the main plot was dedicated to catching this killer. The biggest problem I had with this story was King's interpretation of religious fervor. Johnny's mother was a very religious woman and her coping mechanism to her son's terrible accident was to turn to her god. To me, this is a very normal thing to do. People often seek the comfort in the graces of their religions when the ones they love are in danger. Sometimes it comforts them and gives them strength, other times, it breaks them and sends them into a dangerous spiral of cult like proportions. What really bothered me was every encounter with the devoutly religious (letters and correspondences to Johnny after it became general knowledge that he had some sort of psychic ability) that King decided to write down, were letters from people who were grammatically illiterate and unable to spell things correctly or consistently. One particular letter that comes to mind, the sender misspelled the same word several times, but each time the word appeared it was misspelled differently than it's previous dictation. I felt it is the author's way of telling the world how stupid he thinks people of religion are. That idea itself is very one sided and narrow minded, the very thing he seems to want to emulate about these type of people. I am coming to the conclusion that King doesn't respect anyone of religious background. Carrie's mother was an extreme devote woman who's abusive suppression of her daughter's natural curiosity of the world killed them both. Mother Abigail from The Stand was a supposed to be the religious leader after the superflu killed most of Earth's population. Instead, she ran off into the wilderness to pray and fast and it pretty much killed her. All of these characters of religion met brutal ends. I would love to see him write about someone of faith who isn't 1. crazy 2. unintelligent or 3. fodder for a death scene. Personally, I don't subscribe to any organized religion, but I do feel that they are being unfairly portrayed. But that's just my opinion. I intend to keep moving forward through the works of Stephen King and hope that I find his next book better than this one.

I find myself in a difficult position reviewing this book. It's an astonishingly bad book, but it was recommended highly by many people whose opinions I respect. It's hard for me to know if I'm judging this book fairly on its own merits or comparing it unfavourably with the book I was expecting. I was expecting senstive, nuanced writing, good enough to be classed as literary fiction; optimistic and joyful SF in the style of Star Trek or The Martian; and maybe a little bit of adventure or mystery. Instead, I got a book that was relentlessly "Nice". And so, I feel kinda guilty when I criticise it. Look, it's badly written, badly plotted, badly paced, with terrible dialogue, poorly-sketched characters and very little actual science fiction - and yet, when I say so I feel like I'm kicking a kitten! How dare I be so mean to such a "Nice" book? The crew of the Wayfarer are contracted to build a hyperspace tunnel, and must travel a long distance to do so. Although they are a commercial team engaged in engineering, most of the book has a very cosy domestic feel. The characters refer to themselves as a family often, and business disputes never occur and therefore can't effect their cosy relationships. As they journey, the characters visit family and friends or go shopping. Even scenes that could have been dramatic (space pirates or tyrannical border guards) are curiously flat due to their easy resolution. It reminded me very much of 19th or early-20th century children's books in which each rather tame adventure ends with a character learning an important lesson about Doing One's Duty or The Importance of Hard Work - except here they learn about Not Judging Others or The Importance of Pacifism! In each case, turgid chunks of over-explanation are worsened by the poor quality of the writing. It's littered with annoying verbal tics that should have been removed by an editor. The most striking of these was the overuse of the word 'smirk' instead of the word 'smile', in one instance a character even 'gave a fond smirk'. The moralism of the book is especially infuriating because it's often so shallow. Characters learn about the importance of getting along with each other - but not about truly important things. This is difficult to discuss without giving massive spoilers, so I'll try to focus on the least spoilery cases. One of the crew, Sissix, is Aandrisk: a repitilian species who lay eggs. They do not view their young as full people until they are grown and so are very cavalier about their high infant mortality rate. She would never, ever understand the idea that a child, especially an infant, was of more value than an adult who had already gained all the skills needed to benefit the community. The death of a new hatchling was so common as to be expected. The death of a child about to feather, yes, that was sad. But a real tragedy was the loss of an adult with friends and lovers and family. But let us consider this for a moment. The Aandrisk are a space-faring species, so it cannot be predators, parasites or disease destroying their young; they would surely have the technology to deal with these things. What else causes high infant mortality in reptiles? Neglect? Cannibalism? This is getting pretty bleak, isn't it? It's not very nice. So, naturally, the entire issue is completely avoided. When the crew visit Sissix home, she is very loving towards two children, who are obviously sentient beings and not half-formed half-people. The callous Aandrisk attitude to children is never seen, just referenced as one of those wacky alien differences that must be tolerated. One of the characters in the book is a sentient AI. By any measure, the AI is a full person. She both thinks and feels. She has desires that do not necessarily align with the needs of her owners. The love story between the AI and a crew member is one of the few plot lines that had genuine consequences. Yet, legally, AI are not people. They can be deleted on a whim and are denied any rights whatsoever, and laws are in place to prevent them acheiving independence. She's an off-the-shelf model that is common on ships through-out the universe. The implication is that there are billions of AI, just like her, through-out the universe held in total, abject slavery. That's not very nice, is it? So, of course, this story line does not touch upon the horror of this galaxy-wide slavery at all. This plot is all about the love story - and the lesson that the characters learn from it is that perhaps they should be a bit nicer and not take the help for granted. I said at the start of this review that 'Niceness' is no excuse for bad writing. But more than this, niceness is a frequent and cowardly excuse for avoiding difficult confrontations and important questions. Through-out this book the world-building sets up ethical dilemmas - questions concerning the definitions of personhood, the rights of robots, medical consent. And everytime, these difficult questions are overlooked in favour of a trite homily on friendship. Eventually the niceness of the crew of the Wayfarer is not heart-warming. It is not charming. It is a total failure to engage meaningfully with the universe around them. A blind preference for easy comfort over true justice.

This book and its characters grew on me as it went along. The first part comes as a heavy-handed attempt of a grown-up giving undercover advice to teens through the voice of the MC recounting what he has learned. But that fades away (minus one monologue from MC's friend on what being a good friend really means -- though I really liked that part and think even adults could find use for it), and a lot of messy, tough, good situations happen that are ripe for mulling over. Full of 90s nostalgia, a lot of it seemed pretty foreign to me: people smoking inside buildings, the problems of cordless phones, teens getting ahold of alcohol with zero problems, strong clique culture... Anyways, I really liked this book a lot, but if you're a parent, you should probably read this book at the same time as your kid so you can talk about it.

2.5 STARS FOR "FANG" BY JAMES PATTERSON Y'all, I can't even... I think James Patterson stretched out these books and plotlines far too much. The first couple of books, I thought this series was fun to read when I needed something lighter to entertain myself with. But sadly, I think this series has regressed to the point where a lot of the characters - characters that I used to love - are no longer themselves. In the previous book, we'd at least finally got some resolution for the Max and Fang romance after all that buildup and wishywashy behavior. But then Patterson did the worst thing an author can do to me: he included a love triangle. And not only does it not make sense for Max to suddenly start catching the hots for some random newbie when she literally just together with Fang, but Dylan is the most bland, vanilla character I've ever read. He does absolutely nothing except talk about how he was created to be with Max. I'm sorry, James Patterson, but Dylan is boring. He adds nothing to the advancement of the story, and I get that while he's physically attractive, I don't understand why Max feels anything for this guy. Just because he was created to be with her, it doesn't and shouldn't automatically make her feel anything towards him. Max and Fang shouldn't even be remotely threatened by his presence in the group, yet here we are. Whomp. Dylan was just unnecessary drama at this point. Max and Fang's issues of needing to prioritize the flock over their relationship is drama enough - we didn't need indecisiveness about Max's feelings. What I think happened, now that the plot has shifted away from just mere survival to saving the environment, is that James Patterson lost his way with the plot... and so he decided to contrive some drama this way. And Angel just became the biggest brat ever in this book. I couldn't stand her, especially with how unsympathetic she was towards the people who practically raised her and kept her safe. I mean, she's super power hungry, kicks Max out of the group so she could be the leader, and does not care at all about her "visions" of Fang dying. I think she's a sociopath, you guys. I'm honestly shocked that the others allowed Angel to be their leader once she started making careless and reckless decisions for them. Sure, she has cool powers, but she's seven and is not ready to lead an entire team of people. One small thing that threw me off was Fang's letter in the end. What fifteen year old boy do you know who says "sweetie"? I don't know, that just did not sound Fang-like to me at all.
Terrible. A total waste of time. I skipped many b-o-r-i-n-g parts. The "serious subjects" were mixed with soooo many aweful cliches.. Seriously, I don't get why people love this book so much.

*I received this book from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review* I really wanted to like this book. I loved J.A. Redmerski's Edge of Never series, and so I was very excited to start Song of the Fireflies. The problem was I never really liked Bray. She didn't really resonate with me. I definitely preferred Elias, I felt like he was more steady and clearheaded. Plus, it was difficult to read from Bray's point of view when she just seemed so flat out crazy. I did really enjoy how Elias and Bray loved each other. I think that was amazing, and I loved that they were willing to do whatever they could for each other. Bray was just so messed up, and it bothered me that she was willing to take Elias down with her. For me being in love with someone is being selfless, but the whole book Bray was overly selfish. I also started feeling like there were alot of similarities with some other New Adult books I had read. Especially Bray's bipolar disorder, I just really felt like there was another character that she seemed modeled after. It also bothered me at the end how Bray went from horribly suicidal to suddenly being fine. Granted it was the epilogue, but I didn't get to see her transition from one to the other and so it felt disjointed. Overall, I did really enjoy this book, and I love Redmerski's writing style. I was sucked in the whole way, but the character of Bray just fell flat for me. I give Song of the Fireflies 3 out of 5 stars, because it did draw me in, even if I didn't love everything. *This review was first posted to Moonlight Gleam Reviews http://moonlightgleam.com/2014/02/son...*

Stop playing games and use your words! They are so sweet together, but I want to smack them 90% of the time.

** spoiler alert ** 2.5/5, mainly for plausibility reasons, but also because the first third of the book was way more interesting than the middle and end. I really enjoyed the book for the first 150 or so pages. The writing was quite lovely and the shifting perspectives made the story more interesting than a simple day in the 1930s. The war section was just mundane though. It didn't grab me like other war novels. The third part was not boring by any means, but I think the issues leaking down from the first part affected my enjoyment of it. Also, I can't like Briony after what she did, so her hard job elicited no sympathy from me. My biggest issue, though, is that I also don't understand how Robbie could have possibly been convicted. The testimony of children is always questioned very thoroughly, as they are prone to lie and get confused and imagine things. True, Briony said that she "saw" him, but any lawyer worth his salt would bring up the suggestion that any of the other men were of the same, or similar, height and age. There's some reasonable doubt for you. And Robbie knew that Briony read the letter, which would been evidence that she was confused or frightened, thus diminishing the power of her testimony. Not only that, but Lola seemed like such a stupid, wimpy girl - any manner of rigorous interrogation would have likely made her break down and tell the truth. Also, it is pointed out by the author that everyone noticed Lola had bruises on her wrists before the boys took off, and that the real rapist had a new scratch on his face. I don't understand how the cops/lawyers/forensics/etc seemed to miss these simple facts. And not only that, but Robbie's lack of prior convictions, his hard work, his patronage by Briony's father, and his relationship with Cecelia would have been considered by the judge and likely would have reduced his sentence to time served or something, if he had indeed even been convicted. Then again, I may be thinking of today's court, but the sheer black-and-white approach to Robbie's conviction doesn't make any sense to me and really confused and annoyed me throughout the rest of the novel. I mean, think of To Kill a Mockingbird, which takes place in the same time period, different country to be sure, but the court case in that book dealt with extreme racism and prejudice, and it still utilized evidence and forensics and innocence until proven guilty. It doesn't make sense that Robbie was instantly convicted. What I was expecting was that Robbie would have been acquitted and Briony's lies simply would have affected his reputation, schooling, relationship with the family, and money given to him by the father. When it was revealed that he spent 3 years in jail I was surprised. It seems like McEwan was more interested in fueling the concept of "atonement" than actually crafting a clever lie to get Robbie in jail. Seriously, the testimony of one little girl, who wasn't even the one assaulted, who claimed to see the guy in the middle of the night, is not enough to put a guy in jail. Notwithstanding all the other evidence for his innocence. Not impressed with this author, no matter how nicely he writes!

Let it be known that I really enjoyed this book. Let it be known that I was secretly hoping America Singer would die. That said, I can now move on to my praise filled rant of a review. This book, much like it predecessor, The Selection, which I read back in 2013, is extremely addicting. It's like watching really bad reality TV, but with wars, and kingdoms, and royalty, and all that good dystopian stuff. And you know what I have found? I actually love this kind of crap. Now, I am all about giving credit where credit is due, so I must admit that this book was technically well written. This book was entertaining. It was fast paced and never lagged. It was interesting to the point that I could not put it down, reading it one day. It was like a life or death episode of the Bachelor, and it was great. The great flaw of this book was the main character, America Singer. Oh, America Singer. Sweet, idiotic America Singer. Never has a more 'wishy-washy' character been written. A more infuriating, frustrating, selfish, annoying, self righteous protagonist has never been put on paper. I hated it! This girl spends the entire book going back and forth between Aspen and Maxon. The she realizes that she loves Maxon, and what does she do? Pushes him away, because obviously, that is one does when in love with a prince. Then she goes and gets angry at Maxon for things out of his control and doesn't talk to him for a week. Of course, then she has the audacity to be angry when he dares to pay attention to another girl, after ignoring him for days. Poor Maxon is just getting dragged along basically. He was the only one I was cheering for in this whole thing, because Aspen too was getting annoying after a while. America is also very stupid. Now, let it be known that America is not an unintelligent person. She is actually quite knowledgeable, she's just kind of an idiot. She is rash, never thinking things through. It's like she never expects her actions to have consequences, and then it's never her who deals with them, it's usually Maxon who has to pay the price. Again, Maxon is getting the short end of the stick here. He can do so much better. I don't think America has caught on to the idea that the selection is a competition. That the girls there want to win, not just a husband, but a crown. She goes on and on about how she wants to change things and make the world a better place, but then decides that she doesn't want to play the game. Then gets mad when other girls play to win. This is a competition! No, America. If you want Maxon, which you do, and you want to change the world, you deeply desire, you must win the game. You must become a princess. And to do that you must play by the rules, not go around doing idiotic things just because you are upset. You need the kind on your side, at least until you win. And what do you do? Find every possible way to piss him off because you are a self righteous idiot! You can stop pretending when you get the man and have the crown, in the meantime don't make the one man that can ruin your life hate your guts! But that's just me using common sense. Anyway, as you all could see, I had a lot of emotions about America. Still, despite my dislike of America Singer, I also must admit that I also kinda loved her. She would make a great contestant on the Bachelor, if only for the entertainment factor. I can't wait to read The One. Also, as a prediction for book three, her dad is totally a spy for rebels. He was being hella sketchy at that party. If you've read it, don't tell me if it's true. I'm just calling it now. This, and other reviews, can be found on my blog, The Book Cover Girls

**ARC provided by author/publisher in exchange for an honest review** After reading a review by a friend I was very intrigued to get my hands on this book. I didn't completely understand what I would get myself into when I started this book. I went in with a very open mind. I am a big fan of taboo reads and not many things really surprise or turn me off in books. This book definitely was taboo but on the other hand the characters in this book are not the characters you find in your every day novels. Wavy is a little girl with so much responsibility and has been hurt so many times in her life. My heart BROKE for her, there were a couple of scenes that had me crying because nobody really understood her. To people she is weird, antisocial and does things "normal" people wouldn't do. She was unique and so grown-up for her young age. She was fearless and strong, and I just couldn't wait to see who she would grow up to be. Her parents are no good drug dealers/users and don't pay her any mind. They have scarred her so badly with their horrible behavior and teachings. She only has her younger brother who she is very protective of. They are all alone until they meet Kellen who takes a role as their protector. Kellen has his own problems but I just loved how he took Wavy under his wings and helped her out so much. Their friendship was one of a kind and so heartbreakingly beautiful. This friendship turns into more. I had mixed feelings because of the age difference (especially because Wavy was underaged). There was definitely very inappropriate things happening but I think I could overlook them because Wavy wasn't your typical young girl. In her young life she had been through things others wouldn't go through in their lifetimes. There were a couple of times she came across as immature but other times so grown up. I was blown away by this book. Wavy and Kellen were both two broken souls that healed each other. This book isn't for everyone because of the taboo elements. Be open minded if you do decide that you want to give this book a chance. I don't think I'll be able to forget this book easily, it has wormed its way into my heart. The characters are very dear to me! I love that there are multiple POVs and that they aren't very long. It really gave a great perspective of how the outside looked into Wavy and Kellen's life. Review originally posted at Step Into Fiction I love Angel and Fallen Angel books; I've put off reading a lot of them lately because it was getting tiresome reading all about the same thing, you know? It wasn't hard to figure out the ending of this book. I'm not sure if it was supposed to be that obvious or not but there was really no surprise, which was a bit of a disappointment. I was hoping I was suspecting someone all along and boom, it was someone I didn't see coming. I always love those books but alas, this was not one of them. It left me a bit bummed but not enough to make me not like the book. Julian is sexy, masculine and surprisingly loving. As a Fallen Angel, he's someone the Nephilim are supposed to kill because there are no gray areas. All Fallen Angels are bad and that's that. We all know in everything there are always gray areas; always. I'd make an exception for this man, I mean Angel because he's never done anything to show Lily that he means her harm. I know, I know - looks can be deceiving but you'll never know until you try, right? A female Nephilim is a rare thing so someone like Lily is heavily cherished, if you will. All the other, older, male Nephilim look out for her and almost considered her like the baby sister. It's kind of cute, in a way but this girl doesn't need looking out for. She is one of the greatest hunter's among all the Nephilim in the DC area. If you're wondering what Nephilim are, it's simple - they are the child of a human woman and an Angel (who either falls due to this or has already Fallen). Michael, who up until recently thought he was your average joe looking for a career change. He had a nice job with great pay but wanted to do something different so he became a cop. Little did he know his life was about to change even more. Turns out, Michael is a lot more than just average - he's a Nephilim who never appeared in any of their records. There's a lot of mystery surrounding Michael and I really, really want to get to know him even more in future books. I feel like we've only peeled away the outer layer and there's many layers left to remove. I can't say this is the best story I've seen from Jen but it's not bad, by any means. I definitely want to read the next book because I've fallen in love with the characters, the story is intriguing and I really want to know where the future of Nephilim stands and also where Julian stands. It is adult so younger readers, beware - it's not a story for you. Any fan of Jen's will definitely enjoy this and any fan of Angels/Fallen Angels will also enjoy. London...1812. Prinny has been regent for one year. England is still at war with France, and on the brink of with with America. And Lady Helen Wrexhall is finding out that she possesses a special power that can help rid the world of demons. Welcome to The Dark Days Club Lady Helen has been brought up to be a proper young lady. She knows that all she can hope for from life is to marry well, set up her own household, and have children. But when Lord Carlston appears, and explains to Lady Helen that she has a special gift that will help England, and possible the world, can she really give up everything she knows and wants out of life to become a demon hunter? One of the best things about this book is that Lady Helen has a choice. She can choose to join Lord Carlston and the Dark Days Club, or she can choose to remain a society lady, marry a Duke, and live the life that she has been preparing for. In most other books, when a power or destiny is revealed to a MC, that MC has no choice, but to except that power/destiny. In this book, Lady Helen always had a choice...right until the very end...it was always her choice. The other great thing about this book is the secondary characters. They are all well thought out and written true to the Regency era. Lady Helens' aunt is only concerned with making sure that Helen makes a good match in her marriage (preferably to the Duke of Selburn) and, of course, the latest fashions and what balls and dinner parties she can wear them to. Helens' uncle thinks that a woman should be seen and not heard, and can't wait for the day that Helen gets married and becomes another mans problem. Darby, Helens' maid, turns out to be a very good friend. At first I thought that she could not be trusted, but she turned out to only ever have Lady Helens' best intrest at heart. Lord Carlston is arrogant, handsome, rich, and extremely frustrating all at once...which makes him the perfect "I hate you, but I really kind of like you" guy for Lady Helen. All in all this was a great book and I cannot wait to read the next book!

This review was first posted at http://www.rubysreads.com. I DNF'd Little Women and Me. I kind of think I shouldn't have read it considering that The Twin's Daughter was a mediocre for me. I was, however, enticed by the prospect of a different ending to Little Women. I mean, are there people out there that don't think Jo and Laurie should have ended up together? Or that don't go "Amy!" (in the style of Jerry Seinfeld saying "Newman!") every time they consider the book's ending. I guess that, given such a reaction to the original story, I hardly thought Little Women and Me could irritate me more. However...I didn't even make it to the end. Why? Three little words: It was boring. The story begins in the present tense, with Emily, the MC, facing your typical teenage issues--annoying siblings and crushes that don't realize you exist--but quickly gets to the action of the story. Which is: Emily traveling into Little Women. Let the yawning commence. From that time on, Emily is immersed in the dreary domestic life of Civil War New England. Probably true to life--but that doesn't mean it makes for interesting reading. Also, it took forever for Laurie to actually enter the story. Innumerable pages were spent on Emily's integration into the March family, on the fact that Jo's awesomeness in book form is annoying in person, how Meg is stiflingly principled, Beth is so sweet you feel awful having any negative thoughts about her, and Amy is terribly vain. Not to mention that Marmy is so intent on giving to the needy that she doesn't recall that charity begins at home. The charm (and joy) of retelling classics is that it's (in theory) bringing new life to an ageless tale. Little Women and Me did not do this. It was a boring retread that utterly failed to hold my interest. To be fair, I'm sure this was, in part, due to the fact that the character was a 14 year old, which made the tone more Middle Grade than Teen. I did peek at the end, but it wasn't enough to make me want to go back and read the intervening pages. It's too bad. Little Women is definitely a book with an ending I'd like to see retold.

Ryker. Okay, so I have a major crush on ALL of the Cold Fury Hockey men, but Garrett Samuelson has been my favorite from the start, even when he was just a lovable secondary character. Can they find a way to make a love hot enough to melt ice last, despite the obstacles standing in their way? Well, tie me up and slap me silly. Oh, that's not an exclamation of surprise about this book - I mean, I knew it was going to be good because, hello, I love this author and this series. No, that's more a suggestion of what I would like Ryker to do...to me. Because I have it BAD for Brick. He's strong, and he dirty-talks. He also braids hair and has hilarious, occasionally girly chats with his teammates. Oh, and he respects his woman, his boss, believes in her and still makes her come like a freight train. It still hit all the right notes in terms of tension, drama and angst - my heart was racing for Gray at one particular moment - but it was oh, so amusing and enjoyable. Gray and Ryker just...worked. They had good balance, between jokey playfulness, scorching hotness and emotional rightness. As a matter of fact, the story as a whole was perfectly balanced. It launched right in to the good stuff, making me fall for kick-ass, genius Gray and tough, tall and touching Ryker right off the bat. Or maybe I should say stick, since you know...HOCKEY. Regardless, it simply flowed perfectly; never slowing down completely, but never bombarding me with unnecessary or overworked problems. It had enough going on to peak and keep my interest, and make my heart race, so that I categorically could not put it down but never was it too much. I loved that Sawyer Bennett, who really excels at making her females strong but vulnerable, needy but never weak, made Gray a woman of power. She was brilliant. She felt like she could be a real person. A friend. And I've already said she wrote Ryker as the perfect man. My perfect man, when it comes down to it. Sorry, Garrett, you've been benched... ~ Beth, 5 stars So after reading Zack (the last book in this series) I was really looking forward to the next book! I was hesitant when I learned it was Ryker because he is so sweet. But let me tell you, that sweet boy can dirty talk and screw like a bad boy. Read as: Restock your battery supply! Now to the part you have all been waiting for... The sexiness level of this book on a scale of one to five is a 17. I don't not give this rating lightly. As always, I can't wait to see what other delightfully naughty and hot things Sawyer has in store for us next! ~ Devlynn, 5 stars Sweet baby Jesus, these Cold Fury Men just keep getting better and better! Tris and Four are NOT the central focus of this story- which I enjoyed. Their love story, which I thought would probably be the main focus, is instead placed into turmoil and doubt. Still no release for the sexual tension, but in this book, it's okay- because the rest of the plot is sufficient enough to carry the story. In the first book, the main focus is on passing initiation into their faction and then later identifying a potential threat to their way of life. The second book is a full-fledged war against the enemy. Well, I think Veronica Roth has finally done it: Created a sequel that is BETTER than the original book. Or at least, it improves upon it. I have to say.... Veronica answered all the questions that needed to be answered, while opening up new doors and posing new questions. She left me at the edge of my seat for most of the book. She did pick up the pace for the second half of the book- which was a great way to build up to the climax of the story. I thought Tris' reactions to the events were very realistic. If she did not respond to having killed someone, or the deaths of her loved ones, she would be an unsympathetic character. Yes, I was frustrated with Tris for not standing up and being brave as I thought she should- until I put myself into her shoes. Although the words PTSD are not mentioned in this book, I think Tris suffers from it and for good reason. The relationship with Four develops not out of blind infatuation but in a genuine understanding and acceptance of one another, even though it is difficult and frustrating. That, too, I thought was very realistic. I was a little annoyed that constant "introduction of a character" -> "that character dies two chapters later" aspect of the book... And if there were anything I would change about this book, that would be it. It seems to me, though, that Veronica thought of a great story, and then spread it out equally throughout three books. Many others (cough, Hunger Games, cough) have a great premise for a book and play it out in the first book- leaving the remainder of the trilogy wanting for a captivating, believable conclusion to the story. "Insurgent", however, continues the story with the same momentum as "Divergent" and builds upon an already interesting plot line. I am very pleasantly surprised by this book. Perhaps I'm getting too soft, or perhaps after reading the train wreck of "Matched" and "Crossed", my expectations are pretty low. But all in all, I think this series has great potential. Thank you, Veronica, for creating characters that I actually care about, and can't wait to see how they end up in the conclusion of the trilogy.

I have never felt more outraged at a plot twist before. NEVER. There are tons of things that you could fault this book, but Chase dying and the way he died, with all the things between them so unresolved IS NOT SOMETHING I AM OKAY WITH. I have no love for Harper. Up until half the book, when THE THING happens (and one could even make an argument that she was largely responsible for even that,) literally EVERYTHING that happened to her was because she was just to dumb to live without parental supervision. I called the pregnancy the SECOND they were together. And then the symptoms. Please. Talk about cliche. I feel like a jerk for saying this, but Harper embodies everything I found distasteful in a book. I also generally dislike books with cheating on them, so this book was most definitely not for me. The craft is tolerable, but that's about it. Even then, I could've find it in myself to forgive it all. Maybe. I possibly could have. EXCEPT CHASE DIED. AND EVERYONE JUST ACCEPTED IT AND MOVED ON IMMEDIATELY. EVEN HIS PARENTS. EVEN THE MOTHER OF HIS CHILD WHOM HE WANTED TO MARRY AND RAISE THE BABY WITH NEVERMIND HE WAS BASICALLY JUST THE REBOUND GUY. NO ONE MOURNED HIM EXCEPT FOR ME AND THAT IS JUST SAD. HE WAS TRYING TO GET IT TOGETHER AND THEN BAM IT WAS ALL GONE. Again, I feel like a jerk for saying this, but what happened hit me really hard, and I was a sobbing mess and I didn't even like him all that much. So it stands to reason the people that loved him would've been devastated, but I didn't get that from them. Harper married Brandon, they had another kid together, and Chase just drifted into nothingness. I guess there is a metaphysical argument here, but I didn't really see the point other than having Harper end up with Brandon without dumping Chase. Like, the author thought to herself.. "mmm.. What should I do with this guy? I know! Let's just kill him off." I'm sorry, but that doesn't work if you are not George R.R. Martin. No. Just no. My heart was completely crushed and I didn't even get closure. Ah. Just remember another thing. Brandon was okay with not having a sexual relationship with her. I really respected him for that. BUT HE IS TOTALLY AGREEABLE TO THE FACT THAT HIS GIRLFRIEND GOT KNOCKED UP BY ANOTHER DUDE AND EVEN VOLUNTEERED TO STEP IN WHEN CHASE DIED. Yeah, that is totally normal behavior for a guy in his early twenties. PLEAHSE. He was my favorite character until he got back together with Harper. Man, have some self-respect. Rant over. At least until I can remember other things that pissed me off about this book because it's been a while since I read it.

This little book packs an impressively large punch. There are essentially only two characters - the Captain is a Civil War vet living in Texas who travels the countryside, reading aloud from newspapers to make a living. Johanna is a young girl who was taken captive by the Kiowa and grew up in their culture, then was later found and entrusted to the Captain for return to what's left of her family. It's really these two characters who make this book special. The Captain drifts from town to town, still reeling from the loss of his wife. Johanna tries to escape what, for her, is a completely foreign and hostile world and return to the only life she can remember. Neither one entirely feels at home in the world, and watching them grow to trust each other is really satisfying. The politics of Texas at the time were very complicated, with bandits and raiders and ex-soldiers and violently conflicting loyalties, which also gives the journey some fun action scenes and a sense of peril. The book is somewhere in the neighborhood of 200 pages, but it offers a solid sense of history, action and plot, and a real emotional connection to its endearing characters. Some authors can't do this well in twice the pages, but Paulette Jiles has really pulled it off.

This is a hard book to rate! There are some things I really, really loved about it, mostly in the gender-swapping of some traditional issues -- Georgie works all the time, Neal stays home and takes care of the kids, Neal is upset Georgie doesn't prioritise her family more and doesn't prioritise him more -- this is the stuff of a thousand novels but usually it is the man with the career and the woman who is at home. And it is done without ever casting any aspersions on Georgie for having a career in the first place -- she has a lot of self-doubt but Neal is shown as actually being a very devoted homemaker and father. And I loved that it was about marriage, real marriage, not melodrama, and not just the falling in love phase, but the living together every day phase and the how you make big decisions often without meaning to, and all of that. Also, I loved that Georgie does figure out what is going on -- that she is talking Neal into coming to propose to her 15 years earlier. A lot of books with this kind of time slippage never let the characters figure it out, or not until the very end. And her "list of possibilities" when she first realises something weird is going on was so funny I laughed out loud. But it is only three stars because there is a lot of repetition and circling and some pretty boring scenes; it could easily have been a shorter, tighter book, I think. I did not like Georgie enough to want to keep spending time with her while she worried and fretted and had yet another conversation with Seth, I wanted the plot to move along and the revelations to get revealed and the end to happen.

4.5 stars from me. Why? This book tore my soul out. Oh my feels hurt so bad. SO BAD. Full review can be found here: https://agingerlyreview.wordpress.com... This is only the second book by Adam that I have read and it blew me away. I mean... the title is a bit of a spoiler but it did not stop me from reading this story. Instead, it drew me in and made me what to find out why. Short recap: In the not so distant future, if you are destined to die, Death-Cast will call you between 12a and 3a to let you know. You will have 24 hours to live and this is known as your End Day. They will not tell you how you die but you certainly will die. This is the story of Mateo and Rufus' End Day. What an interesting concept for a story! An algotherm, which is never disclosed, knows when your last day on the Earth is and you are warned about it. It makes me wonder what I would do if I knew it was my last day on Earth? Would I call everyone I loved and tell them that? Would I curl into a ball and cry all day? Would I shut myself away from the world and try to beat the odds? So many possibilities. Adam discussed these and so much more in this story. The story does focus on Mateo Torrez and Rufus Emeterio, two teenage boys who received the call from Death-Cast. Both teens have had rough lives and feel they are being slightly cheated out of a full life. They both download an app, The Last Friend, and choose to connect with people who have either received the Death-Cast call or people who want to be a friend to those during their End Days. Sure, it had its odd freaks but somehow Mateo and Rufus find each other. They set out to help each other have the best End Day possible. Little did they know that a romance would start between them. Just thinking about the romance between Mateo and Rufus is bringing tears to my eye. No lie, I'm slightly crying thinking about it. A lot of people didn't think their attraction towards one another was believable since these two knew each other less than 24 hours but magic can happen anytime, anywhere. My heart broke for these two because no matter what... they both die at the end. I got a little ahead of myself... sorry. Silvera did a brilliant job of interweaving and tangling the lives of Mateo and Rufus. These two boys came from completely different backgrounds yet they still understood each other. That's not easy to find regardless of who you are or what your situation in life is. The development of the characters flowed and just worked. To me, it was believable. It pulled me in and never let me go for a single moment. This was a hell of an emotional roller coaster and I'm still not fully healed from it. I'm not sure how much more I can say about this story other than I really want everyone to read it. It broke me in a way I didn't know was possible. It was masterfully done and it has now made me a Slivera fan for life.

Why do I continually buy popular books? I haven't met one yet that makes me actually glad to have read it! I fear I may be slightly masochistic when it comes to reading books, buying into the hive mind and attempting to ascertain the raw knowledge and emotion that the masses love. It is a desire which can only be fulfilled by misery, wherein I read such awful novels and then ponder how the readers who loved them managed to do so. Then I stay up too late and review those books, knowing full well that my comment shall not leave a lasting mark on the world, and that my retyping of badly spelled words on my tablet keyboard is all for naught. Don't forget, dear review reader, that oblivion is the future of everything. If that little blip was annoying to read, then don't read this book! For some reason John Green thinks every teenager is somehow a huge philosophical thinker and that each one spouts off SAT style words like nothing. I can assure him that no, they do not. Also, who smokes metaphorically? I swear I have never heard of anyone making so many references to metaphorical stuff. Also, the love rang very shallow for me. Almost reminiscent of Twilight in the beginning. Not a good sign. Maybe a teenaged girl in love isn't the best character for him to write. Personally I would have preferred it from the point of view of Gus. Also I felt like the book placed way too much emphasis on her favorite story. I was left feeling like the parents who had no idea why their kid was crazy for it. I can say that, somehow despite all of this, I did feel some emotions. Yes, this guy actually had me tear up a bit. I don't think I would have the same reaction, or any kind of sympathy for her character, if it weren't for that. All in all, a cool concept that was ruined by horribly over aged teengers, even the non cancer inflicted ones. I mean, this level of philosophical ranting replacing normal converstion is akin to the problems in the Jurassic Park series, but even Ian Malcom had a reason for being that philosophical. Not everyone is a scholar while on their death bed. In conclusion, read it if you want, but don't say I didn't warn you. I will add that I loved Will Grayson, Will Grayson, but mainly because I thought it hilarious and laughed out loud while reading it.

I'd probably say this is a 4.5 star book, but that's ok. This is a book I would have clearly judged by its title and cover, had I not seen rave reviews of it. It is about Plum, a self-hating fat woman who longs to be invisible. She has failed every diet she has attempted and is counting the days until her weight-loss surgery. A woman starts stalking her and eventually hands her a book that is an expose of the diet industry. This leads her to a community of feminists that aim to show her her self-worth as is. This is a far simplified way to discuss how women are only valued for the "fuckability" and adoption of societal standards of beauty and behavior, though it's an effective one. It is one of those books I know I can't hand to everyone I know because of the guerrilla feminist revenge story that is the other thread of this book, and partially because of the implications of handing a book with the word diet on the cover - another proof that this book is needed. This is often a very funny telling of Plum's experiences, the characters she meets along the way, and what eventually happens to Alicia, the skinny woman inside her. This is a little bit like She's Come Undone, but also a little bit like Valerie Solanas' SCUM Manifesto. It is an important book and despite my hesitation, I want to give it to every insecure girl I know.

Real Rating: 4.5 stars First off, I just want to say this is my first Kasie West novel--I know! I own PIVOT POINT and need to start it--and I was pleasantly surprised! I'm a big plot lover but the characterization of Caymen is what truly impressed me. Caymen is your typical high school senior who is working way too hard to keep her little family afloat, never wanting to let her mom down. She works long shifts in her mother's doll shop, willing to risk her education and her own dreams. In walks Xander, the heir to a 500 hotel chain franchise. Caymen has had it drilled into her that people like Xander would never want someone poor like her. In this worlds colliding novel, the two characters start a quest to find a future for each other that does not involve their predestined ones. Filled with highs, lows, and witty, sarcastic humor, THE DISTANCE BETWEEN US is a great contemporary YA novel you can't help but devour. I'll start off with Caymen. I loved her attitude. You can immediately tell how much she hates working in that creepy doll shop. You can tell that she'd much rather be doing other things but is willing to sacrifice her own fun for her single mother who is just trying to make ends meet. I loved the devotion she had to her mom. Even though her life wasn't glamorous or her ideal version of fun, she still appreciated everything her mother did for her and never seemed to take anything for granted. But that certainly doesn't mean she doesn't have some of that teenage rebellion in her. Caymen is probably the most sarcastic person I have ever "met" in my life. She's so quick to make a comment, she doesn't miss a beat. I loved every remark that came out of her mouth. I'm very sarcastic and have the dry humor like she has but man, that girl is good. She comes up with the perfect thing to say at exactly the right moment. I usually think of good things, after the fact. (Fun fact: this is called "L'esprit de l'escalier"). Sometimes I did think that she got a bit whiny and jumped to conclusions way too soon but overall, she had a great head on her shoulders. This brings me to Xander. Xander is the kind of guy you wish would walk into your place of work and fall in love with you. I mean really. Caymen gives him all these rich boy stereotypes that he just completely shoots down. He's sweet, he's super thoughtful--I wish I had a guy to bring me coffee on my way to school everyday!--he fires away sarcastic comments right back at Caymen, and he's just the all around good guy you can't help but love. I love how he never once looked down at Caymen for being someone not in his social class. Besides beckoning at her when they first met, he treats her with the same sort of respect he would treat his mother. He takes her on all these elaborate "career days" and when she takes him to a graveyard, he doesn't even bat an eye. He enjoys spending time with her and could care less about the money issue. I do wish he would've stated his feelings for Caymen sooner. Although he did all the gestures that point exactly to that, girls can be silly and don't believe anything until they hear it come from your mouth. If he had said something sooner, I feel like a bunch of the drama that took place could have been avoided--see above mentioned jumping to conclusions part. As Jess said in her review of this book, we miss out on a lot of the relationship building between these two characters. She says it more eloquently than I could. Here's the gist: we know they have feelings for each other, it's super obvious, but we don't get to see those feelings evolve into something more. Again, check Jess' review for better explanation! I did love the plot of the story, though. I loved the idea of these two perfect strangers planning fun "career days" for each other. These showed just how much they paid attention to each other. Each day was unique and let their personalities shine. I think this is a great way to truly get to know someone! Aside from the great characters and plot, West teaches the readers a very important lesson. Firstly, don't judge a book by its cover. Always take the time to get to know somebody, they may surprise you. Next, take time for yourself. While it's nice to make others happy, you have to make yourself happy too. Do what you love and take some risks. And lastly, learn forgiveness. One of my all time favorite things about YA novels are the moral lessons that are in embedded in them. I adore authors who take the time to show true character growth and learning. It's what life is all about.
