My problems with the book: A Flat Main Character- As a character Amy, or as I mentally referred to her throughout- 'Sad Sack' - is just too sad. Everything is terrible, no one likes her, everyone is mean to her, her mother is a drug addict who doesn't love her, she lives in a sad trailer park, her mother steals her money, she is bullied and manipulated by other people, etc... it just went on, and on, and on... we get it already Sad Sack is the sympathetic character. The author attempts to flesh out Sad Sack by making her appear to struggle with a variety of 'moral' choices but these feel so contrived and one sided that they merely emphasize her flatness. A Cartoonishly Terrible World-The world of Oz is so over the top terrible as to be ridiculous. I've read some reviews that describe it as being like 'The Nightmare before Christmas' and I feel like that's a fair characterization. But sometimes less is more- especially with books, and describing weird henchmen- one of whom shoots deadly bubbles from a tube in their mouth, and another who has a bicycle for a body- isn't creepy-- it's stupid, and it emphasizes how unrefined every other aspect of this book is. A Poorly Plotted out Plot- throughout the book we build to what is initially portrayed as a complex assassination plan but eventually boils down to attempting to stab Dorothy at a dinner party-- and it doesn't even manage to deliver in that respect leaving us with a cliff-hanger ending, and the unappetizing prospect of a sequel or 2. Teenage Nonsense- Sad sack manages to fall in love with every one with a Y chromosome in the book for no discernible reason other than superficial attractiveness. We are also treated to a wide range of unnecessary commentary regarding everyone's clothes, footwear, makeup, and hairstyles while artfully skirting anything approaching meaningful character development. This book will likely only appeal to teenage goths, or fans of similarly terrible books like Twilight, or A Discovery of Witches.

Continuing my reading of all things cyberpunk and tech-dystopian, I bumped into Tokyo Ghost, a preamble into what I assume is an epic exploration of life in a fully robotic modern world. Despite the bad tropes of epic stories, not in the least the Eastern-European distrust for centralized power, Tokyo Ghost is a very appealing graphic novel. I am curious to see how it follows. The environment follows the negative (and more dramatic, and surely non-Asimovian) line of Manna: after robots were developed and allowed to take most human jobs, an overwhelming majority of humans are wasting in unemployment. They degrade to couch potatoes, constantly looking for the next Internet- or drug-based fix, controlled by large tv and pharma-meagcorporations. There's also the "naturalistic" (environmentally friendly and of course totally sustainable, a la Ecotopia) enclave, the human-on-human televised battle (a la Battle Royale, but with monster trucks and velodrome audience), etc. Very interesting to think about and compare with what the authors propose. The story is for me the weakest part: the endearing characters She (smart, cute, in love) and He (previously in love, now taking heavy drugs), are pushed by thugs and reality from the dystopian future LA to the utopian neo-Tokyo. Just why they are not able to do better, why She is named chief of environmentalists, and plenty of other whys, remains unclear and a strong disincentive to read further. The drawings are robust, a bit cliche, and with too much gore for my liking. But there is art behind the ugliness, and quality overall.

I read The Hunger Games more than a year ago, finishing it despite my strong dislike of its protagonist, Katniss. I made it 100 pages into Catching Fire before I could take no more. I hoped that watching the movie would make Katniss feel more human to me. More someone I'd like to root for. It did. I resumed reading Catching Fire, and was able to finish it by imagining Jennifer Lawrence in the role. I still didn't like it, exactly. I just wanted to see how the story ended. I'd heard such dismayed reviews about the conclusion of the trilogy that I expected I, too, would find it unpalatable. Instead, I found myself finally both unwilling to put it down and truly feeling Katniss. Not just being in her head. Not just hearing her mental rundown of the actions she's taking or planning to take, but feeling her. This is what I crave from a protagonist, and I'm so glad to have found that connection at the end. And what an end it was! I finished with tears in my eyes and goosebumps rippling up and down my arms. It's not an ending without sadness, but it is, indeed, an ending full of truth, love and halting, wary but real hope.

This review includes many spoilers, because I don't care. You see, this is why as a reader you should try to review the books you love. Because, I truly enjoyed Marriage Games and Separation Games by CD Reiss, but I wasn't motivated to review them, so now you're stuck with this rant as your first impression of my impression of this author. Oh, well. Let's just say that Bombshell was a disappointment. More than a disappointment, actually, because it takes a lot to fuck up this trope for me, and Reiss definitely fucked up this trope. I was so excited to read this! I mean, it's a Hollywood romance. It's a surprise baby romance (my kryptonite!). And, it's also an off-limits love story. Literally (and by 'literally' I mean figuratively; I'm not a moron) this book was the chocolate, peanut butter cookie from the Barnes & Noble cafe--a perfect mix of ingredients. But, I bit into it and it was... I'm so upset. And what's worse, is the fact that I wasn't only disappointed--this isn't a simple 'meh' read for me, I actively disliked this, pretty much from page one. The writing is subpar, the story is trite, and mainly, the hero is a... ...and a fool. I mean, this guy is so annoying that I hoped there was a love triangle twist, and y'all know how I feel about those. Let me give you some backstory on my whole Bombshell experience, so you'll understand why I'm not recommending it. This is going to be long. Bombshell follows...shit, I already forgot their names. Brad and Cara! But, the story opens with Nicole, a hysterical five-year-old screaming a public bathroom, standing in her mess, while her nanny tries to calm her the hell down. (Okay, kids shit themselves--whatever.) Then, the nanny's friend, Cara, enters. She has an instant connection with aforementioned screaming child who calms down just as her new dad walks into the bathroom. Eyes lock, sparks fly, heat simmers. (Not a bad meet-cute. There's potential.) Cara leaves. Then, new Dad freaks out and calls the agency to get her out of a previously agreed to contract so that she can come help raise his daughter, because of course he's a control freak. (Insert your preferred eye-roll gif here.) Cara agrees to come in as a consultant, because she absolutely refuses to work for a celebrity family, but finds it hard to say no to the compelling movie star. They both meet at his house to discuss the babe's future and end up betting, over a game of pool, how to pick her preschool and her caretaker. Did I mention that this poor babe was "dropped in [Brad's] lap" because her mother died? Yep. So, that is the first sketchy move these so-called adults make regarding this child. Fast-forward to Brad hiring TWO nannies to help with his kid, because god forbid he put any real effort in, and my patience was threadbare. Brad is a child--seriously, he's so immature, selfish, and clueless that I have no idea how anyone would think him a worthy hero. NOT ONLY THAT, but the writing is...not good. I expected more from this author, since I found the prose in Marriage Games pretty compelling, but her sentences in Bombshell are careless and unfinished. There are too many fragmented sentences. So many that I thought it was a glitch related to editing, so I switched from my ARC to a KU edition, and... So bad. Then, I tried rationalizing that it was just the guy's POV, and that might be why he seemed like such a moron, but, nope. Cara's POV might've been a bit more smooth, but overall the narration is mediocre. Because, Cara's really no great hero either. It's clear that she loves her job and the kids, but how could she let a fool like Brad distract her from what she knows is right? I will say that I didn't hate everything about this book, or else I would've stopped reading. I enjoyed the romance, the scenes with Brad and Cara, since I thought their sexual chemistry was pretty hot. Also, their banter was okay, once I got over how much of a douche Brad was and over my annoyance with Cara for putting up with Brad's foolishness. Honestly, minus the kid this would've been a pretty good Hollywood romance featuring a selfish playboy and down-to-earth, unimpressed heroine. But! That's my point. There is a kid in this book, and NO ONE IS CONCERNED THAT THIS LITTLE GIRL JUST LOST HER MOTHER. There's a small, very superficial scene about it, but other than that, nada. Basically, these are the adults: Oh well, your mom just died, but your new dad is just concerned about how his life has gone off track and your nanny cares, somewhat, but fighting off sexual feelings is way more important. Oh, and she can't get too close, because she's not supposed to get attached to her charges... Um, you're a fucking nanny, get another job. And, this is what Brad thinks. The one line I highlighted in this train wreck: "She's like glue, she holds everything together." Um, no, you need to get your own shit together. Honestly, if I was one of their friends, I would've called CPS on them. But, I'm trained in psychology and education, so I have no patience. *Sigh* This book, is just...don't read it. Or, read it if you want. Whatever, you're a grown ass person, live your life. I'm moving on, and I probably won't read this author again. Oh, there's also a "secret" that's supposed to make Brad more sympathetic, but I saw it coming a fucking mile away, so... Also, there's another reveal near the end that actually took me by surprise, but it managed to erase any good will I felt for the protagonists, so I'm gonna...

(Book chosen for review by poll) This is, of course, one of the most discussed books of recent years, usually for either a) being rubbish or b) its supposed novelty value and taboo-breaking or shocking ideological angles. Like a lot of very popular, much-discussed books (cf. Twilight, Fifty Shades of Grey) it's actually not particularly radical or original. The "conspiracy theory" it expounds is largely fictional (which would be unremarkable if so much of the "buzz" around it didn't revolve around the teasing of the possibility that it was all true) and in fact so similar to the non-fiction book Holy Blood, Holy Grail that the authors of that book tried to sue Dan Brown. Similarly, fiction that portrays the Catholic Church in a negative or villainous light or that uses theology to spin a thriller plot is hardly revolutionary. The above paragraph was just to get all that out of the way, since I'm more interested in talking about The Da Vinci Code's merits as a novel (or lack thereof) separate from any brouhaha over its subject matter. I read it (via charity shop, like so many) sometime after it came out to see what all the fuss was about, and the two main impressions I gained from it were: 1) It was pretty dull and not at all worthy of so much controversy - I probably had a more exciting and memorable time scrambling around out-of-the-way bits of my Oxford college library looking for resources that might indicate whether there was any grain of truth in any of the Biblical conspiracy stuff. 2) In addition to generally dull/clunky writing, it committed a massive, blatant basic storytelling fail. It was largely this (combined with its undeserved fame) that caused me to put it on my "hall of shame" shelf. The big writing fail, to which most of the rest of this review will be devoted, is, put simply: the book has the wrong main character. Robert Langdon, our nominal hero, is thoroughly dull, seemingly existing solely to spout exposition and solve puzzles (I can't remember a single distinctive personal detail about him, not even some mundane Characterization 101 element like how he takes his coffee, what he wears, or even what he looks like). Worse, he's not only largely unengaged emotionally with the central plot, but he already knows much of the central "mystery" (with the only thing at stake being proof of this central conspiracy theory which he knows of but doesn't seem to care strongly about). This would be bad enough, were it not for the fact that the book has a much more suitable protagonist in Sophie Neveu. She has significantly more emotional investment in the plot (since it's her estranged grandfather who is murdered at the beginning) combined with the skills to actively assist in solving it (unlike a typical bereaved relative in a murder mystery), and all of the Biblical conspiracy theory flim-flam is new to her but not (to a great extent) to Langdon. All this means that our "hero" spends most of the book as something of a detached tag-along and exposition dispenser on the much more emotional and potentially much more interesting, but largely unexplored, journey of another character. The obvious reason for this, of course, is that this is the second book in a franchise revolving around Langdon, a sort of nerdy middle-aged James Bond (complete with "getting the girl" at the end, uuuurgh), and so he has to be the central character. (One could hypothesize that the other obvious reason is that Dan Brown prefers to write a middle-aged know-it-all male American protagonist, even in a novel set in France about religious attitudes to women, and if one were to go full gender politics on the subject, label this Mansplaining: The Novel.) This, to me, simply exposes the obvious problems with writing a franchise about a globe-trotting action-hero professor who solves mysteries others have more personal investment in, and isn't really a good excuse even if one accepts the franchise concept; it's perfectly possible to write a novel from one character's perspective that is more about another character's struggles and/or emotional journey; this article discusses the idea, using To Kill A Mockingbird and The Great Gatsby as examples. However, I suspect that Dan Brown isn't really too concerned with Novel-Writing 101 concepts like "who is this book about" or "what is the emotional journey", as opposed to lurid violence and grotesquerie (I didn't even mention the questionable "mad albino assassin monk" character), routine plot twists (WHAT A TWEEST!) or clever-sounding exposition about historical trivia, conspiracy theories etc. that keeps people reading and the columnists controversy-ing. So I guess my conclusion, like so many others, is that he's simply a writer of high-concept plot-driven airport thrillers who's managed through clever marketing and adherence to formula (apparently analysis has shown that his writing style is highly suited to keeping people turning the pages) to make it really, really big. (Not that there's any reason why high-concept thrillers have to insult people's intelligence or neglect interesting characterization - see for example Neal Stephenson's Reamde, which I've often described using the phrase "the best airport thriller in the world".)

The girls are either baby makers, zombies are eating brains, or love is forbidden and girls are paired up with boys they're initially madly in love with... until they meet "the bad boy." But I think she could've done a better job with the ending, instead of halfways tying up all the "loose" ends and cramming everything into one final chapter. I needed more. And honestly, I was thinking of a 3-4 star rating, but I really despised that ending. So 2 stars it is.

I received an ARC from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. When was the last time you read a laugh out loud, can't stop reading, contemporary YA about a rebellious teenager living in a very traditional home? I thought about that after I read SINCE YOU ASKED. It literally has been years since I've read a book that has made me laugh as hard as this book has. The summary on the book does a pretty awesome job at telling you what this is about. Holly is a hysterically sarcastic teenager just trying to survive her sophomore year of high school, and survive living with her very traditional, no-nonsense mother. What started off as a way to pass the time, Holly now has a column in the newspaper where she goes on and on about what is wrong with teenagers these days. She covers everything from the homecoming court to Thanksgiving to summer expectations. Her column is awesome and I would've loved reading something like that in my school newspaper. One of the best parts about this book is the structure of the writing. Not only do you get the typical chapter style narration, but you also get to see Holly's column, the mysterious love notes she receives from an admirer, and her own doodling, albeit copyedits or a seating chart. I thought including these things really added to the overall feel of the novel. So you get to read about Holly's year in high school and feel like you are right there with her as she's going through life. Holly was great. She said everything that I thought when I was in high school. Goo's ability to make her characters realistic is impeccable. I have quite the sarcastic dry humor myself, so I instantly connected with Holly. The secondary characters were great, as well. They all were completely different from one another but together they were a group of friends that I would love to have. Their personalities, while opposite, complemented each other nicely. They always stick up for one another and even if they get in fights, they know they could never stay mad for too long. I loved how the book didn't just focus on Holly's new-found journalism hobby. While the story was a light, fast read, you still get to experience some deeper issues like Holly's struggle to be something her parents are proud of while still keeping her individuality. Growing up in a traditional Korean household is not something Holly resents but something that sort of clashes with her rebellious spirit. It's all about balance. Holly has to learn to how to still be herself but while keeping her parents and their way of life happy. It also touches on the issue of not judging a book by the cover. You can't always assume how a person truly is unless you sit down and try to get to know them. If you're looking for a fun, fast read with enjoyable characters, I highly recommend this book! Maurene knows how to create a story that you'll eagerly gobble up in just a couple of sittings. You'll love Holly's witty sense of humor and how unafraid she is of being completely blunt. Filled to the brim with pop-culture references, realistic truths, and lots of teenage angst, you can't help but wish you went to school with Holly and her friends! This review can be found at: The Bookish Daydreamer

Storyline: 2/5 Characters: 5/5 Writing Style: 4/5 World: 5/5 This was like watching a street show where a visiting foreigner kept ten plates simultaneously spinning on long poles when delivering a lesson on physics with perfect grammar in his second language while periodically interjecting self-deprecating ethnic jokes as he nodded and smiled, encouraging you to enjoy yourself. I was entertained, and then impressed, then educated, and subsequently humbled, humored, abashed that I was humored, and somehow still fully satisfied by the end. This was one of those rare opportunities to hold something wondrous, a work of art from a genius. The work shifted from an entertaining novel with science fiction trappings to a serious discussion of how things could have been. It lectured while amusing. It deplored and mocked the evil of the enemy while reminding us that not every enemy was evil. The Man in the High Castle taunted Allies whose self-satisfaction and superiority depended upon the frail bases of destiny, divine plan, and history written by victors. It held nothing sacred, yet used the sacred to unfold the story. Philip K. Dick lowered himself - stepped down from the High Castle - so as to help guide the reader through the maze of concentric circles he had laboriously structured. He then taunted and teased readers for thinking they had understood the pattern and what it all meant. I read the last chapter, literally on the edge of my seat, waiting to be permitted in on the joke, the lesson, the secret handshake. I'm no Juliana. I'm not going to say I understood it all. It was enough for me to stand in the presence of greatness and view the masterpiece. An aside: I wouldn't mind joining a book club and reading this again or perhaps taking a literature course that taught this book. It's not an easy read, and it is not an exciting read. If you read it, don't read it for the story - the plot isn't that interesting. And come to think of it, don't read it for the alternate history, not really. The book isn't there to shock you with how terrible things have been. If anything, the book is there to show us how normal this terrible future would have become. I read it as being about people, about we who inhabit this the-Allies-won-the-war reality. And I found that to be the gem in the story.

** spoiler alert ** I thought this book was okay.The parts about what the North Koreans thought about the outside world were interesting. Kim's internal conflict between wanting to tell her students the truth about the world, and the desire to not make her students lives harder was fascinating. Kim talks about how, in North Korea, you are always being monitored by someone, and seditious thinking can be very dangerous. If the students learn the truth, then instead of believing sincerely the DPRK's propoganda, they will have to pretend to believe, which will be much riskier. Given this, is it ethical to dump truth on them, especially knowing that it may make you, the Westerner, feel better than the amount of good it will do them? It's unlikely Kim's students will band together, start a revolution, and overthrow Kim Jung Un. More likely is the possibility that they will simply find it more difficult to behave in the ways necessary for their survival, and they will therefore be at greater risk of being sent to the gulags Kim so abhors. It was also very interesting to learn about the huge list of topics that were verboten for the teachers to discuss. Basically, the missionaries are playing the long game. They are not focused on immediate results but on results two or three generations in the future. Therefore, they are very careful to try and obey the rules laid down by the North Korean "counterparts," though they still try to sneak in some veiled Christian stuff. This kind of super-subtle proselytizing is really the only kind possible, taking into account the balance necessary between educating/evangelizing the North Korean students, while being permitted to stay in country. One of the things that bothered me about the memoir is Kim's seeming unfamiliarity with Christianity. She is posing as a fellow missionary to her coworkers, but she is actually an atheist. Kim lashed out at one of the missionaries for saying that life on earth is temporary and their focus is on the North Korean's eternal lives. Kim responded angrily asked "How could you possibly look at people in gulags and tell them that it is temporary?" - the implication being that the missionaries were not doing what should be done and were in fact doing something incorrect. However, this is the only way the missionaries would be allowed to continue working in North Korea, and Kim herself is doing nothing different from what the missionaries are doing. I think Kim is misunderstanding the focus on eternal life as a focus ONLY on eternal life. "This reminded me of Ruth's claims that God has his reasons, and the sufferings of North Koreans were a temporary stage on the way to heaven. Gulags, then, served a purpose in the name of Jesus, much the way my students were taught to follow their Great Leader despite the famine. Or rather, because of the famine, which was reinterpreted as a form of martyrdom, necessary to the building of a powerful and prosperous nation." These two things are not automatically linked. Saying the first DOES NOT MEAN you are also saying the second. Kim has made a huge assumption here, and she gives no evidence to support her interpretation of what Ruth said earlier. This is particularly ironic, because this comes after a long discussion of how foreign the idea of giving supporting evidence is to her North Korean students. The fact that Kim could live with the missionaries for so long and not grasp this makes me question her ability to grasp the psychology of the boys she taught. Kim does mention, however, that she was raised and remains atheist, so perhaps more of a shared culture exists between her and the students then between her and the missionaries, making her insights into the students more well-founded. Kim also frustrated me when she acknowledged that her publishing this book would upset her former coworkers. Instead of making a case for why she felt she had to publish, or what publishing would do in a positive way, she says she hopes her coworkers will forgive her because they believe that God made her, and that therefore God also knew about her betrayal and made that happen too. This is, again, a weird misunderstanding of Christianity. Christians believe in free will, and therefore in responsibility for your actions. To receive forgiveness, you need repentance. It's entirely possible the missionaries might believe that God let this happen to test them, or that God sent her to test them, but that's not the basis on which anyone should seek forgiveness. It is kind of offensive that she would say she hopes they forgive her because they believe God made her, especially because she is an atheist. Why argue for forgiveness based on a premise you yourself don't accept? Does Kim even believe she needs forgiveness? I feel like Kim's lack of respect for Christianity really informs this book. She argues against things people didn't say (or at least, that she didn't report them saying), she uses misunderstood doctrine to demand forgiveness for endangering PUST's future, portrays Christians as gullible, and participates in one of Christianity's most important rituals, communion, without regard for whether that's appropriate. I would not participate in another relgion's rituals or ceremonies, because even though I don't believe in them, they do, and it's disrepectful to them to treat them as meaningless or make-believe in front of them.

We begin to see the true complexity and depth of what exactly happened to her. And how everything... everything is connected. This book dove into real character development and understanding. You can really see the way the characters are entwining with one another. They are becoming a real, functioning unit. I loved the characters before. Now we were handed more history. Jennifer Lynn Barnes created another knockout mystery thriller. Weaving a web that I'm completely entranced by. And, I am still finding myself utterly surprised by the ending.

DNF @ 32% Wow, third DNF in a row! I am really surprised that I didn't like this book. It had a great intro and I fell in love with Nao immediately. I also heard great things from my older sister (Her friend loves this book), so I thought I was going to love it too. I didn't have super high expectations though. I went into this book pretty clueless. This book has two POVs: Ruth and Nao. Each "chapter" has mini chapters and it makes up a part. I'm not sure how many parts there are because I stopped in the beginning of part 2. I love the writing style in Nao's chapters. It was really cute because it was in a young, teenage girl's perspective. It was really interesting seeing the thoughts of a teen her age in fiction because I usually read books with more mature teens. I loved that Nao was writing in a way that makes you feel like she's talking directly at you. It was like having a conversation with a fictional person. (I already do that...) Her voice seems mature for her age, but it had the right amount of maturity, if that makes sense... I found her really weird, funny and a bit pervy. Her thoughts are very... interesting. It was very entertaining, shocking, and made things escalate quickly. Then we have Ruth. I thought that it was the author's POV, but it was just a character with the same name. The author made it even more confusing by making the character so similar to herself. Anyway, I found Ruth's chapter a total bore. It wasn't really about anything other than her life. I don't think this book needed another life story. It really distracted the "shining star" of this book-Nao. I think the book would have been better if the whole book was in Nao's perspective, until her story is finished, where you then discover it was someone reading her diary. I know, tough train of thought to follow. I guess you can skip her chapters, but you would be missing something-I only read her chapters because I thought I was going to miss something.

Compelling and seductive. Between The Lines is the story of a group of actors who, while on the set of a movie, find themselves battling their own inner feelings. Reid Alexander is hot and he knows it. Being a Hollywood star, he gets whatever he wants and he just landed the lead in his next movie. With surprising chemistry, his co-star ends up being Emma Pierce, a not very well known actress. But, also on filming with them is Reid's ex-girlfriend Brooke and well to say they don't get along would be an understatement. And then, there's another contender... Graham Douglas. Graham is Brooke's friend and is reserved and smart. While these four actors film they also find themselves tangled with secrets, family, and emotions. Between The Lines is told from Reid and Emma's view points and I have to say I enjoyed reading from both. Reid is the all around eye candy. He's got the looks, the personality, the girls, and the connections. But, what he doesn't have is Emma. With their chemistry heating up on screen, Reid finds himself falling for Emma... or is it something else? Reid doesn't normally fall for girls but, all he knows is that he wants her and Graham stands in his way. Reid isn't only dealing with his feelings for Emma though, but with his family. His family has issues and I honestly felt sorry for Reid during parts of the book. Emma on the other hand, while she is infatuated with Reid, she also feels the chemistry with Graham and she is completely uncertain of what way to fall. I liked Emma a lot. It was intriguing to follow Emma, because I'm sure we all know what is feels like to like two guys at once. And if one is showing interest, but the other is backing off, well what do you do? And what happens when you thought there was a connection but nothing seems to be coming out of it? Plus, Emma deals with her family and tries to continue to lead a normal life. Emma just seemed so real to me. Real as in, she acted and felt how any normal person would act being her situation. My favorite character though was probably Graham. He's so caring and cute. I also love the fact that he's 20 years old and he's been through a little more and he knows what he wants. Graham and Emma's interactions through out the story completely made me smile. They have the perfect banter and routines. I really enjoyed the realness of this story. There was also a twist I was not expecting at all, and it goes to show you that you never really know all of someone's secrets. It also shows you that sometimes what you need is right in front of you if you just open your eyes. While I was pleased by the ending, I still wanted more. And low and behold there is a sequel! Though I must admit even though I'm excited for it, with the synopsis for Where You Are, I am a little nervous. Between The Lines was a fantastic story and I cannot wait for the sequel.

The very first thing I thought when my copy of The Twelve fell through my mailbox was whether I needed to re-read The Passage before throwing myself back into Justin Cronin's world. In the end, I did re-read it, but in hindsight it wasn't strictly necessary as I remembered far more than I thought I would, and the first part of The Twelve recaps what happened in The Passage in biblical verse. It sounds like an odd way to recap a book, but it works pretty well from my perspective. One feeling I had from The Passage is that the world building would be revealed bit by bit in the next book, and I'm happy to say I was right. The fall of Denver is particularly closely examined, and the fates of survivors are spread through the first part of the book. More on the background of characters that only flashed up in The Passage are also revealed, and although some of the character interactions have a strong feeling of familiarity, not having these connections would have lessened the tension and emotion of the story. There's also more information on the infection, and the different strains and how they were discovered and introduced to the public. Most of the characters from The Passage are back in The Twelve, and almost all of them have changed and matured in the intervening period. There are also new characters introduced, which for anyone that has read The Passage is enough to sound overwhelming, but they are all quite unique and it's actually good to have a few fresh faces after the intensity of the first book. After The Passage I really didn't think Justin Cronin could rachet up the horror and tension any further, but he definitely succeeds in doing so with The Twelve. A new community is introduced, and the cruelty and deprivation of the regime that controls is in huge contrast to the community introduced in The Passage. I don't want to give too much away, but in some ways it mirrors real events in human history that shocked and appalled the world. Although not told in flashbacks as such, the time period shifts back to the outbreak and moves forward from there, eventually jumping past the period that the majority of The Passage was set it, to five years after the ending of The Passage. Unfortunately, once again, there is a lull in the middle of this book, despite it being significantly shorter than The Passage. However, because it is a shorter lull, it doesn't feel like stalling quite as much as The Passage. Overall, I did enjoy The Twelve more than The Passage, and mostly that is due to the world-building. However, I'm giving them both the same rating as The Passage had a more epic feel to the journey. Read more of my reviews at The Aussie Zombie

This is one of those series you read for the journey, not the destination, because there are no real surprises along the way. You can pretty much see what is coming from the first book, but Mead manages to keep your attention anyway, which is no small feat. My main quibble with the series comes from the unnecessary and relentless slut-shaming that runs through the whole thing. A whole group of people is written off as "blood whores," for the grave sin of, apparently, having sex that is enjoyable and having children out of wedlock - children that are absolutely required and depended on by the entire society. And yet, no one thinks anything of completely dismissing them as worthwhile people throughout the whole series. Even Rose, who has some time to get to know Dimitri's family and see their lives up close, still falls back pretty quickly into dismissing them and their choices as soon as she leaves again. Also on the subject of sex, I would really like to retire the YA trope of "as soon as you have sex with a guy, something terrible is bound to happen next." Buffy did it, Divergent did it, every horror movie ever does it...it's a little tiresome and predictable. And I know this is a YA book and the author is writing for that audience, but I don't think it does anyone any favors when sex occurs, but the characters will only say that it was "too magical for words." Well, no it isn't. There are many words to describe it, the author/character is simply choosing not to use them. And that's fine. If the author/character wants to draw a veil for the sake of privacy/propriety, that's one thing. But again, I don't think imbuing sex with this mystic, "it is unknowable until you do it" quality does teenaged girls any favors, either. Either tell it straight, or say "I'm not going to tell you."

I also don't like that the fact that Gemma was completely changing how her family members were acting with her magic was never addressed. For someone who hates having people tell her what to do, she was oddly fine with compelling herself whatever kind of reaction she wanted from them. It was odd to me how she stripped them of their freewill without any thought of wrongness. I ended up liking characters that I didn't expect to like and I was never quite sure who to trust, much like Gemma would have felt, so bravo for that. As a whole, I would not recommend the series. While it has it's good points, I don't think wading through half a book is worth the good parts at the end. The interview with Libbra Bray makes me really sad that I didn't enjoy this series more. She seems like a super cool lady (and she hates math. I can totally get on that ship).

Le Summary Taking place in 1990s England, Never Let Me Go is the autobiography of a young woman named Kathy who grew up in unique circumstances. Among her earliest memories, Kathy tells the tales of meeting both Ruth and Tommy, her best friends at the Hailsham house, and their adventures together there. However, the Hailsham house quickly is noted for its oddness compared to other schools or orphanages in the fact that none of the children speak of their parents and all of the teachers and care takers are referred to as guardians. Also, Kathy tells how in order to receive spending money, aka tokens, each student creates artwork to trade and to hopefully be sent to a mysterious Gallery, owned by a woman only referred to as 'The Madame'. Despite the strange circumstances from an outside viewer, Kathy's storytelling never points out the uniqueness of the Hailsham house. As the children grow up, more often Kathy notices the guardians and leader of the school, Miss Emily, drift off in their lessons. Not understanding what they are saying, it isn't until much later that Kathy questions what they were referring to when it was repeatedly rumored that the children at the Hailsham were 'being told by not being told'. For example they are told at age 5 that they will donate several times in their lives, but it is so early that none of the children can understand this. Then as the guardians begin to explain more as the children grow up, they tell the lessons in monotone along with history and math so that it blends together and the children are never aware that their lives could be so much different. Confused, Kathy's life becomes vastly more complicated in other areas when fellow students begin having sex. Though it is a known fact that none of the students can get pregnant, as repeatedly explained by the guardians, sex is much more honest and open between students and feelings are often hurt if a girl rejects a boys offer. However, she is side-tracked when Ruth and Tommy call a quits to their relationship and an opportunity presents itself that she could be with Tommy. Again, everything is explained very matter-of-fact. The plans are ruined though when Tommy and Ruth decide to try once more before moving out of school. At the age of 16, Kathy moves with some fellow students, including Tommy and Ruth, to a farmhouse where they will spend their last years before being trained to be a carer of donors. With most days absorbed in reading and gossip, a rumor soon spreads that if you can prove your love to 'The Madame' she can put off your donations for three years just so the lovers can be together. Most of the time this rumor is suppressed but Kathy quietly wonders if it's possible at all. As the months pass, Ruth and Kathy's relationship deteriorates when both begin to hide things from each other causing Kathy to enlist for training earlier than some of the others. It isn't until years later that she asks to become Ruth's carer since her first donation did not go well. The friends do not patch everything up until they take a trip with Tommy to see an abandoned boat in a marsh. Ruth then admits that she had purposely trying to keep Kathy and Tommy apart and gives the Madame's address them. Months later, Ruth completes/dies soon after her second donation. After mourning for a year, Kathy asks to be a carer for Tommy where they rekindle their friendship and eventually start a relationship of their own. The Madame's address is never mentioned until news comes in that Tommy's fourth donation had been called in. Because most complete afterwards, the couple decides to try to track the Madame down and ask her for a deferral. However upon arriving, they find not only the Madame there but Miss Emily, the former head of the Hailsham house. Miss Emily sadly explains to them that the rumor is unfortunately false and their happy upbringing was a miracle in itself. She explains how society has always looked down upon clones and believe they are only a means to end cancer and provide organs. Miss Emily goes on to describe a political movement which provided them with the funds to create the Hailsham house where they used the children's artwork to show the world that not only were the clones sentient but proved that they too had souls. The conversation is soon ended and Kathy and Tommy take the long drive back to his hospice. Tommy then asks Kathy to not be his carer for his fourth donation because he wants her to remember him as he is now instead of being nearly completed (aka dying). Kathy agrees and the novel ends when Kathy sits in a field several months after Tommy's death looking forward to retiring as a carer and becoming a donar herself. My Thoughts Despite the depressing nature of this story, I really enjoyed it. Never Let Me Go was so original in the way Kathy approaches her life in such a straight forward way. Thoughts of changing how things are done or even a revolution are never mentioned. Often I asked myself, why don't they fight this?! I mean they are raised in this incredibly isolated boarding school where the kids can almost get away with anything but always know they will more than likely die before the age of 30 due to donating organs or anything else society needs. But then I really thought to myself... what could they do? Honestly? Except make the best of it and since they knew no different...they had no basis of comparison why would they fight? Hope yes. But fight...? I thought about it more and I know for a fact one day I will die. There is no stopping it and from a very young age I was told this as a matter of fact. It's going to happen. But it never truly sinks in until later but there's nothing I can truly do about it. Other forces are at work, depending on what you believe, and I can literally do nothing. Depressing yes, but it is a similar mindset for these kids. They never were lied to about their fates...yet they were never told what their lives could be if things were different. It felt so wrong. Also I really enjoyed this story because Kathy took her time narrating her story. She has twists and turns and though everything eventually comes together, it's a mystery what these kids are until much later in the book when you are able to figure out they are clones. Very sad, but also very beautiful. If You Enjoyed ______, You'll Enjoy This and Vice Versa The House of the Scorpion by Nancy Farmer Unwind by Neal Shusterman

At the end of the first book Cat and Griffin are a couple in front of all his friends and family in Sinta. The second book opens with drama, Griffin has discovered Cat's true identity and HE IS NOT HAPPY. I liked the way that this was done, I was immediately thrust into a domestic conflict. I thought Amanda Bouchet did a good job of recapping the events of the first book without it being a total information dump. As what I expect will be the second book in a trilogy (I don't know if any further books are planned after the third), this book moves the plot along significantly and logically. Unfortunately, most of the advancements are too spoilery to share. I think one thing which was hinted at in the first book is confirmed Cat is pregnant , otherwise the book shows Cat and Griffin progressing with their plans to unify the three realms of Sinta, Fisa and Tarva. I did feel that the second part of the book was reminiscent of one of the early Kate Daniels books. The Agon Games reminded me of Magic Strikes and the Midnight Games. Overall, I still love the fantasy mixed with Greek mythology, I think the smexy times intrude too much, I felt like I was being beaten over the head with the number of times Griffin tweaked Cat's nipples or pressed his 'sword' against her (pnarr, pnarr). I want more of Cat's diabolical mother, more of the Magoi, more of the corrupt royal families, more of the Gods, more fights. Nevertheless, I have pre-ordered the third book. I still think this is a innovative, fresh approach to fantasy and I am looking forward to the BIG confrontation.

I am so annoyed right now. I love Adam, but this isn't the Adam I've come to know over the past two books. The only thing that felt Adam-like was his love for his brother. This guy, whoever he is, thinks Juliette is some weakling who needs protecting: "I knew she should've stayed behind. She's not built for this-she's not strong enough." "The smart thing would be to hide her somewhere. Keep her safe. A weak link can bring everything down with it." "Kenji and Castle are always blowing smoke up her ass when they shouldn't, and honestly? It's dangerous. It's not good to make her think she can do this kind of thing when really, it'll probably get her killed." These thoughts both shocked and angered me, because the Adam I know wouldn't think such things. The tagline on the cover says "I will not lose her" and about half way through the novella he says he's not ready to give up on her or whatever, but towards the end it seems as if he has given up on her. Apparently he's not sure if he wants to rescue the girl who broke up with him and left him and his brother. He also doesn't want to be on the run again and put his brother in danger (which is fair enough, but it completely goes against his character. I thought he didn't want to lose her?) So, Kenji who is desperate to find Juliette (and btw, seems more worried about her than Adam does) has to convince him to come up with a plan to brake her out. Yes, you read correctly. He has to convince him: "Dude, what the hell are you talking about? Aren't you in love with this girl? Where's the fire under your ass? I thought you would be dying to get to her right now-" What happened to the Adam that once said: "You have no idea how much I've thought about you. How many times I've dreamt...how many times I've dreamt about being this close to you. God, Juliette, I'd follow you anywhere. You're the only good thing left in this world." Also, when Kenji and Adam were talking about how ruthless Warner is, Juliette's reaction kind of irked me. I get that she saw a softer side to him in Unravel Me, but she can't honestly be surprised at the things they were saying. The only good thing about this novella: Kenji's awesomeness. Prior to reading this I at least had some hope for Adam and Juliette, but now? I'm not so sure. I have this horrible feeling that maybe Alia will become Adam's love interest in Ignite Me. This novella has made me a feel a bit angry towards Adam, and that, quite frankly is upsetting. This review also appears on my blog The Page Turner.

Wow. Just wow. It's been days since I read this, and I'm still not sure how to do review this properly, because I still haven't processed it. I absolutely loved it. It started out a bit slow, but the pace just got faster throughout, and I have to say, the slow beginning actually added to the plot, to the tension and excitement. Sal felt realistic and relatable, and I loved to see how they grew through the book, and I also loved the romance. It didn't take any attention from the action or the plot - in fact, it only added to the tension. I loved reading about Sal! Despite Mask of Shadows being a High Fantasy, Sal felt very realistic. It was easy to relate to them and it was interesting to read about them. Sal also grew a lot through the book, and it was amazing to follow their journey. And I have to say something about the diversity in this book. Way too often in Fantasy, I feel like there isn't any diversity, and if there is, it feels a bit like it's there just for the sake of it being there. It's the complete opposite with Mask of Shadows, it feels completely natural and it's so important. The romance was really sweet and so intense! I really liked how the author portrayed the romance between Sal and Elise, it progressed slowly through the whole book, which made it feel realistic. Also, I have to say they are simply too cute together! I shipped them from the moment Sal robbed her, which is definitely a first for me. I just really love how they interact with each other, from the moment they first met - not to mention the tension that is there from the beginning. This is how romance should be portrayed in Fantasy books! The world-building is what dreams are made of! First of all, the author has created such an amazing, unique and utterly interesting world - from the first page, you just have to know more, making it impossible to stop reading, even for just a moment (who cares about school, anyway, I can study after I'm finished). I had no idea what to think about anything, because Miller breaks every single popular trope, and I loved it! And secondly, she does it in such a great way, leaving small hints and pieces of information that only leaves you wanting more. Any author who wants to know how to hook a reader should take lessons from Linsey Miller, because she has it down to an art. The plot had me hooked from the first page! As I mentioned earlier, the plot started out a bit slow, but not slow enough that it was ever boring. Instead, that slow start worked as build-up, and the tension and action only intensified from that point. It grew and grew and grew, until I had trouble breathing and reading at the same time. The writing is bursting with tension. The writing is seriously amazing. No matter what type of scene it is, there was always a ton of tension in the writing, and I swear my heart never stopped beating frantically in my chest. The writing just had that unique quality that is hard to put your finger on that has the reader on the edge of their seat, holding their breath, anxious for what's going to happen next. I can go on and on about everything that was amazing about this book, but the truth is, no matter how great the plot, characters or romance is, in order to enjoy a book to this extent, that tension in the writing has to be there, or you won't enjoy it that much. And Miller's writing has it and so much more! This is a book everyone should read! It's filled to the brim with emotion, and it is honestly incredible how well Miller portrays every feeling, making it hard to separate the characters' feelings from your own. With relatable characters, world-building that is out-of-this-world, and tension from the first page, Mask of Shadows will take you on a journey that you won't forget. But a piece of advice before you start reading (and you need to read it, okay? Just do it); make sure to read it on a day you have free, because you will not be able to put it down.

Gorydamn Prime. Bloodydamn Gold. I am deeply overwhelmed as to how this trilogy ends. This book didn't have me because it was pumped with graphical actions, tactical space war, dramatic defeats and glorious victories (well it does, but only for a fraction of a greater sum). It owned me when Brown decided to write Morning Star on a larger scale. A story beyond Darrow, beyond colors. He set it in humanity and what binds us all amidst cruelty-Family and their love that anchors us. It was how he set Darrow in a glorious path from the previous books and takes us to the scenes where he committed mistakes, struggled with his weakness, experienced failures and humbled him and shaped him to be the man who learned his lesson. A man who leads, who takes risk, who is robbed by choices but tried his best to do the lesser evil and break the chains to make a change. The journey was not just about Darrow, it is also about the people around him, how they were essential in shaping him to a man he should be, a man the Solar Republic needs. I love how Brown writes the entire series of how politics really works, that there aren't only two sides of the paradigm. Power and the greed of men tempts them to conquer it and men like those does exist, not only in books but also in reality. Brown set his book in a very complicated manner that shook me, knocked me out, and surprised me in all ways possible. There was so much in this world and tyranny never ends, men won't stop defying those who are above them no matter which sides they're on. The conflict continues and that is how the world works and I admire how Brown ends this trilogy, to stick to what really is. How human we are, despite the wars our ancestors have witnessed, technology evolves and so does humanity yet we stumble on the same weaknesses. Greed, power and glory. However, our human hearts may be the only thing that saves us from those weakness. This book set the bar high and I can't wait to revisit this world on 2018 in Iron Gold.

I don't understand how this got such high ratings. It's a cool idea (aren't most stories? ), but I was drowning in detail. "It was an ordinary day, a Friday, twenty minutes till lunchtime, five hours till quitting time and the weekend, ten months till vacation, thirty-seven years till retirement. Then the phone rang." WOW. What a great opening. "This was Martin Lastvogel, my instructor, and we shook hands and agreed it would be sensible to use first names." Not "hi, nice to meet you, call me by my first name", but instead told quickly and cutely and I loved it. Little truths like this: "I sat forever in Rube's office then, turning the pages of old copies of Life, discovering again, as in a doctor's waiting room, that it's very hard to tell, looking through back issues of Life, whether or not you've seen them before." There there were the passages that made zero sense to me because the book was written in 1970: "And then, like a computer finally producing the right card, my mind said, How?" But mostly it was page after page after page of detailed descriptions of 19th century clothing, buildings, and New York street names. The author also felt the need to remind us again and again how much simpler life was and how glad the protagonist was to be in the past. Towards the end I was just skimming and ignoring full paragraphs because it was all detail and no story. And though this book left us with a great cliff-hanger, I will not be reading the sequel.

Let's see. First of all, I had no idea what to expect because this was my first experience with the author, but I can say it was quite pleasant for such a tricky plotline. I loved her writting style, not overly-descriptive but throwing here and there a few well-chosen adjectives which really contributed with the narrator's style. I also thought that the idea of the fonts changing to match each chapter's point of view bloody BRILLIANT. It really made a difference to me by giving an individual mood and personality to each character, beyond that which is explicitly written. The story in itself is quite complex, with everyone battling their own personal demons, and managing to be quite relatable to a certain point. It did have a few details I would have done differently. One of the things I was a little frustrated about was the way Delia's character behaved. I have a personal dislike for people who do not own up to their actions, and Delia had a (quite frankly annoying) habit of demanding certain behaviors and then not being able to bear their consequences. It made liking her a little hard for me because I associate that manner of thinking with a certain childishness for which I have no patience but that also made her flawed and, somehow, more real. The other thing that I felt was a bit of a shame was the need to bring up a certain subject in the climax which, although made the story develop quite nicely, felt like it was needed to make sure the reader was on board with the author's point of view. I guess this is just me, but I liked the moral ambiguity that was happening before that, because it was so arguable for either side. Once that point was made, that interesting ambiguity was gone and everything was kinda black and white, which I felt was unneeded. All in all, a complex, sometimes difficult to read but still really captivating storyline.
I'd call this "psychological thriller-lite". It's a quick read and not too "thrilling" but a good enough story.

Orson Scott Card correctly mentioned that much of contemporary "literary" fiction indulges in super-sensitive protagonists who have a gift to see the world in a way no one else does (thereby not-so-subtly suggesting that the author is a superior being). Also, he's a hot shapeshifter prince, which YES PLEASE. Lorelai is also cool. She's a little TOO good at things for my taste, but whatever. She's calculating, analytical, a great fighter, a strong big sister, steady on her responsibilities but also caring, fights for what's right but avoids unnecessary deaths... Yeah. Lorelai is awesome. IRINA! Irina is awful. She's conceited, twisted, and evil. But man, that old axiom about the villains being the heroes of their own stories is totally upheld here. She has REASONS for everything she does, and at points I truly did feel sorry for her. (Shoutout to my man Viktor!) That's how you write a villain, folks. Ewwww the stuff that happens in this book gets gross. That thing with the one lady and the apples? Nope. Nope nope nope. THINGS I DID NOT LIKE: Before a certain point, it was just too easy for me to put the book down. I think much of that was my fault, not the book's, because I anticipated certain plot points turning in predictable ways and wanted to avoid the fallout (they didn't; I was pleasantly surprised every time), but it made for tough going at the beginning. I didn't understand a character's reasoning at a fairly crucial point. Another character could have chosen a path that would have seriously damaged the paths of two other characters, so I know from a plot standpoint why that path couldn't have been chosen, but from a character perspective, I don't see why the first character turned the second character away from that bad path, especially considering their history. ** spoiler alert ** Frankly, I'm appalled that this is YA. Emer has been a brutal pirate in the Caribbean for years, yet when she decides to retire, she get rid of the cannons on her flag ship "so she has room for food" to make the transatlantic trip home. Like there's no other pirates in the Carribbean. Or like she has no clue that she has other enemies. How convenient. No really. How conveniently stupid. But necessary if the end of Emer's life is going to happen the way the author has been promising since page 1. (I kid you not. The prologue shows Emer's death. The rest of the book is only necessary to put that scene into context.) On top of that, the romance between Emer and Seanie, while sweet at first, was totally bland when they finally meet again. I couldn't have cared less about them being together. Seanie had become a non-entity by then. A mere plot necessity. In the end, I disliked pretty much every character except the poor, abused dog that so conveniently leads Saffron to the treasure. (Another convenience for the author.) Not recommended unless you really want to know what your kids are reading.

I can't fault Hillbilly Elegy for lack of ambition - even at age 31, writing your memoirs and then extrapolating from you own experience to draw conclusions about the environment you grew up in is no joke. But I can and will fault it for its surface-level approach and lazy prose. I actually think this book would have benefited hugely from a narrower scope - either stick to the memoir passages and expand them to include incidents that maybe don't have an obvious object lesson to draw; or stick to the sociological study of Appalachia that makes up the book's other half, roughly. Trying to do both in well under 300 pages means that everything feels rushed and disorganized. There are mixed metaphors and cliches on every page - after another incident with his mother promising to get her life together, Vance observes, "but the road to hell is paved with good intentions," with all the gravity of someone coming up with that analogy for the first time. To me, that's something an editor should have caught - this book could easily have been tighter and more cohesive with a few judicious edits and some reorganizing. I also feel duty-bound to let you know I listened to the audiobook and it was... not great. Vance reads it himself and I realize that's common practice with memoirs, but it was maybe not the best choice here.

She is not willing to change her attitude toward dealing with her difficult past, tainting her chances for brighter future. She believes she doesn't need anyone, in fact, she believes that needing someone is a weakness and she doesn't want to feel week and out of control one more day in her life. Here comes the hero - Tyler. This man is a definition of determinition. He goes after what he wants not accepting a failure. He does everything neccessary in order to reach his goals. His only problem is defining his priorities. He is a very succesful entrepreneur, upcoming state Senate candidate and not to mention his teenage son, with whom he doesn't have a close relationship. What happens when these two strong willed individuals meet? Is there any chance? Easton and Tyler first meet at a Mardi Gras ball, they share few intense and captivating moments together only to part ways. Six month later and Easton finds herself being introduced to Tyler as a new teacher of his son. They both know that it might be trouble. The beggining of their relationship was a rocky one, Tyler being an incredible asshole and jerk (thank you Penelope!) - seriously, you want to throtle him. He's condecending and patronizing, arrogant and felt entitled to everything he wanted. And even though he exceeds in business word, he fails at prioritizing. How to jugle a demanding carrier building his empire, approaching announcement of his candidacy for state Senate, his long estranged son and a budding relationship? Slowly he opens his eyes to discover what is important the most to him and sometimes a man has to make a sacrifice in order to do the right thing not just for him, but for the people he loves the most. Easton took a journey of her own - she had to learn how to let people in, to trust them and their motives. How to open up to them when she knows that consequences of her actions (direct or indirect) can be catastrophal? And is it a real weakness to need and want and love someone? Overall I liked this book, but it's more of 3,5 read for me. I am used to some gut clenching tension, something more thrilling, just something more. It was supposed to be a taboo read, but it didn't really felt that way. Ok, she was his son's teacher and he was older, but not by too much and I don't really see the "teacher-student's parent" relationship as a taboo. I couldn't really connect to the horror of Easton past - maybe if it was more described, if it got more space and not just those 5-6 sentences in the whole book. Somehow I just couldn't find a real sympathy for her, because I couldn't imagine what she went through, therefore I didn't feel the need for her to close up. There was no real climax, no real danger or plot, mostly it was about the h's and H's struggle with their own problems then battling any outside forces or any forces at all. It just lacked some drama. Easton was good heroine, temperamental, she could be a real bitch (and mostly I don't like that), but she was smart, strong (in her own way), she gave as good as she got, she never withered under Tyler's assholeness (which I applaud! Tyler was a good asshole. I really liked in the beggining that he was different than any other classic heroes with kids. He didn't put Christian as his first priority, which was the reason they didn't get along and he had to find his way to understand that somethings are more important than money and power. It wasn't given for him and his character went through real development. I just wondered what happened with her brother Jack after discovering he was the one screwing with her apartment ? I read Corrupt some time ago and that was more my speed. Penelope Douglas has an amazing ability to write about heroes that are AA - amazing assholes that you hate to love and love to hate and heroines that don't hide from them and give as good as they get. And I really like that.

I am incredibly torn as far as how to rate If We Were Villains by M.L. Rio--and, for that matter, quite torn on how much I enjoyed it even without any sort of arbitrary Goodreads rating. I went into the book knowing it was going to be some kind of Shakespeare-related murder mystery, the latter genre I am not quite so fond of, but at the same time I follow the author on Tumblr and was prepared to give her the benefit of the doubt. The trouble is, now that I've read the book, I am unfortunately filled with more doubt than I had hoped for. Perhaps my expectations were too high or my nerddom too lofty, but I was disappointed with the way neither the plot nor the characters seemed to be very fleshed out developed where the inclusion of such heavy themes--Shakespeare, tragedy, death, etc--would make sense. If We Were Villains is the story of a group of conservatory theater students who study Shakespeare every waking hour of the day. They are so caught up in their lives--and dramas and tragedies--surrounding their education and performances that when disaster happens in their friend group, they all have to come to terms with how to deal with it. When they don't, their friend group starts to unravel, as does each individual character, as the pivotal event affects every aspect of their lives, both on- and offstage. The story was quick and entertaining, if predictable. The foreshadowing in the beginning is incredibly strong, that it was nearly impossible for me to be surprised when the ending came--yes, the how of the climax wasn't clear to me, but it was no surprise what generally was going to happen. Because I am a huge fan of Shakespeare, having some of his play's plots come back into play for this story was a bit of a plot-ruiner as well, once it became more obvious which character in If We Were Villains was like which Shakespearean character. In that sense it was an interesting read, and though ti was predictable, it was fun to put the pieces together in a sort of dramatic-irony type of situation. I read the book in one day, in more or less one sitting, since I wanted to know what happened after a certain point. However, the dependence on Shakespeare as a plot device to keep all the action going--whether it was symbolism or parallelism or tragedy arcs--seemed a bit heavy-handed in certain places. Certainly some uses of Shakespeare's works were very effective, which I noted with glee, but others were a bit pretentious in any context and ended up making me roll my eyes. As I said, I love Shakespeare, and I was familiar with almost every single reference Rio included in the book (haven't read Pericles yet), so it is not out of a lack of understanding of Shakespeare's words or themes. No, even for me sometimes it was overdone. Some of the quotes and the parallel structures felt very forced to me, like the author was purposefully inserting them but not really understand how they would connect with the rest of the plot. (The disjointedness between the characters and their actions was hard to look past in some places.) I do understand the effect that pretentiousness had on developing the plot, however, thinking about how all these students are trapped in this classical conservatory world, in which Shakespeare is their life. In that sense it worked, but Rio didn't seem to make it work as well as I would have preferred. I also could not decide if I liked the inclusion of Detective Colborne for this reason: On one hand, he seemed disconnected from the world of the conservatory students and thus out of place; but on the other hand, his detachment from that thespian world may have been for the better, to serve as a reminder that not everything happens the way a bunch of Shakespeare-obsessed college kids think it does. Which, in turn, I suppose, is a good lead-up into the ending, when revelations are made and judgments are formed and shattered. My biggest regret with this book, and probably why I cannot rate it higher than three stars, is because of how poorly the characters were developed. As I was reading, the direct and indirect interactions between everyone started off interesting as I was just discerning who each of the characters was. But after a while, their stories turned into those of an ordinary sitcom, with jealousy and anger and a complete lac of communication. There were zero subplots to make things more complex and interesting and show off different sides of the characters. They were not multi-faceted when it came to each of them dealing with situations that arose in their lives. The ending was the only part that impacted me as far as character connection went, and I won't give away spoilers, but it was only at the end that I really felt the humanity and the sorrows of the characters, like I was finally emotionally invested in them. It took 350 pages to get there, unfortunately. My review of If We Were Villains could be entirely more nit-picky than this, but I will leave it at that. It wasn't a bad book by any means: certainly an entertaining read, and I did want to know for sure what happened next, all the way to the end. But its predictability and pretentiousness outweighed some of the more positive aspects of it. If you like murder mysteries and you like Shakespeare, this one is a fairly fun one, but definitely more a light read that won't make you think too hard.

In a nutshell: In 1985, a string of three murders in D.C. indicate the work of a serial killer. The victims are all children and they become known as the Palindrome Murders, as all the victims' names are palindromes. The murders are never solved. In the present-day, a teenager is murdered in a manner that recalls the Palindrome Murders. Some wonder if it's the same killer resurfacing again. Review: This is the first book that I've read by George Pelecanos, though I've seen the first season of HBO's The Wire, where he was one of the writers. It was not the author's television credentials that drew me to The Night Gardener, however, but rather the fact that it is a non-political D.C-based thriller. Pelecanos clearly knows the area well, much more than I do. I live in the suburbs and my knowledge of the District proper is more limited. So at first, I was impatient with Pelecanos' level of setting detail. It almost seemed that he wanted the reader to plot out character movements on a map. Here's a random sample: "Conrad Gaskins came out of a clinic located beside a church off Minnesota Avenue and Naylor Road, in Randle Highlands, Southeast . He had been up since 5:00 a.m., when he had risen and walked over to the shape-up spot on Central Avenue in Seat Pleasant, Maryland." To be fair, Pelecanos does not just name-check street names and locations. He describes the type of neighborhood it is, whether it's a place that police ignore, or a place that is getting gentrified, and so on, so that you get a picture of the D.C. environs. Furthermore, that level of street-name detail came to be valued by me when Pelecanos started describing extremely familiar places in the Maryland suburbs. One of the characters lived less than five minutes from an apartment in Greenbelt where I lived for a year. That was fun. So that's my requisite ramble about setting. The Night Gardener follows a small group of characters, most of them police. The main character is Gus Ramone, who was a cop when the Palindrome Murders occurred. In the present-day he works as a detective for the Violent Crimes Division of the Metropolitan Police. I loved that Ramone was a family man and how Pelecanos showed Ramone balancing his work and family life. It's refreshing as usually police detectives in thrillers are unlucky in their personal lives. Indeed, overall, The Night Gardener has fleshed-out characters. I liked how Pelecanos used different characters to display the range of approaches toward police work. In addition to Ramone, there is a retired police detective who gets reinvigorated by the new case's similarity to the serial killer case which still haunts him. There are Ramone's fellow detectives, a few who are stand-up true partners, and some that are not quite up to par. More than the solid characterization, the descriptions of police work feel grounded and credible. This is a book that was engaging throughout, but I wouldn't call it a page-turner. There is a definite climax to the story, but it's not predictable. What would be red herrings in another mystery are actually used as full story arcs in their own right. They may not relate to the teenager's murder, but that does not mean that they aren't worth reading about. Based on my enjoyment of The Night Gardener, I would definitely read more by this author.

** spoiler alert ** I'm going to be really honest and say that this book had a shit ton of problems. Did I enjoy reading it? Definitely, yes. But I also had to overlook a lot of the issues I had with it to enjoy it. Did I mention there were a lot of problems with this book? I feel bad that I had such high hopes for this book and I ended up being disappointed with it. Let me start by saying that I really liked the writing and the creativity of the story. The book started off great, and at first I thought Mira was an intelligent 15 year old who wanted answers about her life. After not getting background info from her overprotective godmothers, Mira runs away to the small town where she was born hoping to learn more. But the town of Beau Rivage is far from normal. It is literally a fairytale town. Mira is completely clueless when she arrives,and must rely on the help of strangers. Unfortunately, she meets 2 brothers and is immediately thrust between them as they fight over her - Felix wants her to stay so he can 'help' her, but Blue wants her to leave. NOW. The story gets even stranger when Mira meets Blue's friends. It takes a while, but Mira finally figures out that they are all characters from fairytales - and they are all cursed to live out the fairytales which they are from. Mira learns that she is also a character that is destined to live out a fairytale. Sounds weird, I know, but it all seemed so normal to them that it almost started to feel normal to me. I had quite a few problems with this book though. We are instantly hit with a love triangle and insta-love. Like BAM with a sledgehammer, head over heals insta-love between Mira and Felix. Completely inappropriate because Felix is 21 and Mira is only 15! Can we talk about how illegal this is in all 50 states? Inappropriate behavior continuously overtakes common sense, and we get Mira in a sexy nightgown strutting herself through a casino while trying to find Felix to seduce him. No 15 year old would be allowed on the gaming floor of a casino, so this was just a lame attempt to show how far Mira was willing to go to get her man, whom she met 2 seconds ago and barely knows. Blue attempts to tell her how stupid she is and comes to her rescue about a million times, and even saves her from Felix. But Mira refuses to believe that she is in danger, even when Blue tells her YOU WILL DIE if you don't leave. What a stupid and selfish little girl. I don't know why Blue even bothered with warning her about his brother or why he tried to get her away from his brother. Oh wait, I DO know why. Blue told Mira it was because HE saw her first. And his brother, Felix, always wants what Blue has. I really hate to blast a book because it offends my morals, but this book just had so much inappropriateness going on that it is hard to overlook. However, I really did like the writing. I thought the idea of a land of fairytales right in the middle of ordinary society was clever and very creative. I liked the secondary characters - fairytale characters - and how they all interacted with each other, even though they knew what their futures held. I enjoyed learning about how the curses came to be, and the 'gifts' that fairies can bestow to lessen the curses. I thought that the birthmarks that all of the characters have was really different. I really wanted to love this book. There was so much promise, but it didn't live up to my expectations. I didn't hate all of it, but I didn't love all of it either. I wasn't able to connect with or relate to any of the characters. The ending was unbelievable and just so-so, and some of the plot lines were left hanging. Kill Me Softly is definitely a book that I would not recommend. Even if it is a creative story, it still has so many issues that I can't imagine telling anyone it's good enough to spend (or waste) their time on.
