A charming tale of an Irish village, where unearthing a body unearths everyone's secrets. The main problem with this book is that the author's voice, so distinctively familiar to British readers, wouldn't go away. I could hear him reading this to me the whole time. That could be a plus; he's an engaging personality (although he's also profoundly irritating to some), and he does have an Irish accent, so it helps the sense of place. And the sense of place is something this book excels with. Both place and time, including the desperation of the teenagers in the 1960s to touch any part of the world they read of in magazines, are deftly woven through beautifully crafted prose. The story is full of description, which keeps it at a pace suitable for the location, but equally will keep some readers in fits of frustration. The characters are generally well-built, sometimes literally, and the author certainly gets inside the head and heart of his overweight - okay, obese - protagonist. The trouble with the characters is that they are very familiar from various rural episodes, and head towards stereotypes. This makes any pretence at a cosy mystery superfluous, as it's pretty obvious from the start who the body is, even with the misdirection, which only serves to confirm deeper suspicions that are finally released near the end. I was reminded of an infographic I saw recently distinguishing between the genres, crime, mystery and suspense. If only I could remember the detail. But I think this falls into the heading of 'suspense' since you know early on who of three did it, and the flags are pointed early enough for you to narrow it down to the (right) one, but there still remains an interest in how they get found out and whether they get their comeuppance. After getting through the first character exposition, I found the extended journeys back into the histories of each inhabitant tedious. I suspect many readers will find the same. It's well written, and a good first novel, but has its faults, not least tendency to wallow. I wonder if it would have reached the surface of the publishing wannabe heap had the author not been well-known? I wonder if I would have read it differently if I had remained in ignorance of his identity? We will never know. A good first novel; fluffy but enjoyable.

This book is, in a word, amazing. In the world that Laure DeStefano has created, genetic engineering has caused every young man and woman to live only a fraction of what their usual lifespan would be, with men living to the age of twenty-five and women only surviving to twenty before they become violently ill and perish. It is in this setting that the protagonist, sixteen-year-old Rhine, is introduced, being transported in the dark along with a carload of other frightened girls and young women to be sold into marriage. The characters in this story are all SO well written, and I found myself becoming very attached to all of the main characters, even little Cecily, who annoyed me to no end at first. What makes this book so outstanding, however, is the imagery that is woven throughout this book. The description of the girls being transported in the van reminded me of accounts I'd read of prisoners being taken to concentration camps during the Holocaust, and this connection only served to accentuate the tension and fear for the characters that I felt even from the start of the book. If there's one thing that can really be said about this book, it's that the words paint a vivid portrait in the mind of the world that has been created. I agree with the suggested age-range of grade 9 and up, with the emphasis being and up. As beautifully well written as Wither is, it does deal with some very mature topics, which may be uncomfortable for late Jr. High/early High School students. There were some moments that I was downright horrified, especially when the age difference between thirteen-year-old Cecily and twenty-one-year-old Linden really struck me. As much as he was intended to be "the bad guy," I couldn't help starting to like the character of the husband, Linden, since he seemed very genuine and naive...very much a child himself after being sheltered and lied to by his father his whole life. The complexity of his character really helped make me want to continue reading, especially when the story came to disturbing or difficult parts to read. I really hope that there is a sequel to this book, because it deserves it!

Daikichi is a thirty year old bachelor who notices a six year old girl he doesn't recognize when he attends his grandfather's funeral. He finds out that she is the illegitimate daughter of his grandfather (and thus technically his aunt), and as much a surprise to the rest of the family as to him. Despite having just lost her father Rin is treated as an inconvenience and when the family sits down to "discuss" her future, clearly already having made up their mind to ship her off to wherever will take her, Daikichi decides to take care of her himself. Bunny Drop is a slice of life story that grows from the consequences of Daikichi's decision. It focuses on day-to-day life and discussions of "mundane" concerns. For some this may sound boring but the characters are thoroughly engaging, things are well paced, and real attachment forms as we follow along with their lives. Daikichi is in over his head but willing to learn and compromise, and Rin is a largely independent child who none-the-less is still only six, with all the wonder, weaknesses and needs that go along with it. This first volume sets the stage nicely, and sets up developments and questions to be explored in future volumes. The art is simplistic, but very well done and the style suits the story being told. I really hesitate to bring this up here, but it's been a big enough issue for some that a small warning is appropriate before people start reading. Without getting into specific spoilers, the series is much different in the second half, and that has "ruined the series" for a lot of readers. I still think the series as a whole is wonderful and well worth reading, but I understand the complaint and felt it worth mentioning. Bunny Drop is a charming tale of an unprepared yet caring bachelor who suddenly becomes a father, and of growing up for both him and his "aunt."

Read more of my reviews on YA Romantics or follow me on Bloglovin I've read all of Gretchen McNeil's books and there are always aspects of them that I enjoy. She has a lively, funny writing style and is always switching up genres. I'm Not Your Manic Pixie Dream Girl had its appealing points, but also some things I didn't enjoy. At times, it felt to me like this book was a bunch of classic movies (Mean Girls, Election, Garden State, Clueless, Revenge of the Nerds) thrown into a blender and then poured into a computer. There were two main plot strands: 1) a romantic "win the guy back" plot, which I was really not feeling for most of the book, and 2) a plot about Beatrice trying to win a college scholarship by making a mathematical formula by which high school nerds can reinvent themselves. At times the two plots worked together, as when Beatrice reinvented herself as "Trixie" to win her guy back, but at other times I thought these two plots were sort of moved on parallel tracks. Beatrice was, for the most part, hard for me to relate to. Yes, she's smart, but she's also not the nicest person on the block. She schemes and she plots. She's bossy and egotistical. At times, she treats the people in her life as pawns. The romance was all over the place. As the story starts, Beatrice is madly in love with Jesse. I guess the blah-ness of their romance was part of the plot, but I didn't get what she saw in Jesse or why she wants him back after he dumps her. I'm really not a fan of the "winning the guy who dumped me back" plots because ... why? Why do you want to grovel and connive and get back a guy who didn't know the value of what he had? Find a better guy. I also didn't love the fact that all the characters in this book start off as the most extreme stereotypes (the math nerd, the popular girl, the gay best friend, and, of course, the Manic Pixie Dream Girl.) Yes, they do finally break out of their stereotypes, but that happened at the 95% mark on my kindle. Plus, I felt that the book's message on self-acceptance was all over the place. You should be yourself. But if your family moves a lot, it's okay to reinvent yourself. If you reinvent yourself, you might be elected class president (I seriously doubt that). But if you do reinvent yourself, you might lose all your friends. By the end, "Trixie" learns her lesson about being nice and being herself and getting the (right) guy. But getting there was a bit of a bumpy ride! Thanks to the publisher for providing a free advance copy of this book for me to review.

** spoiler alert ** Recommended for lovers of "The Prisoner of Zenda" who always wanted a girl to save the day! Are you ready for a contemporary Ruritarian romantic adventure that will take you to a small middle European country you will swear must exist - but doesn't? (Don't recognize the word Ruritarian? Go hit Wikipedia. I'll wait. Seriously, think "The Prisoner of Zenda" as a feminist tale.) Then you're ready for Sherwood Smith's tale of an American girl who finds out that her roots are not what she expected - and that some secrets may be literally deadly. Aurelia Kim Murray, a 23 year old history and language buff, has abandoned her position on her university's champion fencing team to go in search of her roots. Her ill grandmother refuses to speak, and the family suspects Gran's malaise is rooted in Europe, which she fled at the end of WWII, infant daughter in tow. The clues are slim, but Kim makes her way to Vienna and professional genealogy hunters. Her questions turn out to be less innocent than she thinks, when a casual drink with an attractive native causes her to wake up on a train heading deep into Eastern Europe. Kim's a fast thinker, and not afraid to toss her suitcase and herself out the window when the train slows near a town. Thus begins her adventures. It turns out that her grandmother was a princess of an obscure little Carpathian Mountain country, Kim is a dead ringer for her missing cousin Ruli, and that Kim apparently can see ghosts. By the time her fling in mythical Dobrenica is through, ghosts will seem almost commonplace compared to some things about this country. In true Zenda fashion, Kim is talked into masquerading as her cousin Ruli in an attempt to smoke out the missing aristocrat. In the meantime, Prince Alec Ysvorod is dealing with a possible coup attempt, a wedding he and Ruli must perform, because magic, of all things, enters into it (And explains how the country literally appears on some maps of Europe, and is missing from others) and also growing curiosity about Kim. You will be fascinated and stunned by the detail Smith has put into her tiny country. Kim is the best and worst of an LA just-past-teenager, too trusting for her own good, but not at the mercy of the scheming aristocrats and bureaucrats managing and mis-managing Dobrenica. The magic that is worked by the elders of the country - no matter what their religion, prayer, in any language, has a lot to do with magical power - is fascinating and mostly hinted at. Complexities in language and culture are smoothly handled, giving us a travelogue even as the mystery advances. Kim's grandmother gave up her share of the throne because she would marry only for love. But what happened to her? Who is Kim's grandfather? And will Kim stand by and watch the man she is coming to love marry a woman he does not care for, to cement a peace with a restless faction? You can write a Ruritarian homage in one novel, but if you want a happy ending, it's going to take more than one book. Warning! Although many things are resolved, clearly, another book must finish Kim's story. It only took me about 35 pages or so to forgive Kim's annoying mannerisms and want to know what happened next. By the end I was rooting for her. Looking forward to the next one!

"It was okay" is the best explanation for how I feel about this book. I didn't really enjoy reading it because I felt that the first half was just so boring. The story did pick up for the second half, but not enough to really capture my attention. The continuation was a bit off in this book for both timeline and character traits. I had a really hard time keeping track of time, so the progression of the characters travel left me a bit confused from time to time. I also had issues with the pain tolerance of the main character. For example, one second the main character has been slammed to the ground from a moving train and she's in agony and can hardly breathe, but the next minute the next she's running and acting like nothing is wrong. There were also a number of YA cliches that I didn't really care for, so they may have affected my overall feeling of the book. However, I did really enjoy the overall storyline, the idea of the powers, and the personalities of the main characters. I just wish this book had more oomph. I think this book is definitely worth a read, but I wouldn't read it again. Favorite passages: But the champion was swaying on his feet and downing another drink. I wasn't sure he could hit the ground if he tripped, never mind anything else. My bullet caught it square in the chest. Black guts scattered across the sand. The thing screeched again. And this time, from the deep of the night, a hundred identical voices screeched back. ...there was no arguing against belief. It was a foreign language to logic.

Blue Sargent, the daughter of a psychic, had been told that if she ever kissed her true love, he would die. So when she sees a ghost for the first time, and finds out that he is either her true love or she is his killer, she is immediately apprehensive, because he hasn't died yet; he will die in less than a year. Following this, she meets Gansey, Adam Parrish, Ronan Lynch, and Noah, four students (Raven Boys) at the private Aglionby Academy, who are on the search for the mysterious and supernatural ley line, in order to wake it up and discover the king from antiquity, Glendower, who will grant the waker a wish. I'd read a lot of good things about The Raven Boys, and The Raven Cycle in general, from tumblr. I was a bit wary, partly because I have a friend who doesn't like it, and because I tried to read The Scorpio Races, but couldn't get into it. Even though the book started out slow, I was enjoying it. The slowness of the first half of the book is my main complaint and the reason why I didn't give it five stars. While it was nice that Maggie Stiefvater was taking some time to establish the characters, it was a bit frustrating as well, and there were times when I put down the book just because the action was going so slowly. At no time did I want to stop reading the book, because I liked the characters and the plot, but I did need a break from the slow action. Around halfway through the book, the action became more fast-paced, and I really enjoyed the second half. Except for Ronan and Noah, I really love the characters, and Ronan and Noah are growing on me, and I'm pretty sure that Ronan's character will be explored more in the next book. I really liked the twist with Adam and Blue's relationship, and I'm interested in seeing how that changes given what I know from tumblr. I love the friendship in the book, with the group as a whole, and specifically, Gansey and Blue, Gansey and Adam, and Gansey and Ronan. Gansey is just an interesting character in general. I also liked that Stiefvater addressed topics such as being friends with the wealthy, and abusive relationships. While some people are willing to let the rich buy things for them, I'm happy that Stiefvater had characters who wanted to prove their own worth and not be beholden to anyone else. She also addressed the complexities and frustrations of being in an abusive relationship and knowing someone who is in one. Despite the slow beginning, I ended up really enjoying The Raven Boys, and I can't wait to read the rest of the books in the series.

As I walked to my car, I said good-bye to Emi, the girl who begrudgingly went to frat parties and football games; the girl who pretended like everything was always okay while unenthusiastically teaching Intro to Writing classes; the girl with no past; the girl who wasn't real and didn't exist. Trigger Warning: Abuse Swear on This Life was not my favorite New Adult novel, and even though I was expecting to like it, I had lots of problems with it. The only reason why I bought it was because my friend Amber wrote a positive and wonderful review about it, giving me high hopes and expectations of it, while my friend Mikee didn't enjoy it as much. I was hoping I would like it, since I normally enjoy reading NA novels I always decide to pick up, surprisingly. I was also in the mood for a sweet and fast-paced contemporary, so I was hoping this was it. It was fast-paced, sweet and cute at times, depressing and sad other times, but it wasn't the best. I haven't read Renee's other books, so I'm not very fond with her writing and familiar with her taste, but that didn't change much from the way I looked at this book. Now, I wish I read her previous books before. I always do. For some reason I haven't been enjoying the recent contemporaries I've bought or checked out, and this one was no different. Swear on This Life is pretty much a novel about a novel. Emiline, the protagonist in this novel, is a writer who graduated and got her masters degree in creative writing, going to a University in San Diego and trying to full-fill her dreams. The problem she has is that she isn't able to find her voice and see what the problem is, trying to write something and accomplish it. It's like she never was made to become a writer before and can't figure out what to write of, getting her friends and professors ideas but not taking them for granted. One day, her friend Cara, who is a successful writer and gave Emiline an idea that wasn't taken, lets her borrow a book that she fell in love with immediately. It's a bestselling debut novel that has become one of the best and most gifted literary works out there, being sold to many people and leaving them shocked as to how this story fit in. Emiline has never heard of this book called All the Roads Between, but as soon as Cara lets her borrow the novel and Emiline reads the first line, finishing the first and second paragraph, Emiline is shocked and notices there isn't something right about this. The reason she is so drawn into this novel and knows what it is about is because the novel is about her, about her past and how she had to suffer with her unloving mother, abusive father, and first lover that somehow faded away from her life and left her alone. As she is reading this, she realizes this book was written by her first love; the boy that left her alone and promised to stay with her even when he didn't; the boy she fell in love with; her childhood friend; the boy that became her first and best friend; the boy she told everything to, Jason Colbertson. He doesn't go by that name for some reason, now going by and being known as J. Colby, but he's still the same Jason, the same Jase Emiline grew up with. Now, what Emilie wants is to finish this book and see where it ends to, and find Jase and see why he wrote this novel about her past, and in her perspective. Even with her past being the main key, J. Colby even added more details and changes a lot of the scenes, making them more dramatic and realistic. And as Emiline is reading this novel as time passes, she realizes there is a reason Jase wrote it in her perspective, and realizes the message it was supposed to carry and deliver. Like I said, Swear on This Life wasn't a big hit for me. Emiline is Emerson, Emerson is Emiline. Emerson is the fictional name of Emiline in All the Roads Between, making Jase Jackson, and Jackson Jase. Even though this whole story is about the novel Jase wrote, I felt like there was no point in it. I really didn't understand the whole reason for writing a book about a childhood friend's past after he left her, alone. I enjoyed the beginning of it, but then I was annoyed with the fact that the whole story is about Emiline's past and I couldn't even figure out what the whole story was really about. I mean, I know what it's about, I mean I didn't get the point of it. I didn't understand why this wasn't all about Emiline and her current and future life, but instead about her past and bringing back past and horrible memories. I also didn't understand why Emiline decided to even read the book after crying when she finished the first page. Emiline is our protagonist, but so is Emerson. They felt like different people, even when both are the same. My problem was how Em acted as she was growing up. Even as she was growing up and becoming a woman, I hated how she took it really far and didn't even bother acting like a child anymore. I also hated how she took all this adult life to a whole other level and didn't even want to consider hanging out with Jax anymore as "playing." I don't get it, you're only 13 and you're already freaking out because your breasts are growing, your period started, your hips are getting wider, and your crush is getting cuter. Well, according to the novel and to Jason's writing, that's how it went. It really bugged me how she was changing so much and sometimes she would want to be with Jase but other times she would push him away. Also, what was she doing being 15 years old and already having her first love touching her and running his thumb over her nipple? Wait, it is 2016 so I guess that's normal.... She was strong in both, the past and present, but she wasn't my favorite. She cried a lot, but I understood that because of her past. The reason they were different to me was because I was able to know more about Emerson than Emiline. The fictional characters had more details to explain that the realistic ones, not knowing anything about them except for where they are and what they were doing. As to our other character, Jase, I didn't swoon over him. Sure, he was sweet and caring, but sometimes I didn't understand him and/or his personality and attitude. He went from caring about Em to trying to push her away because of the things that were happening in his life, but sometimes I wished he didn't do that because she was the only one who understood him and was available to help him. I hated some of his decisions and I hated the way Jason wrote the book in Em's point of view, leaving a lot of specific details out and changing everything. Jason and Jackson were different people as well, in the past and present life. Even though I couldn't relate to any of the characters and can't see this in my life, I could see Em having trouble with her mother and stepping up to her mother after all those years. She even was able to forgive both of them after everything that happened, and I was actually glad and proud. I did cry when her father punched her, yanked her hair, kicked her, and slapped her, even when he called her a slut because like dude, I can only imagine that. I felt really bad for her but I was glad Jax came and literally saved her so that was good. I admit, I liked their relationship more than reading only about Em, but again, I wasn't feeling any OTP feels or swooning over them, crying and rooting for them. In the past, their relationship started off as kids hating each other. Suddenly, Jax is that loving and cute kid who apologizes to the girl he called medusa because of her horrifying hair, and suddenly growing up with her and becoming her best friend. As time passed, they both turned 15 and things changed. Ever since Jax's brother, Brian, died, Jax wasn't the same. He was growing and becoming the man he was made to be, growing and becoming stronger. He was still sweet, but still different than the young boy he was. People change, I know that, so I was okay with the change he made, but then at the same time I hated it. He had his own past to deal with, including an unloving father that left his brother and him with his mother, and an alcoholic mother who became a bitch to him after Brian died. His past was similar to Em's, except her mother left and his father became the abusive, unloving, rude, and alcoholic father that calls his daughter a slut and whore and blames her mother for it. Because of that, they both had their similarities and were able to trust each other, tell each other everything and be open about it. The relationship and romance wasn't my favorite thing about this. Nothing really was. It didn't feel real, only because they were kids who fell in love as they were growing up and nothing felt real. I didn't feel connected to them and didn't feel any romance between, not even in the end. Even though they loved each other, they were only high school sweethearts having sex. It's New Adult, but it's not at the same time. When both are adults, they don't have any sweet moments. All they do is talk and make up, but as they're teenagers, they're having sex and hiding. It felt like they didn't know what love meant at a young age, and after the end of All the Roads Between, it finally felt like something. There was finally something shown between both and I wished there were more moments of them being together when they were old and adults, but Jase had to change it all up and end it with them being 50 and over. Now when we come to discussing Emiline and Jason, there really isn't much to talk and discuss. They hadn't seen each other for 12 years, and suddenly they see each other and they start hanging out, communicating, and even start a relationship. I didn't get it, and I didn't like it. I hated how Em still loved him even when he left her and was the reason for her therapy sessions. She was trying to get over him and bringing past memories in her therapy while he was writing a novel about her novel and not giving her credit. Other than that, he was with other girls and even when he didn't feel the word "love" in them and didn't feel like he was in love with them, I still hated him for what he did without even getting her permission. I also hated her for forgiving him so quickly and not being so pissed off about it. Their past was more enjoyable and a lot better to read from, since they had an actual relationship, whereas their present relationship or whatever they had didn't feel real. Another thing I did not like was the whole Trevor and love-triangle thing. I wished she wasn't into Jax and didn't admit it to him after dating him for 7 years. First off, they have been dating for 7 years. After all those 7 years, the sad thing is that they both don't know much, anything really, about each other and have never been open to each other. Even with that, they have never said I love you to each other which was even more sad to read about. A 7-year relationship where secrets were kept and truths were hidden, nothing felt real between them, even more fake and boring than Jason and Emiline. They didn't feel like a happy couple and I wished they broke up in the beginning. I'm not only blaming Trevor, Emiline was the bitchy girlfriend as well. She would ask for his advice and wanted to know what he thought of her work, and even asked for his honesty. As he gave her his honesty and personal thoughts about her work, she got mad and decided to go for a run because she was all mad and hated him for saying that. Well, if you didn't want him to be honest and instead lie about it, why didn't you just ask? I hated their relationship more and I wished there was more background between them. Also, I couldn't believe she would always say "I love you" to him right after she said she still had feeling for Jase, and then suddenly had to say she would think about their relationship and see what she thinks about it. Oh boy. Overall, this wasn't much of a disappointment but it's my first NA novel that I did not enjoy thoroughly. I hated the past and present times and I wished it was only told either in the past of present, finding a way to make up for the way Em found out. If that didn't make sense, I just wished there was a better way of writing the relationship between Emerson (Emiline) and Jax (Jason). It upsets me to not like this one because I really did enjoy the beginning of it, and most of the middle, but then it got to the part where Em reunited with Jase, feeling things because she still felt in love with him and would pretend she wouldn't want to kiss him when he wanted to kiss her because she had a boyfriend. I'll probably still pick up Renee's other works and future novels, but it upsets me knowing this one was a drag. It's always new novels that are disappointing and it's so upsetting because you can go from loving an author and considering them your favorite, to not knowing what to think about them and questioning yourself why you enjoyed their previous work.

It's a shame, because I adored The Iron King, the prequel; I tore through that one in less than three days. But where The Iron King was innovative and engaging, The Iron Daughter was trite, maudlin, and predictable. My favorite characters, Puck and Grim, don't even come in until well over a third of the way through the novel; instead, we are treated to the asinine teenage woes of Meghan, who is just so in love with her forbidden Darque Prince (tm). Their relationship in the last novel was my least favorite part; I liked that Kagawa spent more time building up her heroine and telling her story than sending her head over heels after the first dark and mysterious faery she could find. But the sequel can't seem to go three pages without Meghan pining after Ash, worrying about him, wondering why he doesn't seem to love her the way she loves him, whether she's just a replacement for his dead girlfriend, blah blah angst. The novel starts off with the typical "I'm being a dick to you to PROTECT you" trope, with Ash giving Meghan a very cold shoulder (hyuk hyuk) in Tir Na Nog. Meghan, naturally, is immediately convinced he must loathe her very existence, and spends the first part of the book pining away, wondering what she did to deserve his scorn, and trying not to cry about it. Every time he seems to show a bit of warmth, she instantly melts. She's been in this place for a while, now; you'd think she would have a) caught on that he was doing this to protect her, especially after he said as much, or b) learned to deal with it. Or, my personal preference, c) dumped his sorry ass and moved on. But no, she just cries and moans and when they eventually escape, there are several scenes that I imagine are supposed to be heart-wrenching, where Ash keeps saying they can't be together and Meghan makes out with him anyway. Then she makes out with Puck, because everyone knows the only real cure for a broken heart is screwing around with your best friend's. The plot, to Kagawa's credit, is interesting. There's a new, false Iron King on the throne, and after he steals the Scepter of the Seasons, which will inevitably wreak havoc on the mortal world if not returned, Iron Horse (you know, THAT IRON HORSE) decides to help Meghan recapture it. Iron Horse, as ever, is wonderful, even if he does tend to fall into the "socially awkward muscle guy" stereotype. Grim is just as dry and inexplicable as in the first novel, which almost makes up for Meghan's increased weeping, Puck's idiotic one-liners (were they this bad in the first book? ), and Ash's insufferable stoicism. Still, I couldn't finish the book. 250 pages in and I just couldn't make myself read it anymore. Incredibly disappointing.

"I wasn't sure if I wanted to hear such a big secret. It might not fit in my head and then it would spill out everywhere." A Head Full of Ghosts begins as many horror stories do. The Barrett family is a pretty normal group. Mom, Dad, and sisters Marjorie and Merry live a peaceful life in their suburban home. Things change when older sister Marjorie begins to exhibit odd behavior. The doctors and specialists can't seem to find a medical explanation for her condition. Dad turns to the church and becomes convinced that Marjorie is possessed by a demon. Given their unusual circumstance, the Barrett family does what any American family would do. They cash in on their troubles by allowing a television crew to film their life and attempts at exorcism for a reality show. What ensues is the tragic erosion of a once happy family. The parents don't agree on how to approach treatment for Marjorie, Merry is ignored by the rest of her family, and Marjorie is pushed to physical and emotional limits. Is the girl truly possessed, or is the Barrett family merely enacting a hoax for financial gain? A Head Full of Ghosts is a refreshing addition to the horror genre. Paul Tremblay writes with a self-awareness that gives an original perspective to an otherwise familiar story. Tremblay clearly has an extensive knowledge and appreciation for all things horror. There is nothing overtly shocking or gory about this book. Rather, the story unfolds with a slow build that gives just enough suspense to keep us hanging onto every word. I like my horror stories to make me think and fill with dread. By that mark, A Head Full of Ghosts is an excellent novel that will leave you with an anxious paranoia of every little bump in the night.

** spoiler alert ** I enjoyed this book. It dragged once or twice but mostly kept me engaged until the end. It is very much "hard" science fiction in the classic vein whereby the science is the star, not the characters. And there are some really great ideas and scenes here, such as the nature of the "lock" that will stop all human technological progress, and the destruction of the ship. Unfortunately I had a few issues that keep it from being a truly great example of the genre in my mind. The biggest by far is the presentation of the "Three Body" video game that takes up much of the middle portion of the book. This whole section made little sense to me. Sometimes it's implied that the other players in the game are NPCs, and in a contradictory fashion sometimes it's implied they are actual humans, but they don't really behave like either. Moreso, it's not really clear to me why this game would be considered so challenging or mind-blowing, since the main "mystery" behind it is pretty simple and there didn't seem to be anything required of the player after this mystery is solved in order to progress (GameFAQs would have a field day with it). Likewise, there's a lot of pages both within the game and without devoted to various methods of solving the three body problem, but as is clearly explained later, this is all completely irrelevant because the Trisolarians have to leave because their planet is going to be destroyed someday by one of its suns no matter what. So why does the scientist who is going to solve the problem (which they've also claimed to have proved is unsolvable) need to be killed? I don't get it. Finally, the international publication of this book was somewhat botched as the editor chose to include a spoiler in the back cover copy. I don't know if this blurb was originally in the Chinese edition, but either way it's clear from the way the text is written that the fact that aliens are involved in the narrative is not meant to be revealed until nearly the second half of the book. It's debatable how necessary this is or to what extent it ruins the book as a whole, but in my mind knowing something I'm not supposed to for a full half of the story definitely counts as subtracting from it.

I have loved every volume of this series except for the Fables-Jack of Fables crossover arc. I recommend this series to everyone I meet.

This review appears on Happy Indulgence. Check it out for more reviews! Do you believe in the concept of soulmates? Whether you do or you don't makes it crucial for your enjoyment of this book. It starts off fairly innocently, as Fallon while having an unpleasant lunch with her dad, meets Ben. He becomes her fake boyfriend and they instantly hit it off, with an unusual and intense connection. For reasons I'm not entirely convinced on, they decide to meet on November 9 every year for five years, with no contact in between. Now you'll wonder as I wondered, why would they choose to do this for someone they've known for mere hours? No matter how convincingly their attraction was written, their deep connection and their past, I found it hard to believe. It's surprising how year after year, they would be committed to meeting each other despite not knowing anything about each other except for their physical attraction. Upon first meeting Ben, I found him a little too good to be true, as he delivers cheesy line after line to Fallon. It's like he's almost manipulating the situation, as he feeds Fallon, who's insecure about her scars as a burn victim, exactly what she needs to hear. While I liked his commitment to their pact, the depth of his feelings and his loyalty to his brothers, there was something about Ben that I didn't quite trust - and it turns out I was right. During his first meeting with Fallon, he forces her to wear a dress that she doesn't want to wear. She's a burn victim and wears long sleeves to cover her scars, but even after honestly explaining to Ben why she doesn't want to wear a revealing dress - he makes her do it anyway. She's not entirely unwilling, but I'm like dude, if the girl says no, that means no. He also insists on saying really awkwardly uncomfortable things in front of other people, concerning her panties and her boobs, which I found more disrespectful than awkwardly charming. And the fact that Fallon always comes to him, and he doesn't come to her. I saw two sides to his character - the perfect emotional writer, which he acts like around Fallon, and the controlling and disrespectful alpha male persona which came through his actions. Fallon on the other hand, is the damaged girl who needs to heal herself before getting into a relationship. She goes through major character development over the course of the novel, and in 5 years, changes from the self conscious bitter girl to one who is confident and ambitious. But because of the way the novel is written, only giving us a snapshot of each year, I missed a lot of Fallon's development and what caused her to change and grow. Which brings me back to the one trope I have with "damaged character" books - that romance changes everything. Here it's relied upon heavily and that didn't quite fly with me - because the reader is told to accept that these two characters have pulled themselves out of the depth of their personal hells because they've met each other. And they don't even really know each other! Yet they're blindly committed to this cute idea they made when they were 18. It just doesn't make sense. Colleen Hoover's writing is addictive and filled with emotion, but another issue I had with November 9 is that it heavily features cheesy romance tropes. Damaged characters, a hidden past, and secrets being kept on both sides. The cheesiness, insta-love, and manufactured romantic drama also made it feel inauthentic. Everything seems to be resolved a little too easily, particularly since you can just skip a proper resolution by just going to the next year. I enjoyed the concept of having a couple meet once per year in November 9, however much of how the novel was structured year by year was it's downfall for me. I found Ben to be too unrealistic, Fallon's development was skipped over, and it relied too heavily on romantic tropes and cheesy lines to deliver an impact. The big twist of the end is also featured in other NA books that I've read before, which was disappointing and predictable to say in the least. Sadly, I feel like the magic's starting to wear off. The ending was fulfilling, not rushed in anyway (but by no means boring), and left you with a sense that a squeal would be welcome, but not needed. Some things were not to par when compared to some of Hale's previous novels, however. The romance plot seems forced and very repetitive. The adults in this novel did not seem realistic to me either. As an adult, I could not understand the thought processes that they went through when they made decisions. The pacing seemed a little off as well. Some chapters seemed to drag on and sometimes the pace picked up only to be dragged back down again. I felt like Hale tried to cram in more action into this novel than was absolutely needed, and ended up dragging it out a little too much. Overall, I enjoyed this novel and it was a welcome addition to my Shannon Hale collection, but I feel like it could have used a little more time in the editing process, skimming off some of the more pointless plot lines and scenes.

I've decided I don't like Sarah Dessen books. Don't get me wrong, though - her writing is wonderful and I've only read two of her books, so I'm not really one to judge. My main problem with it, honestly, is that it's too realistic. Yep, you heard me. I don't like Sarah Dessen books because it's too realistic. That's totally insane, right? This is why I'm going to say you don't have to listen to my opinion on this. Dessen's writing is fantastic, and all her characters (for the most part), are believable. The reason I don't like them is because I'm one of those girls who doesn't like being realistic. I like fairy tales and romance that lights up a room, where the two people are obviously soul mates. The pattern I've noticed with this book and the only other Dessen book I've read, Along For The Ride, is that the romance actually happens like it would in real life, meaning the feelings develop at a painfully slow pace and nothing too heart stopping happens at all. Most of the scenes are pretty much every day life stuff. My favorite character was Delia, which I find interesting because she may be the first female character I've actually really really liked in a book. She was great, and I could picture her clearly. I had one other problem with this, though: Macy's mom. And honestly, it's because I relate. Macy's mom has this perfect little mold in which she wants Macy to forever stay. She doesn't accept her when she changes, even though she changes for the better. My dad is just like this, never accepting anything I do on my own. And I suppose I should have felt good about relating to it, but it just made me really mad because Macy was understanding to her mom, even though her mom didn't deserve it. Which is so dumb for me to think that, because that's obviously the better thing for Macy to do. I don't know, basically, the two reasons I didn't like this book were because of personal problems. I don't read spy novels, generally, although I like thrillers at the movies. Something about Ludlum et al leaves me cold. This book was much more approachable for me. First, unlike many reviewers, I love a book that skips back and forth in time. It adds a layer of complexity to the unravelling, instead of just laying it all out for you in order. I was actually thinking that the book would lose something if translated into film, because some of the time-jumping would no longer work--you'd recognize the antagonist, for instance. Next, also unlike many reviewers, I loved the fact that Kate was nervous and distractable even when in full spy mode. It seems much more likely to me that spying is tense and difficult, not smooth and effortless. Oddly enough, I know an ex-CIA guy, and while he certainly carries himself with confidence, and continues to work as a PI, I also know he's human, not Jason Bourne or James Bond. He says one reason he went for the desk transfer before quitting altogether is that it is actually really unpleasant to risk both killing and being killed. And finally, I enjoyed the juxtaposition of bored-expat-housewife reality with the spies and double crosser fantasy world, and the ways the two bled into each other.

Perhaps, unfortunately, it was this experience that led them to include everything but the kitchen sink. This book has got Gorgeous Teens in Exclusive Prep School! on a Secluded Island! with a Scary Abandoned Mental Hospital! and a Dark Forest! and Secret Societies! and Neurological Tampering! and also Underground Tunnels! and even Nazis!! Also, a main plot point -- an extremely repetitive one -- is that the main character, Sarah, has hyperthymesia/eidetic memory (although, curiously, doesn't remember a helpful detail about her family background until the VERY END). And she's beautiful, but doesn't know it, because apparently people in her experience at various foster homes have been harsh on bi-racial girls, or something. There's also a terrible attempt at a love triangle with one boy who is a complete jerk most of the time (and already has a girlfriend), and another boy who seems nice but also leads some strange and sinister doings... including sex parties in the underground nazi tunnels... because ... OK, never mind. I'm done. There are SO MANY IDEAS in this book, and most of them are not good, and they all hold together not a whit. If this were a movie, I'd recommend it for its sheer ridiculousness. But it's a book, and I recommend it not at all. ** I received an ARC of this book via NetGalley **

If you do any kind of research on The Magicians at all, even just reading the back of the novel, you will find it compared constantly and fervently to Harry Potter and The Chronicles of Narnia. I tend to take such comparisons with a grain of salt. With such epically amazing series, it's unlikely that the comparison will do the book in question a favor, because it will merely disappoint, clumsily ape the better novel or actually have nothing in common whatsoever with the book to which it is being compared. The Harry Potter series is definitely among my favorite books of all time and Narnia, although not a favorite due to the Christian allegory, is still incredibly well-written and not to be easily matched. With that said, Lev Grossman managed to mine both for inspiration and create something new, wonderful and completely his own. So yeah, I kind of loved it from the beginning to the end. Like Harry Potter, this series follows a main male character, Quentin Coldwater, in the third person, revealing only that which Quentin personally observes, experiences or is told. For those of us who still dream sometimes about receiving a Hogwarts letter (or the American equivalent) and a time turner, by which to go back to the right age, we have yet another magical school to lament not having received an invitation to join. This school, Brakebills, is even more exclusive: just having witchy powers does not guarantee you admittance. You have to be a genius, not just smart but incredibly brilliant, and also possess a certain something to get to go. It saddens me that I am not smart enough to have ever gotten to go to Brakebills. The story is told in four books, all of which have their own themes and arcs. The first book is what I like to think of as the Harry Potter arc. In this section, Quentin gets his invitation and takes the test to go to Brakebills. The students there are of the age to go to college, older than the HP crew, but they go through similar schedules with classes and holidays and all of that. This part is where you learn about the rules of magic and meet the cast of characters, most notably Alice, Eliot, Penny, Josh and Janet. In Book 2, they have all graduated and are living it up in New York, in a the world is ending kind of way. They're all completely crazy and screwed up, but in a familiar way; many people make these mistakes once out of college and unsure what to do next. Basically, they're disillusioned and spoiled and depressed and without motivation, waiting for some sign of what they're meant to be and do. This section is painful to read, but believable and necessary. Let me sidetrack for a moment to talk about Quentin as a character. Overall, I kind of don't like him, because he can be so dumb for one so smart. Why? Quentin sees the world in a very black and white, childish kind of way, which is why his mood does such crazy rockets from the heights of happiness to the depths of despair. He has huge expectations from his life and is monumentally destroyed and depressed when life does not meet them. He has high standards for others and judges them for their mistakes, but blames his disappointing life for his own. He always expects the next new thing to fix all of his problems and bring him the perfect paradise he always knew he deserved (thus the Fillory obsession). Since I didn't do a summation at the beginning, allow me to explain Fillory briefly now. Fillory is the Narnia equivalent, a magical land from a novel series written for children. These books are about children from a family who manage to pass into another land via a number of means (such as a clock) and there are made kings and queens and have adventures, although they are always made to leave at the end of each book by the goat gods of the world. Book three of The Magicians is the Narnia portion. It is very like Narnia and yet so very, very different and much, much darker. The fourth book largely sets up for the sequel, The Magician King. I can't say much more than that without spoilering, which I most ardently do not wish to do, because I want everyone to enjoy this book as much as I did. This landed somewhere between a three & a four star read. The writing was fantastic and the story was interesting enough, but my only reason for not absolutely loving this story comes down to my own personal preferences. The description of the hero was lacking for me, in my opinion. I just could not wrap my head around it. A bit too much hair and the description of his pubic hair being a 'nest' just made me cringe. I am a 'shave it all off' kind of girl. So it was a little difficult to fall head over heels in love with this amazing hero, I just never got the image out of my head... but on to the story... Lilli is moving to a new town, a town that is in the middle of nowhere. Signal Bend. It's a town without a police department, little activity and a MC that is pretty much the law. So catching the attention of the MC President, Isaac wasn't unexpected; but it sure would have made it easier. Isaac has lived in Signal Bend his whole life, the MC has been his life as far back as he can remember. But his MC is not just about the illegal activity, booze and women. He and his brother have been protecting the people in his town for years, ensuring that the dirt doesn't stick too close to home. But his attention is about to be diverted, when a stranger moves to town and catches his eye. Lilli isn't what she seems. Isaac knows she's hiding something and is bound and determined to get to the bottom of it. But with outsiders moving in on his town and her secrets mixing into his club, Isaac is going to have to make some hard choices... his brothers or his woman. And for Lilli, she had one goal in mind when she moved to Signal Bend, but falling for the President of the Night Horde was not one of them. Let's just start off with Lilli - complete kick ass heroine. She was feisty, independent and not at all immature. She was one helluva leading lady. She easily became an instant favorite. There was a lot of flash backs into her life, and life sure did like to shit on this girl. But she took it all in stride. Isaac was not your typical alpha MC. Living in a small country town allowed this biker to be much more laid back and I loved this slower paced MC read. He and his brothers might have had some unsavory ties, but you could see that beyond loving their club - they loved their town. The people were what mattered to them. This was a surprisingly good read, beyond my own issues with the furry nuts and what equates to a more realistic description of a biker. Other than that little detail, I thoroughly enjoyed this book and am looking forward to the next in the series.

I love books that take place in long-forgotten kingdoms with magic thrown in. Books that have magic thrown in. However, most of those books take after the kingdoms in Northern Europe--France, England, etc. The Thief took me by surprise--it was set not in a fantasy kingdom modeled after Northern Europe but the kingdom's of the Mediterranean--Italy/Greece. It took you through groves of olive orchards. Honestly, I was sick and tired of reading about olive trees by the time this book was done. It also included a religion based on Italy and Greece's pantheon, a major factor in the book itself. It was an interesting change from other books that I have read, even going so far as to include more modern technology (guns, for example). As for the book itself, though, I felt that it could have been written a little better. I was sometimes lost in what was happening and what was going on--to the point where there were a couple times I had to go back and reread to get the snippet I didn't realize I had missed. Not something I would read again, though an interesting concept. I'm thinking about continuing the story but I am as yet undecided.

Jeez, he's my knight in shining armor, whether I want him to be or not. I really really really like this book. It's really quite adorable. Starting from the 5th grade and her first kiss with her next door neighbour, Jaydn shares her relationship with her best friend Phillip through her school years, through college, and after college. It's definitely a girl's diary, but I liked how through each chapter, you can see Jaydn growing up just a little bit more. She keeps up a running commentary of her observations, questions and problems. She seems immature for a while but then tragedy strikes and suddenly the book had substance and I was really curious to see where it was going. Jaydn's a tomboy and has no problem keeping up with the guys. She's a bit of a wild card, reckless, fun-focused, a party girl. She's sarcastic, fierce, and scoffs at the teenage girl drama that her schoolmates engage it. She much prefers hanging out with Phillip and Danny, her two best friends. Her relationship with the boys is questionably platonic. There are a few kisses over the years, some lusting (admiring) moments, but no dating, and they generally behave platonically. Is it a love triangle? No. Their friendship is so much fun. I liked seeing their conversations and the scraps they got into. Jaydn and Danny are hilarious together. They snap and bicker a lot and it's all very flirtatious. The boys aren't that different from each other. They both play football, they're both hot, smart, and ambitious. Phillip's portrayed as a rule-stickler who says nice things to Jaydn. He's the type that oozes, "I'm here for you," but he also tells her off like he's her dad, or a very protective lover. Danny's a bit more sardonic and meaner but a whole lot more funny. He's not afraid to tell her she's hot or give her naughty looks. Their relationship ends up more of a friends-with-limited-benefits.

In the fourth (and as of now, final) book in the Jackson Brodie series of mysteries by Kate Atkinson, I'm left happy for having read it, disappointed that there aren't more in the series, but then wondering about the inconsistencies in this series of books. I've given books in this series 2 stars and 4 stars, but am ending with 3 because we just completely "lose track" of people from Jackson's life while others stick around entirely too much. Jackson's number one annoying trait, besides starting nearly every conversation with "I used to be a police officer", is fixating on long-gone relationships to an annoying degree. Jackson is a brooder. Stop brooding already, Jackson, you have two kids and a dog, it doesn't matter that you've also had lost loves. The mysteries in this edition are interesting, and tied together nicely. There are some event which remain unanswered, however, which is like life I guess. I'm glad he's finally got a paying client again, as Jackson needs to earn some money now that one of his foolish romances emptied out his bank accounts. I liked Tracy and Courtney, but there were too many other new characters to keep straight. All of these cops charging around in 1975 and also in the present, it was hard to keep them straight in the audiobook. The descriptions of fat old white men did not draw a compelling distinction, somehow. And, the author seemed to be fat-shaming Tracy through most of the book, focusing entirely too much on what she was eating and how large she was and couldn't find attractive clothes and whatnot. I liked the plot of the aging actress as well, but thought perhaps too much time was spent with her lost and confused in various shopping centers. And what was the point of Julia having a role on that tv show, not sure, other than yet another way for us to have to endure the annoying existence of Julia once again. To have more Louise and less Julia should be a goal for any future books in this series, I would think. I also loved the dog, but think The Ambassador is a pretty terrible name for a cute little dog. Bass could be a short nickname, and it would sound like he's named after a fish rather than a diplomat. Overall, an enjoyable read, but it wasn't as enjoyable as the first and third books in this series.

FINAL DECISION: This story had promise, but I got tired of the secrecy of this story and just when things seemed to be moving story wise, the characters would engage in sex and stall the story. Not as exciting as I would have liked. THE STORY: A year ago, Kate was devastated when the love of her life died in a plane crash. On a beach, a man approaches her and Kate is shocked to see her dead husband Price. Price tells Kate that he has been in hiding for a year and she has a choice, come with him without questions or they will part forever. OPINION: I thought this book was uneven. Parts of it I really enjoyed, but parts were difficult for me to get through because I got bored and distracted. I thought the book had a good premise and I was intrigued by how these two married people would find one another again. My first problem with the story was that there was too much sex that interrupted the story. I don't have a problem with an erotica story where the characters develop their relationship through their sexual encounters, but I kept thinking as the story went on that just when the story seemed to be moving, there was a sex scene. The other problem was that there was never really any issue with Kate and Price being together emotionally. That made the relationship part flat for me. As a result, the first problem was even more glaring. Despite that, I enjoyed parts of this book. I wanted to know what would happen and I like the characters as people and I wanted to see them have a happy ending. That was satisfied. WORTH MENTIONING: This story is an attempt at an erotic romantic suspense, but isn't entirely successful. CONNECTED BOOKS: This book is the second in the Misadventures series. This series, however, is a series of standalone books where there is no crossover or connections other than the hot and spicy nature of the stories. STAR RATING: I give this book 2.5 stars. NOTE: I received an ARC of this book via Netgalley in order to provide a review. I was not required to write a review or to write a positive review. All opinions contained herein are my own.This review was originally posted on Top10RomanceBooks.com

"Finn said art isn't about drawing or painting the perfect bowl of soup. It's about ideas. And you, he said, have enough good ideas to last a lifetime." June has a special relationship with her Uncle Finn. Finn is a famous painter who lives in an apartment in New York. June has always had a hard time fitting in with her family and peers. Finn offers her an escape filled with culture, exploration, and understanding. He accepts her for who she is and indulges all of her quirks and curiosities. The year is 1987 and June's world is beginning to change. Finn has been diagnosed with a mysterious illness. Her parents, both accountants, are in the thick of tax season and spend little time at home. Mom has been very muted about Finn's illness. June is only allowed to visit him during weekly trips with her mother and sister. She knows little about AIDs, but June sees the debilitating effect it is having on her beloved uncle. After weeks of deterioration, Finn finally succumbs to his illness. June is devastated. The only person who truly loved her for who she was is dead. Mom seems eager to put the whole ordeal behind them. While the rest of her family seems keen to leave the memory of Finn in the past, June wants to know more. Who was the strange man at Finn's funeral that had Mom so upset? Did that man really kill her uncle? And what has become of Finn's apartment and possessions? In Tell the Wolves I'm Home, author Carol Rifka Brunt presents a deeply moving coming of age story about love, loss, and acceptance. By having fourteen-year-old June narrate the novel, the author makes the heavy topics a bit more palatable. We feel every emotion of June as she discovers the cruelty and ignorance that surrounded the AIDs crisis. At its heart, Tell the Wolves I'm Home is a coming of age story that manages to weave larger themes into its foundation. From the very first page, the book captured my emotions and imagination. Tell the Wolves I'm Home is a stunning debut novel that will have you contemplating its layers long after the final page.

And not til just before did she do something about her appearance. You'd think she'd get her scars covered up before she went back, knowing she'd potentially taking her clothes off. And surely she would have built up strength, come up with a plan b. She just seemed totally careless. The sex seemed unreal too. Anal with a bit of spit? I'm hoping the romance with Jace will improve, he seems 'nice' and they have a little friendship going on. But that's it. I'll carry on with the series, but I just hope there's no more contradicting behaviour.

I like the protagonist Cameron, but I wish the book had been edited. There's entirely too much detail! Do we need to know the name of every song she danced to at the prom she attended when was in ninth grade? (Yes.) I think the book would work as well, if every other sentence and every other scene had been left out. I like foreshadowing, but the holy roller church her aunt has her attend, we know it's going to be bad news, couldn't Cameron have saved herself a lot of grief by going back to the Presbyterian Church her parents attended? Maybe, but that wouldn't have been Cameron. And the detail made this read more like an adult coming of age book, than a YA coming of age book. Cameron and the other characters in the book has a complexity usually missing in YA books. I loved the setting, rural eastern Montana; where the swimming pool Cameron's swim team meets at is a pond. Where the highlight of the year is Miles City Bucking Horse Sale. Where her girlfriend Coley gets her own apartment in town, because she lives forty miles away on a ranch. (Where it seems to me that Coley's brother's drinking is much more of a problem than Coley and Cameron's gayness.) When Cameron was twelve her parents were killed in a car accident. Afterwards, she lives with her aunt and grandmother. Her aunt is horrible, but she thinks she loves a version of Cameron. Just not the version of Cameron we readers see. This is a very, very good novel from a debut author, who I hope gets a lot of deserved attention and writes a lot more.

I'm struggling to gather my thoughts about this book. As a psychological thriller, it was pretty good; I thought it was well-plotted and the twists were totally shocking and unexpected. However, there were a lot of problems with this book as well. For one thing, half the chapters don't have quotation marks, which was extremely annoying. Sometimes it was unclear whether a sentence was spoken out loud or just in the narrator's head. Another thing that bothered me was the characters. Both the narrators, Emma and Jane, were difficult for me to understand and relate to. At the beginning of the book each of them has been through a tragedy, which is supposed to explain why they choose to live in a house with insane rules. But even with the things that had happened to them, I felt it was a stretch that anyone would agree to the terms of this house. I also couldn't understand why they each chose to have a relationship with the architect who built the house, because he is clearly insane and extremely controlling. I understood why they were drawn to him in the first place, but these women ignored and explained away so much horrible behavior on his part that I found it difficult to sympathize with them. All the characters in this book felt like one-sided caricatures with no real complexity.

Thank you, NetGalley, for providing this book from St. Martin's Griffin for review! Maya was cursed since the day she was born. Because her mother died and she lived, the other harem wives of her father, the Raja, believe in Maya's horoscope: her marriage is one of death and destruction. When the Raja asks Maya to give her life for her kingdom on the brink of war, Maya painfully agrees to do so -- and instead finds herself in Akaran with Amar, a raja who promises equality and power. But strange things are happening in Akaran, and as Maya tiptoes the edge of secrets, she's thrust into unraveling an ancient mystery, one that could alter thousands of lives and truly bring about devastation. I wanted a love thick with time, as inscrutable as if a lathe had carved it from night and as familiar as the marrow in my bones. I wanted the impossible, which made it that much easier to push out of my mind. What a ride. There are no comparable titles, only authors, that I can give. Chokshi's writing is vivid as Erin Morgenstern's and as otherworldly as Laini Taylor's. Toss in the beauty of Indian myth and folklore, and you're destined for an adventurous read. I haven't read a YA fantasy quite is unique (and steeped in non-Euro culture) as this (either ever or in a long while!). Chokshi is like a breath of fresh air! Maya's journey is unique, yet familiar. Though there are words and beliefs and myths completely unfamiliar to me, it's Maya's quest for answers and character growth that's recognizable. The last third of the book heavily relies on Indian mythology, I felt, with a fantastical, otherworldly quest Maya must fulfill in order to restore the balance between the mortal world and Akaran. Hang on tight. It may seem a little confusing, but it's entirely worth it in the end. You are, along with Maya, experiencing several reincarnated lives, and every word in this book matters! "I know your soul. Everything else is an ornament." Amar is also a great character for a love interest. It's easy to see why Maya's drawn to him, and it's understandable when her trust begins to falter. How can someone so ethereal, composed, and determined to show compassion and equality also refuse to tell her anything deep about himself, about his world, his past? What is he hiding? And why can't he share it with her? All this complications made for an intense relationship, and a key to Maya's quest, and I deeply enjoyed the character exploration. Chokshi is officially on my watch list. I'll happily read anything else she publishes! *quotes taken from uncorrected proof

For this review and more, visit my blog at Idle Pursuits Book three of this series also has a small, several page, short story from Finnigan Lane's point of view called, Wasted. Compared to Finn's other POV story, Poison, this one was much better. We had more of the adult Finn we know and love and less of the awful teenager Finn. We can also see how well he can handle himself, something he has only done off-screen, and only incrementally until this point. So, if you like Finn being Finn and also shooting people, this is the short story for you. Compared to the other books, Venom, didn't feel like it held quite as broad of a scope. It was pretty focused as far as plot was concerned. Gin's baby sister Bria has taken Donovan Caine's place on the police force, so we get the all new dynamic there, where Gin wants to both have a relationship with yet another straight-arrow cop, and somehow keep being an assassin without going to jail. So far, Bria doesn't know that Gin is the Spider, hasn't put two and two together. So we don't actually have to deal with that drama yet. I really like Bria. She can handle herself, and I can't wait to find out more of her backstory. Eventually, I assume, it will all come to light, but as a cop and a thorn in Gin's side (in more ways than on, also that's a rose joke, get it), she's absolutely fantastic. Gin, herself, seems to waffle between being super rude to Bria and giving her free pieces of her favorite pie. So, we'll have to see how this relationship develops over the course of the series. Gin's other relationship with Owen Grayson has come to bear, and he (and those goddamn violet eyes, Jesus) play quite a role in this story. Okay, so, I get that like part of the plot was for Gin to go to Northern Aggression (the sexiest sex bar to ever sex ever), but for Owen Grayson to just be there, and then to be like, "Oh, yeah, I took my sister who I'm hella protective of here," just like, doesn't make sense. If you want to keep your little sister safe you don't bring her to a club where people are literally boning under tables. That just does not compute to me. That is not a place you take your baby sister. What sort of literal weirdo are you, Owen? Clearly quite a weirdo. He gives zero fucks about Gin's occupation. He gives a few fucks that maybe she stormed into his house and took some of his swords, but those fucks are soon forgotten. He just doesn't have any substance yet and it's pretty glaringly obvious. There was that shoehorned bit where Gin saved him once from starvation and the cold and now he's rich because Fletcher Lane decided to step in because Gin was feeding him like a lost puppy. But, like, that doesn't overly give him substance or feelings. It just adds more to Gin's backstory (though, that was touched on in Poison slightly). I dunno. I'm just not feeling Owen. I know more about the scar on his chin and the color of his eyes than anything else about him and it's slightly infuriating. Donovan Caine might have been the lamest goodie goodie, but at least I knew what I was getting with him. He had substance and character and wasn't just places to promote plot movement. Also, we literally got to 90% of the book before there was any sort of sex. I was pretty into the fact that there wasn't any, that Gin wasn't going to rush into it. Nah, we got a weird shower scene because Gin showed up to Owen's dirty and bloody. Just more weird 'because plot' for Owen Grayson. Like I said earlier, the plot for this is pretty condensed. Gin is after one of Mab's goons, Elliot Slater. He's a huge giant with a proclivity to abuse women until they're dead. He's set his sights on Roslyn, whom Gin feels indebted to. So Gin goes after him, fails a few times, gets beat up. You know the drill. The only thing I didn't like about this book, overall, was that the entire conflict made me uncomfortable. The entire conflict was abuse and rape and subsequent murder. They don't paint Elliot Slater as a good guy, but literally no one steps in to help Roslyn except Gin, due to the fact that he's on Mab's payroll. It was mentally taxing and upsetting. I think it was meant to be, but abuse and rape as a plot point really grinds on me. Anyway, three books in, and by the time I'm said and done, 13 more to go. This book had some interesting parts, good action sequences, and also some real squicky bits. Overall, I really enjoyed it. Time to start Tangled Threads.

Stitch is the first volume of a new series called gothika. I love dark, gothic romance stories, and I love m/m. I was a bit disappointed last year when there didn't seem to be many new things out in m/m for Halloween that were, well, Halloween-y. So Jamie Fessenden and I started talking about doing an anthology together. And we had so many ideas that turned into a series of anthologies. We were fortunate enough to get Sue Brown and Kim Fielding to agree to participate. Et voila. Each volume of gothika will have a theme and include four novellas. The theme of Stitch is Frankenstein/Creature. In other words, one of the MCs is a man-made man. I have always loved stories like this and there aren't many in the m/m category. The stories in this volume include: Made For Aaron -- by Sue Brown The Watchwork Man -- by Jamie Fessenden The Golem of Mala Lubovnya -- by Kim Fielding Reparation -- by Eli Easton My story, Reparation, is a sci-fi/dystopian novella, 33K words. It was heavily influenced by Wuthering Heights, one of my favorite gothic novels. We'll have a second volume of gothika out for Halloween 2014.

As this is an anthology of stories from existing series, I will read it in sections as I get to each story in their respective series. Bas catches the scent of his future mate and even discovers her in a sweet little human kindergarten teacher, but there is something different about her scent and they soon learn why. Kirby has issues with abandonment and she is just learning more about the changling race after moving where there is a large concentration of them. Bas captures her senses and her heart if she dares believe in him to truly mean that they are together now. This was sweet, heartwarming and passionate with a little mystery about Kirby's background. Is it terrible that I loved seeing overprotective Mercy and sweet though no pushover Kirby meet? Another great edition to the series. Magic Steals by Ilona Andrews 4 Stars I was excited to see this was a continuation in Jim and Dali's story along with a cunning case for them to partner on. Dali was somewhat frustrating with her issues of not feeling good enough. I thought she was over it after Jim started showing fixed interest in her in Magic Dreams, but like most of us, I guess she needed mom's boot up the butt to get her head on straight. Now, Jim? Holy Hot Panther Man! He made my knees weak the way he focused on Dali saying and doing all he could to show how he felt about her. Nice addition to the series.

Loved it. I like a book with angst and this one definitely delivered on that. Loved the relationship between Evan and Jo. Loved the "sixth-sense" element. Loved the writing style. Evan's adoptive parents infuriated me, but I think I sort of get it. Some questions that came up about them while I read: Why did they adopt him when they were able to have children of their own? Why did they let their kids treat Evan the way they did? I imagine they freaked out after Evan's "episode" in the classroom during the shooting, and his subsequent stint in the mental institution. Maybe they were afraid of him after that. Maybe that's when they gave up on him. I wonder if their relationship was at all good before that? Anyway, I relished in all the feels the story gave me and I thought it was fantastic the way everything fell into place at the end. It made me understand why everything happened the way it did. . Great book, and I will definitely be reading more from this author.

I'm actually really sad. I really enjoyed the other Shadow books! However I'm about halfway through and I think I missed something. When did this turn from a gripping story of world war, politics, betrayal, and revenge, to a rant about babies? First of all, the chemistry between the two main characters, Petra and Bean, is awkward and forced. I don't get that these are two people who, despite being geniuses, find themselves falling completely in love. It's a little odd how Petra suddenly decides, "Hey, I'm going to have your babies. What, you don't want to have babies? Okay, come talk to this gay dude. This gay dude says that the meaning of life is to have babies. What, now you guess you'll have to marry me and have babies? Sweet." It's just not how people go about getting married. And as someone familiar with fertility treatments, I know that it's really not how someone goes about deciding to do IVF to have children. I would have kept reading the book, however I am also pretty offended by the underlying view that the meaning of life is to have lots of babies. 'Oh, but I guess if you can't, then you can adopt them...but you're not really a part of the 'web of life', so you're sort of second rate.' What, a military genius who helped saved the entire world isn't already a part of the web of life? By the way, it's also very weird how the characters seem to want to have these babies out of some sort of duty to the human race. Lastly, Card's thinly-disguised political rants were a distraction from the plot. I'm even a Republican, and I rolled my eyes at his references to marriage and family and how he thinks it should be. I'm sorry, Shadow series. I'll ask a friend what happens and move on.
