Review by The Blogger Girls. There is a reason this series is one of the very few on my m/f paranormal reading list - it delivers every single time with no signs of slowing down any time soon. From the very first pages, I was flooded with memories of this wonderful series, smiling at the humor and fun the characters I know and love are having as they play a role playing pirate game as this story begins. There is never a dull moment in Mercy's life, whether she is out getting into trouble of her own, or at home in the midst of her now very large family. It doesn't take long before things get a bit more serious and Mercy is kidnapped, by vamps! I've been waiting a long time for more vamp exposure in this series. Stefan is back in the fold, as he, through his tie to Mercy, helps Adam in her recovery. I absolutely love Ms. Briggs' style. Right from the beginning, she tells us we need to pay attention to Mercy's notes because things happen in kind of a wonky order. Mercy keeps us posted though, and it was not difficult to follow along at all. Now, normally, I tend to not enjoy a story where the characters spend more time separated than together. But I didn't mind it all all here. The time spent with Adam and his crew was exciting and wonderful, just as much as the time spent with Mercy trying to get out of her situation on her own. And, truthfully, through their bond, they never really felt that far apart, even though they were. This might be one of my favorites of this series. I loved how the different factions came together to help Adam (and Mercy) when they were needed. Even Elizavetta, who is not a Mercy fan, stepped up to the plate! And I loved the twists and how everything came together. If you are a fan of shifter stories and have not picked this series up yet, I cannot recommend you do so highly enough. Each story is just as good as the previous one but with new elements or events that never feel over the top - this series just works, and it works well. It has unique and interesting characters, and a family of relationships that exist beyond the pack dynamics. Mercy is strong, loyal and even though oftentimes falls into trouble, making it through on her tenacity and connections (and even a bit of luck), I have to agree, she is definitely one of the most powerful elements in the Tri-Cities and beyond.

The ending was just so underwhelming that it's all I can think about for this review. I was disappointed by the choices she made at the end. And I was kind of irritated at Collins for making Katniss have kids without any indication that she actually wanted them. Lame.

The storyline was just too unbelievable from Nan getting involved with the X's again, to her accepting the horrible position at Jarndyce, to her husband's disappearance to Africa. And the plot dragged throughout a good portion of the book. I finished b/c I was hoping something would happen or get resolved, but ..... not so much.

I will say that the last 10% of the book was easier to get through, but only because of the realisation that everything is drawing to a conclusion. There is a number of things that annoyed me endlessly. The fact that the characters were so very much the same, that they all just felt something or knew that something bad will happen - did they all participated in a Shop experiment dealing with "Lot 6"? Even in near death experiences they feel and see the same thing, I mean really. Another thing was all the self-pitying going around. Could there really not be one semi-stable person in this story? In the end even the male characters are labelled crazy, or strong on their way to crazy town. There is one positive point I would like to make: In an accomplished director's hands; this will make a very good movie. One of those rare one's were the movie is better than the book.

I really don't have words, as someone in the LGBTQ community, to express how disgusted and betrayed this book made me feel. Is the writing beautiful? Sure. Is Einar's story one that should be told? Absolutely. But this is not that book. The Danish Girl, instead of talking about what it might have been like to undergo the first sex reassignment surgery ever performed, takes a highly fictionalized story about an intersex person who almost certainly has multiple personalities, possibly schizophrenia, and presents it/names it as a story about the transgender experience. I mean, everyone's experience is different, but nothing in this story even comes close to capturing what it's like to be trans*. This does unbelievable damage to the trans* community, a group already severely marginalized, by both confusing transgender and intersex as well as associating transpeople with mental illness. It plays into every harmful stereotype out there. I don't understand what could possibly have motivated Mr. Ebershoff to do such a thing, especially as a gay man himself. I really don't understand what would have compelled Penguin to publish something so inappropriate. And how on earth did this win awards? I hate that I wasted hours of my life supporting this nonsense.

From what I recalled from my first read through that never seemed to be the case to me but upon the second time I can agree with that conclusion. A big part is the interactions between Ren and Kelsey in which Kelsey doesn't find herself good enough for Ren and Ren is wholeheartedly convinced that Kelsey is the one despite having known her for such a short period of time. Just about all the characters are bland and are simple as can be; nothing makes them too unique. A person had mentioned how despite being much older than everyone else Ren and Kishan don't act much different from everyone else in the 21st century. Irene is still competent, but Kai gets kidnapped early on and is pretty much absent for much of the book. Vale is also mostly absent, and there is nothing new about Alberich and Baramont. In many way this was better written than the first one, more tightly plotted, and yay, for the female character to be saving the male ones instead of being relegated to the sidelines when push comes to shove. But the problem is that I can't warm up to Irene and that I honestly don't care what the fae are up to in Venice, and that war that's brewing. How can I not care? Fae! In Venice! And yet I don't. The Fae are all nasty pieces of work, and I've come to consider the book basically racist, against fae, against werewolves; they're all of them more or less despicable. Only the humans have some variety (Kai might also be the sole dragon exception).I noticed it in the first book already,but while I recognize actual racism fairly quickly these days, this is racism against fictional creatures,so what does it matter. Well, it matters to me-- I like my fictional races to be more complex. Once again the characters I care most about don't receive much screen time (the Horse), the library hardly plays a role at all, and this author has written a book with glimpses of interest that alas I couldn't care less about.

dnf @ 53% I tried with this book. I honestly did. While I wasn't enjoying the beginning, I was really hoping that if I got farther enough that the novel would get better. I mean, this book is so popular and so hyped I really wanted to enjoy it. For me, personally, I didn't though. (Warning: spoiler part may be ranty & if you like this book I am in no means trying to offend you. If you don't wanna hear it, then don't read it.) I have not read a lot of books which talk about important issues like suicide, so this book is definitely valuable in that case. But while reading it, it almost felt like Jay Asher was glamorizing suicide. I mean, seriously? Hannah Baker definitely went through a lot of problems with her life, and I am definitely not disregarding that or trying to belittle that. She felt like she had reason to commit suicide and I am NOT going against that fact. But what I found as a problem in this book that Hannah, literally BLAMES these people for her suicide. "I committed suicide because YOU spread a rumor about me and YOU pretended to be my friend". No. No. Stop. I understand that these people hurt you, and in the end, you felt helpless against them. But it's one thing to to tell them to change their behaviors and another thing to commit suicide to prove a point that THEY made you do this. While reading the novel, I kinda despised Hannah. All Hannah did was repeat the same things over and over again, continuously emphasizing that her suicide was this person's fault. Honestly. Read this quote, directly from the book: "And yet the whole time Courtney was using me, she thought she was polishing up her image in my eyes. Can you say... backfire?" What? What does this line mean? "Backfire"? Are you seriously saying that you killing yourself is revenge at her for using you? "I'm gonna kill myself. That'll show her." That is LITERALLY what the line translates to. To me, Hannah was just such an annoying character. Every single time she kept repeating 'you're to blame for MY death' she was being too dramatic. I know I am supposed to feel depressed for her, as this is a SUICIDE novel, but I just couldn't. Hannah was petty, overly emotional, and literally committed suicide to make a point to others and I just don't condone that. Maybe Jay Asher wanted to make this book relatable for suicidal people, but after reading reviews from ACTUAL people who had thoughts of suicide, they confirmed my suspicion that this book was just written based on the overall generalization of suicide. It's kind of like The Fault in Our Stars-- that book is based on the overgeneralization of cancer and a lot of ACTUAL people with cancer can't relate to it. Like I said before. This book glamorizes suicide and I really don't think it's okay. Another thing I disliked about this book was the writing. Besides the fact that I found the entire book to be problematic, the book just seemed to drag on forever. The book is written in a fashion thought to be of how teenagers talk, and I found it SO annoying. Lines were literally repeated over and over. All the characters kept repeating questions instead of any actual answers being provided. Clay: "Why did you do this Hannah..... Why didn't you do this" LITERALLY THE ENTIRE NOVEL (well at least up to the point I read to). Anyways, reading further would just kinda be like torturing myself, because I could not connect to Hannah in any way at all and I just could not read it. I found it boring. Simple as that. Anyways, despite finding this book to be extremely problematic, the only reason I decided to read it was so I could watch the Netflix series. I'm still gonna give the show a try, because maybe the problems that were emphasized in the book are not as prominent in the show. Again, I never EVER want anyone to misunderstand my dislike for this book as belittlement for anyone who actually has suicidal thoughts. Everyone SHOULD think before they act/speak. Although it seems as Jay Asher TRIED to send out that message, it came out completely malformed to me. It seemed more like a girl blaming a bunch of people for her choice, rather than teaching them to think before acting.

I read Cecilia Grant's A Lady Awakened not so much over Christmas as on Christmas, ignoring my partner's family, the Queen's speech, and even Toy Story 3 to finish reading it. Because it's honestly that good. I think it's unavoidable to make more of the things you read at the end of the year compared to the beginning, but A Lady Awakened simply has to stand has one of the most original, intriguing and tiny-mind-blowing books I read in 2013. The book opens with the heroine, Martha Russell, childless, newly widowed and about to return to her brother's home to live out the rest of her days as a quiet burden upon his family, a fate she has no choice but to resign herself to enduring. Her solicitor, however, encourages her to remain at her late husband's estate until it is absolutely certain that no heir has been conceived. Martha knows that she isn't pregnant, but she has her own commitments to Seaton Hall: specifically the servants and tenants, who rely on the family for their livelihood, and the building of a local school, to which she has given her support. She also learns that the man who stands to inherit is a dissolute character, who previously forced himself upon some of the women of the household. Realising that all these problems would be solved if she was pregnant, Martha strikes a deal with her new neighbour Theo Mirkwood, temporarily exiled from London for extravagance and general debauchery. They'll have sex every day for a month, and Martha will pay him, "regardless of issue" to quote the lady directly. What follows, I suppose, is a lovers-to-friends story, except they're not really lovers because while their daily sexual engagements are...something. What they're really aren't is lover-like, much to Theo's dismay. Martha is determined that the arrangement remain strictly business, and while the first half of the novel is this excrutiating awkward-off of unsexy sex it's also completely fascinating to watch two people with completely irreconcilable worldviews, motivations and value systems clash, fail to understand each other, and then gradually, and subtly, begin to move through acceptance, and understanding to friendship and love. And to situate the most visible expression of all this emotional and intellectual development in the bedroom is unbelievably bold, clever and impressive. Ms. Grant, I totally take off all my hats. Full review is over here at Heroes and Heartbreakers. Yay!

I don't know what to rate this (5 stars, or 1?) My Harry Potter lover side tells me 5 stars, but then again I was hurt (yes, actually hurt) by some of the decisions made regarding the plot of the novel. I'll start off with what I found most important about this play, which I think all Harry Potter lovers will agree with: There were a couple of scenes, words said, moments between characters - that had been missing from the series but which were included here. And that warmed my heart up, more so than the actual plot itself. So yeah, that's the number one thing I like about the book (and what makes me want to rate it 5 stars - and it's enough of a factor to push it that high up into my rating.) The next thing is my love for Scorpius, because I actually think his character was excellently developed and very realistic. And thirdly, I like how this book stands quite on its own, how it's a whole world apart from the other books in the series. (It's not even part of the series, it's a standalone - so that says it all right there). The reason why I like that is because if it had tried to be an imitation of the rest of the series... I probably would've despised it. But it feels so far off that I don't really associate it with the ACTUAL Harry Potter, you know what I mean? Anyhow, let's just get to the cold truth of this: Yes, some parts were fabulous, but many others weren't. Instead, they were awfully cringy - like badly written fan fiction. In a sense, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child IS fan-fiction, because JK Rowling didn't even write it. But still, I don't see that as an excuse, because I don't understand why she agreed to the plot of this play, why she agreed to take part in it - is this REALLY what she imagines to be the next part of Harry's story? Here are the two things that I think are a complete dishonour to the series, and which I can't get over why JK Rowling could possibly agree with: Firstly, Ron is portrayed as a weird, almost pointless background character throwing around stupid jokes. How could this possibly honour Ron? I just cannot agree with Ron turning out as a pointless, cast aside character. Secondly, Voldemort has a daughter. And with Bellatrix, on top of that. Excuse my language (and I don't often speak like this), but what the actual F**K????? I cannot possibly IMAGINE for one second that this is what JK Rowling believes to be true in her world of Harry Potter. Maybe I'm wrong, but I just don't believe this. It's so fake, and I think everyone wants to vomit at the thought of it. In the end, Harry Potter "8" had SO many expectations from fans everywhere, myself included - and it's important to remember that this book isn't another 7 book series, written in the same way and with the same feeling. Our three main characters have grown up, so how could reading this still feel like it's the same, like its the Harry Potter series we know? It can't. I was very scared about reading this book, because I knew it wouldn't feel right, it wouldn't be right to have a next Harry Potter - yet I am still glad for the parts of it which warmed my heart and added what was missing from the 7-book series (like I mentioned above). But here they are, in more detail: how Petunia kept Harry's blanket - I feel it's something she actually would have done - , being able to relive parts of the Triwizard tournament again - I particularly liked the description of Hermione clapping loudly for Harry, and learning that the Yule Ball jealousy was what truly defined Ron and Hermione's relationship. I was also very, very much warmed by the scene where Snape learns Harry had named one of his children after him. So yes, there are moments I loved in this. But it's also true that I hated the larger concepts. I won't rate this book, as it's a 5 star and a 1 star all at the same time - and it's not like I can simply find the average score. For me, Harry Potter will always remain the 7 books JK Rowling wrote. Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is something separate.

Confession: When I was a teenager I sold movie tickets from a glass booth like the one on the cover, part of an old art-deco theater with red velvet seats built in the 30s. I loved that job. And in my off time, I volunteered with the homeless. So when I read the synopsis for this book I got a WEE bit excited! This IS an amazing story, but unfortunately the bizarre formatting makes it anything but readable. The story is told as the memories and diary entries of a dozen people, but instead of devoting on chapter to each, the author changes POV several times in every scene. So each page, at times, will have three or four different people speaking. Combined with the sheer number of narrators, and the fact that each one is coming from a different time, the overall effect is nothing but a confused, chaotic cacophony. For me, at least, it made the entire book unreadable. I have trouble believing that not one editor spoke up and said how hard this makes the story to follow. So I'm disappointed, because this story is just right up my alley. Too bad it was hidden in the chaos.

I enjoyed this more than I thought I would. I put this off for a long time because I didn't like Xhex or John Matthew very much before reading this. Somewhere along the way I fell in love with them as a couple. They talked and helped each other through the tough times. John and Xhex just got each other. I liked it. I'm glad I finally picked the series up again. It's so bad but it's so good. It's my favorite guilty pleasure series (even though it's so embarrassing to read this in public because the sexy times are really detailed). This definitely took time to get absorbed in the Black Dagger Brotherhood world again. I just wasn't into it for the first twenty or so percent. Somewhere after that I got completely immersed, like I always do with these books. The series is so fun and angsty. There was not one Brother related page that I was bored. I didn't like Lash's point of view but I've never liked the lessers points of view. They're just disturbing and boring. I prefer all the other perspectives. Speaking of the other perspectives, my favorites were the Blay and Qhuinn parts. I am SO tempted to just skip the next two books and dive straight into Lover At Last (Blay and Qhuinn's book). I'm not going to but I really want to. Their parts were so angsty and full of romantic tension. I like the way their relationship is going. I don't know how to explain it but their relationship is just so perfect. I mean, it's not really a relationship now but I love the angst so far. It's done really well in my opinion. In fact, the relationships in this book and in Rehvenge's book were done very well. The characters are the main reason why I stick around in the series. They make the book in my opinion. The way that the Brothers interact with each other makes me feel so happy. They would do anything for each other which is amazing. Plus, it doesn't hurt that all of them are hilarious in their own way. The banter is so funny! I wish there was more of that. John and Xhex surprised me, as I said earlier. I didn't expect much from their relationship but damn did it grow on me. The way that they just clicked and knew what the other needed was perfect. John would have done anything for Xhex, even if it meant that he had to leave her. I wasn't a fan of how the Brothers treated Xhex. They treated her like she was a fragile woman, like their wives. But she's not. She is so tough and kick butt. They treat women like their just objects. I get that it's a Brother thing but I'm not a fan. Anyway, the development of the relationship was on point. Little by little they learned to trust each other which made me like their relationship more. I like developments in relationships. This was a great example! I am a big fan of them now! Overall, I really enjoyed this installment. It's not my favorite but it isn't awful either. I liked that this wasn't just a filler book, like Phury's and Butch's books. There was a nice balance to John and Xhex's story, other character's drama, and the overall lesser plot. This series is just a guilty pleasure read for me so it's not like I'm looking for an amazing story. I don't know what else to say other than I really enjoyed this. I can't say I'm excited to read the next book about Payne. We don't know much about her at this point so I'm not sure what to think of her. Oh my gosh, maybe it was the fact that I was listening to Ready Player One on audiobook and the narrator was actually talking in my ear, but the main character really, really gets on my nerves. Which is really disappointing, because this is a book I've been wanting to read for a really, really long time. A not-so-distant future where human civilization has used up most of it's resources and has left the earth ravished, where life basically sucks for everyone and the only highlight is the fact that the Oasis, a free-to-play virtual reality game, exists. Of course, with the real world being so terrible (as the narrator clearly states), the Oasis becomes an escape from real life. To call it wildly popular would be a gross understatement. Everyone is on Oasis, you can even go to school with the virtual reality system. The author spends time creating the world, which is refreshing in the sense that... it's kind of plausible for it to exist. Cline talks about the energy crisis and global poverty and a whole mess of other problems that don't seem like the fantastically futuristic elements of science fiction. Instead, they feel real, and right around the corner. So, kudos for world-building. The heart of the plot is the fact that the eccentric billionaire who built the Oasis has died, and has bequeathed all of his wealth and shares in his software/video game company to whoever finds the Easter Egg he has hidden within the game. The main character is an orphan being raised by his aunt, incredibly poor and unloved. The Oasis becomes his escape, something he needs to survive. He plunges into the hunt, seeing it as his only ticket out of his desolate life. The setup is great. The execution is where things start to get iffy. See, the main character is a monologuer in the extreme sense. There's a ton of narration, and after a while it gets to be excessive. The second problem is--I'm just gonna say it--the Oasis developer is obsessed with 80's culture. What does that mean? Well, it means that instead of being a look into the desolate future with all that it doesn't have to offer, we take a trip down memory lane via the main character's pages and pages of rambling about how he knows soooo many different old video games and comic books and whatever else. He thinks he's superior to everyone, and with his vast knowledge, he may not be wrong, but that doesn't mean that it's fun to read. And also, at one point he does this whole build up to how he wished he had been "told the truth sooner" instead of being lied to by adults, but he won't tell you what the "truth" he's referring to is. He goes on for pages. I thought it was going to be that he thought the Oasis was real, and that he's crushed when he realized he can't actually go there. Because, seriously, with augmented reality, what three year old is going to figure out that this stuff that looks like it's right there is fake, all a created world. Wouldn't that make him even angrier at the current state of things, knowing that the world he's been born into is so terrible, and an escape is at his fingertips and yet it's not even real, it's just simulated? What a complex relationship he would form with the game, loving it to the point of resentment, the wish that it were real becoming a painful twist in his gut. But nope, the truth is that God isn't real, and anyone who believes in religion is a big ol' idiot who's lying to themselves. And obviously since he figured it out, he's sooo much smarter than everyone who still deludes themselves. Which, I mean I get why some people don't like religion and don't understand why people believe in God. But whenever someone is this much of a jerk about it, it kinda sets alarm bells off in my head that, wait a minute, they just might be a jerk in general. Which, surprise, he was. Also he may think people who believe in God are idiots, but he came off pretty hypocritical since he basically admits that his own form of religion was the hunt for Halliday's easter egg. [God/religion] was a pleasant fantasy that gave her hope and kept her going. Which was exactly what the hunt was for me. In conclusion, since I wasn't alive in the 80's this book felt like less of a nostalgic trip down memory lane seamlessly blending the old and new, and more like a chauvinistic asshole talking down his nose at me. So yeah, I won't be continuing this.

Series Review (for books 0.5 - 5): I've been hearing great things about the Mythos Academy series for so long, that I finally had to take some time and read these books. I can see why people enjoy these books because they're very reminiscent of Vampire Academy, the Covenent books, Harry Potter, and Percy Jackson. There's mythology, a boarding school setting, a strong heroine, and different powers. What's not to love? Interestingly enough, Gwen got on my nerves quite a bit in the first couple books, but I liked her enough that I was still able to get into the books. Even though she drove me crazy, I kind of liked that she wasn't all sunshine and rainbows. Her situation sucks, and her defense mechanism is to be snarky. Gwen is definitely very judgmental at first about the school and its students. She tends to make a lot of mistakes by being rash and jumping into things. What Gwen also is, is very lonely because of her gift, and therefore very loyal to the people she does have in her life. Gwen definitely grows as a character as the series continues and she becomes more willing to learn from others. As you would expect in a mythology based urban fantasy type series the central theme is a fight against evil, Loki in this case. The boarding school that Gwen attends is full of warriors who have different abilities. Gwen is a chosen one, a champion for Nike, who has to figure out how her ability will help her in the fight against Loki. The books feature lots of action, with some high stakes coming up occasionally. I definitely enjoyed reading the Mythos Academy books. I feel like the series keeps getting better, because while I liked the first couple of books, I didn't love them. But the next couple? A lot more exciting.

Anyone who is interested in young adult literature needs to read this book. Speak is one of those novels that changed everything. It inspired a lot of copycat books and is required reading in many middle and high schools. Speak is about Melinda, a freshman in high school. Her old middle school friends will not speak to her because she called the police about their party the year before. As the book progresses, the reader learns that something very bad happened to Melinda at that party. I love the fragmented way that this story is told. The pacing is a little slow, but Melinda's voice more than makes up for the slowness. Melinda is funny and authentic. Many teenagers (including me as a teenager) have the same attitude that she does toward high school. She hates it and doesn't take it too seriously. The humor is wonderful and surprising. I love this book. I'd recommend it to everybody, especially if you are interested in quality young adult literature.

1.5 stars. I'm sorry, but this is just torture porn masquerading as symbolic, deep writing. Bick uses the small town environment to create a horrible, terrifying atmosphere. Well, I made it through this novel, I think I deserve a prize. It very much reads like a YA novel, but the heroine is 24 - even though she acts like a dim 17 year old (I have a 17 year old, I know how they act :P ). There are many, many flaws with the premise of the book, with the spelling and grammar... makes you wonder if anyone still employs editors. Most amusing mistake by far, was when she ran her fingers 'threw' her hair. I would be so annoyed if someone threw MY hair! The one thing I will say in it's favour is, at least there were more clues as to who the bad guy was than there was in the first Sookie Stackhouse novel. By clues, I mean it was glaringly obvious. It starts with our heroine, who grew up in a series of foster homes, and is now a is a poor, friendless orphan, living in a crummy bedsit in London, walking home from work and realising she is being followed. Stupidly she heads AWAY from busy, brightly lit streets and is surprised when she s caught. But, surprise! Her magic powers kick in and she zaps herself across the street, and heads home. She takes great pains to be quiet when she gets home. She doesn't put on the lights, tiptoes around the flat, and then puts on the TV! Facepalm. Lo, the Brotherhood (for this is indubitably whom her attackers are) find her and attempt to burn her out of her flat. Surprise! She is rescued by a witch who can zap herself about, intentionally! They escape and fly to America. Stella is surprised to be given an American passport, which, she is assured is hers and all legal and above board, even though she didn't apply for it, or sign it or anything. Oh, but her new friend knows her father was American. More than our heroine knew! She arrives in America, is welcomed by a wealthy American family, who are old family friends. Gee wonder where they've been her whole, sad and sorry life? Oh, but look, here is her family lawyer! What's that? Her parents were rich? They have left her money and property? Where the hell was this lawyer all these years? Why has he not done his job before now? He's the executor of the will! His job was to find her and make sure she was set up with her inheritance, not left to rot in the British care system! But, she doesn't mind, no big deal. This family has a son, he kisses her. The super magically protected house is magically attacked! Nobody is suspicious. They pack Stella and the son off to a 'safe house'. Where she meets hot but moody Evan, her new teacher. Marc gets jealous. Marc goes off. Stella sleeps with Evan, learns to control her powers and becomes BFF's with the bubbly ex-girlfriend of Marc. Stella's room gets riffled, oh look, Marc's back. Nobody is suspicious. Marc's daddy turns up, finally figures out all that has been going on, and gets killed just before he tells her. Rocks fall, everybody dies. Well, not EVERYONE, the survivors bugger off and leave Stella, who decides in her infinite wisdom, to bugger off too. She takes immense pains to cover her tracks, so she is not followed - and goes straight to the house her parents left her! You may now proceed to question my sanity, for in lew of anything else to read I am going to go read the sequel. It might explain where the hell certain people have buggered off to. Maybe. To be fair, the budding romance was nicely, written. Mostly.

Having heard so many amazing things about Megan Whalen Turner's The Queen's Thief series, I finally snatched up the THE THIEF. This fantasy world is rich and evocative-an almost Greek-like setting, but with a unique series of gods/goddesses and their own histories-and the character development is top notch. None of the characters we start out with as a reader are left unchanged by the end. I've heard the second and third installments in this series are where the story really shines, so after a thoroughly enjoyable tale in THE THIEF, I'm pumped to pick up THE QUEEN OF ATTOLIA. Atlanta Burns is a kind of YA contemporary that is dark -- so dark that the world in which the titular character exists is almost a caricature of itself. I've seen the book described as noir, which is something I usually associate with detectives in oversized coats, but that works here in the sense that Atlanta's world is bleak. Almost everyone is corrupt, incompetent, or outright evil. The handful of characters that aren't evil are damaged as a result of being the victims of those who are. These include Atlanta (mostly) and the two boys she befriends at school, Shane and Chris. It's a tough read. One I enjoyed, but at the same time -- oof. Firstly, if you are triggered by any of the following, this isn't the book for you: rape, child abuse, torture, suicide, animal harm, homophobia and violent racism. Also, if swearing and drug use bother you, again, maybe don't go here. (I told you it was dark.) Atlanta is the survivor of childhood sexual abuse -- a situation she extricated herself from by buying herself a secondhand gun and shooting the perpetrator. She was then sent away to therapy for either six months or a year (my copy of the book says both -- oops). The story opens up two weeks after she comes home to a mother that seems to be terrified of her and former best friends who don't even want to make eye contact. Atlanta suffers PTSD and panic attacks, but her particular coping mechanism whenever she's bullied, or sees anyone else being bullied, is to confront the bully with extreme prejudice, cans of mace and her trusty shotgun -- generally without thinking anything through in advance. She's quite fragile beneath the bluster, and afterwards she suffers, but in a crisis she is as hard as nails. Maybe this reaction is a result of the same personality trait that made her buy the gun in the first place, or maybe it's a result of therapy gone awry. It's unclear. Of course, given the world Atlanta lives in, there's no shortage of opportunities for her to leap in and make things worse. Which, given her fire and lack of planning, she generally does. In many ways, Atlanta Burns was a satisfying read. As a reader, nothing frustrates me more than when I see a character that is sufficiently evil get away with their evilness. And I've learned I'm kinda sorta bloodthirsty (as a reader, honest! ), in that I love to see the bad guy get comeuppance at the hands of the good guy. Atlanta's lack of impulse control and readiness to resort to violence meant I saw all sorts of bad guys get hurt. It was very satisfying! Where it got a little unrealistic was when the bad guys didn't seem to strike back as hard as I thought they would or should given their other behaviour. Atlanta does quite a few things to goad people without actually killing them, and their reactions don't seem to match up to their apparent level of evilness. The other thing that bothered me was that I kept trying to apply my understanding of the real world to the situation, and Atlanta's world clearly wasn't like mine. In the world of this story, the police can't be trusted and the only adult in her life is her useless, timid mother. The teachers are largely non-entities. I realise that Atlanta going all vigilante defender of the weak does require a corrupt setting (in the same way that Batman needs his Gotham City) but at times I did raise an eyebrow at her thinking she had no other alternative but violence. At least, I sincerely hope that there aren't really places like the town where Atlanta lives in the world. Atlanta Burns is a hard read, but I loved Atlanta as a character. I'm sure I'll go back for the next book, but I couldn't read the sequel back-to-back. I need something a bit lighter to cleanse my psyche first!

Okay, so this isn't When You Reach Me. This is a smaller story on every level, including actual size, and it's firmly in the realistic fiction camp, with no twist of sci-fi. Nevertheless, it still resonates with Rebecca Stead's gift to reach inside the minds and hearts of kids in transition, and illuminate the struggles of little things. The characters in this story felt like real people, with real worries and concerns and reactions to things. I loved how they were middle schoolers who had some "typical" middle school concerns like being bullied or unpopular, and also still did things that a lot of writers would relegate to younger kids--like playing games of imagination or sending messages on scrabble tiles back and forth with a parent. It felt exactly like the real 6th and 7th graders I spend time with every day, and not the the fictional kind I've read so much about. I love the way Rebecca Stead depicts close-knit, but unique families, and the way she captures the intricacies of friendship. The twists in this book will probably take a lot of younger readers by surprise, but there are a lot of clues that older readers will pick up on. The genius of this book, I think, is that one of the twists is designed to be highly guessable....which distracts the reader from noticing the other one. Personally, I was distracted. Not enough to be actually surprised by the other, but enough that I hadn't formed it as a conscious "prediction." The story and writing are strong enough that neither twist actually has to be a "twist" for the book to be completely enjoyable.

American Sniper is a tough book to review. On a technical level, it's frankly mediocre. Many chapters are simply loosely related anecdotes with no story arc. Kyle (and his writing partner) write in a simple conversational style resulting in something closer to a blog post than a novel. For me personally, while I'm interested in soldiers' experiences serving America and fighting for all of us, I'm not into "war stories", particularly play by play and/or detailed descriptions of weapons and their functions. So the deployment sections were pretty boring for me. But Kyle's story was compelling nonetheless. His focus is almost entirely on the fighting, but he also pays some attention to the effect on fellow soldiers, his wife and family, and himself. He is uncomfortably excited about killing for a nom-hunting/non-military person like me. I simply know no one like him. I do know hunters and grew up in a rural area, but I'm basically a city girl (honestly, even more removed - suburban girl). So being all "fuck yeah, let's kill!" Is way outside my comfort zone. But that's the kind of person who does the job he had to do. And what made the book a good read for me is that the reader gets to see glimpses of his humanity and struggles. We also get to see all the empathetic aspects of his personality. As a soldier, a tremendously successful soldier in fact, he doesn't leave out the compassionate side of him. No, there's no compassion for his enemy. But for his fellow soldiers? Unlimited. It's true that Kyle appears to have been a bit of an exaggerater in print and certainly after the publishing of the book based on things I read about him on the Internet in the wake of the film getting an Oscar nod and while I was reading this book. I'm not going to judge him too harshly (sorry Jesse Ventura, not sure what happened there but that's your battle). I can't imagine many people could do what he did and see what he saw and not have some flaws. My edition has a few updates at the end from his wife and the film's screenwriter, which really rounded out the novel.

I figured I would like this book - after all, I adored Anna and the French Kiss. I didn't figure that I would love it as much as I did. Lola is a seventeen-year old who doesn't believe in fashion, she believes in costumes. "Oh no," I thought to myself. "Is this going to be her token quirk, like Anna's obsession with movies? Only this is literally more in your face." Fear not, Lola's love of costumes, while a big part of her, wasn't over the top, and was actually rather endearing. Lola herself was rather endearing! Sure, the girl had flaws, but I like my characters with flaws; it makes them more realistic. She seemed utterly believale as a seventeen-year old girl. Yes, this does mean that she had her moments of fantasizing, of whining, of - gasp! - behaving like a teenager. But I could relate to her, even beyond her love for Pushing Daisies, which deserves every shout-out in the world. Now onto the boys. In this sort of novel, a lot rests on the desirability of the boys, and these ones had that in spades. Mainly the titular boy next door, Cricket Bell. I don't think it's a spoiler to say that Cricket is infinitely more desirable than Lola's boyfriend, Max. I mean, this isn't Lola and the Boy Next Door Who Obstructs Her Path to True Love With a Rock God. It's pretty easy to see why Lola likes said Rock God too, at least initially. He's attractive, he's fun, he's nice, he does everything he can to spend time with her (weekly brunch with overprotective dads? Check! ), and sure, he's older, but he expresses his concern about this as soon as he finds out how much older than Lola he is. So yes, I understand what Lola sees in Max, but then, Max is no Cricket. Sweet, eccentric, charming, slightly awkward Cricket. And that's the real problem when it comes to comparing Max and Cricket because Cricket? Is pretty swoon-worthy. Lola and Cricket are easily my favourite characters in this book, which is how it should be, but I don't want to go without mentioning the supporting cast, especially Lola's family. I loved her relationship with her dads (yes, dads), who are strict but still seemed lovely. It was refreshing to see a perfectly functional relationship between the main character and her parents, though that's not to say the family was without drama. I actually loved having a secondary plot of the family drama, it added a more well-rounded sense to the characters. Cricket, too, had his own family drama, stemming from the book's resident bitchy character, Cricket's twin sister Calliope. I think Calliope (and Max, to an extent) are as big of villains as you get in this book, and I understood her motivations and reasoning, she was well-rounded and even sympathetic. Oh, and I can't mention the supporting cast without mentioning Anna and St. Clair from Anna and the French Kiss. Were their appearances slightly gratuitous? Sure, but that's not to say I didn't love seeing them again! The backstory between Lola and Cricket is wonderful and shows the deep-rooted chemistry between Lola and Cricket. And man, do they ever have chemistry! That's where Stephanie Perkins really shines in the wake of all this YA romance. She knows how to write chemistry between her characters. Sure, the story is slightly formulaic and predictable, but it's also wonderfully enjoyable. While Lola and the Boy Next Door may not be life-changing, it's a lot of fun to read and has some absolutely great characters. As far as chick-lit goes - hell, as far as YA lit goes! - this is one of my favourites.

EVERNEATH is a young adult fiction based on Greek Mythology, about the life of seventeen year old Nikki Beckett. Last spring she disappeared, leaving behind a father, brother and Jack the quarterback best friend/'love of her life'. After a hundred years in the 'everneath' glued to the body of a very hot eternal boy called Cole (who drains her of her life force), she returns to her home where only months have passed. She is given six months to say goodbye before she will be once again sucked into the underworld, but this time a much darker pit of hell awaits her. So...I didn't hate this book and I didn't love it. I read it in one sitting and skipped very little of it, which means it wasn't totally terrible. But there where too many incongruities with the character choices and world building that left me unconvinced. The things I loved where: Jack and his relationship with Nikki. Their love was convincing and touching, it was built up over a long time and based on friendship, rather than the usual angsty instalove. The things that left me feeling rankled: First of all I actually find the whole concept unconvincing. The idea that there is this whole underworld where immortals take people and suck of their souls for a hundred years to then live for another hundred years is a bit odd. I think with these bizzarro concepts you can go as crazy as you like so long as I could see them conceivably happening...like in the Matrix when the computers take over and use us as an energy source, well the reason it was so popular was because it was conceivable. Just lightly using some old Greek Myths was not enough for me. Cole, well he was a bad boy biker/rocker with no feelings...but he is supposed to be in love with Nikki. I was totally unconvinced. I felt like his personality was not fluid or developed and he didn't act like an immortal. NIKKI BECKETT HAD NO PERSONALITY. Well she was just a very average teenager riddled with self doubt and her main trait seemed to be never ending selflessness! Well I know that selflessness is good, but only up to a certain point...eventually the reader is unable to relate. Because everyone has a desire to live life a little and feel like they deserve some happiness! But no, not our Nikki, she forsakes all her own happiness and I find this BORING. The story line about the 'Daughters of Persephone' along with the Meredith story and the other side characters like their teacher and the professor all seemed like they where just added to beef out the story and make it a bit more than just a love story. In reality the only good part of this book is the love story between the quarter back and his best friend Nikki. The memories of when he first saw her, Nikki's shyness and their eventual relationship was sweet in a very very conventional sort of way.

I was lucky enough to receive an advanced reader's copy of this book through Netgalley. I'm really pleased with my decision to see this edgy, quirky YA novel through to completion. It was enjoyable throughout, but it wasn't until the end of the novel that I realized that I was really emotionally invested in these teens' drama that was cleverly hidden a midst a backdrop of comedy and quips. At BHS, the students in Homeroom 10B are close. Really close. There are NO secrets between them; in fact, there can't be. After receiving a contaminated batch of flu shots, these twenty-two teenagers developed the ability to read minds - for better or worse. While they quickly realize the advantages of their situation, unwanted knowledge bombards the telepathic teens, leaving them questioning if they were better off before they developed this accidental talent. By the end of the tale, they'll be questioning whether it is a blessing or a curse to know exactly what is on everyone's minds. It was really fun. Flat-out fun times - even for an ancient thirty year old like me. I had worried that I may be too old to enjoy YA stories set in high schools, but, thankfully, this book was just edgy and mature enough for me to enjoy it. If anything, I might complain that it was just a little too mature for the intended audience - what with all the sex talk and four-letter words. The author didn't spare any detail when it came to revealing what can be on the minds of adults and teenagers. And, as an adult reader, I was okay with that. Would I want my middle-school aged daughter reading about sexy lingerie and condoms? No. (Side note: perhaps I'm only thinking this because I'm in mom-mode constantly now, and the thought of my three-month old daughter being exposed to anything racy or unclean makes me want to have a panic attack. It wasn't really that explicit. I was just surprised by how nonchalant and hip sex could seem in a YA novel. Aside from that, I totally loved all the relationship drama - with Connor and Makenzie, with Tess and Teddy, with Olivia and Lazar. In some ways, their twists and turns were a bit predictable, but it felt cute and comfortable in this novel. Overall, it was a super fun flashback into the drama and worry of balancing family, friends and schoolwork as an emotionally turbulent teen. The science-fiction/fantasy edge really reanimated and re-energized what could have been just another all too familiar story about high school heartache. I would have no reservations recommending this to my girlfriends looking for a fun, easy read.

It features her usual impeccable writing, unputdownable pace and interesting characters but lacks her trademark twists and inventive plotting. I kept expecting the plot to have an astounding turnaround but it never happened. The protagonist guesses the identity of her antagonist early on and is proved correct. Some of the secondary mysteries are also disappointing - the school Principal's denial that George ever existed is initially intriguing but then she later admits that she lied and he did exist. This is preposterously unprofessional, unconvincing in the context of the story and disappointing writing from an author who is usually a master of the genre. The elaborate story of Perrine is also too interesting to be dismissed as mere fabrication. Ultimately a disappointment.

This book did to what only a few books have ever done to me. It made me cry. It kept me up all night reading and then it left me in tears. That doesn't mean that the ending isn't hopeful, it just means that the emotions contained on the page were so strong that long after the book was closed they continued affecting me. This is probably the greatest character arc ever to be written. Colfer stared with this selfish evil little boy and over the course of eight novels turns him into a man capable of the most selfless act. And it works it is all totally believable because in that first book he gives us that little nugget of goodness. As far as endings go it was perfect. I really could have done without the tears but still it ultimate way to illustrate Artemis's journey from Villain to hero. Of course there is always room for more and if it is ever written I will certainly be ready to read it.

I read to the last page thinking it's bound to get better, come on I know this author and I know this story will pay off, but no. I was wrong there is no ultimate love tingle and of course they should be together despite all the reasons they shouldn't because TRUE LOVE. Well true love never happened here and once we get a hint of where these characters are going, it ends. I mean just a glimpse and if you read too fast you will miss it and then THE END no epilogue. I fought through to the end, but must conclude that this was not a book for me. I've seen a lot of positive reviews, so definitely possible that I am in the minority on this one. 1) I went in expecting dystopian -- does that cover say "Divergent-ish" or what? It's not dystopian, but a fantasy. To be fair, I'm not the most enthusiastic fantasy reader. 2) This was the kind of fantasy with too many fight scenes. My mind wanders. 3) Meira, the main character, was someone I had a hard time connecting with. She spends most of the book trying desperately to win other people's acceptance and respect, but not in a way that I made sense to me. She kept rushing foolishly into danger, fighting, and then crushing on two different guys. See #2 and #4. 4) Love triangle-y, and not the kind of triangle that I like. There's this guy that Meira clearly has a thing for -- a sort of long-term, partly repressed crush. Then, in a strange turn of events, she has to spend a lot of time with this other guy. Then, she suddenly seems to like him just as much, if not more, than guy #1. I'm not always opposed to love triangles, or even to fickle adolescent mind-changing, but I wasn't feeling any love in this love triangle. 5) The story world has different kingdoms, some named after the four seasons, and some that had to do with rhythms (??) and despite the book repeating this a lot, I just didn't get it. Plus, all the talk of "Spring conquers Summer, and then Winter fell and Autumn crumbled" just started to sound like a Who's On First?routine. I read and re-read and was still going: Huh? Who did what to whom? Normally, if I were struggling this much with a book, I would set it aside, but I kept reading because I could see a reveal coming and wanted to know if I was right. I was! Meira is an orphan, and she keeps having dreams about these two women and their two babies and it was obvious to me -- or probably anyone who has watched any TV soap operas -- there was a BABY SWITCH. I think this reveal might have had interesting potential if it had happened earlier in the story. It seemed COMPLETELY unrealistic that this crucial information was kept secret for so long. It seemed like the characters were being kept in the dark just to keep the reader in the dark, and that bothered me. I'm sad that I didn't feel this one. But many of my blogger friends have adored it. Try the first few chapters and see where you come out... Thanks to the publisher for providing me an eARC to read and review.

A Stolen Life -- a book you just can't rate! The writing is sloppy, the grammar is horrendous and there are typos galore. But the rules of a good novel don't apply here - what matters is the content. And by golly does Jaycee have a ton to write about and a ton to share. For anyone who followed the Jaycee Dugard recovery with interest, this book provides a good and personal look at what Jaycee went through during her abduction, life with Garrido, and rescue/recovery. The main question I have is personal, but relevant to the story: she doesn't talk about rape after the birth of her two daughters, so I'm not sure if she was raped after her kids were born or if that was the end of the sexual abuse. I wish that had been included in the book, but with so much pain so fresh in her memory, it's hard to say, "Jesus, Jaycee - I wanna hear MORE from you!" Because she has already offered the world so much by writing about her life and experience. Thank you, Jaycee, for writing this book.

"I suppose at one time in my life I might have had any number of stories, but now there is no other. This is the only story I will ever be able to tell." Wow. I want to say so many things about this book but I can't find the right words. This was so beautifully written, both fascinating and completely unsettling from beginning to end. I love everything that relates to Greek, Roman history or mythology so I had a feeling I would love this book but I wasn't expecting it to be so serious, uncomfortable and yet enthralling. This is literally the story of a murder club, composed of young, obnoxious, haughty, addicted young people obsessed with ancient Greek and mythology and aesthetics. I had so many paradoxical feelings about the characters. I both hated them and felt really bad for them. They were fascinating. They represented perversity, arrogance and coldness at its peak. I always find that something, the subjectivity of the narrative probably, makes me loyal to the narrator of the story and his friends no matter what. I wanted both to see them escape and for someone to catch on what they had done and throw them in prison. This was very unsettling. More than anything I find particularly interesting that these characters show their true natures after Bunny's death and all seem to become the opposite of what they seemed at first. The story dragged a bit at some point but it definitely wasn't enough to make me dislike this book. I had heard some people found the book problematic because of slurs on race and sexuality but I feel like it was part of the context and the point of the story. These characters are awful and highly problematic. They are not an example to follow. I can't and I don't want to say more because this story needs to keep as much mystery as it can to the people that want to read it, but READ IT GUYS.

2.5 Stars Antonio stayed the full day at the hospital? I got a great hospital scene but not a single point for the scavenger hunt to be had. Now he's confident about being attractive and he's flirting very heavily. When the guy jerks back after a quick touch, I would assume the guy was saying no but Antonio assumed the guy was definitely interested. He doesn't even consider the guy might already be seeing someone. (A picture he saw doesn't mean a whole lot). He's making a fool of himself when he really needs this guy's help. Antonio's an ass. I don't like him at all. He never even called his live in housekeeper. It has nothing to do with his tricking either. I don't care about his promescuity. I care about how he treats people. Why in these books does everyone have only one grandmother and don't even mention another? Where does Massimo sleep when he stays over if the apartment is so big but here's only one bed? March is only spring the last third. All the housekeepers are women and all the music people are gay men. The only other women are family members. It's so sexist. Once again, a female author. I just don't get it. She was in music herself! Oh, here's a musical female, but of course she's a music teacher which, while honorable and noble, in the context of this book she's just a peon not a world famous musician like all the men. No plot. Falling in love and moving forward in a relationship isn't a plot. I'm so bored. I may need to take a break from this book. I'm only a little over halfway through. From the blurb, I thought there would be some exciting secret Cary had. For some bizarre reason, I had gotten the idea that he was passing off music he had written as his own. Now I realize that was a different book, although the title fits the other book perfectly. Cary did a good job parenting. But I hate that later when Massi was bragging about him he said that he wasn't really his dad. Cary said this frequently. Good that he talked about his angst with Antonio right away. If anyone makes me choose between them and someone else (and this has happened before) I choose the person who's not making me choose. That person has no right to control my life like that or even try to, and the problem is theirs not mine. (Unless it's my kid and then I always choose my kid, but then again, a kid isn't going to be in the position of giving me an ultimatum.) Wow I actually have watery eyes! I guess it was Antonio showing emotion. They cry an awful lot so it was weird when Cary said to himself he doesn't cry. About one of the very few issues in the book involving the mother: Taking a young son from his very good and doting father or mother is not okay. If the father wasn't so great, and hurt the kid sometimes emotionally, then fine. If the child was a teen then maybe. But you make sacrifices for children. If you're miserable in a marriage, get a divorce, because if the parents are miserable, so is the child and the child needs to see his or her parents happy and have loving relationships modeled for him or her. But don't move to another country for a job even if it's a dream job. You made a choice to have a child and committed to what's best for them. Leaving his father like that is even worse than divorce on a kid because there isn't even another parent to see on weekends and in this situation, it's not necessary. You can be happy even if you're not happiest. You can discuss with the father about possibly moving with you but don't expect him to. I hate selfish parents. I gave up my fiance for my foster daughter because she was mine and I knew it was permanent (it was). And now they're thinking of having another child with her when that spoiler hasn't been resolved? Predictable. Boring. Plotless 2.5 stars

It's a setting that just full of possibilities: the Greek Gods of Olympus are still around and most of the principles are living in a rundown house in modern London. With characters like Apollo and Athena and Hermes, there's no end to complications and plot twists, right? Phillips does come up with jobs suitable of her cast - Aphrodite as a phone sex operator just makes perfect sense. And if Apollo and Aphrodite live in the same house, they probably would end up having sex with each other, considering their particular strengths, and despite being half siblings. Altogether, wouldn't we expect the whole clan to be just as dysfunctional in this age as the one they originated in? But that's the problem with this book - the characters do act all too often just as you'd expect. They have almost no arc. I guess that's the problem with characters so deitic - they have no where to go but down, and if that's not your ending, you really don't have much of a story. There are two mortals that get mixed up with this crazy family, and they do have a journey, but you'd think with people like Zeus and Hades getting involved, the whole thing would be more.....epic?
I can't believe I even finished this.

When Graeme Montgomery receives word from the king that he is to marry the daughter of the clan that murdered his father, he is furious. How could the king ask this of him? Especially as the girl is rumored to be daft and unable to have a normal marriage. With the prospect of passing on his heritage through his own blood gone, he still reluctantly accepts his duty as to refuse would be treason and would end up in his death. Graeme gathers his two brothers and his men and heads off to his rival Armstrongs clan, prepared for the worst and willing to accept his duty. When he lays eyes on the lovely Eveline he is blown away by her beauty and also her easy acceptance of him. He makes a vow to himself that he will protect her at all costs but is stunned when his clam refuses to accept her and treats her badly. How can he help his clam understand that they can not punish the daughter for the sins of the father when in his own mind he still wants to destroy the Armstongs? Eveline Armstrong is very secure and protected in her clan, especially after a terrible fall from a horse made her lose her hearing, though no one is aware of this. Circumstances prevented her from speaking as well and to protect herself, she let the charade of her being daft keep going. When she sees Graeme for the first time she actually feels his voice vibrations and she is instantly taken with him and knows he will protect her. But upon arriving at his home and experiencing the hatred and ridicule towards her, she is distraught and wants to leave even though her feelings for Graeme have deepened. The time comes when she must face her past and in the process, she just may lose more than her heart to the rival laird. Sigh....such a romantic, sexy, heart warming, tear inducing story!! I loved it! Eveline was so strong and courageous and faced her demons with a spunk I wish I had. She taught herself to read lips, even though she can not read or write, and was able to hide the fact she could not hear for three years. I loved watching her and Graeme interact, with her trying to explain herself without talking. I admire her courage and what it took to admit the truth about her voice and I admired her even more when an accident occurs and she tells the truth as to what she saw. And Graeme, swoon. I really enjoyed the fact that he was not a womanizer, that he was going to stay true to his wife even if the marriage was not going to be everything he hoped for. Thankfully, our couple is able to express their passion for each other and Graeme's tenderness with Eveline was lovely. We get to meet the extended families of both, each with two brothers and Graeme with a sister as well. I adored Graeme for his understanding of taking away a father and mothers only daughter and I thought the resolution near the end for the rival clans was done very well. There was not much that bothered me about this book expect the fact that Eveline was able to hide the fact she could speak but not hear for so long and one small part that involved Graeme's sister and the women of the clan. Overall, an absolutely wonderful romance book that any romance fan will not want to miss! It made me smile, sigh, laugh, cheer and get angry and had me tearing up. I am so eager for more books from the lovely Maya Banks in this delicious series! 4 1/2 stars Thank you so much to Random House for providing me with this eARC!

I reviewed this book with my blogmate Celeste and our good friend Sim over at The Book Hookup we decided to rate this 1 billion stars, but the ratings max out at 5...so it's a 5 star. And that means top shelf here at The Book Hookup. First Thoughts: Celeste: HOLD. ME. I don't think I can write a review that will do this book justice. It was so good. I had all the feels from book 1, Charade, but now I have ALL THE FEELS. Sim: This book!!! It ripped my heart out... Loved it!! Ana: This book brought the ugly cry, the heartbreak and the flails...it had it all! Plot, Pacing and Style: Celeste: In this installment of the Games series these characters, Delaney and Adrian, are so very broken. And when I say broken, I mean broken. They have had so much tragedy in their lives. I was broken hearted for them. Delaney's goal was to track down Adrian to find some peace from an incident that changed their lives in the worst way possible. But, Delaney never expected to fall for Adrian. The story of their love was so powerful - I couldn't help but be moved. The pacing was perfect: slow and steady, which was so realistic. Nyrae Dawn's writing style, combined with the alternating POVs is so easy to read, I finished the book in nearly one sitting. I will read ANYTHING she writes. Sim: Delaney went in search to help someone, and maybe help herself, but found love instead. Completely unexpected, but maybe even better than what she set out for. Adrian was running from everything, but mostly himself. The love these two develop for one another is a deep one and the poetry that Adrian uses just intensifies it on so many levels. 'Haunt me, my little ghost, Possess me. Live inside me, And scare away my sins Until there's nothing left. But you.' Ana: This story felt so real. The characters were so real, so raw, yet so likeable. The pace was perfect. The heart stopping moments were intertwined with the bits of happiness, the confusion was linked to the past and present and the love was explored with kid gloves and trepidation in such a delicious way. The MCs: Celeste: Holy damaged goods. I don't know who had more of a haunted past, Adrian or Delaney. Both are totally hot, they know it, but are still full of self doubt which makes them so real. The story is told in alternating first person POVs, so we got to get in their heads and I can tell you...I adored both of them. They are down and devastated, but still keep going. Sim: Both have deep intense souls which makes me love them! Throughout all the bad stuff they had to deal with, they fight their own way back at life. You can't help but understand the decisions they made, even if they were not always the right ones and that's a great accomplishment of the writer. 'Her tears rival my rain,' Ana: I fell head over heels in love with both of these characters very early on. I rooted for them in their struggles and cheered them on in their attempts to save themselves and each other. Their relationship was so intense and their struggles so huge yet, somehow, I was able to connect with them. These two characters needed each other in order to find the strength that was deep down inside each of them. Their struggles were heart wrenching but their story was worth the ugly cry and the tissues. Romance /Chemistry: Celeste: Nyrae Dawn hit this one out of the park. The attraction was undeniable from the word go. It's not just the physical side of things (which was AMAZING), but the emotional connection was so strong. "I can't.... We shouldn't..." If you knew, you would want to. You'd throw me out. "I think we can and maybe it doesn't matter if we should." His voice is low, sexy. I shiver. Sim: From a seemingly no-ties hookup, to a deep deep connection that had the sparks flying; loved every second! There's no teasing or fooling around but an intense connection. And the poetry: omg I loved it!!! The intensity: just wow! She's the rapid pulse in my neck and the welcomed ache in my chest.... Celeste: Sim, omg. that quote *dies* Ana: Utter perfection. The chemistry was strong and deep. These two were meant for each other and the intensity of their connection left me breathless! "She knows my words, which are part of my soul, a part I've never willingly let anyone else see, yet I show them to her. I write them for her. She knows those part of me - the only parts of me that aren't a lie." Title/Cover: Celeste: Love them both! The title is seriously perfect, and the cover is just right. It's like they are about to kiss and connect but are still holding back a bit. I feel like I saw another cover of this somewhere and liked that one a bit better, but this is still good. Sim: This cover fits the book better. It could still use a bit more intensity IMO. Ana: Easy to see where the title came from since the word was used several times in the book. The title and the cover suit the story well. Twists and Turns: Celeste: There was definitely something that came up that I didn't' expect and it hurt my heart even more. It was painful, but added so much depth to the story. I loved it. Well done, Nyrae! But you might owe me a box of tissues. Sim: There was one point in the book that had me blown away and gasping for air. It hurt my heart even more but it explained a lot as well. Ana: Well, I didn't see that coming and let me tell you that, from that point on, there was no consoling me...tears, tissues and tweets about how my heart was breaking...yup, that's what happened! Ending: Celeste: The perfect ending was perfect. It was real. Adrian's note to Delaney...I don't even have any words....It's a fantastic stand alone book, but I hope I see some snippets of them in Maddox's story next. Sim: perfect! No butterflies and shiny sunsets but a real ending, fitting in perfectly with the characters. Ana: Great ending! The author must have known that I was all out of tears and it was time to bring it home...and she did a perfect job. Gripes/suggestions: Celeste: None. Well, maybe the fact that it's over and I wish there had been a longer epilogue. Sim: somehow the ending came too soon for me. Other then that: perfect. Ana: None that I can think of. This book captured my heart, exhausted my tear supply and made me a huge fan of Nyrae Dawn! I'm so looking forward to Maddox's story! Final Thoughts/Rec It? Celeste: A million trillion times YES. Sim: yup!!! And I can't wait to find out more about Maddox!!! (Masquerade: coming out January 2014) Ana: Absolutely no doubt...you must read this book!

From the way everyone raved about the book, I thought I would be hungry for Oreos, but I'm left a little homesick for Waffle House. They're just not up here on this side of Canada, and I have yet to find another place that can make a satisfying pile of greasy hashbrowns all the way. I read this book in three freaking hours - sorry, not sorry. It's hard to pick a spot to start from in raving about this. Simon, the funniest teenager with the funniest family full of in-jokes and made up worlds about Oreos? The diverse characters who existed because they were there with their own lives outside of Simon's personal world, not because the author went through a check list of diverse characters to include? The humorous but touching and courageous e-mails between Simon and Blue? I won't delve into Blue so much because I don't want to give away any hints about the mystery, but I have to say that from the very beginning, I knew I would not be disappointed in who Blue ended up being. Simon crushes on him so hard, and it's adorable and sweet. Anyone who could make Simon that twitterpated without revealing their name or face was not going to disappoint me when the reveal happened. Simon himself is a fantastic character. He's awkward sometimes. He's funny. He's introspective. He's a teenager. An honest-to-goodness teenager who doesn't want to make a big deal about his sexuality. His family really had me in stitches, and much of Simon's humor is developed because of them. Their reality show obsession. Their dog named Bieber. The Halloween costumes. The thing they did on Christmas Eve day was the only time I put the book down since I started reading because I had to go to a different room and laugh so I wouldn't wake up my spouse. It was kind of terrible but it was so funny. The story is a little on the simple side, but it's addicting like Oreos because all the characters are so well-crafted. Especially Taylor.

Objectively, this was a good book and I liked it. Objectively, these were the exact kind of smartass found-family criminal desperate theatrical characters that I love. I don't really know what it is about Bardugo's writing which, objectively, is excellent, but I had a similar response to Shadow And Bone. I could see all the reasons why I should care about the characters, but I didn't. I found some parts of the narrative greatly entertaining, and yet still kept putting the book down and not itching to pick it up again. For some reason -- and I think it must just be me and how I think -- I couldn't get into this the way I wanted to. I normally would never have picked up a zombie book, but this is a Diana Rowland book so I just had to give it a chance. One of the main reasons that this was not a five star book for me was that it took me a long time to warm up to Angel, I feel like she had to start liking herself and being willing to turn her life around before I was able to like her. By the end of the book she is a new Angel, and not in a bad way. The book is gruesome in some ways, so if you are one of those people who faints at the thought of blood this might not be for you. On the other hand, Angel is one of those characters who just spits out whatever crazy thought is going through her head (and there's a lot of them) so the book has a healthy dose of humor as well. The main plot is interesting and a good mystery, although it does kind of take a backseat to Angel just trying to get her bearings (it does take a while to get used to the idea of craving brains after all). I was a little bit surprised that Angel never asked any questions like "I wonder where zombies come from?" or "how does this magic stuff work? ", but then again she was a bit busy with the murders and the whole trying to make sure she didn't rot away thing. Overall, the book is really well written, and I did enjoy reading it. Like all of this author's books, the story just kind of sucks you in and it was a fast read. I will definitely look for the next in this series, but I am much more excited for the next Kara book.

Stuck in a tiny fortress situated between high mountains, a glacier, and a frozen fjord, Solveig, her brother Harald, and sister Asa, are surrounded by their father's warriors, a few servants, and a skald (storyteller). The king sent them to the far north for their protection during a war, but no one considered treachery from one of their own. Solveig has always been the overlooked on. She is not beautiful like her older sister, nor a male heir like her younger brother. She's just Solveig. Even her father rarely acknowledges her. But Solveig is important in a different way, as she finds out during the long winter. She is the one whose stories calm the restless warriors during the long nights and bring them comfort when they are struck down by a fatal poison. Thanks to the tutelage of Alric, her father's skald, she learns she has a voice and that gives her power. Forced to face harsh realities, she comes to understand that the fiercest warriors may have the gentlest hearts and the ones you trusted most may have dark secrets. She also learns that courage comes in many forms. Mr. Kirby has written a moving story full of action and adventure that will appeal to both boys and girls. It is the type of story that draws you in and doesn't let go until the last page. Though younger readers may not understand all the Viking references and terms, they'll figure it out through contextual clues, and even if they don't, it's still a great story. For a strong story set in distant Viking times with a touch of suspense, myths, action, and emotional ups and downs, definitely pick up Icefall when it comes out in October. Your tweens will enjoy it - and while you're at it, read it yourself. You'll be glad you did. It's definitely a story worth reading.

I liked how much suspense there was as I read. I was very invested in the story to try and figure out what was going on and what was going to happen next. At first it seemed so linear, lost in a forest, ghost stories, some Cherokee spirits, and the fact that they were stranded made it seem like it was going to be some form of paranormal story but it turned into something really messed up and sinister. The labels on their arms really made everyone wary of each other. Deceptive, Dangerous, Damaged, Darling. Did that mean that the Lucas was the one who was killing people because he was dangerous? Or was Jude the one responsible because he was deceptive and could get away with it? Was Emily damaged and so she had nothing to lose or gain by doing this, and Darling-why was Sera labeled Darling? These were the questions that kept me reading. And as I read, I found that they were more than the labels. They all were so different from each other, but the more shit they went through together, the closer they got, and they became a tight knit group. They all cared about each other and tried everything to find a way out of the woods, and not to mention trying to figure who the killer/psychopath was that was toying with them. In the end, I liked how the author made it seem like the culprit could have been either Mr. Walker, or Madison, or maybe even some serial killer, but I think the reveal was actually a good twist-it certainly surprised me, especially considering the details of every thing/crime the culprit has committed. The story was well told and I definitely liked how it kept me pulled in even to the last page, even if there were a few questions left open.
