A trilogy that redefines what you think about Faerie and the Apocalypse! Here is Janni discussing how she "talks" to her character Matthew @ Not Yet Read The long wait for Faerie After, the last in the Bones of Faerie trilogy, was completely worth it! Simner has a way of connecting you to her characters on an intimate level. Their struggles with each other could very well mirror your own struggles with loved ones. OK, maybe not with all the faerie, post apocalyptic business but you get what I mean. In my opinion, it is essential that we see all sides of a character in order to bond with them. Of course there are going to be traits you love and hate, but these things all serve to make the characters more real. Simner has a deft skill at writing characters I can directly relate to. They didn't read like cookie cutter characters like I've read a zillion times before. Liza can be a selfish nit when it comes to certain things, thinking she knows best but she is also self sacrificing and tries to be honest and do what's right - but even that doesn't skim the surface of who she is. In Faerie After, Liza is thrust into yet more tragedy and harsh realities, about life and death and the gravity of one's choices. She's been through so much and it doesn't seem like she can ever catch a break. I was saddened that Matthew was again absent for a big portion of the book but I was delighted that Allie played a large role. She is a wonderful character and we'll deserving of her own story. Overall this trilogy has tackled some hefty issues like child abuse, neglect, discrimination and hate crimes. The only complaint I have is when I reviewed Faerie Winter (book 2 in the trilogy) I oozed over how I thought the "rehash" of the previous book was done so well - how you weren't hit over the head with it. I have to say I was extremely disappointed in the beginning of Faerie After because you weren't just hit on the head with the recap information - you were freaking face punched with it. I know what Simner was trying to do with using the "Before" reference as the characters call the time preceding the War "Before." But she reiterated every major event as "Before this happened, Before that happened" and it was in a constant stream of this for at least an entire page. We are taken on a journey into Faerie as well as the place beyond where all go when they die. A battle is fought and the very fabric of reality re-woven. What I especially enjoyed was that the book didn't end immediately after the climax. I was eased into letting the story go, which I'm thankful for as I will definitely miss this world.

*Back-dating reviews based on random things I wrote at the time. I just wrote about the three as a whole rather than each book* So, I finally read them. Initially, I wasn't going to - based on everything I'd heard, I figured I'd not like it. On the flipside, I also believe you shouldn't slate a book until you've read it, so once I saw the books floating around the house I thought there was no harm in borrowing them and seeing if I could work out what all the fuss was about. I really can see why it's so popular, but I really dislike most of those reasons. The unrealistic sex, the scale and perfection of everything, the timescale alone infuriates me. This was always my pet hate in fanfictions: guy meets girl, it's instantaneously obvious they'll get together and end up together forever - that's exactly what this book does. Despite it being ludicrous at many moments, I'd rattled through the books so quickly that I just had to know what happened, otherwise it'd niggle at me until I found out. The main theme in the plot that honestly infuriated me was the fact that it all spiraled from jealousy or longing surrounding Anastasia. I'm not saying if you're plain and understated you aren't attractive - far from it - but literally everyone they meet is either instantaneously smitten with Christian, therefore jealous of her, or wants her. No, not going to happen. I understand it's fiction, and I understand it's fantasy, but this has classic cliche fanfiction written all over it. My other issue is Christian. Why I was most annoyed was that - based on reading the first book alone - people I know were romanticising him and praying for their own little Christian Grey. He is a control freak, a bully and no amount of money or pretty hair can change that. This is only forgiven because he's said to be beautiful and unfathomably rich. Would an ordinary guy get away with that behaviour? No, he wouldn't. The idea anyone would romanticise such a horrid person - the negatives veiled by the fact he has money and speaks to lovingly of her - is crazy to me. Just because someone can tell you you're beautiful and genuinely cares for you doesn't mean you should take shit from them. And Anastasia. Dear, sweet Anastasia needs a reality check. Your first boyfriend. Your first everything. A quote sticks out following the announcement of their ridiculously quick proposal: "I love him and he loves me. He wants to marry me and there will never be anyone else for me." Anyone else says this about their first boyfriend and everyone would take them as a sappy teenager in love, but because he's a billionaire that's okay. There's a reason they're popular and it's because they pander to the perfection and ideals in love. Boy meets girl, they fall in love, she fixes him, they get married, they live happily ever after. There are obviously more tumultuous times created through Christian's past, and that's one of the few factors that remotely peaked my interest. But, even then, it was very predictable. Did anyone really not see it coming that Jack was part of the foster family? It's hard to give it credit where it's due, because I can't work out where it is. The writing style was juvenile, the plot wasn't great, the characters weren't very good. She's taken an intelligent girl and presented her as a pushover, someone who'll take a beating from a pretty face. She takes too much shit without knowing that he has a past because he is essentially rich and attractive. This ramble is pointless and it's not really going anywhere. Overall, I can see why it's so popular but that's because it's just very vanilla, plain and tailored to the mainstream. This isn't even a BDSM book, like I had been told, this is a book about a couple coming from two sexual extremes to find a balance and fall in love. Nothing they actually do is extreme and I find it surprising that anyone reading this thinks so. And, a rant dedicated to the reason it's so popular - the sex. I've had issues with EL James' style of writing throughout the whole book. I found it quite juvenile and repetitive. The Inner Goddess drove me crazy and the fact she would put dashes between words to form a description rather than choose one suitable word infuriated me. But when it came to the sex scenes, it feels more innocent. Ana being inexperienced could be one reason to use such poor vocabulary on anatomy - "my sex" and "there" are pretty juvenile ways to describe the female anatomy, as is "his length" for Christian. The other reason I think that really drove the poor language is the author herself. She's notably embarrassed in interviews when she's questioned about sex, and it seems even in her writing - in her own fantasy - she can't write anything crude through a certain shyness. I suppose that makes shy newcomers feel better about reading it; they'd be less embarrassed reading this than reading about cocks and other similar words. I think that had Anastasia been more dominating in the relationship, it wouldn't have been as successful. I, personally, didn't like Anastasia and her pushover nature when it came to sex. I felt she was blinded by beauty and money, despite her saying it's not about the money. She wouldn't have done anything like this for a beautiful bum now, would she? So, the loose language is my main theory as to why it goes down so well. Mix that in with an irresistible billionaire with a troubled past, the fact that you know they're going to end up together happily ever after and BAM! There you have it. That's why it sells. The sex itself has its pros and cons. One key pro is that it creates an atmosphere that avoids a wham, bam, thank you mam scenario. Christian worships every inch of her body almost constantly and it always builds up before sex. That, again, is another reason I think this book has done so well. I, however, did not like it. Not to mention the sex itself is unrealistic. For one, Anastasia is a virgin with no gag reflex. Not unheard of, but mighty convenient. She experiences her first orgasm, if I remember correctly, by him playing with her nipples. Does that even happen? Even if she was sensitive enough for that to happen in the first place, the more sex she has, the less sensational this should feel. Yet it doesn't. It can still get her off completely. And, just throwing it out there, she always comes first and he comes soon after. Sometimes they even come together! There was even an instance in which she couldn't come because she was distracted by thoughts on life, yet Christian says "come" and she does. Again, I understand this is fantasy but the sheer inaccuracy of this annoyed me continuously throughout the series. I'm glad he found his release, I'm glad you crumbled around him, but once in a while he's going to come just before you do and probably roll over and go to sleep. To the BDSM aspect... I think this has been greatly skewed in promotion and what I hear from other people. This is not a BDSM book. 50 Shades of Grey deals with a Dominant and a virgin essentially falling in love and finding a happy medium between two extremely contrasting sexual lifestyles. In turn, it's middle of the road. In fact, it's normal. Spanking isn't taboo, nor are vibrators, handcuffs or any of the objects they used. If they were, you wouldn't be able to buy them on your local high street, nor would they be advertised in shop windows. The issue is Christian as a character. He has defined his sexual desires by his past, though they were really founded through Elena, and then adapted to fit his past. The author, with or without meaning to, puts forward the idea that Christian is only into BDSM because he is damaged, and that is an issue people I know who are into BDSM really have with these books. BDSM is a preference, it is not a sign of emotional baggage or a damaged past, yet EL James really makes the link between his childhood and his sexual desires. His baggage is what causes his stalker nature, his possessive needs and his inability to trust Ana to be safe without him being around. These can be tailored to his damage, but BDSM cannot. tl;dr I rate this series in a similar way to Twilight - there are so many great erotic (and vampire) books out there, so why did this one break through? It's usually the watered down, easily digestible books that break it and, more often than not, they're terrible representations of the genre they become the poster boy of. These books, like the series they spiraled from, are poorly written, have a terrible plot and awful characters. It is completely unrealistic in every sense and, while pandering to dreamers and fantasy is fine in books, this takes the absolute piss. I think the massive rant was me trying to be reasonable, when it's a long-winded way of saying this is a horrid book. You ask for any erotica nowadays and this will be the top recommendation. It shouldn't be. Not by a long shot.

Scooby Doo meets H.P. Lovecraft? Who wouldn't want to dig in with a book being marketed this way? Certainly not me since that seemed quite the, um, interesting pairing. Teen detectives (The Blyton Summer Detective Club) are well known for solving a particular case, and their last one at that, in Sleepy Lake. Somehow, something resonates horrifically with each of them - the invariadubitably (hey, if the author can make up words, so can I - it's fun to say - try it!) large pink elephant in the room! Thirteen unlucky years later, they reunite to go back and face this metaphorical elephant head on. I am so torn with this novel. I want to love it. I really do. But I just... don't. What I liked about it: various ha ha moments with nods such as "Nancy Hardy, journalist", Arkham Asylum and Zoinx River. Cute, very cute. And going in with Scooby Doo being the main factor, it was easy to see how this was more humor and nostalgia than anything else. For that, I can appreciate it. However, what didn't work for me was the writing style. I felt it was all over the place. Set stage one, scene one... and then back to novel style... then screenplay... sometimes dispersed sporadically throughout a section written like a (dare I say) "normal" book. I also learned more about the proper way to destroy a man's testicles than I ever needed to, though I found myself smiling during this part and I'm not sure what that says about me as a person or if I'm just in a mood... *wink*. And that was just in the first 50 pages. Ultimately the story line was fine - I can totally appreciate what the author was trying to do and found my love (again) for the Scooby Gang, er... BSDC, that is. I think the writing style hurt my brain a bit though. I'm off to find the Mystery Machine and Shaggy for some Scooby Snacks.

**Thank you to Netgalley and the publisher for sending me an ARC of this book in return for an honest review :) 4 stars!! If I had to sum up this book, I would say it is cross between the 'Hunger Games' and the 'Maze Runner' but this isn't necessarily a bad thing because it does have some unique elements of its own. The story is set in a futuristic dystopian world where people are segregated based on three colours - gold, silver and bronze. The golds are obviously very rich while the bronze are the poorest of the lot. Silvers are a little better off but they serve the golds. Our MC Maia is a girl that was born of both gold and bronze parents. She holds the key to saving her people from a deadly asteroid that is hurtling its way to the planet. The story is essentially one in which she is trying to reconcile two halves of herself - the heroine and the girl who lived most of her life trying to run away from things. The worldbuilding was pretty developed. I could visualise the world pretty easily. A lot of the nature of the society was based on the constellations and Greek mythology which was intriguing. There are lots of descriptions of clothes and gadgets used. It reminded me a bit of 'Capitol city' especially with the outlandish clothes and wigs. But, nevertheless, it was still riveting. The MC Maia was okay. She seems to be rather level headed and doesn't give into her emotions easily. She is very guarded yet resourceful. She is wiling to go out of her way to protect those she cares about. However, there were times when she flip-flops a bit which can be irritating. This can be seen in her relationships with Caspian and Riser. The romance element of the story is a love-triangle of sorts but a slow burn one. I preferred Maia with Riser because they had more chemistry. Caspian was just a bland character. He wasn't really that engaging. He's your typical good looking guy and that's it. Plus, he doesn't have a very strong personality considering how things change towards the end. Riser, on the other hand, was swoonworthy. He has all of these rough edges but a heart of gold. He is just the perfect book boyfriend. With regards to the minor characters, I think they are fleshed out pretty well. There are a couple of villains in the story which is rather interesting. Their personalities are rather complex and we don't know what their agendas are really. It will be good to see how this plays out in the books to come. Overall, I thought the story was great. The plot progressed really well. There are no boring bits as we are thrown instances of murder, betrayal and action. There aren't many revelations or twists except for one which was fairly obvious at least to me. However, the plot devices used for story progression were sensible and gave a seamless read. I would recommend this to lovers of science fiction and dystopia. You won't be disappointed. I look forward to book two.

Right around a 4. Of the three books I've read, this was my least favorite. Of course, with a series this entertaining, being the least favorite is in no way an insult. Titan's Curse is still heads and shoulders above many of the books out there today. Plot: When Percy, Annabeth and Thalia go to pick up two new potential campers, Annabeth is kidnapped. Artemis and her hunters begin a quest to rescue Annabeth, and Percy, Grover and Thalia go with them. Along the way, they face several mythical creatures, attacks from the Titan army, and eventually a battle with Luke and one of the Titan leaders. Characters: Percy's greatest gift, which some consider his fatal flaw, is that he will do anything he can to keep the camp safe and protect his friends. As he does, he learns more about what he can do and grows more confident in his ability to use his powers effectively. At the same time, he continues to try and figure out his role in the prophecy about Kronos and the destruction of Olympus. Thalia is faced with the same problem, but she is a little more bitter than Percy about being deserted by her father. Grover is a steadfast and loyal sidekick, as is Annabeth even though we don't see much of her. We also don't see much of Luke in this book either, but when we do, we learn that while he is still malicious, he is growing weaker and more scared of Kronos and his soldiers. There are several new characters. Artemis, the leader of the hunters, initially refuses to work with Percy because he's a boy, but in the end, she respects him because of how he fought for his friends. One of Artemis' hunters, Zoe, also plays a huge role in helping to locate and rescue Annabeth. There are also the two campers, Nico and Bianca, who appeared at the beginning of the story. In the book's conclusion, we learn that one of them could be part of the prophecy as well. Writing: The book is very well edited, which I always love. Another plus is Riordan's writing style, which is very laid back and witty. I have been reading it with my son, and there are times that he and I both laugh out loud at things the characters do or say. There's no foul language, but there is (as to be expected) a lot of violence, though most of it isn't too terribly graphic. I'd probably rate the book a PG. The Bottom Line: In comparison to Lightning Thief or Sea of Monsters, there are a few more lulls in the plot. Even with those lulls, there is plenty of action, drama, humor, mystery, and suspense that make this book well worth the read. Like the previous books, Titan's Curse sends some great messages: 1) even when we don't get along, it is still possible to work together to accomplish something, and 2) family isn't always blood. I'd recommend it to readers of all ages.

The premise of this story seemed interesting and even though it took me way longer that it should have, this book was actually pretty good. Lawyer Kate Baron gets a call at her office on a busy day to come to the office to pick up her daughter Amelia who is in trouble. Kate is shocked by this as her daughter had never been in trouble and gets to the office late only to discover that her daughter is dead. She apparently jumped off the roof. A few months later a distraught Kate gets a text from an unknown number, "Amelia didn't jump." The story does something weird here, where you hear the story from Amelia's point of view a few months before the apparent suicide. The author does well by switching the voices between the mother and the daughter. One is struggling with her daughter's death, the other is struggling with surviving the exclusive high school she belongs too. As the story unfolds on both perspectives the list of suspects grows with each page. While Kate has a list of secrets and men who could potentially be Amelia's father and part of the mystery, Amelia gets herself involved in a group who call themselves the Magpies and immediately rubs the leader Zadie the wrong way. Amelia then falls in love with another member called Dylan. The story grazes over Amelia's discovery that she was gay. It was an interesting plot development and I think I appreciate that it was just a thing that happened to be true, rather than what defined Amelia as a person. As the story plays out, the suspects all look incredibly suspicious at different times in the story and the pace is brisk without getting bogged down with the amount of characters you're expected to remember. The story closes in an anti-climatic way and honestly you hate that you got to hear from Amelia and learned to like her only to see her die. You feel sorry for Kate because even though she is moving forward in the end, she lost her only daughter. The narrative voice was odd at times and the book could have used a few edits, but over all I was pleased with the read and the author did a great job at answering all the questions she posed, even the ones you didn't realize needed answering.

I am in love with this book! Going in, I was a little worried about how the author would handle the themes of depression and suicide but I felt she did it very well, especially after reading about her own experiences in the author's note. Theodore and Violet were wonderful characters with great depth and I loved them both. They're both really interesting and quirky - Finch is always changing himself in an effort to find himself and Violet is struggling to rediscover her passion for writing after the death of her sister and co-author. But most of all I love the way they work together. Their relationship dynamic was really beautiful. I can't even pick a favourite thing about this book because it is the way the author incorporated so many cute and quirky details and trips for the two characters that i loved the most. Trailers converted into bookstores, a roller coaster in someone's back yard, a solar system in a closet, running through the snow in winter to find flowers. I'm a complete sucker for cute and imaginative details. Some people have criticised the characters as being completely unrealistic and pretentious but I didn't get this impression at all. Violet and Theodore aren't overly weird names. I know plenty of seventeen year olds who enjoy reading poetry and thinking about life. It's completely normal for teenagers to want to explore and discover. And i think Finch and Violet are amazing characters. Strangely enough, the ending didn't actually hit me that hard. Loads of people have written tearful reviews but I think because I had been expecting it before I even read the book it didn't come as a surprise and I had already prepared myself for the blow. I didn't expect to love this book as much as I did and thought it would be another run-of-the-mill ya contemporary as many people have criticised it to be but I don't believe that at all. It has definitely earned a spot on my favourites shelf.

I have to admit before anything that this review is more than a little biased. The fact that I watched ABC Family's show based off of this book before I read the book obviously leads to a bias, but I believe that even if I had not seen the show first, I still would have given this novel the same rating that I have. Maybe one star more, but nothing less. Chloe King is an average sixteen-year-old girl who has friend drama and teenage sexual tendencies and all of that which makes for an average young adult novel, but the best part about it is that she's not an average sixteen-year-old girl at all. From the beginning of the novel, the prologue that insinuates that she's about to die is intriguing enough to want to pick up the book and read it a little more intently than planned, and it only gets better when she falls off of the top of a tower, but other than that, the book falls short of anything considered spectacular. Chloe's personality was not what I expected at all, and the fact that she just seems to spend the entire novel whining about the fact that she can't get one guy to kiss her despite the fact that she's already kissed/made out with two others is really kind of annoying. I understand the concept of teenagers being obsessed with sex, lies and drugs/alcohol, but I was expecting a little more out of this book, and I didn't think that it was going to revolve around Chloe's determination to get laid or how much alcohol she was going to drink with her friends. The friend drama was also an annoyance of the book, and that seemed to take up a large chunk of the novel. Between Chloe and Amy fighting, Chloe and Paul disagreeing, Amy and Paul dating and just the three best friend whirlwind of drama, it was just frustrating. The only character I actually liked in the novels was Aleyc (I will never stop calling him Alek though, because that is what ABC Family has ingrained into my head). His personality was the best out of everyone's. In my opinion, the worst part of the entire book was the fact that Chloe's powers were barely thought about, almost as if they were an afterthought in this teen drama, and the fact that she didn't even seem to care about them at first, that she didn't care about the fact that she'd fallen off the top of a tower or had claws or could do weird gymnastic moves, was just annoying. I know if anything like that had happened to me, I would be freaking out, so I don't understand her. And the end of the book was the only point where her powers were really talked about, and yet we still really never found out what was so special about Chloe King and why she had all these powers. I am hoping that the next book is better than this one, but if it is not, I might just give up and not even bother to attempt to read the novels that one of my favourite ABC Family shows was based off of. It was just that bad.

As you may have caught in my other reviews, I only give out 5 stars to books that are absolutely amazing...the kind that will always stay with me OR Indie writers who rock and need a little publicity. With over 4k reviews, this one doesn't fit into Indie writer who needs publicity. So that said, 4 stars would be my 5 star rating. This is not that. I was torn on this one. If I could have given it 2.5 stars, I would. But since Goodreads says 2 stars = "It's Okay", that's what I picked. Let me start off by saying the writing is good. It's actually really good. The metaphors sprinkled in the dialogue are often amusing and I think I only spotted one typo issue through the whole thing. Jolie is a fairly entertaining character to read. Rand isn't too bad himself. However there are several "huh?" moments that just bugged me too much to give it 4 stars. The whole beginning premise just doesn't fly with me. It's easy to buy in the first few chapters but the further we get in the book, the more I found myself trying to figure out how the beginning fit with the rest of it. ----Begin SPOILERS----- Maybe I missed something (as I often say, it's likely), but it made no sense to me how Rand stumbles on Jolie. He's doing a favor for the evil wench at the end of the book? Huh? How does this make any sense? And he finds Jolie from yellow pages? Really? Ok. Sure. But still, why are we all of a sudden in a huge war with Bella on one side? If she is so horrible that he's been working to build his own army, why in the heck did he do a favor for her in the first place...um all the way in the US instead of his home in the UK? Yeah, that's the primary thing that bugged me. I was also a bit put off by the triangle with the wolf, I forget his name now because he's not a very memorable character, Trent maybe? Yes, let's call him Trent. The fight in the party where Trent punches Rand read as forced drama. As does Jolie's about-face. I didn't see much in the story to explain why he was as bad as she claims he is. He came off as a decent character...except when he'd let her get jumped. But he had a somewhat reasonable if not foolish explanation for that. And then the whole Sinjin working for Bella but not working for Bella... And the half vampire, half witch who supposedly worked for Rand but then turned out she actually worked for Bella--these two clunky twists were too much for me to swallow, especially with the awkwardness of how the story began. I may continue with book 2 at some point and hope it smooths out but I'm certainly not racing out to get the next one.

The title of the book comes from the observations of Europeans that all swans are white. Much to their surprise, they came to Australia and found their first black swan. The book starts with this story to illustrate the "limitations to our learning from observations or experience and the fragility of our knowledge." As Taleb points out, it very different to think there is evidence of no possible black swans, than there is no evidence of the possibility of black swans. Taleb has received lots of press and admirers given the recent meltdown in the financial markets. The book was published in 2007. Taleb seems to have perceived the coming collapse (and probably got a rich financial reward based on his strategy). His supreme self-confidence (arrogance) shines brightly through in his writing. He has little time for shallow thinking and those who think they understand risk or the financial markets. Another example running through the book is the first 1,001 days of a turkey's life. For a 1,000 days the farmer brings food to the turkey every morning. On that last day, things change dramatically. The farmer shows up with an axe instead of food. A surprise and horrible change in circumstance for the turkey. But all the historical evidence for the turkey indicated that the farmer would show up with food and not an axe. Of course, on the flip side, the farmer saw the axe day coming. As Yogi Berra philosophized: "It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future." It is the unknown unknown that is most dangerous. We spend too much time focusing on knowing what we know. We need to spend focusing some energy in realizing what we do not know and what we do not know what we do not know. As a compliance and risk professional I was particularly intrigued by the story of the four largest losses by casinos. As you might expect, casinos run very thorough security programs, compliance programs and risk management programs. The four largest losses fell completely outside the casinos' models. One was the white tiger's attack on Roy, the second was a disgruntled contractor who attempted to dynamite the casino, the third was the kidnapped daughter of a casino owner, and the fourth an incompetent employee who failed to file the 1099 reports with the Internal Revenue Service. It is also important to draw the distinction between positive contingencies and negative contingencies. The black swan can be one that brings unexpected destruction or one that brings an unexpected windfall. His philosophy is to play it safe, but hedge for a disastrous losses and spectacular windfalls. Mitigate the unexpected consequences. I expected to get a lot of insight from the book. But it was one of the few books that changed the outlook on my profession.

"The only way out of the labyrinth of suffering is to forgive." I have had this book for so long but didn't really have the urge to read it until after I read The Fault in Our Stars. That book was fantastic. So after reading that it pushed me to read more of John Green's books and one of which was Looking for Alaska. I actually have to reread it because the first time I did, it didn't appeal to me that much. As they always say, "second time's the charm." Miles wanted a change. He wanted to move to boarding school. He wasn't running away from his family, he just wanted to have friends and fit in for a change. He was also determined in finding out what Francois Rabelais called the "Great Perhaps". He was sure that he will find this in boarding school. He was right. He found Alaska. The thing I liked about John Green's books is how easily he creates relatable and realistic characters. John Green has this ability to make hard sensitive topics very easy to read. When I first read it my initial reaction was all negative. I didn't like it at all. There was nothing there that I could connect to. But when I reread it I started to see things differently. Being a teenager is not easy. To adults it may seem that teenagers didn't have much to think about but they do. Adults may have work, money and personal relationships to worry about and teenagers have those too just not in the same level. Teenagers worry about fitting in and making friends. Honestly, not having friends at school would really put you down. Not having any friends may lead you to think that you are nothing because no one wants to be friends with you. You may say that it's a very shallow reason but it isn't. Fitting in and being with other people helps a lot. I didn't mean just being with people but being with the right people. At first, I didn't really like Alaska. I didn't like her for the reason that she was reckless and mostly don't think of what she was doing. But as I reread this book again I found myself empathizing for what she has gone through. Alaska might seem carefree at first glance but she was not. She hides behind this facade. She lets everyone see she's this fearless girl who loves to play pranks, have sex and drown in alcohol. But deep down you will see that there was this other side of her that had to be kept hidden away because of what happened in her past. I felt her pain and how she kept drinking and smoking herself to death just to forget all her worries for a little while. Why didn't I like her the first time? Because somehow I saw myself in Alaska. Miles was a different story. I liked Miles the first time I read him. He was the new kid and immediately got along with his room mate. Since he never had many friends back in Florida when he got some in boarding school he decided to try some of the things he never done. I liked his POV. There were no barriers in how he tells the story and I liked it. Miles was the typical new kid who would do anything to fit in. He desperately wants to fit in that he'd join in the stupid pranks that Alaska, Chip and Takumi had planned out eve if he doesn't really want to. He was a little gullible which was cute. I don't know how Mr. Green does it but all his characters were three dimensional that it's pretty possible I might meet one of them on the street. Everyone was whole and complete. You'd know each and every character in this book and its one of the strengths of this book for me. There were however parts in this book that I hoped weren't included. It was a bit dragging on the initial part of the book which I didn't really appreciate. I am okay with slow paced books but only if its necessary and in this case I didn't feel like it was. I was okay with this book being cut in the before and the after of Alaska's death but again so many unnecessary stuff here and there. All in all I think it was still a good book. Not as good as The Fault in Our Stars though but I still liked it. I have to change the rating from 3 stars to 4 stars

There's nothing particularly wrong with this book, it's cute and can be funny at times. The voice is defiantly an authentic teen guy voice, which, as a teen guy who reads YA, I am thankful for. But, this whole book was just...eh. It's essentially the same problem I had with Simon vs. The Homo Sapiens Agenda. This book isn't bad, there's just nothing new about it. If I had to call this book anything, it would be the gay version of P.S I Still Love You, which I haven't read but pretty much has the same premise. The book is about an athletic, popular guy with a semi-but-not-really girlfriend named James who's gay and writes letters as a way to get all his thoughts organized. The book is just him essentially trying to find the courage to actually talk to people and admit his feelings and it was just, so, so boring. Look, I understand the how important the coming out narrative is and I still love those stories, but this entire book is just James refusing to talk to anyone. He absolutely refuses to even discuss anything with anyone and the entire time I'm reading this book I'm just rolling my eyes and screaming "For fucks sake just talk to someone, anyone." I get how scary it is to admit your gay, I get how scary it is too have to say something that will completely change someones perspective of you, but I have never read a book where a character just didn't want to do anything as much as James. That all this book really is, James not doing anything and reacting to the world around him. Despite his voice, James is such a passive character it makes the story seem invisible. He never does anything, never takes action, never has motivation. Even by the end of the novel the only thing that's different about him is that he's out. Coming out stories aren't just about coming out as gay, they're about growth and change. they're about coming face to face with what seems like an impossible decision and being brave enough to make that decision. This book takes that decision away from James and gives it to an outside force he has no control over, robbing him of the only thing this book was really about. There are better LGBT books. There are better coming out stories. Where this book stands is kinda in the middle, not bad, but certainly not the best out there. But, if this book gives someone the courage or inspires them to come out, then I guess I don't really have anything to complain about.

ARC provided by publisher in exchange for an honest review "Everything was suspended. Time. Pleasure. Pain. It was like the entire world held itself in waiting. For her." Emotional. Raw. Poignant. Heartfelt. These are a few words that comes to mind when describing The Truth About Him by M. O'Keefe. Ms. O'Keefe has once again had me devouring this second installment as she spellbinds and lures her readers into an emotionally charged second chance romance. With her gorgeous and heartfelt prose, Ms. O'Keefe has readers like myself fully invested into the complicated love story of Dylan and Annie. "Sometimes, maybe we don't know exactly what we have until someone shows us." In The Truth About Him, the story of Dylan and Annie continues and picks off where it last left off in Everything I Left Unsaid. The relationship of Dylan and Annie can only be described as raw, intense, passionate, and complicated. So many secrets and truths of their past has yet to be revealed. Their emotional burdens keeps them from being truly honest with one another. And in this second installment, both Dylan and Annie must come into terms of their relationship of how far are they willing to let one in emotionally, physically and sexually. As the revelation of Dylan's past comes to surface, are they willing to fight for their love? Can love and forgiveness heal a broken heart and shattered past? "The mess of me all over the beauty of her." The Truth About Him had everything I wanted, expected and much more in the continuation of Dylan and Annie. I loved how the author was able to douse her readers with raw emotions allowing us to feel for their strong tangible and palpable connections. Your heart will ache, swoon, and be moved as we delved deeper into their past. While in Everything I Left Unsaid was mainly focused on Annie, The Truth About Him was more focused on Dylan. I loved the way M. O'Keefe stripped her characters raw, allowing readers to really see their vulnerable sides while weaving mystery, suspense, erotica, and romance into the storyline. Overall, I loved the conclusion of the story of David and Annie. M. O'Keefe was able to maintain a sexy storyline while keeping it emotionally charged, raw, and heartfelt. So yes, I would highly recommend readers to read Everything I Left Unsaid and The Truth About Him. Both books are highly addictive and will leave readers yearning for more of M. O'Keefe's books. This review is also available on my blog, Bows & Bullets Reviews Ridley Duchannes is a bad girl, the absolute worst. A siren with enough juice to persuade anyone to do as she bids, she's out for her own. But after losing a poker game, she's in a world of shit and she can't seem to get out on her own. Wesley "Link" Lincoln just wants to make it big in the big bad city. Off to New York to start a new band (or join a band) on his way to fame and success. Link, though, is a southern gentleman at heart and he also really wants to be with Ridley. Can the two love birds make it work or are they going to crash and burn in NYC? I've been avoiding writing this particular review because I have only negative things to say. I hate writing negative reviews on books I got just to review. X_X I might as well get it over with, right? Ridley and Link are just the same as they have always been, but we get a few new cast members here. I honestly won't go into details about them because I didn't love any of them and that's part of where this series failed as a spin-off. With Beautiful Creatures (and it sequels) I loved most of the characters and generally wanted their success and happiness. Here I was pretty ambivalent about the new people. Hell, I was even a bit ambivalent about Ridley herself. Her determination to remain a "bad" girl and the idea that it was all she was capable of doing drove me fucking nuts. She refuses to even try to be better. And we all know she is capable of more, but she is just so damn stubborn. It really made me sad because I loved Rid in Beautiful Creatures & Beautiful Darkness. The only cast member I really loved was Link. Sweet, devoted Link. He should irritate me. He's a pretty stereotypical southern boy, but he's got so much charm that it just works somehow. That's probably why I was still rooting for the Rid/Link duo, because I wanted to see him happy. But we don't get that here. This veers straight into love triangle (square) land, with both Ridley and Link finding new love interests, but somehow still being interested in each other. It was a bit confusing because it was clear they were both moving on and then the thing at the end? WTF? Another issue for me was this was exceedingly boring. I know I received an eARC for review, but I just couldn't get through it. I ended up getting an audiobook copy and listening to it almost entirely that way. Even with audio, it was a struggle to get through. I didn't care about the characters. Without a connection to them, it is hard to muster up emotions about their journey. Then there is the villian. I won't say who he is, but I'll give you a hint. It's the same one as the previous books, which was another problem for me. How many fucking times do we need to kill this guy?!? And then there is the horrid cliffhanger ending that you don't see coming. You don't see it coming because when it ends, the audiobook still has well over an hour of time left (which is obnoxiously filled with excepts from Kami's & Margaret's other books). But the thing is over and it is a cliffhanger from hell and I wanted to punch my computer when it happened. I know I am OCD about finishing series, especially ones that I once loved, but I don't know that I will read any more of these books. Things for me starting going downhill in Beautiful Chaos and they have just kept rolling downwards. This was no improvement. I wouldn't say it's a bad story, but I've come to expect more out of Ridley and she just doesn't delivery. Maybe you'll love it to bits, but it just pissed me off. ****Thank you to Little, Brown Books For Young Readers for providing me with an eARC via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review****

Picoult has won several awards for her work as well as an honorary Doctor of Letters degree from Dartmouth College and the University of New Haven. Several books have been made into television movies. Her book "My Sisters Keeper" even made it to the big screen. Jodie Picoult is currently living in Hanover, New Hampshire with her husband, three children and several animals. In their childhood they played together as teens their relationship develops in an intense love story. Chris tells the police it was supposed to be a double suicide but the local police officer is not convinced. Her questioning unravels a tragedy in which both families loose everything they thought they were certain of when Chris is taken to trial for the murder of Emily. Honestly I will not even think about it probably in a week or consider telling someone to read this book cause they are missing out on something. It is a truth universally acknowledged that there is no point to writing a review of this book, because even if you haven't read it, you probably already know what it's about. It is also a truth universally acknowledged that "truth universally acknowledged" Austen jokes are pretty played out, but I proceed in defiance of both of those pieces of wisdom to tell you that Pride and Prejudice is, you know, really good. The suspense of any romance is not "will the couple get together?" but "how will the couple get together? ", and Austen elegantly and wittily draws tension out of that with Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy. There is, throughout, a very real feeling that personal flaws can get the better of even good, well-meaning people, and ruin their happiness, especially when the rules governing their interactions are so strict, and allow so little directness. Austen knew that Regency-era courtship was an intricate game played for very high stakes, and here you get both the sense of fun and the sense of tremendous investment. And aside from all that, it's a funny, sharply-observed novel, with a great way of putting things. Here, for example, is the narrative's treatment of Elizabeth leaving her parents and home for a few weeks' visit: The only pain was in leaving her father, who would certainly miss her, and who, when it came to the point, so little liked her going, that he told her to write to him, and almost promised to answer her letter. It's social comedy as much, or more, as it's romance, and if you like clever banter and the occasional bit of cringe comedy from someone making a fool out of themselves at great length, you would like it. There is also something moving, and useful, about the way the novel presents two people discovering their failings and trying as best they can to work to change them. (And, given that their example is surrounded by examples of people never realizing their faults, realizing their faults and doing nothing about it, or realizing their faults and trying to change and failing, it's a very realistic optimism.) The satisfaction of the ending, where everything comes together neatly and amusingly, is perfect.

There's the classic Hollywood lifestyle bashing, the height of which occurred during a scene where Layla is with Trip at a pre-production meeting and is introduced to two 'groupie sluts' who proceed to fill her on in why she'll never fit in: "'It's a whole 'nother world out here, honey. You might want to wake up and realize it. Sex is money out here.' Chrystal Lynn high-fived her slutty friend and added, 'And there's a helluva lotta rich people!'" Layla mentally accuses every woman she meets of being one of Trip's former 'sluts'. She needs a dress for the Academy Awards, so Trip sends her to a boutique owned by a friend of his. When Layla gets to the boutique, she meets the stunningly gorgeous proprietress and this happens: "This gorgeous woman has just referred to my boyfriend as "Trip" instead of "Mr. Wiley." Friend my arse. Ex sex-slave maybe. But there was no way this chick was just a "friend". It was like being in a bad, real-life version of Pretty Woman. Only I was not the hooker in this scenario." We then have a "claustrophobia-inducing limousine" (I'm not sure how that works), an indecent proposal (no, for real), page after page of Layla talking about how utterly hawt, talented, and perfect Trip is, and trite, banal dialogue that I'm convinced was masterminded just to push people into thoughts of suicide. Layla actually mind quotes the smelly pirate hooker line from Anchorman. Really! Most of the writing is just plain bad. "The music was pumping through my body; Trip's tongue was invading my mouth. We were totally making out." "I didn't want to tarnish her impression of the glamorous Hollywood facade she'd come to know..." How does one come to know an impression of a facade? When they're attacked by the paparazzi at one point and one of them tells Layla to smile, she thinks, "Smile? It was all I could do not to break down in tears. Who was this man and why were his hands on me? I didn't know him; we weren't friends. What gave him the right to even say my name?" Note to self: do not address anyone by name unless getting confirmation that we are, in fact, friends. Apparently, I don't have that right otherwise. Layla and Trip are trying to communicate more effectively (i.e. for the first time ever since they met a decade and a half ago)... "Striving for better communication wasn't always easy, but our recent efforts had been an improvement between us..." Fucking smoke signals would have been an improvement. Flag semaphore would have been an improvement. And there's the real rub; after spending the first two books pulling at my hair and mentally screaming at these two to just talk to each other, I ended up wishing they would just shut the fuck up and die.

(www.bookburnn.wordpress.com) Never have I felt so fooled than this. The concept. A duel between two well trained magicians? Count me in. A duel between two well trained magicians AND lovers? Give it to me. It all sounds right to me. It sounds perfect. I think this could be a perfect match for my frozen heart. This could be it. And then again, I could be wrong. Before I rant, I would like to say that I really wanted to like it. I wanted to. I tried to. And after being promised of a "fierce competition", "duel" and "headfirst into love", lies are what the book told. Maybe it didn't help that I read The Golem and The Jinni first. Now, try as I might, it's impossible for me not to compare the two, especially since its soo similar--forbidden love-esque, the presence of magic, toying with fate/destiny. Nonetheless, I still had (false) hope. That maybe, just maybe, in the end it'll be all worth it. And let's just say, it was a complete waste of my time. The writing, didn't speak to me, it felt (sort of) fake. It was supposed to be magical, entrancing, dreamy. But it felt like it was trying too hard that it came of as a bad imitation of what it should've been. What I'm trying to say is that it didn't feel real; it didn't felt true. And again with the lies: Fierce competition. When did that happen?! Did I miss a chapter or so? They weren't physically or mentally fighting. The continuity of the performance is the sole basis of the said "competition". So basically, it's just an endurance test. And it just goes on and on and on and on and on and on and on and on and on and on and on.. This book itself is an endurance test--whether you're strong or foolish enough to finish it. Duel. You can say that again. There are no flame-throwing, gesture-binding and tongue twister spells involved. More like a snap of a finger and boring written spells. See, they're trying to redefine things. A true duel would mean that they would meet and fight. But no, they don't want it to be that easy. Do they? By duel they mean, no contact with the other "fighter"--yes, they did meet; but whenever they do, they don't fight, not ever--and no "round one, fight!" --so basically you NEVER know when they're fighting because they themselves (characters) don't know either. By duel they actually mean, fighting but without an actual fight. Headfirst into love. By part three, they immediately KNEW they were in love. And no, they did not FELL in love. For your own sake, skip this. Do I like it: I wish Recommended to: To people who like wasting their time

It took me awhile to gather my thoughts over this book. I had to ruminate on it and check out a few other reviews that could more clearly describe how I felt about it. I believe I gave myself a sufficient amount of time inbetween this volume and Heartless, which I listened to two months ago. And yet, listening to this final volume was still a complete drag. I feel like Carriger lost her will for any effort. Now that Alexia has a baby (as well as Ivy), the entire story becomes a giant fangirl roleplaying game, or a "day in the life of." I can remember how fun it was to create large fandom families that I wrote with friends, and how fun it was to write what every single character was doing at any given moment - which...is what happened in here. Multitudes of moments and pages were dedicated to reminding me that Prudence is a baby who basically has a three word vocabulary, that Alexia has to admonish someone, that Lefoux is STILL untrustworthy, and don't forget that Ivy's babies have to speak at every moment as well. Much of this book felt like a giant "Now that we have all of these characters and babies from everyone we love, let's let them all prattle on for several pages before we get to a real plot." It was deplorably boring and I found my focus waning often while listening to this. Unfortunately, because of this, some pretty important plot development went by almost completely unnoticed. I would usually have started screaming when Biffy and Lyall got together but by the time I realized it was happening, it was too late. I was too bored with all of the slow plot development and prattling to realize a fanfiction I love was taking place. Lord Maccon's "death" was also wildly out of place with the tone of the book; I continued through that part of the book in cool disbelief, only to find out that my gut had been correct. A failure of a shocking climax and fan jerker, IMO. The plot itself was also incredibly underwhelming; I know the mysteries in this series are very simple, but when this one came to light, it was almost insultingly simple. Ivy's transition into a vampire queen was also done far too quickly without proper development or reactions from other characters. Floote's double crossing, though shocking, was also left to the dogs with a shrug, because apparently it's not that important that Alexia's man servant from before she was even born betrayed her (and we don't even hear an explanation about it....or the Order of the Brass Octopus....OR the nature of the soul stealers, for that matter) I did like how Lord Maccon's mortality wrapped up in the end so that he could grow old with Alexea. Very sweet. I still love Lord Akeldama and would love reading more about him. I was incredibly enraged with the reappearance of Felicity, and still cannot believe that she isn't given the appropriate punishment she deserves. Overall, this novel was frustratingly slow, lacking meaty plot and reasonable climaxes. A real disappointing ending to a decent series. I will not be looking into the series about Prudence. I wouldn't mind picking up the prequel about Alexia's father but I wouldn't know where to find it. One last note: seriously, a character named Bumtrinkle, or whatever?

This book is probably the best action-adventure fantasy I've ever read. The author's world-building is breathtaking. He even uses dialogue from several fictive languages (at least I didn't recognize them). A young boy (Kvothe) travels with his parents in a caravan of actors/musicians from town-to-town. This is their heritage and their talent. He learns about the use of sympathy - a form of magic - from an arcanist who travels with the troupe for a time and decides he wants to go to University to learn how to be an arcanist himself. Then things take a turn for the worse in his life. The story does not really slow down at any point. Although there are sections that seem a little slower than others, the pace is really perfect. There is an overarching plot, which I suppose is the glue that will hold this series together, in addition to many subplots. One of the most interesting things about the way this story is told is that it is in the first person because Kvothe is telling the story of his past to a Chronicler (in the present). That part of the story is told in third person perspective. A hard trick to pull off, but it felt seamless to me. In the present, there are several other points-of-view. But when Kvothe is telling his story, it is all in first-person limited - that is, only from his perspective. It works, believe me. Highly recommended - run out and buy it now.

Pages read: 23 What struck me immediately was the writing. I feel like Johnston's writing is technically very good, but it also feels very forced. The style is more on the ornate, stylized side, but that only works well when it flows naturally. As a result, A Thousand Nights felt stilted and dense to me, without giving me a real sense of the time, place, or people through the writing. I was also annoyed immediately by the name Lo-Melkhiin. Now, please correct me if you can tell me the origins of this name, but based on some preliminary googling, I can't find any similar names in the Middle Eastern region where qasrs would be. Every time I hit the name I stumbled. Which is a lot, since it's one of the only character names in the book. This I gleaned from reviews and a comment down below, though I'd already been wondering why I didn't know the heroine's name or her sister's. While this technique is clearly award-bait, I find it problematic to give only a murderer of hundreds of women a name but not his victims. (Plus I was hoping for more names so I could try to figure out where exactly it was set and if Lo-Melkhiin was a realistic name.) Still, I was going to give A Thousand Nights a real chance and determined to wait for the romance. Apparently, though, according to Brandy, there isn't romance. For her, this is a positive, but it's a kiss of death for me. I encourage you to check out her review for a different opinion, and I thank her for including enough detail that I can safely say that A Thousand Nights is not the book for me. I'll be over here snuggling my copy of The Wrath and the Dawn.

Aight y'all listen up. Basically this is The Breakfast Club except with murder, at least that's what the summary on the back of the book says. I can tell you that is false. For maybe about 50 pages it's "the Breakfast Club" with murder. Now with that subscription, I was expecting most of this book to take place in detention while the characters were trying to figure out who killed Simon. I was also expecting it to be more of a thriller than it was. Neither of these were the case. So as I said, the beginning of the novel was The Breakfast Club with murder. I definitely expected to get more time with Simon and get to know him a little better, but he was killed off within 30 pages and I was like what?! Also the whole breakfast club thing only lasted about 30 pages as well. There were about five point of views, which wasn't too bad. Sometimes I got confused as to who's POV it was. Doctorow's books always make me feel smarter by the time I'm finished reading them. Part of it is the integration of Doctorow's vast techie knowledge, the rest is seeing the parallels in the real world. In this one, there are teens all over the world, playing MMRPs and getting paid to do it. On the surface, it sounds like a great deal. Until you realize that their employers are totally shady and violent. What are a bunch of gamers to do in order to be taken seriously as workers? Form a union, of course. Doctorow brings in tons of behavioral economic theory as well as a healthy chunk of labor union history to make the story work. Toss in a pirate-radio host and you've got a revolutionary concept. And that's just what these kids are after: a labor revolution. One where they have the same rights as other workers. Since it's online, they can take it to a global level and transform the way the games themselves work. Once again, this is a pump-your-fist-in-the-air-and-shout-"viva la revolution! "-type of novel. Only problem is just how long and dense it is. At 500 pages, it's no light-weight (not to mention small print and margins, unlike most YA lit) and the settings/characters shift frequently. A typical chapter can take you through Mumbai, California and Singapore with a few stops in Shenzhen along the way. One must also be prepared for plenty of gaming lingo, which can take some getting used to for the non-gaming crowd. I had my high school kids read this for our monthly book group and most didn't wind up finishing it. They liked the concept, but the book itself wound up being too much of a challenge for them to finish.

Wow, this was absolutely not my cup of tea at all. Clearly this book has received otherwise very good reviews, so I forced myself to struggle through the first 1/3 of it before I just couldn't take any more. The story seems to consist completely of non-stop "witty banter" (I suppose you would call it) between the various main characters. For me, however, it was just plain ridiculous. Non-stop ridiculous characters and non-stop ludicrous dialogue. This is just one such example from chapter one (and keep in mind this dialogue is between two characters -- Gary, a unicorn without a horn, and Sam, a wizard apprentice -- who are currently tied up being held captive by the "evil" wizard, Lartin): "Horse?" Gary snarled. The pretty unicorn act dropped immediately. Red sparks shot from his nose. "Did you just call me a horse? Listen here, you two-legged bag of shit. I'm not a motherfucking horse. I am a unicorn, and I am magic and a beautiful creature made of fucking sunshine and rainbows and good feelings." "I knew it," I whispered. "Get your ass over here so I can stomp on your face," Gary said to Lartin. "Untie me, lie down on the ground, and let me stomp your face." "You don't have a horn," Lartin pointed out. "That's just rude," I said. "I didn't point out that your nose is really big. Why would you say something like that?" "Sam," Gary said tearfully. "He called me a horse." "Hey," I said. "Hey. Look at me." He did. His eyes were wet, and I wanted to punch Lartin in the spleen. "Who is the most beautiful unicorn in all of Verania?" "Me," Gary sniffed. "And who has the prettiest mane?" "Me." "And who is a badass motherfucker who'll gut a bitch?" "Me!" "Damn right." Ugh. More dialogue between Sam and Gary the unicorn from the same scene where they are captured by Lartin the bad wizard: "He's a villain," I said. "It's what they do. They have to broadcast their entire plan when they think they've won because no one else will ever listen to them." "Lame," Gary said, glancing at Lartin. "Girl, I really don't care. Unbind my legs before I scratch your eyes out." "You don't have fingers," I reminded him. "You can't scratch anything." "He's lucky I don't have my horn back yet," Gary muttered. "There'd be so much goring, it'd be unreal. It'd be like Gore City up in here. These roots are chafing. He should undo them." "Are you going to undo them?" I asked Lartin. "Uh, no?" he said. "You know I captured you and you're my prisoners, right? "Did he?" I asked Gary. "Well, we are tied up," Gary said. "And not in the fun way." This is the tone through the whole book. To be fair, some people clearly derive enjoyment from this and have rated the book quite highly. I, however, am absolutely not one of them and had no idea what I was getting myself into based on the book blurb. Big disappointment.

Fantastic concept, horrible execution. I know it's a translation, and that's why I persevered longer than it really deserved, but the narration was poor - it didn't flow, it had no spark to it, and it meandered far too often. Every time we got inside a character's head for a flashback or extended bit of introspection, my eyes glazed over and I came out of those dense, dry paragraphs forgetting where I was. The characters were as flat as they were unlikable, so much so that I found myself wishing the Black Rock Witch would just let loose and end it all. As for the concept of Black Spring and project Hex itself, I give Heuvelt full credit for trying to bring several classic horror tropes into the 21st century, but the attempt just didn't work for me. There were far too many leaps of logic required to make the town work, and far too little understanding of the human condition to make the project believable - everything that was happening to 'break' the story to the world, I would have expected decades ago, and I can't believe the government wouldn't take more drastic measures to keep new people out. As for the Black Rock Witch, she was a cool concept with a great backstory. I found myself wanting to know more about who she was, about what really happened to her son, how she came back to curse the town, and where the original settlers went. Like the story of the Roanoke Colony, it was the mystery and the speculation that made her tale so compelling. As much as I appreciated what Heuvelt was trying to do with his reversal of the trope, the story that reminded me that horror works best when the monsters are kept in the shadows, teasingly glimpsed, but held back for a climactic reveal. I admit, I skimmed a good chunk of the second half, just to see how it ended . but the final few chapters did nothing to redeem the book. Disappointing.

Well, now that I'm done with this book, I wonder why it doesn't receive more hype than a few craps I've read for the past couple of years or so because All Our Yesterdays is pretty good. More accurately, it's a pretty good efforts by a debut author, Cristin Terill. I tend to be very selective of reading any time-travel books because they can be mind-blowingly awesome (until it can cause me insomnia) or just purely bad. All Our Yesterdays surprisingly sits close towards the mind-blowingly awesome category which is a first for me. The blurb simply gives practically everything away and to be honest, I could predict the ending from miles away. Also, I didn't feel invested in any of the characters. I was frustrated not because the evils that a character has done (because we didn't really get to know how he transitioned from an innocent braniac into a ruthless scientist), but I was frustrated at how weak-willed the characters who supposed to finish him behave. Yeah, I know the author went around saying how if they are weak, they would kill him at the first sight blablabla but as the fate of the world is resting on their shoulders, they did a lame job of trying to save the humanity. As if that's not a strong enough motivation. The world building was pretty weak too. "How's outside? Bad?" "Worse." Don't give me that shit. Details matter. Otherwise, how would the readers truly understand the dire of the situation. And I swear two of the chapters had a wrong heading. It was confusing as hell. Ugh. Overall, I know this may sound like a negative review but trust me, it's actually a pretty good book. It kept me awake until 3 in the morning. I can't remember when was the last time a book managed to do that but I think it was years ago. So yeah. Although I would suggest you watch Loop (film) or/and Stein:Gate (anime) if you're looking for a better time travel story.

Classification: XXX The Pogrebin is a Russian demon, barely a foot tall, with a hairy body but a smooth, oversized grey head. When crouching, the Pogrebin resembles a shiny, round rock. Pogrebins are attracted to humans and enjoy tailing them, staying in their shadow and crouching quickly should the shadow's owner turn around. If a Pogrebin is allowed to tail a human for many hours, a sense of great futility will overcome its prey, who will eventually fall into a state of lethargy and despair. When the victim stops walking and sinks to their knees to weep at the pointlessness of it all, the Pogrebin will leap upon them and attempt to devour them. Easy to care for, it emits a low humming noise when contented. From time to time a very long, thin, pink tongue will emerge from the depths of the Puffskein and snake through the house searching for food. The Puffskein is a scavenger that will eat anything from leftovers to spiders, but it has a particular preference for sticking its tongue up the nose of sleeping wizards and eating their bogies. This tendency has made the Puffskein much beloved by wizarding children for many generations and it remains a highly popular wizarding pet.

I have this thing where I like to guess what rating I'm going to give a book after I finish it. So after reading about fifty pages, I took a guess. I liked it but I wasn't hooked so three stars easy. But then I kept reading.... After Hello is the most beautiful book I have ever read. Watching Sara and Sam come to terms with their pasts and growing closer was a complete pleasure. The two are so alike yet they look at things differently. The pacing was spot on - never too slow or too fast. In fact, I'd describe it as flowing. Everything, even when they were pressed for time, felt like an easy flow. Even when Sara and Sam didn't have a lot of time, they still took the time to appreciate each other and the life around them. Following their story was as gentle as following the breeze. I didn't exactly know where it would take me, and neither did they, but it was easy and wonderful to watch their story unfold. Both Sam and Sara have baggage but neither of them wear it on their sleeves. They spend a whole twenty four hours together but they were talking and getting to know each other during that time. They were helping each other work through the difficulties of life and their current situation. They were their for each other no matter what ugly memory decided to rear its head. Like Sam, I too believe that these characters were kindred spirits. This wasn't a love story. After Hello is about two people overcoming barriers that kept them from truly being happy. Yes, they eventually kiss, and quite honestly, I wanted that to happen long before the end, but Lisa Mangum can write a love story even when a book isn't about the love story. She held and protected that first kiss until the perfect moment. That moment was beautiful and full of possibilities for both characters. And those possibilities were simply beautiful.

I liked this least of the Sherlock Holmes books I've read. I only liked the parts that had Sherlock in them; I wasn't interested in the larger story, and skimmed it. This book is a single story, not a collection of short stories like most of the other Sherlock books. The free audiobook available from Project Gutenberg has excellent voice talent. Quote Some touch of the artist wells up within me, and calls insistently for a well-staged performance. Surely our profession, Mr. Mac, would be a drab and sordid one if we did not sometimes set the scene so as to glorify our results. The blunt accusation, the brutal tap upon the shoulder - what can one make of such a denouement? But the quick inference, the subtle trap, the clever forecast of coming events, the triumphant vindication of bold theories - are these not the pride and the justification of our life's work? At the present moment you thrill with the glamour of the situation and the anticipation of the hunt. Where would be that thrill if I had been as definite as a timetable?

The only reason why I bought this book was because of the gorgeous cover. My excitement over this book only grew more once I read the synopsis. I absolutely love stories where the characters escape to virtual worlds. I was not a big fan of this book. It was an uphill battle to read. I didn't particularly enjoy the writing style, mainly due to the main character rephrasing what was implied in the previous sentence. I understand why Regan supported Patrick while simultaneously rifled through the lies with Josh, I just wished she realized who was in the wrong sooner. Yes, Elusion is her father's second child and she wants to protect the last thing she has of her father. But when the proof is staring her straight in the face, it drags out the story. Lies. Lies. And more lies. This book wasn't terrible, it just wasn't my cup of tea. I did enjoy the scattered plot twist and mind puzzles thrown in throughout the book. But I found it difficult to predict the outcome if the main character is caught up in her own problems. That leads me to another thing. I think the story could've done without Regan and Josh getting together. Only because she began to question everything soon after they met. Not that is not necessarily a bad thing, but when she doubted her trust in Josh numerous times it felt like useless fluff. Especially when she took one glance at this face and instantly trusted him again. Again, I this book has potential and could be really enjoyable to some. It just wasn't for me, which I hate to say because I already bought the second book.

1.5 stars It boggles my mind that this book has such fantastic reviews. I just don't understand. The first 50 pages were good, as well as the last 30 or so, but the rest was just goddamn awful. For a book that is not even 400 pages, I felt like I had been reading and reading for hours and never making any progress. The first person POV was so monotonous, it made it seem like Fitz had absolutely no personality. To make that worse, there were no side characters good enough to hold my attention either. Oh, and don't forget the fact that the whole thing felt like it was being told rather than shown (isn't that supposed to be a sin in writing?). Combine all that with chapters full of info dumps and you get one incredibly dull book. I didn't care about the characters, I didn't care about the supposed Red Ship conflict that was happening. The only thing I had any vague interest in was the political stuff, and even that was just bothersome most of the time. Am I going to continue on with the series? I suppose I'll try the next book, since I own a copy of it, but if it doesn't get better halfway through, I won't force myself. I think that's more than fair at this point. By the way, for a book with the word 'assassin' in the title, there sure isn't very much assassinating going on.

Ugh. This is one of those books that the more I think about it, the more I hate it. The first half made me curious enough to keep slogging through, but I really wish I hadn't. There are so many things wrong about this story that it's hard to know where to begin. Maybe I should start with the characters. Besides the fact that the author chose the most bizarre of names for the hero and heroine (Dank and Pagan? Seriously? Are they goblins? Do they steal babies and live under bridges? ), they are ridiculous, inconsistent, and unbelievable. The heroine is touted over and over as being this insanely unique "soul", but the only reasons ever given is that she sees ghosts (which isn't that unique because she runs into another character in the book that has the same ability) and because she's really self-sacrificing, kind, and brave. Being those things aren't unique. There are lots of people in the world that have those qualities and the heroine doesn't even really have them anyway. She is selfish through and through. For most of the book, she's dating this guy she doesn't really care about, but won't break up with him because she doesn't want to give him up. Not because she cares about him or is really worried that he'll be hurt, but because she wants something "normal" in her life. One minute she's making out with the guy she really likes and then is doing the same with her boyfriend the next. I can accept and understand someone who is torn between their feelings for two people, but that doesn't excuse her cheating on both of them. And she is the farthest thing from brave. She is weak. The only time she's really willing to make a hard decision is when the life of the boy she cares about is in danger. If she were truly this amazing soul everyone keeps claiming, she would be willing to step up and do something more than spend half of the book crying and moaning over the fact that she can't be with the guy she wants. And that brings me to the hero--AKA Mr. Self-Centered. Their relationship wouldn't have developed if he hadn't pursued her so strongly from the beginning. He moves into her school, stalks her, constantly pushes himself into her life, and then when she finally cares about him and wants to be with him, he pulls the "we can't be together" card. Even with her initial attraction she wouldn't have gone any deeper into that relationship if he had just left her alone. But he didn't. And every time he pulls away, he reverses again, makes out with her, and then tells her that he just can't help himself because he wants her so much. That is the definition of selfish--putting your own needs and desires over the well-being of others. The "love" in this love story is juvenile, self-centered, and insulting. The hero and her boyfriend (yes, two separate characters...) go about trying to get her attention by making her jealous. In private, they are kind and sweet, but then jerky to her in public. Yes, that changes eventually, but having a guy be a tool to you shouldn't be a turn-on. The characters all care more about their relationship than how it's affecting those around them. When they are separated, the world comes to an end and they will never survive this heart ache. And then it's packaged as though that's what true love is, as if any widow or widower or parent who's lost a child who doesn't fall apart completely and are unable to function after losing a loved one is less caring or in love with that person than this idiotic girl and her tool of a love interest. This book reminded me so much of Twilight, it was gagging, but at least Twilight had an interesting world and mythology that held up. This book doesn't. Supposedly, the hero (again, I'm going to point out that his name is Dank. That's right, Dank!) is Death personified and his job is to collect souls so they can move on. It is even stated that they cannot move on unless he does his job, but when the world average is 2 deaths per second, he spends an awfully long time hanging out at high school, chasing girls he can't be with, and playing with his rock band (yeah, rock band...cue eye roll). And this novel's take on reincarnation is weird. Add to that whole mess a very bizarre section of the book where the heroine is committed to a mental institution for PTSD. Apparently, in that world people with no history of self-harm are committed without even trying therapy first. And apparently, rather than putting her in group therapy home or something along that lines, they choose to commit her to an insane asylum where she is locked up with truly unstable people. Yes, she did have a freak out moment where she needed to be sedated, but she isn't committed until several days later and it's by her mom's decision. One minute they're talking about her going to therapy and after one session she's committed. That makes no sense. The ending absolutely clinched my dislike for this book when rather than ending it properly, the author decides to throw this major bomb (which had been set up in the plot) about one of the characters and cut off the story. I could go on and on about all the things wrong with this story (I haven't even covered how awkward the dialogue is in many places), but I'll just end this now before this becomes a full-blown tirade.
