I hated this book. It was just full of unlikable characters. I should have quit when Cooper's dad after leaving his wife and two kids to go live with his side piece(A side piece he was having an affair with for 5 years) makes Cooper visit him at his side piece's home and the side piece's son proceeds to call him dad in front of Cooper. They just couldn't help themselves, their love was just so amazing who cares if the lives of two children and an innocent woman was blown apart. Cons: I tried to give Butcher the benefit of the doubt. After 6 books, I've given up. This series is NOT a cleverly meta satire on Dresden's sexist perspective of women. The writer and protagonist are truly "chauvinistic pigs," (in their own words!) plain and simple. I initially figured Butcher was poking fun at Dresden, whenever he tried his "nice guy" act. It's okay, because he's demonstrating how growing up without female role models can stunt your emotional growth! That is, apart from a weirdly incestuous relationship with his adoptive sister. However, Dresden actually DOES see women as sexualized objects in need of his benevolent assistance. And as time goes by, it seems increasingly clear that Butcher does, too. Murphy, the badass police lieutenant lauded by Dresden's fan base as proof of his "woke"ness? At the first sign of trouble in the vampire basement, she cries out "What do we do, Dresden???!?!" Help me, oh wise male benefactor! Would the tough-as-jerky police officer Butcher describes her as lose composure like that in a crisis? Did we REALLY need to mention Lara Raith's high heels twice? Once, when Dresden ogled her, and the second time, when a vampire knocked her out of them? And if Lara Raith is so much stronger than Thomas, why does she look terrified at the first sign of a stronger opponent, when Thomas (shot, immobile, about to bleed out) can KO an opponent with just one swipe of a leg? Let's talk about Murphy's sister. I got SO tired of the "pretty dumb girl" stereotype after... maybe the 3rd paragraph or so? Yes, dumb blondes exist. So do dumb brunettes, redheads, people with black hair (do we have a word for that?).. People exist. We don't all make smart choices. Deal with it! Just because you insult Murphy's sister doesn't mean that you're being an ally to feminism, Butcher. You know what would help? Just regular old characters, who happen to be female. Also, that exchange between Kincaid and Murphy is horrifying. I think Butcher's intention was to illustrate how obnoxious men like Kincaid mistreat Murphy (don't underestimate Murphy for being female; short doesn't mean weak, etc.). However, his execution is so cringe-inducingly clumsy that it negates his intentions. Pros: Plot development earns Blood Rites its one lonely star. *spoilers* Thomas Raith reveals their brotherly bond, they adopt Mouse, they move in together, Dresden gets pissy because Ebenezer dares to be besmirch his morals, blah, blah, blah. And that's just the B plot. The A plot involves a gig with a porn studio, vampire basement stakeout, and attacking Lord Raith on his home turf. Lots of plot packed into one book. Still... I get that good protagonists should be flawed, but Dresden is SO FLAWED that it detracts from the reading experience. Actually, it would be awesome if instead of being brothers, Thomas and Harry had instead been 1) unrelated, 2) commenced a "Welcome To Night Vale" style vampire-and-wizard relationship. I'd buy that book. ...actually, that would put an interesting twist into the ongoing wizard/vamp war. Huh. Butcher also deserves credit for executing a dick joke that is 1) central to the plot, 2) consistent with the rules of magic in the Dresdenverse, 3) does NOT involve any softcore porn scenes. Basically, Dresden's mother cursed Papa Raith with the equivalent of ED for vampires. In fact, this installment doesn't stop for any sex scenes at all. Kind of odd, considering that this one's client du jour is a porn video director, and the previous 5 books have all featured random sex scenes. Sure, Dresden complains that he hasn't gotten any in a while, but that's all he does. Heck, BOB sees more action in this volume. In conclusion, I've finally seen the light. Dresden Files is trashy adventure fantasy AIMED at the lowest common denominator in the male populace. And if that's the case, Butcher's target demographic deserves better. Ladies and gentlemen, you don't need this book's distorted perceptions on male and female relationships. Go read SAGA, or any damn thing. Have a little self respect. If only the magical world in it weren't so well-developed... Someone needs to write a series in the Dresdenverse, but MINUS Dresden and Jim Butcher. I'll probably keep reading the series, but mostly so I can discuss the magical lore with my workout buddy.

This book is one of the best ever! Oh my gosh. There are no words to describe this book. It is now one of my all time favorites. There was so much loss. Loss of lives, loss of beauty, and loss of one's identity. There was horrible guilt, as well, because Ambrose is the one who convinced his four friends to join the service with him and they didn't make it home. Ambrose Young was the most beautiful of young men with everything going for him until he was critically injured in war. He was a wrestling star that had the opportunity to go to college on a wrestling scholarship. He had what all young men dream of. It is the tale of one girl's (Fern) love for a broken boy, and a wounded warrior's love for an unremarkable girl. A friendship that overcomes heartache. The Book Description say it like this: Modern tale of Beauty and the Beast, where we discover that there is a little beauty and a little beast in all of us. Fern had loved Ambrose from afar. She knew her appearance: fiery red hair, braces, thick glasses and a very small stature were not appealing to guys and there was no way she could compete against the beautiful, curvy gals in her school. But, our girl Fern, she knew and loved the real Ambrose, the one underneath the beauty and the wrestling. This book was remarkable, the writing excellent, and the storyline gripping. It pulls you in and doesn't let loose until you have read it all...and then I didn't want it to end...ever!!! Amy Harmon is to be commended. Added to this story is a wheelchair bound young man, Bailey, Fern's cousin and best friend. He is an incredible young man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. He displays great courage and heroism and was so completely lovable. DO NOT MISS THIS BOOK!!!!! I read more than 300 books a year and have for many years and this book ranks in my top 5. Words cannot efficiently describe how wonderful this book was. There is angst; you will cry; you will feel so sad; but you will also rejoice in the power of love!

4 Stars Read full review here: https://5171milesbookblog.wordpress.com/ What I admire most about YA dystopian authors is their massive imagination and their creations of new worlds, new societies, new rules and new ways of thinking. Nothing is impossible. Some dystopians focus on a new world and a society that was only recently formed as a result of a war that our current society caused. Other dystopians focus on a world and a society that existed for hundreds or thousands of years because our world as we know it never existed in the first place. The Winner's Curse by Marie Rutkoski is one of those dystopians. It focuses on seventeen-year-old Kestrel and the world she lives in. New worlds, societies and rules in dystopian novels need to be explained to the reader. And while some authors explain those worlds in long discriptive passages in a few chapters, Rutkoski revealed the Valorian and Herran society mostly through dialogue and only through a few descriptions. The revelations were scattered throughout the book and the reader learned bits and pieces here and there, which I really enjoyed. It was confusing yet fascinating to watch Kestrel and Arin interact with each other. With each chapter it became more obvious that Kestrel and Arin's initial master-and-slave-connection merged into a more affectionate one. But as quickly as their initial connection changed into a more intimate one, they were just as quickly to put their feelings on hold. You see, on the outside it looks like they come from different worlds, but the more you learn about their respective societies (especially before the Valorians started the war), you quickly figure out that they are not that different after all. Although they have a lot in common and share feelings for one another, they both want what's right and best for their people. Their struggle to stay committed to that was difficult. They were always tempted to decide against their societies and their way of thinking was a constant back an forth which resulted in a few sacrifices at the expense of their societies. The possibility to escape from our everyday lives into a completely different world is great. I enjoyed getting to know Arin, Kestrel and the world they live in. I'm eager to pick up The Winner's Crime soon to see where the journey will take them. Review to come!

Sometimes I really do not understand YA ratings on this site. To All the Boys I've Loved Before, a book that was really fluffy and had some character development/consistency issues, has a 4.08. This book, with a fantastically developed protagonist, believable conflicts, and, honestly, a really fun writing style, has a 3.55! This book was way, way better than To All the Boys I've Loved Before. The good: The Spectacular Now is a truly impressive character study. I love books like this, because by the end I feel like I know the protagonist inside and out. Sutter is a funny guy, but he has a huge heart, both of which make the story enjoyable to read. He's also much more dependent on alcohol than he himself thinks. For that reason, the ending makes your heart ache, but I admire the author for creating a realistic ending instead of making Sutter change dramatically, because that would have felt a little cheap. It's a good reminder that even in YA, stories don't always have fairy tale endings. The bad: The end of this book left something to be desired, and I can't decide if it's because Sutter himself left so many loose ends or the author did. I think it's a little bit of both. I want to be clear, though, that I don't mean the actual ending itself- because I absolutely loved that- but more the fact that when the book came to an end, literally nothing had been resolved. I don't necessarily think that's a bad thing, but it's a book that won't give you a lot of closure. You're going to want to read more that isn't there. Also, some people will probably hate Sutter and think he comes off as a flippant hedonist. I personally adored him, but if you don't like the protagonist, you probably won't end up enjoying this book. Overall: This book is surprisingly deep and poignant for YA. Sutter is a truly memorable protagonist, and I loved being inside his head for the duration of The Spectacular Now.

Holy wow! What a book!! This was an impressively written novel that covers such relate-able content in a way that I feel would make it accessible to both pre-teens, all the way through to adults, guys and girls alike. 16-year old Samantha (Sam) works her hardest to keep her overly anxious brain that "messes with her mind" and severe OCD from being discovered by anyone - especially her core group of friends, the Crazy 8s. Those friends (think the girl pack from Mean Girls), are the epitome of frenemies...best friends since kindergarten, but in more recent years, they've been pushing Sam to her limits. Despite this relationship from being rather unhinged and more than a little unhealthy, Sam strives to maintain that friendship as a way of self-identifying. Finally, on the first day of school in her senior year of high school, Samantha is introduced to a group of people, and a world, that completely throws her into a spin and forces her to start taking the initiative in taking control of her mind, her thoughts, and her life. Seriously, wow. I mean, I felt that this reflected and rang true on so many levels, I don't see how anyone - even those without something as serious as OCD or an anxiety disorder - can't NOT feel the truth in this. Everyone has had the experience feeling the highs and the lows of the social ladder, and the main character - as well as a number of the rest of the cast of characters - are just so easy to identify with. Whether you are into poetry or not (personally, I've never felt much affinity for it), it works so very well in this story. **I feel the need at this point to mention that this is NOT in verse and the book is for the most part just a book, not stanzas of poetry front to back - so those of you who shut a book as soon as you hear the mention of poetry, please don't. I really appreciated the realism that Stone put into this work, identifying CBT (cognitive behaviour therapy) techniques, as well as showing a psychiatrist and a few other adult characters as positive, and supportive people that Sam and the other teens recognize as people who they can trust (something seriously lacking in the YA genre). I also really liked the fact that while there was sex included in this book, it was not the be-all and end-all...it was just something that happened - it was kept real and not exaggerated in any way. Tamara Ireland Stone, thank you for a beautiful book! I wish I had something like this to read when I was a teenager. I think you highlighted something that is so very simple, and yet also so true, that we often (even adults!) trick ourselves into forgetting: mistakes in life are necessary for us to learn; it's all one big trial-and-error experiment, we just have to let ourselves learn from those mistakes.

She has begun to fast and her mother has removed her from school so she is basically a prisoner in her room. Anna, the 11 year old child, has been fasting for four months and apparently thriving when a committee of townspeople hire two nurses to supervise her. They want to find out if it's a hoax or a miracle. One nurse is a nun and the other is a Nightingale nurse who served in the Crimea, Lib Wright. She is unsurprisingly tough nut who is determined to get to the bottom of this purported miracle. The family and child are deeply religious and this grates on Nurse Wright immensely. As she spends her time overseeing the child, it is mind numbingly boring. She can't take her eyes off her as she may be trying to smuggle food. The only activity is prayers and more prayers. And under her supervision, the child's health starts to fail. This is a perfect book for a book club. It really makes you want to discuss the situation, the choices the adults make, how little power a child has and the impact of religion on lives. It's one of the more thought provoking books I have read in a long time. After I thought I could not read one more page of the endless routine, the end snuck up on me and really blew me away. I didn't see it coming.

Revelations was one of my more anticipated books of 2013, since I loved Renegade so much! And with the ending of Renegade? Hell yes I wanted to get my hands on this. Diving right into the review, I found that while I did miss the world of Elysium, Mother always chasing at our characters' heels, Revelations was intriguing and chilling in it's own way--just in a different way than Renegade's. We're introduced to the Surface which we now know for sure is a futuristic world and seeing Souders perform her worldbuilding magic here too was stunning. There are certain bits of Renegade and Revelations you can see sort of reflect each other and it was unbelievably fun figuring it out as you went along. The number one thing I loved about Revelations was how bits and pieces of Renegade, of Elysium, would sneak into Evie's brain. She would say something that we could recognize immediately or she would do something that she'd done before. I always did love amnesia stories--but knowing everything our character's forgotten? I never realized how much the anticipation can kill you! You just keep hoping, waiting, for her to remember everything. And does she? Evie is a rather fascinating character, even with her memories gone. In some ways, she's more innocent before, without her memories of bloodshed and escape, but we can clearly see the wear on tear on her with not remembering anything. (At times, I just wanted to shove Renegade in her hands and tell her to read anything--but of course I couldn't do that.) Evie is still a fabulous character though. While she could be called a damsel in distress character, her personality just drew her as a strong and independent character--not quite the DID after all. We are introduced to a new character--Asher. I'll admit, I was completely worried about a love triangle at first. After all, two hot guys? And Evie's traveling with both of them while having a ton of alone time with Asher? Oh yes, I was wary. But REST ASSURED. There's no love triangle here--instead we get a brother like figure who would do anything for Evie--just not quite the same way as Gavin. Speaking of Gavin, we would get little bits and pieces from his POV and it was rather fascinating putting it all together. His relationship with Evie was absolutely adorable and you could see how fiercely they loved each other, and how desperate Gavin was to keep Evie safe. The plot was absolutely thrilling. I was always anxious to find out what would happen next and there are some undeniably creepy things that go on. It turns out the world of Elysium hasn't changed much--and Mother? She's still as psychotic as ever, and still the perfect villain. We learn more about Evie's past, and just a bit more about Mother. And the ending? Oh God. J.A. Souders writes a heart pounding plot in Revelations, making it almost as action packed as Renegade while also introducing us to the new addition to Evie and Gavin's little duo. Not suffering from Sequel Syndrome at all, Revelations is a brilliant book to continue the series! I'm dying to read the third one and anxious to find out what's next for our characters in their world. A seriously amazing series, I can't stop recommending this to everyone!

** spoiler alert ** UPDATE: I decided to think about it for a couple of days and discuss my feelings with a couple of people, and we are agreed. The cover copy and the quoted book reviews give a false impression of what this book is about. I feel like I signed up to read one book and was given another one completely. That being said, I stand by my review and my rating. ORIGINAL REVIEW: My primary emotion when I finally finished this book was anger. Just about every review I read of this book--glowing, all of them--focused on the humor, how funny this book was. When a book is universally described as funny--not dark humor, but funny--I expect a certain amount of levity. What I don't expect is a dead mom, an absent dad, a mentally ill sister, and a young girl who is kidnapped and sexually assaulted by a pedophile. I might have liked this book better if I had been given any indication of how dark it was, in both tone and subject matter. And I say might: it's entirely possible I wouldn't have. The book collapses under its own weight at times; there are so many metaphors, and the language is impossibly dense at times. This reads like a series of stories that were pasted together in novel form, but they don't quite fit together: about halfway through the book splits into separate storylines, which (at least for me) disrupted the narrative flow. This is a slow-moving book, with perhaps too much attention to the language and not enough to the structure. There are some good things: the history within the story, and the Bigtree family mythology. But to have a young girl--she doesn't even wear a bra--telling her abuser she loves him, and to include a violent sexual assault that serves no other purpose than to finally get the girl to run away from this predator and that apparently has no lasting impact on her . well, I don't think that's "heart-warming" or "exuberant" or "bewitching" or "scathingly funny."

An advance copy of this title was provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review. A copy of the audiobook was also won from the author. This review can also be found at The Starry-Eyed Revue. The Star-Touched Queen is a story of many things: love, loss, redemption, revenge, learning and knowing oneself...and then some. The heart of the story finds its origin in the Greek myth of Hades and Persephone, but I also found myself captivated by reminders of other favorite tales, like that of Bluebeard and Beauty and the Beast and even The Neverending Story. Basically, this novel combines so many aspects from my favorite stories and yet somehow manages to remain unique and compelling. And it's a stand-alone!! That, like, never happens anymore: a fantasy novel that comprises the pages of a single book and yet manages to convey the magic of three. The magic was all over the pages of this story, and what a lovely story it was. I'm actually kind of impressed with myself that I was able to savor it, rather than devouring it in one sitting. The first time I read it, anyway. ;-) I won a copy of the audiobook from the author and that I did devour immediately upon receiving. And if possible, the story is even more majestic, nay hypnotic, on audio. The narrative is simply gorgeous and poetic, no matter which way you experience it. I could lose myself for days in a story of this caliber. It felt like a story of before and after, and yet it spans so much more than that: a love that will not be denied, a betrayal that unbalanced the worlds, and a need for vengeance so deep that it threatened to destroy the worlds completely. I cannot fathom how Chokshi could fit so much into such a tiny book and have it turn out so lovely. She must have a bit of Otherworldly magic of her own. She so seamlessly weaves the Indian culture and the mythology in this story. It's a true work of art. And gorgeous to behold, from the descriptions of life in the palace of Bharata to the incandescent beauty of Akaran. (I'm actually super glad I listened to the audiobook because I was saying practically every proper noun incorrectly. And it sounds so much lovelier in Priya Ayyar's velvety voice.) The characters were all so full and bursting with vitality. Yet, I never imagined that a flesh-eating demon horse would become one of my favorite characters, maybe of ever. But somehow, Kamala wormed her vicious way into my heart. Honestly, this was the aspect of the story that reminded me most of The Neverending Story because I felt like Kamala was akin to Falkor, joking about eating the main character and becoming a source of companionship and encouragement throughout the story. I've always wanted my own luck dragon, but now I kind of want a demon horse, too. Which is probably the best testament to how amazing and compelling this novel is. You're living and breathing the story right with the characters, and then you're wishing you were part of the story, too. Funny how that happens. I've read this book twice now and I still can't get enough of it... GIF it to me straight: First Falkor, now Kamala. I'm going to need a zoo for all of my favorite imaginary friends.

An interesting, thought-provoking book that's not really for those readers who need a strong plotline. Anna is fifteen, angry at her mother and probably feeling a little displaced (her mom is expecting a new baby) steals her mom's girlfriend's credit card number and buys herself a ticket to LA to stay with her older sister, Delia. Delia, in turn, is a struggling actress who is sleeping with Roger, her creepy, egotistical director behind her boyfriend's back. As a way to pay back the money she "borrowed," Anna gets a job with Roger researching the Manson girls for a movie he wants to make. Through the story, Anna discusses one Manson girl after the other. American Girls had the kind of drifty plot I can enjoy if the writing is good, and it was. And I always love a slightly seedy LA setting (much better than the glitzy LA setting imo). Though this was supposedly set in the present, I kept having this weird sense that the story didn't feel current -- Anna felt like one of the kids I knew growing up in the 80s. (There were a few cell phones thrown in, but I wasn't entirely feeling the 2016 vibe). Anna's fascination with the Manson cult did feel very real to me -- at her age I went through a huge Ann Rule reading phase. Anna's overall assessment of the Manson girls was a little troubling: she seemed to think of them as just girls who were in the wrong place at the wrong time and made "bad choices," like she did with the credit card. I found this takeaway a little disturbing and highly debatable -- while I do agree that one mistake can change the course of a person's life, I really disagree that anyone in the wrong place and the wrong time could just .... whoops ... deliberately go out and murder a bunch of innocent people. This could make a good book club discussion! Read more of my reviews on YA Romantics or follow me on Bloglovin

This book! I can't. Here's the thing. Once upon a time a young girl was seduced, under the pretenses of true love, marriage and happily-ever-after. Of course, nothing like that happened, the girl is ruined and pregnant at sixteen. She is despised by everyone, condemned, they're calling her a whore and whatnot. It's the nineteenth century after all. If you're a girl, you better be a virgin or you can drop dead, nobody would care. So this girl vows revenge on everyone, they are all going to pay for the way they mistreated her and her daughter. She creates this alter ego, pretends to be a man and manages to fool the whole world.Chase, her alter ego, is smart, wise, ruthless, cunning, and with her three partners she creates an exclusive gaming hell where all the aristocrats who once made her life living hell, now lose their fortunes and respectability. She creates another version of herself, Anna the prostitute (she isn't really a prostitute), so she can monitor everything that happens in the gaming hell from the front rows. Ten years later, she is the ultimate puppeteer. She has all the threads in her hands. Chase is one of the most powerful men in London. The king has nothing on him. But now, her real self needs a respectable husband, so that her daughter has a shot at normalcy. And here's what makes no sense to me. Everyone, I mean everyone, knows of your scandal, knows your daughter is a bastard (it's the same as with non-virgins, if you're a bastard, you just better drop dead, no one cares about you) and yet you still insist on marrying a viscount, thinking that somehow this marriage will save your daughter. How? You think she's gonna find a family where that won't be held over her head? It's roughly the Victorian era, people are judgemental hypocrites, it will not be easy on her, any way. Logic flaw aside, she doesn't even love that viscount (and it was strongly hinted he might be gay). She is in love with the second most powerful man in London (after her ofc) , the newspaper magnate, Duncan West. Plenty of drama ensues. My god, you would think that a woman who rises from the ashes with no one's help, all on her own, is a strong, confident, brave woman, who takes life by the balls and allows no one to tramp on her. Yeah, no. Georgiana is a wuss. She is insecure, she is a coward, she is a friggin sheep and Duncan her sheppard. She allows him to blackmail her, to humiliate her, to disrespect her, to push her around. She is pathetic. Duncan on the other hand is a lying hypocrite with a hero complex. Apparently he wanted Anna for a long time, but she a ho, so no go. Only when he found out she's really Georgiana, a daughter of a duke, he's after her, wants to save her from that awful life in that gaming hell. Duncan requests that Georgiana gives up all her secrets so he can protect her from Chase, who is using her and who is terrorizing her, while in the meantime he evades every question she asks. Georgiana explicitly says that her relationship with Chase is not like that, not even sexual, but Duncan won't hear it, because she's a stupid female, what does she know about anything. She needs rescuing and that's it. Dear god, this story had so much potential! Imagine a power play between the two most important people in London, while battling an ever-growing attraction to each other. Imagine them realizing that battling is counterproductive, and then unifying their forces to beat every one of their enemies. Imagine them living as equals, being a family and just enjoying what life has to offer. That would be something worth reading. Read and decide for yourself. As for me, I've outgrown this kind of stories. Never Judge a Lady by Her Cover might have been once a tolerable read, but like everything in this world, my reading tastes have evolved.

This review was done by KissinBlueKaren I really enjoyed the first book in this series The Fire Sermon. Map of Bones is the second book in this series. **This review contains major spoilers for book one. Map of Bones continues with it's dark setting and bleak future for the survivors of nuclear fallout. This story follows Cass after the death of Kip. Cass is accompanied by siblings Piper (the former leader of the Omegas) and Zoe. Zoe is an alpha twin who chose to stay with her Omega brother and be part of the resistance. Once they join up with other resistance Omegas things move at a crazy pace. They are gonna make a discovery that changes everything for the Alphas in control and might be enough to gain an edge for the resistance. I really liked Zoe and Piper. I think both of their backgrounds lead Cass to the place she needs to be as a seer for the resistance. This story starts off a little slow as they gain each others trust and figure out how to live together. Zoe and Piper add so much to this story, that I don't think a review can be done without mentioning them. Zoe is an alpha so her very presence shows that some people can overcome their prejudices and live together. Once they meetup with other Omegas and the soldiers for the resistance, we are back to square one with the prejudice about seers. Actually, prejudice is a reoccurring theme in this story. I can see that almost everyone in this world harbors a little prejudice and it keeps them from co-habitation. Alliances are made for some different groups but it is not without problems and daily struggle. I honestly didn't enjoy the first 50% that much. I was really sad thinking I would have to write a negative review after liking the first book so much. There was a lot of idle time traveling and back and forth in conversations. I felt like these characters are on the run for so long, and then after that 50% mark the focus is off running and on to something else, (it was a weird transition). I almost gave up on the book, to be honest. I am glad I didn't but readers should be aware that the beginning is slow going. There are some big things revealed in this story. One thing that is revealed answers a lot of "how in the hell?" questions I had in the first book. The other gave me major angst for the fate of Cass. Those big things saved the story for me and made me so excited to read the next book in this series. They didn't completely save my rating though.

It's been a while since I read RED RISING, so I feel like a missed out a little with GOLDEN SON. Don't get me wrong, if you liked the first book in the series, you'll like this one, and probably better than the first, because everything is bigger: bigger stakes, bigger battles, bigger worlds. The action is punched up, and if you like your sci-fi on the range of solar systems, you can have it here. Whereas the first one was like the Hunger Games on a terraformed Mars, GOLDEN SON is more like an episode of STAR TREK where everyone's favorite bold space explorers have to engage in a little diplomacy with the Klingons (and everyone knows how well that works out, right?) There's less transformation here and more politics. There is probably more death, and death that was supposed to hit me hard, but it's been too long since I read RED RISING for me to be invested in the characters. You won't find much "remember how this happened?" in GOLDEN SON--and I wish there had been, because as much as I liked the first book, I only had the vaguest sketches of what happened in my head (the curse of reading too many books, I guess). Regardless, this is a great book. The action is tight and the world-building is vast. Betrayal and revelations are around every corner. I just felt like there was an undercurrent I was missing because I didn't remember some of the plotlines from the first book. Also, beware the ending--you'll want to know when the next book is out, and why it isn't out already, because you will probably want to throw GOLDEN SON at the wall when you finish. Book 3, MORNING STAR, can't come soon enough! Received as a free digital ARC via Netgalley and the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

Reviewer: Diane Genre: M/M Contemporary 5 Hearts Review: Jake and Nate are the same age, they have been friends since birth since their mothers were best friends and the two boys became best friends as well. Jake was the athlete, Nate was the "scary smart" one! Nate came out in 8th grade, first to Jake, who supported him - and if the smart did not make him a bully target, add gay to that and if not for Jake, school would have been a lot more challenging! The story is told from the alternating points of view of Jake and Nate. These two men were first introduced in the first Home story, He Completes Me, so that could be a bit of a spoiler for the ending, however, that book does not explain how they came to be a couple or what challenges they had to deal with to get there. Boy, does this book do that in spades! Okay, this is two in a row where the author had me crying early on in the book! And for anyone who reads my reviews, you know if a book can make me cry, I usually love it! That was the case here, especially with Jake who sees so much and makes some very tough choices before he even finishes high school! Then to put himself on the line to the man he loves, his bestfriend, who then does not believe him! As the story progresses, they each go back to memories of key events with each other growing up. My translation says these are 3rd year B class (second semester) junior high students (9th grade) but I can't help thinking that they are really supposed to be 3rd year middle school students (7th grade). This would make an enormous difference; but let's not quibble. The omniscient narrator probes the head of his male students pretty well (not so well with his female students) but the writer also assumes an eighth grade (let me split the difference) mentality. Shuya might fantasize about (**spoiler alert**) overpowering a boatload of trained SDF soldiers (with a bullet in his shoulder, no less) but this stretches credibility beyond anything reasonable (I can believe that, with enough exposure to junior high student, many people might be willing to send them to The Program). I did like the ending, although there was no need to (**spoiler alert**) kill off any potential epilogue-love-triangle with Shogo. What Takami doesn't explain, however, is why The Greater East Asia Republic is sponsoring The Program ("instilling paranoia" is not good enough). I think it might be better explained as a means of controlling the underclass. We traditionally think of the underclass as limited to the chronically unemployable--but really, we should extend this classification to anyone doing a job that is relatively meaningless (unrewarding, with positions easily filled through the minor training of random individuals). A successful society has to breed a fairly extensive underclass (you never know when a war or plague might make it useful). I believe it was Voltaire who suggested that whenever European nations fought, 100,000 men would be facing each other, half of them being ravaged by syphilis. War and disease were the means by which nations traditionally controlled the size of their underclass. But our wars are now too small, internal medicine too successful, and our population too great. In some parts of Japan, only the Xiong (oldest son) was traditionally allowed to marry and have a family (see The Ballad of Narayama--1983). While this left the Chang Nan Yi Wai noNan Xing horny-but-non-reproductive, I can't imagine anyone remaining so un-copulative today. However, if you had enough of these programs (Takami is almost there) you could use them to cull your underclass. This might be a better explanation--in fact, this might also be a better explanation for the Hunger Games--although, then, I suppose, you'd lose The Capitol's network coverage. But why junior high schools? Why not nursing home? It wouldn't be as interesting, but might solve the nation's social security/aging populace problem. Maybe they could call it The Chronic Constipation Games--give them bedpans instead of gladii.

First of all, can we please thank Laini Taylor for writing books? Because she could have been anything else in life but she chose the right path. Laini is a ray of light in the darkest part of the forest of young adult and fantasy books. She captures words like a thief and turn them into magic. The pace of this story was slow at the beginning but the writing serves this story in absolute reverence and this only happens when you're one hell of a write! But ok, now let's skip to the topic that is Strange The Dreamer. This book is very slow paced for the first 60% but i think you really need to savor every word you get from page to page. Then everything happens. Strange The Dreamer was a dream itself and a story to remind us that we need to believe. Lazlo is a young orphan librarian that travels to his dream world to unlock a secret and only through his fervid imagination he can succeed with his task. I can't get enough of Lazlo's magical journey. The worldbuilding is incredible, characters so relatable and there are gods, goddesses, magic, dreams, ghosts, secrets, legends and stories. Absolutely imaginative and dreamlike, a journey that celebrates the wonders of our mind. The cities, the culture, the background is incredible, the characters are so well defined. Plus, I haven't felt that invested into characters for a long while, maybe since Crooked Kingdom (and i have read so many books i loved since CK!) and i want to hug Lazlo forever. My favorite character is Sarai, she's so conflicted, so beaten up by life but still, she's the real dreamer! i'm still crying all my tears if i think about her I also loved the dynamics and the message about diversity, about relationships and about different cultures. It's a book about feral feelings, about human ferocity, of long-term hatred and prejudice. But mostly, it's about hope and learning. Acceptance, the magic of discovery something unusual, different from us and feel the excitement and the wonders of discovery. How someone apparently different is somehow just like us. To see how difference enriches us, not divides us. So, if you want to enter a world of gods, legends, secrets, hidden treasures, monsters, ghosts, romance (but the kind we want to read about) and above all, dreams that will take you to an enchanted universe, drop everything you are doing and start Strange The Dreamer.

** spoiler alert ** I have to say...I am underwhelmed. It is a classic in the sense that it's old and it's still read, and in that it was an idea unique in its time and even...kind of unusual now. I have to say I've never read anything quite like it, in both good and bad ways, although it did have kind of a Robert Louis Stevenson feel to it, now that I think about it. But don't ask me to explain or substantiate that claim, because it just popped into my head and I can't defend it. The problem I had was the cardinal sin of a book for me: I didn't like the narrator. When I don't like a narrator, 9 times out of 10 I can't get over that and like the book, especially when it's told in 1st person limited POV. I can't get out of Prendick's head, and because I don't like him and don't agree with his interpretation of events, I can't get past him to enjoy the story. I'm trapped with someone I don't like, it's like being locked in an elevator with some jerk who won't shut up, so even if what he's telling you is interesting, all you can think is "Oh my God, are you done yet?" I feel like I could have enjoyed it even Prendick such a...well, dick. (Ha! I see what you did there, H.G. Wells, even if you had no idea you were doing it.) He gets to the island and is locked into a room because Moreau and Montgomery don't feel ready to tell him what's going on, and he can hear a puma being cut open in the next room, while it's still conscious. His reaction is...I can't find the exact quote, but this is pretty close, "There's nothing about vivisection that a modern man of science would find repulsive." Are you serious? ARE YOU SERIOUS? And from that moment on, I hated him, because he was completely indifferent to having animals sliced open while they were alive and screaming in agony. He repeats that sentiment several times throughout his narrative, that if it were "only" vivisection, it wouldn't be that big of a deal. It bothers him that animals are being sliced into each other to create abominations, in the sense that they creep him out, but not in the sense that they've been tortured by a madman. This guy is a Nazi forerunner, and Prendick just reguards him as a scientist who went a little overboard in his research. R u srs? In fact, Prendick dislikes the only other human on the island, besides him and Moreau, because Montgomery is "too sympathic" to the Beast-men, and tries to befriend them and make them more human. Apparently, according to Prendick, being too friendly with animals can make a person cruel to humans. Huh. I guess he missed the memo that the people who become serial killers are usually the ones who torture animals, not the ones who feel bad for the animals that have been tortured and mutilated. I know, I'm shocked too. I think it is entirely possible that I am trying to put modern attitudes over the ideas of the time, but either way, it's jarring to me, and we don't likes it, precious! Next, I think I'll read The Invisible Man, to see if it's just this Wells that I don't care for. The man is one of the founders of sci-fi/horror/fantasy, the least I can do is give him a fair shake.

Once in a while you'll come across a book that really keeps you reading. Not your average page turner, but something that really excites you & keeps you reading. This is one of those books. Where to start? First off, I love how realistic the characters are. Emily doesn't have some unrealistic quirk to her & while she's definitely not one of the "beautiful people" she's not the specific target of anyone's ridicule. (Her friend Megan did have that dubious honor at one point in her past, though.) She could literally be one of any thousands of average teenage girls out there. That's what makes her nocturnal changes into the wild child Emily all that more potent. Another thing worth crowing about is that there's no romance in this book. Sure, Emily has hormones but those take a back seat to her fright over how she's been acting & how it's been impacting her daytime life. Again, another touch of realism. (There will probably be romance in the next book, though.) The only thing about it I could say kept me from enjoying it as much as I'd like is that when we DO discover what's going on with Emily, it kind of comes a little out of left field. Sampson does a good job of trying to blend it into the story but when the discovery is revealed it's kind of "huh... that's a surprise- doesn't entirely make sense, but I'll run with it". It's not anything that will ruin the book for you but it might make you step out of the story for a minute. Overall this really was well worth reading & I can tell that this series is going to be pretty popular, up there with greats such as Soul Screamers & Wicked Lovely. (ARC provided by Amazon Vine)

Posted to Almost Grown-up: I love, love, love Jackson Pearce's work. I love, love, love fairy tales. And above all of them, I love, love, love The Little Mermaid. So raise your hand if you're at all surprised that I loved, loved, loved Fathomless. Fathomless is the third in Pearce's fairy tale retelling series, but you don't necessarily need to read the other two to understand this one, as they're all companion novels. Pearce simply has a very obvious talent with words. Her prose shines whether we're with human Celia or Lo, who is a creature of the sea- but her talent is especially evident when we see the world through Lo's eyes. The sea and Lo's sisters are mysteriously sinister. Not only because of the fact that the only way for them to regain their souls is to kill, but because they lose their concepts of "self" as time moves on. Is there anything more terrifying? There are so many strengths to this novel, and one of them is the strength that we find in the main characters Lo and Celia. They begin thinking of themselves as weak or powerless, but progress beautifully until their strengths shine. Not really their physical strengths, but strength of character. It's also wonderful to see that when a (rather swoony) love interest is introduced, it doesn't at all subtract from the girls' strength. A major theme of this book (and perhaps the series overall), is sibling relationships. Celia and her sisters don't always see eye to eye, but they love each other. Despite the paranormalcy of the triplets and the events surrounding them, there is so much truth to their relationship. Rating: 5/5. I'm almost sad that this series of retellings has concluded, but I can't wait to see what future novels from Jackson Pearce bring.

This and other reviews can be found at herbookstacks. This is seriously a long time coming. And I can't believe I am actually saying that this is my review for THE BECOMING OF NOAH SHAW. That it is possible that there is a sequel to the Mara Dyer Trilogy. I find the idea of it absolutely ridiculous but I can't stop my hands from typing out about this because this is seriously insane. Okay, enough rambling. Let's get down to business here and get into it already. Can I talk about how beautiful this cover is? I was an enormous fan of design behind Mara Dyer, but I kind of love this aesthetic even more. I'm not sure what it is about it that I love - but I think it's embers. It's got this great color contrast and really pops off the cover. Plus, I love that it has a different spirit and tone that the Mara Dyer books had. And when I think about it, I feel as though those books were colder and dissonant (like Mara!) and this cover is warm and fierce and like a crashing crescendo of stringed instruments roaring against the large open spaces of the orchestra halls. It's just pretty beautiful. This book is dark. It is super dark and intense and vicious and visceral and all of these things that I was blown away by - Michelle Hodkin is a brilliant storyteller. There is no doubt about that. I felt like I was beig twisted and thrown about - feeling one emotion after another. But I can guarantee that felt shocked and awed through much of the book and xouldnnot believe when things were happening. I will say that I have read other people's thoughts about this book and have heard them say that nothing really happens in this book. I think a lot does. Just because something isn't FIGURED OUT and there are no real answers to ease a reader into the ending of it doesn't mean that nothing has happened. Sure, nothing is solved, but do not be mistaken that that book has a lot going on. I didn't think that Michelle Hodkin could DO MORE with world. At least not much more but she continues where she left off with RETRIBUTION and it is a wild ride. Also, I think Hodkin has always been one of those authors that has straddled the line between young and new adult. There are some rather racy scenes that happen. Even before thirty and I was fanning my face. I am a huge sucker for those sort of scenes and you obviously know that it's gotta do with Mara and Noah and those two are like two sticks rubbing on kindle to start a fire and once it starts, it burns. I am a fan of those sort of scenes and I know that there is definitely sexual undertones to the entire story, especially when it comes to Noah talking about Mara. It won't be everyone's cup of tea and I'm sure people will think it's inappropriate, but I think Michelle does a great job in finessing those undertones in. I will say that everyone is insanely suspicious to me as a character. Something begins happening to other carriers and everyone seems like a suspect, especially Mara. I think that the one issue I had with the POV being Noah's was that the autonomy of other characters, like Mara, suffered. I was suddenly asking who the heck she was and where the girl from the Mara Dyer trilogy was. I became suspicious with her and if she was behind things that were happening. I started distrusting Jamie because of his own motives and Noah's suspicions regarding him. And then I started to dislike Jamie. I was not a huge fan of his in the original trilogy and I feel like the only reason I liked him was that was he a support system for Mara. There are definitely some new characters to meet. And some old ones come back. I love that Michelle Hodkin has expanded to more characters because it just means more characters to like, but then it also means more characters to hate and no one wants that. I mean, there were some characters that I was really, really disliking (LEO!). I was delighted to see Daniel again in the story and I wish that there was even more of him. He is such a great character. It's hard to imagine regularity when the story is saturated with these uniquely-powered characters. And I love that Daniel is the character that grounds the rest of the story to the real world. And even more, I love that he is a rather loyal confidant to Noah, who I think really needs one. I would have loved to see more of him, but he does go through betrayal in this book and it HURTS. Oh, does it hurt. To be quite honest, as I'm writing this, I really feel like The Shaw Confessions are giving me ORPHAN BLACK vibes. It's sultry, dangerous, high-adrenaline, intense, mystery. You know. It's kind of crazy. I will say that the ending - I did not expect that ending. It kind of blew me out of the water because it was NOT what I saw coming at all. I knew that there would not be any clean and tied up ends. It would be messy and sad and visceral and AHHHH. But oh my gosh. I really don't want to spoil it, but let us just say that Noah meets someone from the past - someone that we have all met before and wondered about since she was introduced into the books... And guys, I am not ready for The Shaw Confessions #2. I am not.

For next month my book club is reading One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel Garcia Marquez. And that was my choice. But there's another reader inside me, too. And that reader likes to read fun books that are quick and consumable and exciting and pulpy and fun. Also, did I mention, fun? That reader discovered Harry Dresden a few years ago. What's not to love? In Jim Butcher's contemporary urban fantasy series, Chicago looks much as it does today. Except that, in the Yellow Pages, there's a single listing for a "Professional Wizard." That's Harry Dresden, and he's an old-school private investigator who solves problems with little help from modern technology (electronics don't do so well around magic). The novels might start like classic noir detective stories but soon the missing artifact or other de rigueur case turns out to have an occult twist. To sum up the awesomeness here, so far we have: 1) Funny series novels set in Chicago 2) Classic mystery set-up 3) Magic. What's not to love? That's harder to put my finger on. But I found that I don't want to read two Dresden novels back-to-back. Butcher's voice grates on me after that and little . flaws? stylistic choices? character idiosyncrasies? in the writing begin to call attention to themselves and draw me out of the story. So I read the books one-at-a-time, with space between, because I really like to enjoy each one. These stories have it all: wizards, magical politics, faeries, goblins, trolls, zombies, vampires, werewolves, angels, priests, fighting, battles, war, romance, you name it and it's probably somewhere in this world. As an added bonus, the main characters are geeks. Another benefit to the slow-read approach is that I didn't catch up to the author for a long time. But when I finished Ghost Story (Book 13, naturally) last week, I was stuck. The next novel isn't due until next summer! And only one per year after that! Alas. If the above description captures your interest, let me underscore that/reassure you in two ways: Butcher's writing improves as the series progresses, and the novels are better than the short-lived Sci Fi Channel series loosely based on the books. If you've tried just one or two of the novels but haven't gotten hooked, I'd recommend perseverance. I was shocked - shocked! - at what happened in Changes (Book 12). It sent me scrambling for Side Jobs, an anthology of short stories and a novelette set between various novels in the series, as well as a novella set immediately after Changes. Then I rushed right into Ghost Story, which left me hanging deliciously. I'm looking forward to book 14 - and it's worth noting that the author does have a planned story arc for the entire series, including an ending - but I think the first 11 novels, fun as they were, were worth reading as prelude alone for all the changes in books 12 and 13. Recommended light holiday reading.

A unique take on the Arthurian quest for the Holy Grail, set in a secondary world that has modern-day technology (cell phones, limos) right alongside knights and sorceresses and basilisks. McKillip usually writes straight high fantasy, so it was unexpectedly delightful to read her take on a more modern setting-the wry humor in her juxtaposition of magic and modernity reminded me of Diana Wynne Jones. ("Yes, my lord," Val answered eagerly, for them all. "We can travel together to this mysterious Friday Nite Fish Fry.") But despite the humor and the short length of the story, this is not lightweight fantasy-I found it to be among the more literary of McKillip's novels, focusing far more on theme and mythic resonance than individual character arcs. This can be a little frustrating at times-I'd get all attached to one character's story, and then the narrative would switch away to someone else entirely. I also feel that if I had a deeper knowledge of Arthurian legends, I'd have uncovered whole new layers of meaning. But still, I found it absorbing and beautifully written (as all McKillip's novels are).

2.5 stars I didn't actively dislike this book at any point in my reading experience, but I also didn't actively like this book at any point in my reading experience. Hence, the 2.5 stars. Yeah the format is cool and everything, but format can only go so far when your story is pretty average. Speaking of format, I found some of the pages in this book to be kind of unnecessary. Let me explain. In the beginning of the book, you're told that everything you're about to read consists of files that "The Illuminae Group" has hacked and compiled. Most of the content of the book is consistent with this. There are announcements from ship commanders, emails, IM conversations, etc. However, some of the other stuff was...not so consistent. Step right up ladies and gents, step right up! For a limited time only, you get two, count 'em TWO reviews for the price of one, for your entertainment I present, I Am Number Four: The book AND The movie. Book Rating: Half a wheat thin out of a full family fun pack sized box. Aliens! Action! Romance! What's not to love? Well... After the Disappointing Days of Daniel X, I was hoping to get a little YA alien action without the cheesy contrived romance that seems to be pervading the market these days. On the whole, it wasn't as bad as it could have been, but to say that it was good would be stretching it. From the first page we are welcomed directly into a land filled with one-dimensional characters, some of which have superpowers because they are aliens who happen to look exactly like humans. Sure, why not? These beings are being hunted by other evil aliens who want kill them. Sounds good. This book will NOT focus on the battle between good and evil, a super-powered alien smackdown or even a heartwarming tale about the last few members of an alien race trying to survive. OK, then what...? This book WILL focus on cheesy romance, a (sorta not really) love triangle, the ever-popular battle between nerds and jocks, and a hayride. Excuse me while I indulge in a sad internet meme. *facepalms* There are a couple of fight scenes, but they're really less of a 'now we have to fight for our lives' and more of 'Oh, it's nearing the end of the book, let's throw in a random fight scene so people will hopefully read the next one and make us more money' kind of way. That, in all, is the biggest problem with the book. It's written coherently, has an amusing and potentially intriguing plot and characters with the possibility for greatness. But it's not telling a story, it's selling one. That's why, on the difference between a fad and style, I predict that this book (and potential series) will hit fast, make money, then fade as quickly as it came. Movie Rating: One whole wheat thin with a few wheaty crumbs stuck to it, but still scraping the bottom of the bag. Alex Mcwhatsisface! Action! Romance! What's not to love? Eh... Well for one thing... 1) Two words: flashlight hands. 2) That chick from glee 3) Number 4's pathetic closeted meltdown, "ahh it burns!" 4) Evil aliens who look like vampires (the non-sparkly kind) 5) Lame super powers 6) #6 arriving too late in the movie to save it. 7) It's associated with JAMES FREY 8) The final battle scene is too drawn out to be awesome. 9) Twu wuuuv! 10) When the acting/plot/dialogue/attractiveness/CGI/everything else not mentioned fails, fall back on EXPLOSIONS! (to be fair, many movies do this to great effect) 11) The dialogue 12) One more word: voiceovers 13) Plans for a sequel What it did have: An original hayride scene that I can honestly say I have never seen anything like before (or hopefully ever again). A trademark teeny action flick, great if you've got a few hours to kill. The verdict: Two stars: one for the book, and one for the movie.

"...stories can make someone immortal as long as someone else is willing to listen." After History Is All You Left me I was sort of sure that I would adore this book just as much and that it would make me feel every kind of emotion you can think of. In the end I didn't get disappointed at all. At first I would like to say I didn't mind the romance that happened near the ending because let's be honest. It might have been rushed but how would you act on your very last day? Knowing you don't have any more days left? I think no one would care too much about rushing into things. That's why I didn't mind the face paced romance, even though I usually prefer slow built up romance. It's the kind of book that will make you think about a lot of things. It might make you ask yourself what you'd do if you had 24 hours left before you die. Did you do all the things you wanted to do? Did you reach all the things you wanted to reach? Are you happy about the last conversations you had with your loved ones? Million of questions went through my mind as I read this beautifully written story. It might be the type of book that will make you want to use your time better, that will make you want to get out and do all the things that you are scared of. Who knows? It might have that kind of impact on you. I know I couldn't stop wondering if I am using my time and if I am really living my life to the fullest or if there's anything that I am missing. It may sound a little dramatic but this book really managed to make me reconsider a lot of things and I think if a story is able to make you want to change your entire life it's definitely a good one. I know most of us will have a different experience with this book. Some might feel the same as I did when I first read it, some others may just enjoy the characters and wish they had gotten a much happier ending. Personally, I am happy that this book had such a huge impact on me and I know for sure I am going to re-read this one many, many times.

Hmm. This story was only recently completed, so it's been awhile since I've read the bulk of it. The first 10 chapters are pretty rough. All the warnings you see, you should take to heart. Torture, cruelty, bestiality, gratuitous violence and extreme humiliation...it goes pretty much non-stop for the first 50% of this story. It was hard for me to read, I'm not gonna lie, but I got through it with the expectation that the story was going somewhere better...that the fantasy world and storyline would be further developed and expanded beyond the narrow confines of the cabin in which the Neko is tortured. Unfortunately, that never really happens to my satisfaction. I don't want to give too much away, but things start to get exciting (and better for the Neko) at Chapter 11. At the time, I thought to myself, "Now the story will really get started." Eh. Not so much. Don't get me wrong, I liked the last 10 chapters MUCH more than the first 10. The story picked up, and I thought we were really getting somewhere. But unfortunately, it kinda fizzles out at the end. To be honest, I got the feeling that the author was having trouble figuring out where to go with the story or perhaps just trouble wanting to go anywhere further with the story. So instead of the story taking off, as I had expected, it just sorta...stops. Ultimately, I appreciate that the author managed to "complete" the story instead of leaving it unfinished like so many other slash authors might do...but at the same time, I can't help but feel disappointed that it didn't go any further. And unfortunately, I think a lot of people who have issues with all the sexual torture won't be able to see past that when it takes up such a huge percentage of the book.

And one thing in the book that had me hollering out loud in frustration: When they are trying to figure out what the symbols on the panels mean they are beating their heads against the wall trying to make "language" out of it, and all I can think the whole time is, "IT'S MATH, YOU IDIOTS!" because everyone who's ever read a lick of sci-fi knows that math is the universal language that all aliens try to communicate with. Get with the program, you super educated linguists who spend months staring at symbols with different numbers of dots and take forever to figure it out!

Binti swept through my friend's list last year, and everyone loved it! I ended up reading (and disliking) Okorafor's Who Fears Death? before I got to this novella, and given my experiences with that novel, I had some reservations picking up another by this author. However, in the end, Binti was quite enjoyable, though I wasn't quite as enamored with it as others. Okorafor excels at crafting protagonists who aren't just white North Americans in future clothing. Her characters are usually of African descent (well, future African, or at least, future person from that particular area of the world, whatever it is referred to at the time), and they read quite differently from what one usually gets in North American SF. Culture is often important in Okorafor's stories, and Binti is an excellent example. Our young protagonist is from a fairly insular community, and she defies norms to go study at the best university in the universe. She is the first of her people to leave in such a way, and much of the story deals with her feelings of isolation and discrimination. The story takes a dark shift when the ship carrying Binti and her future classmates is attacked by hostile aliens, leaving Binti the only survivor. She is saved by a strange device she picked up in the desert, and she negotiates with the aliens and agrees to help them get an important artefact back from the university. Binti's time on the ship that has been taken over is eerie and full of tension. The aliens are quite alien, and one is never quite sure whether Binti is going to live. Fortunately, she does, forging some interesting relationships along the way. A few other reviewers have mentioned that the science fiction aspect of this story is weak. While I don't think that authors need to go full hard SF to prove their mettle in the genre, there are things I look for when reading SF. In particular, the social dynamics need to reflect the way the universe has been structured. I have no issue believing that Earth is still mired in racism. Humans are dicks. Us not changing over the course of a few thousand years isn't terribly surprising to me. What threw me, however, was the way racism/speciesm/classism was treated in the greater universe. At one point, Binti thinks that the university professors are mocking her for her adherence to cultural norms (namely the clay that her people use to clean themselves). I buy that class is at issue on this university planet, and that Binti is seen as less advanced (re: intelligent) than the other people at the school because she comes from an insular community. However, given the fact that the university has a dorm room for students who need a specific gas filled environment so that they can float properly, and the leader of the professors is a spider-like creature, the fact that she uses clay on her skin isn't actually something I think would standout as weird. This, I think, is why people thought the SF was weak. The universe isn't fully fleshed out yet (which, admittedly, is to be expected in a novella), and this means there are little things that can easily draw the reader out of the story. Okorafor gives us weird aliens, but she doesn't shift the social dynamics to take advantage of this much. I am often fascinated with how SF authors deal with discrimination in different contexts, so I was disappointed that this novella didn't think through its own implications more. The novella also starts quite strongly, but meanders to the end. The tension of Binti's time on the spaceship leaves readers quite breatheless at points, but things slow down quite substantially at the university, even though the stakes are so high. Not to say that I disapprove of a story that takes a less explosive approach to negotiations, but the pacing was off. All in all, Binti is definitely worth a read, and I am excited for the second installment in the series. However, it had some lofty aspirations that it didn't quite manage to meet. (To those that really liked this, I also suggest Rochita Loenen-Ruiz's "Dancing in the Shadow of the Once" a gut-punching story of the terrible bargains made between colonised and coloniser that occurs in a much vaster universe than our own currently is.)

My my what a struggle! It took me ten days yes ten fucking days! I had to force myself to finish but I'll start by describing the (few) things I liked. The concept and storyline was very different indeed. In Adelice's world, Arras, the Guild controls and monitors everything via the Weave (a tapestry of threads made of time and matter). Everything has a thread and the Guild can alter or get rid of threads therefor altering and controlling the world around them. Adelice is a spinster, a girl who has a gift to weave the threads that make up time and matter. Spinsters are the only people that can alter the Weave, that's why the Guild treasures them. About three quarters of the way through there was a really good, shocking revelation about Arras and how it'd been woven... I found those ideas very clever and interesting. It definitely made me think about the makeup of the world around us. It's a very clever idea to think of the world as one big tapestry. Plus a few years back I remember watching a documentary about time travel and parallel universes. Lots of theories were discussed, one of them was about the destruction of this universe (entropy) in the far future. It discussed how future civilizations could escape to other universes or perhaps even CREATE their own universe/reality. So that's what the description of this book reminded me of... In fact I'm sure this story is inspired by the strings theory... Seriously though, that's pretty much where the intrigue ends. The rest of this book was literally a lump of SHIT with hardly ANYTHING happening! I mean honestly this was so boring I began to visualize the threads as cobwebs! In fact here's the full process that was me reading this book. STAGE 1. I was excited after seeing this online. I couldn't wait for the release. STAGE 2. Approx 50 pages in "Uh oh I have a feeling I'm gonna be in here a long time.." STAGE 3. Approx halfway "Uhhhhhhhhhhhhh...Zzzzzzz...(Only I wasn't smiling)" STAGE 4. Almost at the end,"What? Did something good happen?" Adelice, Jost and Erik fall through the Weave and land on Earth.. FINNISH! Oh man, I'm so glad can you see my tears of joy? FINAL REACTION/OPINION..The plot was soooo slow and sooooo full of shit! I really don't enjoy reading shit and I fail to comprehend how so many people have given this high ratings. The characters all felt really dull and unreal. Why did this story drag so much? It was so so boring, the only thing I was looking forward to this past week was finishing this crap! Now that I've FINALLY (at long fucking last) finished, I really feel like a weight has been lifted. I feel like I've accomplished something big! *clap* *clap* *CHEER! I'm really starting to agree with Melissa Marr "Life's too short to bother with books I'm not enjoying." But with me I just have to know what happens at the end, which was a cliffhanger of sorts. I highly doubt I'll be continuing this series but we'll see.. I just really hate books that build you up for something big, then let you down with a truly crap story. So to close up this "review" I'll say there were some awesome, mind-blowing ideas that had huge potential but were pitifully wasted in this...SHIT!

Can't finish. Gahhhhh. It seems like a very cool concept--a noir police procedural set in a near future where actual and virtual realities have been melded. But the writing. It is multi-narrator, present-tense, second-person narrative. Whyyy! I mean, I know I'm rigid about narrative styles; I tend to dislike present tense, but I'll tolerate it for a good story. But second person? I mean, how many people do you know who refer to themselves as "you", e.g. I must have zoned out, you realize nervously. I tend to adore unreliable first-person narrators, and I even think I could have coped with a Gollumesque/royal "we". But a story changes narrators every chapter, and all the narrators speak in present tense and refer to themselves as "you?" I just can't deal. It's like a choose-your-own adventure story where you have Multiple Personality Disorder and don't actually have any choices. The concept is very cool, and I think it could be a fun story. If you can deal with the narrative style, I'm sure it's a fantastic read. It was gripping enough that I hung in there for a while, but ended up deciding I just couldn't cope. And now I have a headache.

Kitty Norville works as a DJ during the night shift, and is getting bored taking the same old song requests. She is also a werewolf, and fully aware that there are vampires and other creatures that go bump in the night, so one night she engages one of her callers on supernatural matters. Very quickly, she has a popular call-in show called "The Midnight Hour", where she offers all sorts of advice to human and supernatural callers alike, and is being syndicated on a number of radio stations. Not everyone is happy that Kitty is becoming popular and successful, however. The alpha of her werewolf pack is worried about the attention she is attracting, and one evening there is a werewolf hunter sent to kill her, live on the air. Her secret identity is rather spectacularly revealed, and she suspects the local vampire leader may have ordered the hit. She makes a deal with the hunter, and saves her life. Once the police are forced to accept the existence of supernatural creatures, they call in Kitty to consult on a series of extremely grisly killings. It's obvious to Kitty's advanced sense of smell that the serial killer is a werewolf, and he is not one from the pack. This opens questions about whether the alpha's control is slipping, since he is unaware that a were has been killing young women. As well as helping the police try to catch a serial killer, Kitty has to deal with her pack not being happy about her getting more and more independent and figure out who paid a guy to kill her. Amazon kept recommending the Kitty Norville books to me, based on the fact that I read a whole lot of other paranormal fantasy series narrated by a first person supernatural protagonist. A quick count reveals that not counting the Kitty Norville books, I'm reading 12 other series, and that's not counting some of the Young Adult books. So it's not surprising that Amazon thinks I might like it. Possibly because I read quite so many different series, and really do love some of them, this just fell a bit flat to me. Kitty was an ok character, and she's clearly still developing, still trying to get used to being a werewolf, establishing her identity in the pack and outside it - but I just didn't care that much about her, or the stuff that happened to her. Having browsed through the blurbs for the rest of the series on Amazon, nothing there interests me enough to make me want to continue the series. It wasn't bad, it just didn't make me want to add a 13th series to my reading list.

(Re-read, rating: no change) I forgot about all of the craziness that went down in this book and I just read it two years ago! Its a little bit scary how the brain works...I remember more about what happened in the first couple books in this series than I do with Frost Burned and this is book 7 out of 8. The events of this book didn't occur that long ago. There were little bits and pieces of weird information that I remembered but all of the important stuff and big reveals... couldn't remember to save my life. But I loved it because that meant I got to experience a lot of the "what the hell is going on" feelings I had when I read it for the first time. Mercy can never just have a normal life...She's always into something. As soon as her body has recovered and she no longer needs crutches or a cast, when her black eyes and cuts have healed, something gets thrown in her path that leads to her getting bruised up and beat down all over again. But what I love most about her is she's always up for the challenge and she will fight to her very last breath if it means protecting the ones she loves. Some idiot has taken the pack. I mean the ENTIRE pack, Bran has shut down all communication and Mercy is on her own with no idea where to start in getting her family back. But the Coyote is a clever animal and Mercy is nothing if not resourceful. Frost Burned sees Mercy pulling out all the stops to figure out what is happening and why and with the help of a few friends the threads begin to slowly unravel and the bigger picture is revealed...and it doesn't look pretty. From the very first chapter of this book until the very end, this book was ON. There wasn't a moment that passed while reading this book where I wasn't afraid, nervous or worried about what was going to happen next. For this to be a re-read, I couldn't believe how many times I had those "I need to just see how this is going to play out before I put this down" moments. Usually when you re-read a book, once you get in the grove of a particular scene or sequence, pieces come back to you and you remember what happened. But there was so much action and craziness in this book I really had to just read it through to see what was going to happen next and make sure everything was alright. Mercy of course is always a pleasure to read. Loyal to a fault, never completely fearless but always brave, daring and willing to risk her life for those she loves and for those who cannot fend for themselves. Her relationship with Adam is always fun to read. I love how he's super protective of her but he knows the kind of person she is, he knows she can defend herself and despite how much it scares him to do it, he lets her be who she is. My favorite crazy werewolf made an appearance in this book! I swear I'm going to name my first born child after him. And then of course there's Tad. Tad is the antithesis of his dad and I wish we could get more of him in the coming books. He's such a fun character to read. This BOOK was so much fun to read. I wasn't even planning on reading it so soon after finishing River Marked but once I picked it up I didn't want to put it down. I would've liked to have a more of my other favorite werewolf Samuel but there was so much going on, throwing him into the mix would have been TOO much. The great thing about this book is that while there was SO much going on, it wasn't a mess and everything FIT. Patricia Briggs is amazing and I will love her forever for sharing these characters with the world. I can't say this enough...if you like paranormal urban fantasy...you most definitely need to pick this series up. You have no idea what you're missing.

I'm disappointed, to be bluntly honest. Not that the book in itself isn't very good. If you look at it as just that - a lone-standing book, it's very thrilling. But this is supposed to be a prequel. A much anticipated prequel, after The Death Cure left so many questions unanswered. (There might be minor spoilers ahead, tread with caution.) I was hoping to discover more about W.I.C.K.E.D and it's founders, what fate befell them and how Thomas and Teresa came to be the ones who took over. I wanted to know about what our characters - the ones we're familiar with - did before Thomas wakes up in the Box. I went into this book expecting back stories for Newt and Minho and Gally and, well, everyone. I wanted to know more about the characters I'd read about. Maybe how it was for the first group of 20 that was sent to the Maze. Not some random group of people struggling through the after-effects of the flares and the Flare.
