A toddler's family is killed and he alone escapes unseen. A plea from his recently deceased mother touches an elderly couple who take the boy as their own to raise. But they have been long dead and their home is the graveyard. They name the boy Nobody - Bod for short - and they along with the other ghosts spend the next 16 years taking care of him. Also helping is Silas, not a ghost but also not a human and who is quite secretive about where he goes and what he does. As boys tend to do, Bod gets in a fair amount of trouble, much of it being the "other-worldly" sort. The graveyard keeps Bod safe from those who wish him ill, but sooner or later, he must make his own way in the real world. Tinged with humor as well as dosed with scary bits, this children's novel will appeal to all ages and to those who normally skip this genre. Masterfully written, this tale is well deserving of the many awards it has won.

Ellen Callahan is a lawyer and single mother who could do without all the current drama surrounding her twin, megastar brother Jamie, and his girlfriend who lives next door. What she resented even more was the bodyguard Jamie dispatched when the paparazzi started getting out of hand. Caleb Clark, fresh out of the Army and Iraq, thought this would be an easy assignment but he hadn't yet come up against a woman as stubbornly independent as Ellen. Nor had he expected it would be so hard to resist mixing pleasure and business. For a time, Ellen's stubbornness started to wear a little thin but the more I learned about her past relationships, I began to warm up to her character. She had many layers and had learned to be self sufficient as her brother garnered most of the attention even when they were growing up and her ex-husband was a piece of work. She had no appetite for being in another relationship and when Caleb emerges, she's pretty comfortable about considering a no-commitment, sex only arrangement. He, on the other hand, wasn't in the market and had a reputation for being footloose, but not really a player. Caleb's very sexy and clever but she had him at hello. It was enjoyable to have the tales turned for a change with Ellen not wanting a commitment and Caleb really hoping for much more. The sexual tension between these two was even better, complicating their lives in ways they never saw coming. I liked that we were able to have both of their points of view presented so I could be the voyeur while they figured things out. Be prepared for some very steamy times, though, when they do decide to come together. The volatile romance between Jamie and his girlfriend, Carly, added another level of excitement and humor as he worked to get out of the doghouse. Ellen's son, Henry, added an interesting element as he played an important role in the story. Of course, his father added to the drama and not always in a good way. I liked how the secondary characters were woven into the story in a way that didn't distract but augmented Ellen and Caleb's relationship. I enjoyed Ellen and Caleb's story, so much that I rolled right into the next book in the series. It is complex, aggravating at times, funny and had moments that tugged at my heart. (I received an ARC from NetGalley)

He shares Flavia's passion for chemical trivia, and demonstrates doctoring abilities; she responds instantly, perfectly, (like adult?) when his wartime torture memories resurge. She wants to believe in Santa, thinks "affair" means best friends, and is sheltered from the birth process. Does Nialla Gilfoyle, from Porson puppeteers book 2 return to ... demonstrate Flavia's ignorance? Dogger's competence? provoke reader curiosity? provide ontinuity for a later book? philosophize on reincarnation, a life for a death? I don't see concrete contributions. 4.5 stars What I really wanted was not to be a burden to anyone. To be really and truly free. Don't Breathe a Word was an incredibly touching and captivating read. It's one of those books that leaves me wondering and thinking long after I've finished it. We have Joy Delamere, a girl who suffers from severe asthma and is in an unstable relationship with her boyfriend, Asher. She feels her family and Asher are suffocating her, not allowing her the freedom she wishes she could have in life. So, after a night in which Asher went too far in damaging Joy, she escapes into the streets of Seattle, where a homeless boy had offered her protection would she ever need it. She sets out to find him, hoping she could be saved from the suffocating life she had been living. This book was such a breath of fresh air. It's raw and real, and the issues and problems explored in this book were dealt in a tender manner. Joy learns that living on the street isn't as freeing as she thought it would be. She suffers from drug dealers, rapists, thieves, and abusers. She lives in a ratty old shack, with the boy, Creed, and his gang, May and Santos. Together, they pitch in to bring in money somehow, bring in food from the garbage, protect each other from the street thugs out there. Their world is truly heartbreaking. Each teenager is running away from something, each with their own morbid history. We learn slowly why each one escaped their other lives and how they ended up homeless in the streets of Seattle. I loved Creed! He was protective (not overbearingly, though! ), caring, understanding, determined. He had a dream to become a musician, and Joy was there to encourage him forward. I thought they were a perfectly complemented pairing. Holly Cupala really wove this story into a beautiful one, and I was able to connect with Joy on some levels, in her pain and her imprisonment she feels. My only problem was that in the beginning, Joy appears to be a girl who doesn't know how to stand up for herself. She depends on other people to help her--like Asher, then later on Creed. But I got to watch her develop into a fierce and brave girl throughout the book, and I admired the strength she has towards the end. So, overall, I loved it. Joy's voice was real, honest, and Holly Cupala doesn't sugarcoat the horrors of run-away life. I'll definitely be looking into her other books as well!

A signed copy of this novel was won from the publisher. My opinions are my own. This review can also be found at The Starry-Eyed Revue. After reading The Winner's Curse at the first of the year and falling head-over-heels for Marie Rutkoski's beautiful writing style and the beginning of what is sure to be a truly stunning trilogy, I knew I had to make time in my reading schedule for The Shadow Society. I have a signed copy after all. And then I saw that Kristen from My Friends Are Fiction was just starting it, and we decided to do a buddy read. (You can check out her review here.) This turned out to be a great decision because there was soooo much I wanted to discuss while reading, and Kristen was a fantastic buddy-reader. Probably doesn't hurt that we hardcore bonded over our love of this author's writing style, either. To kick things off, I think I'd have to say that this novel has one of the best, most enticing prologues I've ever had the pleasure of reading. I couldn't not read the book after that! It packs a real punch, but it's the rest of the book that delivers. The Shadow Society is this really awesome alternate history/multiverse story, but that's not even the half of it. That aspect comes in to play over the course of the novel, but I wouldn't say it's the focal point of the story. No, that would probably be the war brewing between the Shades and humans in an alternate world where the Great Chicago Fire never happened. But I'll get to that. "You stole it," I finally choked out. I felt as if Conn had seen me in nothing but my oldest, ugliest underwear. I was a little worried about the amnesia plot in this story because those are always so hit or miss. But Darcy's memory loss is due to some traumatic event in her childhood, and I can get on board with PTSD-related amnesia. Especially when the memories return in the fashion that they do for Darcy: little by little, triggered by familiar faces and familiar places. And then those pieces start to add up, and everything falls into place for the reader at the same time it does for Darcy. I had my theories, of course, but considering the Shades are a completely new brand of paranormal creature, I was just as shocked as Darcy to learn the truth. Darcy was a bit of an enigma at first. She doesn't fit in anywhere, but she has this really tight-knit group of friends. She's been passed from foster home to foster home since she was first found outside a fire station at the tender age of five, but now she's got a loving foster mother by way of Marsha. It seems that Darcy has finally found her place in this world...just in time to have it all taken away from her by a past -- another world -- she can't remember. All things considered, I think she handles the fall-out rather admirably. The Shades are, essentially, children of the shadows. In their corporeal form, they look human, but they have the ability to make themselves invisible. And they use this ability to hide among the humans in their world, following them around like shadows and spying on them. For this reason, Darcy is valuable to both the Shades and the humans of that world. But she's especially important to Conn. I don't know if you can call it a pattern when it only exists in two instances, but at the very least, the theme of betrayal is a commonality between both of the books I've read by Rutkoski. I'm equally drawn to storylines involving betrayal, so I get it. And I don't mind...I just think it's interesting how two stories can have the same basic premise but still be completely different and also captivating in their own rights. And as Kristen stated in our discussion over this book during our buddy read, I'd much rather the tension in the story come from some type of betrayal, as opposed to a misbegotten love triangle. He grinned the first time I said it. "Pleasure later, then," he replied. But later was always later than that for me, and he grew sullen. I knew that I could change that, could heal the insecurity that shape-shifted Orion from a sly jester into someone who pouted. He pouted sexily and looked very kissable. Really, he was very everything. But he wasn't for me. In the midst of the lies I had to tell and secrets I had to keep and secrets I had to unearth, it felt important to be true to myself. I guess I should mention that there are two interested parties, but this is clearly an instance of the love T, which I don't mind. Conn, despite his betrayal, is where Darcy's heart lies. Orion was simply a friend who tried to force more from the relationship than Darcy was prepared to give. Conn uses Darcy, but in the process -- and over weeks, while spending time together working on a school project in the Alter (their name for our world) -- they become something more to each other. Neither is really sure what to make of the other, but it's clear (at least to the reader) that Darcy's feelings are reciprocated by Conn, before and after the betrayal. He slouched at his desk, but there was something a little calculated in his slumped shoulders and stretched out legs. I got the impression that he had riffled through his closet, found his Typical Teenager costume, and was trying it on. And now we come down to it. My suspicion: Conn McCrea wasn't exactly normal. My reasons? Let's just say it takes one to know one. Conn was intriguing and confusing for a majority of the story, but he wasn't the only stand-out character aside from Darcy. There were members of The Shadow Society that seemed to share Darcy's concerns for the welfare of humans, especially Savannah and Zephyr, but hardly any of the Shades could really be deemed trustworthy. But after reading Jacks and Queens at the Green Mill , I feel like I understand Zephyr a little better, anyway. Then there were Darcy's friends from the Alter. They were true friends, caring and funny and loyal to the end. And they really shocked me at times, which endeared them to me further. I think I should just go ahead and admit that I'm kind of in love with Rutkoski's gorgeous prose. It was an entirely different experience reading this novel as compared to The Winner's Curse, especially knowing that The Shadow Society is a stand-alone, but I enjoyed this story immensely. I cannot fathom that I have to wait over a year to get my hands on another Marie Rutkoski novel. If you've already read and enjoyed The Winner's Curse, or if you fancy stories featuring themes of rebellion, love across dividing lines, or characters discovering that much of what they know is a lie, then I think you'll find something to appreciate in this novel. GIF it to me straight: This woman can write!

Where to even start with this book... I began reading it with some roommates as a sort of joke, but it's kind of like a train wreck - no matter how grisly and awful it is, you just can't look away. So, I finished reading it in about a week. Honestly, I'm disappointed in myself for reading it - not only do I disagree with the content of the book itself, the writing repulses me. First of all, the ties it has to Twilight are glaringly obvious to the point that I'm surprised there hasn't been a plagiarism suit. Christian Grey has a thing for cars (like Edward and his Volvo), and disturbing past (like Edward and his time not being a vegetarian vampire), plays the piano and has a fondness for classical music, comes from a seemingly perfect family, and has endless supplies of money. He and Edward are both insanely controlling and vaguely stalker-ish. AND GUYS. THEY HAVE THE SAME WEIRD COPPERY REDDISH AUBURNISH HAIR COLOR THAT IS NEVER REALLY NAMED. As for Anastasia and Bella - both shy, awkward, clumsy, self-demeaning, and seem to be reflections of the author themselves. There are literally scenes where I think EL James copied Twilight nearly word-for-word: when Christian takes Ana to IHOP, it's extremely similar to Edward taking Bella to that Italian place, even down to the conversation they have. The writing itself is painful. The analogies, the exclamations, the vocabulary... Ana has both a subconscious and an 'inner goddess' both of which she refers constantly. It's uncomfortable. It's weird. They do various things like glare at her over their half-moon specs, do the hula in a red skirt, hide behind a couch underneath a blanket, and cheer with pom-poms (GUYS I'M NOT EVEN KIDDING THESE ARE ALL IN THE BOOK. I DIDN'T MAKE THEM UP - THESE WERE WRITTEN BY AN ACTUAL PERSON AND OKAYED BY AN EDITOR AND WHYYYYYYY). Now, for the actual sex scenes - I felt demeaned as a woman just reading them. Frankly, it disgusted me that she was clearly uncomfortable with what he expected the entire book and she just let it happen. She drew her limits, but let him cross the line over and over again. WHEN SHE FINALLY WORKED UP THE COURAGE TO LEAVE HIS SORRY BUTT AT THE END I WAS SO HAPPY WITH HER CHARACTER. Obviously, she comes back to him because there are two more books, but I hope that it means he cleans up his act at least a little bit.

What I am feeling right now? Sadness. Why? because the book has ended. Natural Born Charmer is indeed a charmer, from start to finish. This is a beautiful, wholesome story that I wished I can continue to read. I hadn't prepared myself for that last page that signalled its closing, though I was aware I am reading an Epilogue. I want to cry. I desperately want to immerse myself in Blue and Dean's world, not the Chicago Star's world but our main characters' journey after that happily ever after, and that in itself speaks a lot about how the author successful wove and brought to life two people who amidst life's challenges and their own imperfections, were able to find and hold on to each other. It's not only Dean and Blue that I'll miss. There are also supporting characters that stamped a place in my heart, to the point that I felt like I was reading two novels at the same time. Riley, bless this beautiful girl, taught me that strength can be found in different forms and to conquer our fears one step at a time; Jack and April, the happily ever after that is long overdue. These two showed me that it's not too late for second chances. That sometimes, we need to find ourselves first, mature into who we are, and learn lessons along the way in order to love truly. Once again, I remember the saying I love to throw at my friends: "Not destined today, but maybe in the future, when things are different." And that is what this book is all about. Our past shape us to who we are. Our environment, friends, the people who raised us. They are factors that defined us today and if any one of them is different, the you today maybe a stranger. Natural Born Charmer sums this up perfectly and beautifully, and I love it from beginning to end.

I read a few reviews about Belzhar before I began reading it. It generally received average reviews and a few people stated that they were bored while reading it. That was not the case for me. I was intrigued the entire time, especially when we got to learn the back stories of every character and why they were at this special school for highly intelligent and fragile teenagers. The ending is where my four stars come from. Although I was surprised by the twist ending, I wish it went a bit differently. Throughout the whole book, we know that Jam was sent to this school because she was deeply depressed about her boyfriend Reeve dying. The ending was a shock because we find out that Reeve didn't actually love her, he wasn't even interested in her but her mind fooled her into thinking he liked her and she became obsessed. That part I liked and was very reminiscent of the French movie "He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not" which is a fantastic film everyone should watch. What threw me off was the fact that Reeve didn't actually die. When Jam starts describing the moment that she found Reeve making out with another girl (a girl who has been bullying Jam for quite a while) it made it seem like maybe she would snap and accidentally hurt or kill Reeve. When it turns out that she just killed him in her mind I felt kind of let down. Not that I wanted her specifically to kill him, just I wish there was more to it than that. Something small was just missing there for me. All in all, I did enjoy this book more than the average reviewer and I would recommend to at least give it a chance. P.S. I know you aren't supposed to judge a book by it's cover, but I thought this cover was beautiful.

She shadows her father in his duties, and she knows how to run a country, but her isolation has made her unapproachable to the public. Eadlyn isn't a sympathetic character. She does have moments of redemption, which are quickly followed by her making an egregious faux pas. I wanted Eadlyn after talking with Kile, to make a project to help bring housing to homeless. The thought never crosses her mind. With the original Selection, there were more opportunities to test the candidates, but in the Heir there were no such trials... well there was the quiz event. I feel like Cass missed an opportunity here, instead the pages were filled with run of the mill dates, bland summarization of riots and how tired the king looks. It wasn't humanized enough. Random Notes: I'm flabbergasted that neither Maxon nor America ever divulged what happened during their Selection. How do you keep something like that a secret for so long? I don't really get the hatred between Josie and Eadlyn. It's childish. Why is there no back story here, besides saying Josie is obnoxious and takes my things. Henri is adorable. Eric is unfailing. Kile is brilliant. What happened to America's other two brothers?

I was so very disappointed in this book. The magic, which plays so subtly into the background of Chocolat (to good effect) is so blatantly pushed in your face in tis. "Smokin' Seventeen" by Janet Evanovich lets me down. The novelty has worn off and degenerated. Titillation substitutes for substance or substantive humor. Until the end, where she always walks right into danger, her heroine always ducks under the protective arms of two hot guys: one rumpled, one smooth. Stephanie Plum constantly vaccillates between them, so this time her family sets her up with a former high-school classmate, whose prime qualification is the ability to cook for her. I liked supernatural Diesel too. Quotes follow to illustrate her style in early chapters. Suits some; she's a best-seller. The first page sets the scene. Lavender sweatsuit-clad granny narrates dream of a flying horse "dropping road apples" on our girl, dressed only in "a red lace thong". During a fortifying donut stop, her cop boyfriend's gran gives her the "vor-do" evil eye, resulting later in a forehead zit-bump. Her bounty-hunter work site is a crime scene: local club owner "Mr. Tittie" left his rotted beringed hand poking up from the dirt. Local gossip suggest the motive wasn't robbery, or the remains laid a false trail leading to misidentification. Secondary side-plots are chasing two bail-skip cases with her ex-ho cohort. "Holy sh-, holy crap, holy moly! ... I almost got diarrhea, Lula said." regarding a senior vampire-wannabee without his false teeth. The second FTA (failed to appear) perpetrator "answered the door buck-naked. His Mr. Happy was hanging at half-mast and was about the size of a wanger on a champion stud Clydesdale." Typical conversation while they wait: Lula says Steph "could cook the crap out of sh-." Standard supper: Fruit Loops and beer. [Spoilers: I skipped to the end where Steph gets virile Ranger to protect her while breaking into the abode of suspect Alpha aka Twizzler, for his munching habit, to find an incriminating Frankenstein mask. Yet the real criminal waits for her in her own apartment; he stole her key when she invited him to cook earlier. The finale pits him, Alpha, and vengeful skip Regina, all three against the defenseless Plum. She's a lucky lady.]

4.5 STARS Genre: NA without the cliches. Cover: 6/10 Writing: 8/10 Heroine: 9/10 Hero: 10/10 Amount of humour: 3/10 Amount of jealousy: 2/10 Hotness: 5/10 Romance: 8/10 Ending: 9/10 Extra book Details: HEA. Lead Male POV only. This is the first 'Rook and Ronin' book I've read, (not my first J.A Huss book though) so I was somewhat confused (and still am a little) with the Rook/Ronin/Ford love-triangle and relationship, so the first 10% was a little trying for me. I wasn't sure where Ford was coming from in his feeling of abandonment by Rook. Essentially; she didn't love him like she did Ronin, who is Fords bestie. Ford decides to leave. Ford has high-functioning Aspergers. He labels himself weird and unemotional. He was a troublesome child. He's detached from the women he sleeps with, calling them pets, having little to no conversation with them. He doesn't like to be touched, it's painful for him. He's still grieving over his father's death. But he's also super clever, rich and a highly successful TV Producer at 26 years old. Yeah, I know. These lead characters are the kind that have a hell of a lot going on for the short life they have lived. They are the ones that have achieved/done a silly amount for their age. But it isn't too OTT or done in a way that blows smoke up their asses, it totally adds to their characters. On his way to his next TV Production, snow forces Ford to stop in his holiday home-town. Upon entering his hotel for the night, he sees a girl and her baby in their broken down car. He offers them the spare bed in his hotel room and pays for Mum Ashleigh's car to be fixed, and offers her a place to stay while she's waiting for it. This is where the story kicked off for me. Ford is incredibly interesting and he begins to become more and more interested in Ashleigh, who turns out to be kick-ass. There isn't a lot of story to this, it's the characters and their conversations, emotions and pasts that hold your attention. Ashleigh is constantly surprising and challenging Ford. They play games with each other. I loved Fords slogan t-shirts. Found Ford's fascination with the breastfeeding, funny. Loved the road-trip feel. But mostly, I thought the characters were incredibly interesting. Probably my 2nd fave Male POV book. Looking forward to the other spin-off books.

I loved this book. I suspect others will hate it. It's definitely for a certain kind of reader. If you hear "A circus run entirely at night, with a monochromatic color scheme, and magic!" and get excited, this book is probably for you. If you're the type of person who dissects each book you read to see if the characters motivations are 100% realistic and scrutinize every plot element, this book is not for you. The characters are delightful: enigmatic, archetypal, and distinct, but not particularly "deep." The plot is fun, but not particularly sensical. The circus is the true heart of the story. It is the coolest freakin circus ever. Really. Morgenstein could have been three hundred pages of just description of the circus and I would have sat at her feet, wide eyed. I am usually not an "aesthetic" reader. Clever design, beautiful details...I appreciate them, but I mostly connect with books when I find emotional resonance with the characterization. In Night Circus, Morgenstein captured the childlike awe of the circus and then transfigured it for adults. To age it up, she didn't make it unneccesarily "dark" or "gritty" and although the book occasionally embraced an ironic tone, the circus itself inspired genuine wonder. That was enough for me. On a personal geekery level, I loved the character of Isobel and usage of tarot throughout the book. Morgenstein is a tarot deck creator herself and her deep knowledge and love of it show in the text.

I took a chance on Done Dirt Cheap. Nothing about the book description sounds like a book I was liable to enjoy, but something (the cover, maybe, or okay that Lenore told me about a sex scene) made me want to give it a try. Done Dirt Cheap surprised me. It's Daughters of Anarchy, and it's awesome. Okay, so I've actually never watched Sons of Anarchy, but I'm assuming. Done Dirt Cheap is about the daughter of the head of a motorcycle club and her friend, who's getting close to them for her creepy lawyer, drug-runner boss. My personal pitch is that it's like Sons of Anarchy meets Veronica Mars, since there is a mystery/taking-on-the-man component that reminds me of VMars. Lemon's writing is absolutely lovely. Though not poetic or as pretentious, there's something dark and luscious and edgy about her prose that's reminiscent of Elliot Wake. The characters have southern accents but Done Dirt Cheap isn't written in dialect. Lemon conveys the environment with subtle cues, but not with style. Lemon's writing doesn't seem like it should fit the story but it's somehow perfect. The book's also total crack; I couldn't put it down once I started. There's constant drama and romantic tension and action going on, so you really just want to keep turning those pages. I wasn't emotionally invested, but I was definitely constantly excited to find out what would happen next. Lemon manages to tell a very melodramatic story in a way that makes it seem way more reasonable and not like a massive drama llama. I'm also totally into these ships, which are so not my usual ships at all. Tourmaline and Virginia aren't the sort of girls I've ever known, but they're well drawn and sympathetic, as is the rest of the cast (minus the villains). Done Dirt Cheap's a beautifully done novel, compelling and gorgeously written. Even if it doesn't necessarily sound like your sort of book, it may be worth a try.

Actual rating: 2 1/2 It would be much easier to tell this story if it were all about a chaste and perfect love between Two Children Against the World at an Extreme Time in History but let's face it that would be a load of crap. I'm really on the fence about this book. It was okay, I didn't absolutely despise it. It was just really strange and I feel a little...numb after finishing it. Maybe not numb. I just don't know where my feelings lie, which shows me that this book didn't really hold a place in my heart. Let me try to explain. I'm kind of on a controversial romance book splurge right now. I found this for four dollars at Half Price Books and I knew this book involved incest, but I didn't know much else about it so I just bought it because it was so cheap. I guess I was expecting it to be more focused on the relationship between the two cousins, but it wasn't. This is more of a survival/war story which isn't exactly my favorite thing to read about. The book begins with Daisy being sent to live with her Aunt and cousins in England from the United States. This is where my disbelief begins. I mean, I understand that Daisy was being problematic because she didn't like her stepmother so she wasn't eating and all that. However, I can't imagine her father sending her to a country where there were rumors that a war was rumored to be coming. I'd understand if she was a little bit older, but fifteen seems kind of young to be sending your child away to another country with people you hardly know. Then we have the romance between Daisy and her cousin Edmond. These two have zero chemistry. It's not even because I'm comparing it to the sparks that flew off of the incestual couple in Forbidden. The author glossed over any scenes between them. I don't even mean physical scenes between them. I mean emotional scenes with dialogue (which this book lacks in). You can't expect the reader to root for these two to find each other the whole book when you don't make it believable that they "love" one another and have this weird "connection." The writing is something I liked but also disliked. It reminded me of Chaos Walking (my favorite series, I might add) in the way that it really puts you in the shoes of the main character. It really felt like you were reading a book written by a fifteen year old girl. Well, most of the time. Some of the things that "Daisy" said felt much too mature for age, leaving me confused, and I'm a few years older than she is. I can't decide if that one is more of a positive or a negative. I thought the plot was interesting enough. Although I wish their relationship was built upon more, I liked how the book didn't revolve around solely romance. It was more about persevering even when the world is in chaos and survival seems impossible. There were many scenes where Piper and Daisy were struggling in the wilderness that made me shudder because they were just so raw and emotional. Oh, I was going to give this book three stars but found this article about the author saying that authors need to stop having agendas for diversity in their books. Dropped a half a star because I try not to base ratings off of the person that wrote them, but this really irritates me.

The Sellout (2015) has been on my radar for about a year now. I'd seen a couple of people on Literary Twitter talking about it but I've yet to actually see a physical copy of it in any bookshops. I had almost forgotten about it until the longlist came about. So I read it first. The Sellout is a satire about race in modern America. The novel begins with our nameless black narrator sitting before the Supreme Court. We soon discover (through oneiric but lucid prose) that he is being charged with owning a slave and segregating a school. Before you have a chance to do a double-take the narrator brings you back to his childhood. We discover that he grew up in the town formerly known as Dickens but the town is now disappearing, it barely even appears on maps anymore. Overwhelmed by a literal lack of place our narrator attempts to bring Dickens back from the ashes. In order to achieve this, he 'employs' one of Dickens' oldest residents and last remaining Little Rascal, Hominy, as his slave, a job that he is more than willing to do (he even insists on calling our narrator 'massa'). He will stop at nothing to bring Dickens back. This is a very heavy book when you think about it. However, Beatty never lets you think about it because scattered between the paragraphs on the ethics of slavery and meditations on modern blackness are jokes. Lots of jokes. This novel about slavery and segregation is one of the funniest books I've read in years. However, I wouldn't go around advertising The Sellout as a 'comic novel'. Beatty himself has said that people are reading the jokes and forgetting what the book is actually about. I see the humour of this novel as a necessary antidote, like the porter telling dick jokes after the murder of Duncan. Beatty's approach is brazen but brilliant. He will have you laughing and then a couple of seconds later you'll be thinking about why you are laughing. The Sellout is one of my favourite reads of the year thus far. It's one which plants itself into your frontal lobe and refuses to leave, like a satirical tumour. I'm scolding myself for putting this one off for a year and a half but now I'm calling shotgun on the bandwagon (if it hasn't already left).

This is a young adult book. It's sci-fi, not horror. Nevertheless, it is quite possibly the scariest book I have ever read. It takes place in a future where, between the ages of 13 and 18, kids who grossly misbehave or who are orphans not considered to be useful or talented enough or who are specially chosen "tithes" are taken away to be "unwound"--broken down to all their component parts and distributed among those who might need a new heart or lung or hand. Each part is kept alive, so it's not really murder, right? If you think that's creepy, it's nothing compared to the details of how they actually do this. There's a sequence about 3/4ths of the way through the book where characters are taken inside a Harvest Center and...oh my god. I don't want to spoil anything by going into detail, but think of the worst thing you can think of. It's worse than that, and Shusterman writes the hell out of the sequence. It's truly impressive. And, you know, traumatizing. After I finished reading, I had to fight the urge to call my mom. I wanted a hug. The one real problem I had with this book was the idea that unwinding was some kind of compromise between pro-choice and pro-life arguments. I have an admitted HUGE HONKING BIAS here (part of me thinks, "Yeah, I could see certain pro-lifers going for a system like that..."), but I have to say, I think this misses the point of what being pro-choice is about by, well, several dozen light-years. Luckily, this bit of backstory is not the focus of the book; if you can ignore it or handwave it away, there's an engrossing, intense (SCARY!) adventure story to be had here. I don't think I would ever give this book to a kid, though, unless it was a kid with parents I really, really hate. Have fun dealing with those nightmares, hypothetical frenemies!

Having being "blown away" by the first two books in this series, http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/16... and http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/16... , I knew that Edible was going to be another fantastic read....and I was so right!! Edible is a brilliant, beautifully written love story, filled with emotion, love, pain, romance, humor, sexy and hot love scenes and believable, quirky and lovable characters that you just can't help falling in love with. Rachel and Cole were a perfect fit for me. There was so much more to them than what we first thought. Underneath that quirky (I loved her style), strong, smiling, in control exterior, Rachel is more broken than she realizes. She feels disconnected and lonely. Cole ...wow what can I say about this man??? Confident, domineering with the well-put together look of a professional but he has a side that is hot and sexy...very very sexy. Piercings tattoos...a delicious wicked side that I so understand Rachel not being able to resist. The man is too f***ing much--cocky, arrogant, sexy, and bad. Oh yeah, and it didn't help that he look in his eyes and the tone in his voice screamed all the bad things he wanted to do to her. Oh Rachel, I so totally agree!! Their chemistry is intense and they have an incredibly deep emotional connection that jumps right off the pages. I loved seeing their relationship evolve, the sharing and the trust that grows between them. Great dialogue. I loved the witty and passionate banter between Rachel and Cole. And the interaction between Rachel's family and these two was so hilarious and sweet. Lena & Shelley are so totally "wicked".....i love those two...there's never a dull moment when they're around!!! The understanding he showed as Rachel begins to open up to him was so incredible. For some explainable reason, Rachel felt tears welling in her eyes. What the hell is going on? He was making her think about things she had long left behind. He was making her want things she had decided weren't for her. As he stood before her, showing her an even softer side to a man she wasn't sure she fully understood, she took a chance. She gave herself completely over to him. "I'm scared." "Of me?" he questioned cautiously. Shaking her head, she closed her eyes as she admitted, "I'm scared of how you make me feel." As her confession left her lips, he reached out both hands to cup her face, and he leaned down to press a firm kiss to her mouth. His kindness and the tenderness and care he shows Rachel...... "I don't know what to say," she finally replied. Cole continued to stroke her naked back, running his fingertips over her mantra--Pride, Strength, Hope, Love--and for the second time tonight, he thought that this woman needed to be his permanently. "Just start at the beginning and tell me what happened. Nothing you say will make me think any less of you, and nothing you did will make me look at you any differently. But maybe if you tell me what he did to you, you will see me differently and realize that you are safe here. I am not him, and you do not need to be scared when you close your eyes at night." Resting one hand on the curve of her hip with the other in her thick hair, Cole squeezed gently and pressed his lips to her head. "Let me in, Rachel. Let down that final wall." Cole realizing the depth of his feelings for Rachel pulled my heartstrings. Turning his face slightly, he took a deep breath and inhaled her intoxicating scent, and then he noticed her hair for the first time. It was pulled back into a high top-notch bun, showing off her elegant neck and the perfect tattoos decorating her spine. That wasn't what held his attention though. Her hair didn't have any bright color in it. It was sleek, shiny, and jet-black. When she turned her face toward him, those fascinating blue eyes locked with his, and Cole knew it was all over for him. This is where the search stopped. This is the woman. His heart was now in complete agreement with his head. She was unlike anyone he had met before. One minute, she was fearless and sexy, and the next, she was almost childlike in her joy and exuberance. In that moment, Cole knew without a doubt that he loved her. The scene where Rachel and Cole visit his mother had me almost in tears. As Rachel continued, Cole's mother beamed and began to hum along with her, occasionally slipping into the lyrics. Amazing. Songs seem to live in the soul even when everything else leaves, Rachel mused with a heavy heart, thinking of all the wonderful memories this woman had lost of her son. I LOVED THIS QUOTE.............. "It's beating hard because it wants the one it loves to feel it." No words, Rachel thought as she wrapped her legs around Cole's waist. He's left me with no words. This is what makes me read romance books. The love. The happiness. It's what makes my world go round. "I, Cole James Madison, ask you, Rachel Catherine Langley, to stand beside me through the toughest battles and harshest critics, namely your brother, and to lie beside me through the calmest of nights. I ask you to continue being the exact person you are today and to never be anyone but the woman who turned me into this impulsive man who stands before you here today." Cole squeezed her fingers in his, and his gaze stayed locked onto hers. He was intent on only one thing, and that was the woman in front of him. "I was not expecting you, and that's what makes me so sure. Nothing this perfect could be anything other than right. So, Rachel Catherine Langley, will you be my wife? I loved the characters from the previous books that were woven into this story. Mason and Lena, Josh and Shelley and did I love the teaser for the next upcoming book!!!!!!!! Logan sounds so delicious and I can't wait for his story.........I know it's going to be another book by Ella Frank that I will LOVE too.

Society is the choice between freedom on someone else's terms and slavery on yours. DNF at 92% because I could not find any motivation and self-discipline to continue. To be honest, I read "All the Birds in the Sky" that most of my reactions are probably much milder than the time I was reading the book. Because the book made me so frustrated and indifferent at the same time and still I really wished I'd like it. Because I felt the potential. But it never followed through. Sometimes I encounter a book where I understand that the writer can write but the idea that the book is about is quite ridiculous. In this case, the situation is reversed. The idea is great but the writing is a mess. Yes, it's a good mess, I've read far worse. It's not un-edited mess, no. As a matter of fact, this mess is so polished and every word is so carefully picked that at a glance, you may think what the living hell I'm rambling about. But for me, because it was so carefully polished, because every sentence tried to be the ultimate truth full of wit and geekiness and cleverness and magic, and it was exhausting. I found myself in a bit of a situation where I had to concentrate on an extreme amount to get through a page because otherwise I'd just drift away. And if you happen to drift away, there's no getting back because the story just storms on like a bull who's chasing the fighters. And me as a reader was completely lost. The trap that can be ignored is no trap. Every passage, every sentence tried to be EVERYTHING at the same time - a novel about technology, magic, pop culture, ultimate geekiness, philosophical ramblings, school society, broken families and of course, modern love and friendship. And while it tried to be EVERYTHING, it was it also at a very fast pace. Which was confusing as fuck. "/--/ I shouldn't have destroyed what I didn't understand, and I shouldn't have done that to you." And yet, I liked certain passages a lot. Quotes like made me feel like Mrs. Anders must have a deeper understanding of the dysfunctional that often occurs when a child grows up in a demanding household. If he strained to listen over the dozen cooling fans along one wall of his bedroom, he could hear his parents fighting. Not the kind of fight where anybody hopes to win. Or even find some solution. This was hopeless, pointless, mindless aggression, two creatures caught in a trap with nothing to do but tear each other apart. And: On the long drive home, Laurence tuned out his parents explaining to him that life isn't an adventure, for chrissake, life is a long slog and a series of responsibilities and demands. When Laurence was old enough to do what he liked, he would be old enough to understand he couldn't do what he liked. I like when passages like this reveal the actual truth about how the world works. It's raw and painful but it doesn't make it less true. Deedee was talking about her ska band's latest gig, in which as usual the blue-haired, wiry singer exuded so much raw Kathleen Hanna-esque sexuality, nobody would ever guess that she identified as asexual. I think it's the first book I've encountered that mentioned a person identify him-/herself as asexual. I like that a lot, I think the whole asexuality theme could be the next big thing and I believe society (meaning Average Joe) should know about it more. Raising tolerance and all. There are probably books out there that centre more on the whole asexuality theme but as I said, I've yet to read them and "All the Birds in the Sky" gets points for being First Book that Openly Tolerates Asexuality reward. Or something. Which brings me to the pop culture and physics references. As I said before, this book was like a geek slam poetry, like whole Twitter in one place where every sentence tried to be meaningful and amusing. The text of the article could be "lorem ipsum" as far as Laurence was concerned /--/ In a way, it was quick-witted but also I found myself sighing out loud a lot. In the end, I still cannot decide if "All the Birds in the Sky" was trying too hard or was it just a brainfart. And although, I didn't really enjoy the book nor did I manage to finish it, I feel like I should like a book like "All the Birds in the Sky". I've read some other writers who also produced content which was spiced with inside jokes and sociological musings about how mainstream culture oppressed other, more alternative people, and I quite enjoyed their work. Mon Dieu, even I once wrote something that felt kind of similar. But I guess they were never as messy (nor as painfully long) as "All the Birds in the Sky" managed to be. The other reason why I feel I should have liked the book, is because in general, I'm considered quite geekish. No, I'm not a character from "Big Bang Theory" nor am I a Silicon Valley protege but I enjoy science and science-y jokes. And I also feel that I get science. Usually, books that I've liked a lot involve some sort of a magical element to them so I feel I'm not really that far from the intended reader "All the Birds in the Sky" should appeal to. And I was so, so excited when I heard a book like that was coming out. I mean magic and technology in a battle? That sounds awesome! Unfortunately, in this book's case, for me it never reached further than 'sounds'. In conclusion, "All the Birds in the Sky" is definitely not a bad book. The story is interesting and fast paced and if you can read past the ADHD-styled writing or you enjoy it even, it may be the book for you. But right now, it'll stay in my DNF shelf.

I...I don't know what I was expecting. I don't know what I was expecting, RE: a book on gender conflict from an author that specializes in harsh black and white dichotomies. I guess I just wasn't expecting this. World Without Princes was less a "story" to me, and more a window into how an author can completely and utterly miss the implications of the words they are putting on the page. I think Chainani honestly thought he was writing about magical transformations and book clubs and kisses and a fun battle of the sexes - I just don't think that's what he got at the end. First off, even if we ignore the immensely troubling social perspective of the book...as a book? World Without Princes has got problems. Just like with its predecessor, there is NO adequate sense of the movement of time; it's literally impossible to tell how long our protagonists have been at school, which completely undercuts our sense of tension. Do they have 3 months to solve their problems, or 3 days? How worried should I be as a reader? Who knows! (And yes, I know the comparisons with Harry Potter have been done to death, but seriously, these books need to take notes on how J.K. does it - even in Deathly Hallows, a 700 page book where our characters have no access to calendars, you always have a sense of time. Seriously, it's important.) While World Without Princes does have a little more pick-up-and-go than its prequel, it definitely drags in the middle. Our antagonist's plan is overly convoluted and doesn't really make sense in hindsight, and the novel suffers from Middle Book Syndrome, ending so abruptly that, since I didn't have the book in print, I actually wondered if I missed downloading the last file of the book. All of that? Might have made me give the book 3 stars. But then come the bigger problems. The "Ew, girls!" problem. The main plot of World Without Princes revolves around the fact that Sophie and Agatha's completed wish - to go home together, as friends - has caused the ENTIRE WORLD to decide that the opposite gender is useless and terrible and DESERVES DEATH. Like...okay, I understand this is a fairy tale universe, and everything is amplified for effect, but this is...completely ridiculous? But it gets worse. Because when our protagonists return to the newly christened School for Girls, they discover that everyone is happy! They can eat sweets if they want, they can wear make up if they want, they can pursue all kinds of individual interests! And OBVIOUSLY they want to murder all men or make them slaves, duh! This is called "straw feminism": the depiction of people who want gender equality as ACTUALLY wanting to replace a patriarchal system with a matriarchal one. It is often used to discredit or ridicule actual efforts to level the playing field between the genders. The most frustrating aspect of this, to me, is that Chainani combined this with a lesson on history being written by the victors, and having his antagonist, Dean Sader, go out of her way to alter how history was taught in her school. This is fine, generally (to make another flippin' Harry Potter reference, think Professor Umbridge and how she teaches her whitewashed Ministry version of events), but in World Without Princes, it only serves to demonstrate how our author is NOT thinking of the implications of what he's writing - because this is LITERALLY the opposite of how the world typically functions. Women have traditionally been all but left out of how we teach history, and it is frankly insulting to have a work of fiction try to tell me how horrible it would be if this happened to men, without ever acknowledging the flip side of that coin. I know how horrible it is. I am female. I am Latina. I KNOW. And let's not forget the other groups this book steamrolls right over by not realizing that WORDS HAVE IMPACT! World Without Princes features two boys or at the very least, two people in bio-male bodies who spend the last 3rd of the book "no homo"-ing all over the place in the most obnoxious way possible. Then we might possibly MAYBE get some glancing mention that LGBT people exist (though not explicitly! 'Cause it's not like LGBT kids might ever want to see themselves in a fantasy novel! ) in Yara/Tristan, which I'm hesitant to even count because she/he is then IMMEDIATELY killed off brutally . There were only a handful of references to anyone, named character or otherwise, being anything other than white. The fatphobia was RAMPANT, with every single character who was demarcated as being overweight also burdened with descriptions that rendered them gross and stupid. And the one the one that disappointed me most, because of its unused potential - the revelation from Yuba that gnomes can change their gender at will could have been used as an amazing acknowledgement that gender can be fluid, that personality is based on the individual as opposed to gender, that trans people exist, left completely unexamined . Kids aren't stupid - they know the difference between fantasy and reality, and no single book is going to brainwash them. But World Without Princes is another drop of water in that inexorable wave that is most of our culture, beating at us that there is only ONE right way to be a girl, ONE right way to be a boy, and NO room in our world for those who don't fit in to those narrow categories. It may have been accidental on Chainani's part - but I have little time in my life for books that don't help me or my patrons fight that tide.

But really, what Bea does isn't stalking, is it? It's not her fault that she gets to therapy an hour early and happens to sit in a chair next to a vent that allows her to hear what goes on during Austin's therapy session, is it? I can't remember the last time a book made me so uncomfortable while I was reading it. I mean, I was literally squirming with anxiety for Bea. I wasn't 100% sold on the idea that OCD could make someone a stalker, but Corey Ann Haydu made me a believer (or at least made me say who gives a crap and just enjoy the story). Poor Bea! Such a tragic mess. This was a book I wanted to put down the entire time I was reading it due to my anxiety level (solid 7 for the duration), but somehow could not. Consolation by Corinne Michaels is the first book in The Consolation Duet. It is at once heartbreaking and uplifting, tragic and hopeful, and I simultaneously wanted to devour the book while being very depressed that it was getting closer to being over. A definite hangover book for me. Natalie is very recently widowed. Her husband survived the SEAL's but didn't survive a mission with the security team he now worked for. Needless to say, she is devastated and her grief is all-consuming. The light in her life is their daughter who was born shortly after she learned of her husbands death. Liam is the best friend of Aaron. Aaron is the husband killed in battle. The father taken away before ever getting to welcome his daughter into this world. Liam and Aaron were in SEAL team four together and are closer than most people ever get to experience. That is just the way it is when you not only trust the other person with your life but are willing to put yours at risk to save them. A few short months after Aarons death, Liam moves back to Virginia from California. He takes it uppon himself to break Natalie out of her depression. He succeeds where everyone else has failed. He doesn't take her "fine" at face-value and challenges her to appreciate and actually live in each day. The bond that forms between them is beautiful and breathtaking. The support they provide to each other and the beautiful honesty they share is something to be in awe of. When a devastating truth comes to light, Liam is the one that helps her help herself through it. Natalie is learning that she is able to cope alone but that she CHOOSES to be with Liam because they are better that way. So what happens when the absolutes UNTHINK-able happens? I don't know. That's the problem with cliffhangers, we ALL have to wait to find out. A VERY powerful and emotive story that I cannot wait to finish reading when part two, Conviction is released May 27, 2015.

I'm just going to come out and say this: I wish this story didn't exist. Or at least that it wasn't official canon... To be honest, I think any new addition to this universe (/with these characters) would have been a let down. The thing is, a new story just shines a light on all the things that didn't quite make sense in the original books that we never really cared about because of how much we love the series. I hate to say this, and please don't hate me, but when you think about it, the world building and magic system in this universe aren't actually that good. Which is fine, because they worked pretty perfectly inside the series we all know and love, but with this expansion of the series (and with Fantastic Beasts, but that's a different issue), it starts to fall apart for me. And that's before even considering the story itself. And dear lord, did I dislike this story. I'm sorry, I'm truly sorry I feel this way, but the plot was absolutely ridiculous and just plain stupid. It was a mess and a lot of it felt pointless. Most of the characterisation was crap (well, Albus was fine, and Scorpius was pretty great, even, but the rest? Just no), and the writing... well, the writing probably works a lot better on stage than as a script. I do actually think this would make a very aesthetically pleasing play, with all the magic. It seems quite an impressive thing to pull off. But that's no excuse for the plot to be this bad. And it could have been so much better. I feel like, aside from the inherent problems with expanding this universe, they could have given us a great story. There are so many great storytellers and there's so much possible in this world. And the unlikely friendship between Albus and Scorpius was actually a great place to start. You know, a lot of people have said this felt like fanfiction, and I agree. But a lot of fanfiction out there would provide a much better basis for an 'eight story' play than this. I made so many notes while reading this, but I really don't feel like getting into all of it, mostly because most of it is spoilery. The only spoilery thing I really need to say is this: FUCKING TIME TRAVEL. UGH. Oh and this: HARRY WOULD NEVER BE THIS HORRIBLE TO HIS SON. FUCK THAT. Personally, I'll be counting this as fanfiction and not canon, because I don't want to mess with the love I feel for this world and the original series. Which is kind of also why I'm not rating it. I wouldn't know how to anyway. I'm very up to talking to people about this, because I have a lot of thoughts and feelings, but I'll stop the review here, before it turns into a full blown rant.

1.5 stars. I did not like this book. The only thing I liked was the premise. Tempests are a mythology that I haven't read before and that was the only thing that interested me. However, I found the tempest mythology in this book very thin. It shows in the plot that lacked real depth. On a side note...how is 16 year old Gary, who had nothing, was expecting to get on a plane without a passport or any form of ID even if his friend bought him a plane ticket? Either he had those things, but the author was too vague. Also, this book resembles a MG more than a YA. And 16 year olds act like they know everything, and where they're going in life, even when their situation drastically changes. WOW! Starting from the gorgeous cover, the setting, the characters, the fights - this book is absolutely amazing! I honestly don't know how to write a review of The Greyfriar without spending hours praising its originality, world-building, character development and so on. Imagine people on steam-powered ships fighting vampires in the air with some extra-cool gadgets that only human imagination can conceive. Or Vampires who can decrease their bodies' density so they can float on air and who have driven the Europeans out of their lands and made London into their main stronghold where humans are kept as cattle or used as servants since vampires are no good at~ GAH! I can't even write a cohesive sentence without sounding like a total fangirl. Oh! And let's not forget the flashy bearded Americans with the white cowboy hats, the "British" (here, known as Equatorians) and their obsession with etiquette, the world-wide politics, the kick-ass heroine who has her weaknesses and fears, but is brave and strong-minded nevertheless, the Vampire princes, did I mention the awesome plot twists in the beginning? Dammit, ok, so, obviously, I liked it. But then, why am I not giving it a 5-stars rating? As much as I loved the whole idea of the book, there were a few major problems for me. Sometimes it felt like I was reading two completely different books - one of them is this epic adventure of two future rulers trying to prevent war, while the second one was a very slow, kind of cute, romance that was just too...Ok, I liked it, but it felt like it was trying to keep me away from the better, more action-packed parts of the book. I couldn't wait for the - I hate/like/hate/love/hate/not sure/like/etc. you part to be over so I can get to the fun. What the HELL is Greyfriar/Gareth doing? Why is he putting the lives of so many of his subjects at risk for one princess without even knowing her yet? Not once, not twice, but three times he takes the princess to some human friends, only for them to be massacred because of her presence afterwards! (True, this didn't happen in Edinburgh, but it could've!) I found his actions to be appalling and stupid and it took away from my enjoyment of the character. Why are there no vampires in Edinburgh? What happened to them, why has noone found out about Prince Gareth's affection for humans? Has noone passed by the city and seen the freedom the humans there are enjoying? Don't know why, but this plot "convenience" bugged me. As a conclusion: - This book is amazing! - Audiobook is equally amazing! The narrator is absolutely brilliant, he even screams when he's supposed to (and managed to startle me a few times). He really puts a lot of skills and emotion in his performance and I would definitely recommend checking the Audiobook version! - Will I read the sequels - yes, but not right away. Although I enjoyed it, I still feel there was something missing for me.

I was excited when I saw this book in Borders, because I'd had it on my to-read list on here. It had 4 stars at the time I discovered it. That's not usual for most books, so I had high hopes. Of course, Jen Calonita's books have 4 stars as well, and I couldn't stand Secrets of My Hollywood Life. I should've remembered that, and been more cautious... A Match Made in High School is told through Fiona Shaheen's point of view of the events that occurred just before, during, and after the marriage program her principal sets upon the seniors. Those in twelfth grade have to participate in a program which randomly matches them up with another senior of the opposite sex. Anyone who fails to comply won't receive their diploma. That was my first problem with this book. The Principal's defense of the program was that students have to learn marriage skills to prepare them for the real thing, but the program cannot even CLOSELY be compared to the real thing. At least let the students choose their own partners, someone they care about to BEGIN with; THAT would be close to the real thing. After all, we don't live in a world of arranged marriages, do we, now? Obviously the program would be drastically different, because in real marriage, the two people involved have developed a close relationship already. In the school program, two people who hate each other (like the main character and Todd Harding) could find themselves paired. It's obvious the author thought this would be a cute focal point, but it's not a realistic program. Throughout the book, the parents band together to protest the unfair project and eventually succeed in overthrowing it, but I don't see how it could've been greenlighted in the first place. It's almost as if the author is pleading with us through her characters, when she has the parents list reasons why the program's unjustified. "I know the concept doesn't make sense, look...I'll even say why! Just cut me some slack, okay?" Another problem I have with this book is something it's actually been lauded for: its humor. It did have some chuckle moments, but some gong seemed to sound, alerting me that the author had such banter set aside just to use in this book (this being highly possible, since it's her first book). Is that a problem? Not if it works, of course not, but it seemed so contrived. Someone's also pointed out that the back-and-forth between Todd and Fiona seems a bit too intelligent for high school students, and that was something I noticed as well. Not saying EVERY high school student is drab and unlit, but it just wasn't believeable dialogue. As for the other moments...attempts at humor that just had me facepalming. I just said that Fiona and Todd seem too intelligent in their banter, but they have moments of being ENTIRELY TOO STUPID to be believeable, as well. Senor Shitslacks? Princess Pisspants? The stupidly altered sex doll? The diaper prank that was just not clever at all? Comparing the cheerleaders to "animatronic turkeys"? That's just...uncomfortably dumb humor. My next beef is with the characters, who are all severely unlikeable even just for their cardboard personalities (except maybe Sam, the little girl). Our main character is the most unlikeable of all, due to her crude nature, bitchy attitude, and idiocy for considering herself "in love" with a boy she's barely ever spoken to (TWICE this happens, come to think of it). At least Fiona has a trait or two highlighted: her love for math (oh, no wonder I don't like her) and her love of Jane Austen books. Hey, that's cool. She's actually in the middle of Pride and Prejudice when...oh, oh wait. Elizabeth Bennet, the heroine from the stories, has witty banter between Mr. Darcy. Could that be compared to Todd and Fiona, perhaps? And oh yeah, Elizabeth's known for making snap judgments without giving people a chance. Near the end of the book, Fiona's accused of this, too. Yet another lame, modern spin on a classic tale, and characters who identify with the tale? OH GOD, I'M HAVING Twilight FLASHBACKS. To go along with the last cliche, there's others such as the character undergoing a transformation by the end, and the child who imparts worldly wisdom which changes the main character's perspective. Points lost for predictability, as well, as it was obvious who Gabe's secret girlfriend was. Some might think the end is a surprise, and were actually angered because of it, but...come on, the boy was already involved in a relationship. What did you think would happen? All in all, I felt like I was reading a junior high book that tried to pass itself off as high school material by throwing in swearing and sexual references. Science fiction at its best! Beggars in Spain is set in the near future (year 2008, but it's written in 1992), where genetic engineering has advanced so much that it is now possible to genetically altered fetuses to possess certain qualities, including sleeplessness. Leisha, is one such genetically altered child, a Sleepless. As it so happens, her twin sister, Alice, is a Sleeper or a normal human child. What would happen in a family with two very distinct children growing up together. What would happen if you find out that you're a special child. Or that you and a select few of other Sleepless children have more brain power and more time to learn and accomplish things than other children, or even adult human beings? How would the other "normal" human beings react to this disruptive force in their daily lives, especially if they see that their economic abilities are being threatened by the Sleepless? On the other hand, what would Sleepless do? Do they try to integrate themselves better? Or do they think it's better for them to seclude themselves? The cast of characters are also very believable, especially, I believe, the main antagonists. I've read a few comments that argue the antagonists are unbelievably too extreme in their "badness". But, I would argue that if you narrow down the relationships that you have with like-minded individuals, then more likely than not, you would start to lean towards fundamentalism and/or extremism, because you live in a self-fulfilling bubble. One main reason why I don't give this book a 5-star rating, is because the way to story is being told. I believe in many places, the book feels flat to me. A lot of the events that occur in the book are told after the fact, through some other character telling the main characters of what had just happened. In other words, a lot of telling and not enough showing. However, it's still a very very good example of what science fiction can give to the world: several important questions to ponder on the subject of what it means to be human. I find it especially interesting that Nancy Kress decided to write this book based on economic and political points of view. I believe an analogy of what happens in the book, is currently happening in our real world. Does an economic principles of "from each according to his ability, to each according to his need" work best for all humanity? Or does a more socialism system (everything for the community) work better? The book tries to depict these two opposing economic systems as being unreasonable. For example, the Sleepless under Jennifer Sharifi tries to create a perfect Randian economic system, where only those who can contribute to the community is welcome. However, this leads to the question of what happens if one member of the community, for some reason, ceases to be able to contribute? On the other hand, the United States has set up a perverted, in my opinion, system of social democracy. In this system, 80% of the population are "livers", who get to enjoy the perks of being alive with free everything (free food, free "brainies" drugs, free parties). All they gotta do is vote to get the money. The remaining 20% are called the "donkeys". They are the ones who keep the economy and the government running. They do business. They do legal administration. They are the elected officials who are slightly more intelligent and wealthier than the "livers". However, one thing that I find it strange is that the "donkeys" seem content to want to run things for the "livers". I would argue than the "donkeys" would want to create a separate system of economy from the "livers". Another important issue discussed in this book is the issue of tolerance. How should we tolerate another group that is significantly different than the rest of us, especially if that group is also significantly better, more intelligent, and is more successful than us? Furthermore, this book also warns of the danger of fundamentalism, which echoes what's been going on in our real world very recently. Jennifer Sharifi, in her single-minded focus to protect "her community" from intolerance of the outside worlds, has, inadvertently, created an intolerant community herself. One last, but not least, key point of the book is the ideas that there is no perfect community, and that to affect change one must attempt small changes bit by bit. I would argue that in this book Ms. Kress argues that there's no perfect economic, judicial and political system that guarantees equality and personal freedom to all. Like when Leisha realizes that the Yagaiist economic system isn't broad enough to accommodate all people on earth, because there will still be "beggars in Spain" (interestingly, why choose a relatively developed country in Europe? Why not some random third-world country?). But, at the same time Ms. Kress also argues that complete social democratic system is prone to manipulation without strong check from the populace. This is ironically shown by Jennifer Sharifi herself. In her attempt to create the perfect Randian economic system, she inadvertently creates a community that values sameness. There's no details in the book, but I think the way it works for the Sleepless community is that each individual works on certain projects that can be sold or traded with the outside world. The money from these transactions is then pooled into a fund to be distributed back to the community. However, this system doesn't work, because Jennifer Sharifi tries to control the entire thing. Therefore, to prevent gross abuse of power, there needs to be strong check from the rest of the community members, which requires differences to arise, which means inequality. Thus, there is no perfect system, because humans change.

The Little Lady Agency is a creative and fun premise. Melissa has found herself been made redundant, again, and is looking for a job. Looking at all her natural skills, she accidentally finds herself starting a variation on an Escort service. Only, instead of providing sexual favors, Melissa helps single men cope with things they typically need a "little lady" for. In the guise of "Honey", she helps men complete their shopping, writes thank you notes, refresh their wardrobe, and plans parties. However, as one can imagine, Melissa finds herself in a whole mess of trouble-- with friends, family, and lovers. It's quite a wild ride. This isn't a saucy book. Melissa isn't about to jump into a stranger's bed, and frequently has to navigate those advances! I like that sex isn't a driving factor of the book. It makes Melissa more relatable and realistic. This book then drives away from the type of escapism romance provides, which I greatly appreciated. I love the ultimate message of the book: You must love yourself for who you are. Trust in the people around you-- if you stay true to yourself, you will always be with the right people. This is a critical life lesson that, sadly, few people learn. As Melissa spends more and more time with her "alter-ego" Honey, she eventually realizes that Honey isn't someone else. Honey is the person Melissa can be, if she will stop second guessing herself and setting herself back. Gain some confidence, girl! I will admit, I got quite a bit frustrated by the end of the book. It was obvious that Melissa was breaking down under all the stress. But she got really irritating. For the majority of the book it was hilarious. Melissa was witty and brilliant. Yet, she started to fall apart and snowball into a dreary boring person who was blind to everyone's intentions. ABSOLUTELY EVERYONE. I know that this happens to people, but it happens mostly to 16 year old girls. This woman was probably in her late 20s. Seriously. I just couldn't take it. And the ending seemed very abrupt. That said, I still definitely continue to read the series when I need something light and fluffy. Melissa will surely have many more adventures come her way.
